articles.title: Bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant, prompting evacuations
articles.excerpt:
Peoria officials said a bomb was found at BioUrja Renewables and later defused; FBI said it is investigating

Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an Illinois community on Friday after the mayo...
articles.body_text:
Peoria officials said a bomb was found at BioUrja Renewables and later defused; FBI said it is investigating

Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an Illinois community on Friday after the mayor there said authorities found a bomb at a local ethanol- and alcohol-production plant.

The discovery reported at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria triggered a mandatory evacuation over a one-mile evacuation zone encompassing sections of that city as well as the adjacent municipality of East Peoria.

“It is real – this is a real thing,” Peoria’s mayor, Rita Ali, said, according to local news outlet WMBD. “We know that is a real threat. We know it is a bomb.”

Peoria’s police chief, Brad Dixon, said at a news conference early on Saturday that bomb technicians had rendered the object in question safe.

But Dixon asked for the public’s patience as investigators searched BioUrja Renewals’ expansive facility for other explosive devices, as the Peoria news outlet WEEK reported.

“We don’t know if there are other devices,” Ali remarked.

Meanwhile, Ryan Presley of the FBI, who is in charge of the bureau’s field office about an hour away in Springfield, Illinois, said agents would pursue whoever was responsible “tirelessly” and “bring them to justice”.

At about 7.05pm local time on Friday, the Peoria police department had announced that officers were “actively investigating a reported bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables”. The agency then urged “anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to immediately evacuate their homes and businesses until further notice”.

The police’s statement said the evacuation notice had been “issued out of an abundance of caution while officers and emergency personnel investigate the threat”, which officials initially referred to as a suspicious package. The city offered the Manual Academy school as a temporary shelter, and police said anyone who needed assistance evacuating their home or business could call for help.

In separate statement, the municipal government of neighboring East Peoria acknowledged that the evacuation zone associated with the package at BioUrja Renewables extended into part of that city. That area remained in effect as of 9am local time on Saturday, East Peoria’s government said.

A hockey game, a Comic Con gathering and a dance-themed charity event scheduled for Saturday had all been postponed, as WEEK reported.

“This is not a hoax,” the Illinois state senator Dave Koehler said during the early Saturday news conference. “This has gone beyond that … This is serious. This is serious.”

Law enforcement receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls not infrequently. Even though officials take those kinds of calls seriously as they investigate the claims, they often aren’t verified as credible or substantial.

Friday’s BioUrja Renewables case came amid a particularly chaotic day in the US marked by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration-ordered nationwide ground stop at US airports that was in effect for about four hours, canceling or delaying more than 11,000 US flights.

The country’s nerves were also frayed by a tanker which struck a cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon. First responders had to rescue passengers from the river’s water after the cruise ship turned on its side, and there were more than 30 injuries reported. But none of those injuries were critical, and there were no fatalities reported in association with the crash.

articles.body_text:
Two American tourists drowned in the Bahamas after strong currents swept them out to sea near Bimini Island. Police said the victims were swimming beyond warning signs.

Two American tourists drowned in the Bahamas after a strong current pulled a group of swimmers out to sea Friday, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said in a press release.

The pair — a 38-year-old man and a 40-year-old woman — were swimming with a larger group in waters off of the island of Bimini when the strong current swept them away.

Police said the victims were swimming in an area beyond a sign warning of strong currents.

MOM OF 2 WHO DIED RESCUING SONS DURING BAHAMAS SNORKELING TRIP IS IDENTIFIED

A nearby ferry boat rescued some of the swimmers, but the American duo were already unresponsive by the time the boat got to them, police said.

One of Bimini's beaches found on the west side of North Bimini, the most popular of which is this long stretch of three contiguous beaches in Alice Town. (iStock)

Though CPR was administered to the pair, they remained unresponsive.

WOMAN FOUND FLOATING IN SEA AFTER GOING OVERBOARD FROM ROYAL CARIBBEAN SHIP

"Both victims were transported to the local clinic, where medical personnel continued life-saving efforts. Unfortunately, despite their efforts, both individuals were pronounced deceased by the attending physician shortly before 4:00 p.m.," the police statement read.

Vector map of Bimini Island, The Bahamas (iStock)

Police do not suspect foul play, but are investigating the circumstances.

ROBBERIES, ASSAULTS AND RAPES SPUR NEW US TRAVEL WARNING FOR POPULAR CARIBBEAN GETAWAY

An autopsy will be conducted to determine the exact cause of death, according to the police.

Aerial view of boats anchored near coral rocks off North Bimini, Bahamas on sunny summer afternoon. (iStock)

Fox News Digital contacted the Royal Bahamas Police Force for further information.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.excerpt:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not prope...
articles.body_text:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
articles.excerpt:
Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra

The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Ba...
articles.body_text:
Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra

The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the comeptions at 19 years old

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.

Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.

Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 points

Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.

There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.

Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing

Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.

"It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie.

"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.

They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.

For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.

However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.

The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs

articles.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
articles.excerpt: The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)...
articles.body_text:
The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.

At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.

Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.

“We had 1,000 connection attempts ever four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Transportation Department.

When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.

“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.

The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

Al Jazeera has reached out to L3Harris for comment on the allegations but has not yet heard back.

Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.

“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”

The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added.

As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11 , the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”

Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.

“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

articles.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
articles.excerpt:
Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction

Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van...
articles.body_text:
Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction

Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before  World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

articles.title: Family of Watford woman set alight ‘desperate for answers’ after attack
articles.excerpt:
Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday

The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said that...
articles.body_text:
Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday

The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said that they are “desperate for answers”.

Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Caractacus Cottage View on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition.

Hertfordshire constabulary have said that a 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life but has been released on bail with strict conditions.

Raymond’s family said the attack had left them in “complete shock” and that they were confused over why she was targeted.

In a statement issued via Hertfordshire constabulary, they said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.

“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.

“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda. We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward.”

The family also asked for their privacy to be respected during this “unimaginably difficult time”.

Police believe that Raymond was attacked as she returned home at around noon, with her attackers pouring some kind of flammable liquid on her before setting her alight. Detectives said that an accelerant was also poured through the letterbox of a nearby flat, but have not officially linked the two events.

The decision to publicly name Raymond was made by police with the blessing of her family on Wednesday in the hope that it would lead to anyone with knowledge of the attack coming forward.

DI Adam Bridges, from the Major Crime Unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.

“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.

“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dashcam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.

“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our inquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”

articles.title: New prostate cancer guidelines urge men to start screening at specific age
articles.excerpt:
Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.

The American Cancer Society ...
articles.body_text:
Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.

The American Cancer Society is recommending regular prostate cancer screening starting at age 50 for men at average risk under updated guidelines released Nov. 12.

The update shifts from emphasizing individual decisions about screening to explicitly recommending regular testing for eligible men.

The new guidelines call for PSA testing every two years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69. Black men should begin annual screening at 45, regardless of family history. Other men with a father, brother or son diagnosed with prostate cancer should also begin at 45, with the frequency depending on their family history.

JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS

Men ages 70 to 74 should discuss whether to continue screening with their doctors; routine screening is not recommended at 75 and older.

The American Cancer Society is recommending regular prostate cancer screening starting at age 50 for men at average risk under updated guidelines released Nov. 12. (iStock)

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death among U.S. men. For disease that has not spread beyond the prostate or nearby areas, the five-year relative survival rate is nearly 100%, according to the American Cancer Society.

MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS

"Men think it is going to happen to someone else," Dr. Ash Tewari, chair of the Milton and Carroll Petrie Department of Urology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Medical Center in New York City, told Fox News.

The doctor, who has performed more than 10,000 prostate cancer operations, said the success rate of treating patients is exceedingly high, but that many men still need to be nudged to get screened.

The new guidelines call for PSA testing every two years for average-risk men ages 50 through 69.  (iStock)

A prostate cancer screening involves a simple blood test for PSA, which measures the level of prostate-specific antigen, the protein produced by normal and cancerous cells in the prostate gland.

Under the updated guidelines, a PSA level of 3 ng/mL or higher in men younger than 70 warrants a repeat test to confirm the result. There are other explanations for higher PSA levels beyond the existence of prostate cancer, such as an enlarged prostate, inflammation or an infection.

CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

Screening can also identify slow-growing cancers that may never cause harm. The society recommends discussing screening’s benefits and possible harms with a healthcare provider and offering close monitoring as an initial approach for low-risk cancers.

"We know how to cure 95% of them," said Tewari, referring to prostate cancer patients. "I can operate, we have developed medications … to get to them in time, my approach is very simple: Go right where they are."

To reach more men, Tewari and Mount Sinai have created mobile prostate cancer screening vehicles that are deployed in neighborhoods so men can be examined where they live.

The society recommends discussing screening’s benefits and possible harms with a healthcare provider and offering close monitoring as an initial approach for low-risk cancers. (iStock)

The first bus, the Mount Sinai Robert F. Smith Mobile Prostate Cancer Screening Unit, was sent out in New York City in 2022. Last month, another bus was deployed to the Atlanta Falcons-Chicago Bears game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta. The Winship Cancer Institute at Emory University offered free screenings in partnership with the Atlanta Falcons during the game.

Tewari and Mount Sinai are engaged in other ways to get the word out to men.

The ACS estimates that more than 333,000 men in the U.S. will be diagnosed in 2026, and about 36,000 will die from the disease.

Last month, actress Brooke Shields joined Tewari and directed a public service announcement advocating screening and early detection. The goal is to screen more than one million men for prostate cancer under Tewari's Million Strong Men Initiative.

"We need to be able to talk about ...down there," a son says to his father in the PSA video.

"I never got to have the talk with my dad early enough," says Shields in the video. Her father, Frank, died of prostate cancer in 2003 at 61 years old.

"Prostate cancer is treatable when detected early," she adds.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Prostate cancer is often a disease that families don't talk about until there is a reason to," said Tewari. "We want to change that. Starting the conversation early can give men an opportunity to learn about their risk, talk with their doctors about screening and act when appropriate."

articles.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
articles.excerpt:
'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop

A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire up...
articles.body_text:
'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop

A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.

The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.

Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.

What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if you're affected

Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.

The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.

"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.

Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."

Duffy told a news conference that the US government did not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack

No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.

More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.

Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.

Questions remain on why US ground stop happened when it did, former TSA boss says

Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"

A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

articles.title: US officials say flight stoppage stemmed from ‘routine maintenance’ as travel chaos continues
articles.excerpt:
Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding

The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ...
articles.body_text:
Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding

The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance.

At a news briefing on Saturday, the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said that the issues began when a contractor was performing “routine maintenance” at a remote FAA facility to “switch telecommunications lines” from copper wire to fiber optic cable.

“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said, “or did they install a faulty router.”

He added: “Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online,” and the ground stop was lifted.

However, travel chaos continued across the US on Saturday.

At the briefing, the FAA’s head, Bryan Bedford, apologized to passengers and said he believed that the worst of the disruption “is behind us”.

“We will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” Bedford said. “Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday.”

“I want to reiterate: we see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” he continued. “So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was.”

Even as Duffy and Bedford spoke on Saturday, airlines worked to recover from Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flights.

By of 11am ET on Saturday morning, more than 4,000 flights within, into or out of the US had already been canceled, according to FlightAware, adding to the more than 8,000 cancellations recorded on Friday.

The disruption, which marked the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, left passengers stranded at airports across the country and facing uncertainty about when they could reach their destinations.

Duffy on Friday had blamed the ground stop on an ageing air control system, saying that the communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and was starting to cause inconsistency in the data”.

“Because of that, we shut the system down,” Duffy said.

Duffy on Saturday again mentioned the US having a “decades-old air traffic control system”. “It’s not just old equipment – we have an incredibly old telecommunications system,” he said.

“The work happening was due to the age of the copper wire that we were replacing,” Duffy said on Saturday. “What we’re working determine was whether … it [was] user error or installer error.”

Duffy echoed Bedford in saying “we don’t believe” the disruption resulted from a cyber-attack or some hostile foreign nation.

“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” he said. “Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment and causes the outages.”

Duffy also warned that it would “take us time” to “resume normal operations”.

Among those affected by the fallout from the ground stop on Friday were sports teams traveling for games over the weekend. In college football, the Southeastern Conference announced that Mississippi’s game against Oklahoma had been rescheduled to Sunday – a day usually reserved for the National Football League (NFL).

Meanwhile, a men’s college basketball game between the University of North Carolina Greensboro and Cornell University, scheduled for Saturday, was postponed. NBA and NHL travel was also disrupted for the weekend.

On Saturday morning, there were reported flight disruptions at airports in major cities including Boston, Washington DC, New York and Miami.

American Airlines said in a statement on Saturday that “while we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations”.

Delta Air Lines also warned passengers traveling on Saturday that they “should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft” after the FAA-ordered ground stop.

The UK’s Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) also issued a statement on Saturday morning warning that “while US flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to re-book affected passengers and get all services back to normal”.

Friday marked the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA this century. The first occurred after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. And the second took place in January 2023, during the Biden administration, after a pilot notification system went down.

During Friday’s briefing, Trump administration officials urged Congress – which until January is controlled by the White House’s Republican allies – to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, called on Duffy to resign. She also called on Congress to “launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again”.

articles.title: Bill Maher warns Democrats not to 'go back to bad ideas' after sweeping midterm victories
articles.excerpt:
"Real Time" host Bill Maher on Friday issued a warning to Democrats, telling the party to not go back to the "bad ideas" that cost them in 2024.  (Real Time With Bill Maher/Screengrab)

Comedian Bill ...
articles.body_text:
"Real Time" host Bill Maher on Friday issued a warning to Democrats, telling the party to not go back to the "bad ideas" that cost them in 2024.  (Real Time With Bill Maher/Screengrab)

Comedian Bill Maher issued a preemptive warning to Democrats following their sweeping midterm election wins, urging the party not to mistake its victories for a mandate to revive "bad ideas" that could drive voters back to the GOP.

"Now that Democrats won the election, let’s not get high on our own supply like the last crowd did and interpret the W as a sign to go back to bad ideas," he said during Friday's episode of "Real Time."

As examples, the liberal comedian pointed to "defund the police" and a refusal to enforce shoplifting laws, arguing that such approaches hurt the people progressives claim to help.

BILL MAHER WARNS DEMOCRATS THAT SOME ON FAR LEFT WANT 'COMMUNISM' AFTER MIDTERM SWEEP

Maher also mocked progressives he described as the "lawn sign people," accusing them of using yard signs touting equality, science and kindness to advertise their moral superiority.

"It's all well and good to declare yourself the morally enlightened ones, but when your policy ideas are based on how good they make you feel and not on how much good they actually do, that's when people lurch to the other even worse extreme," he said.

JAMES CARVILLE CAUTIONS DEMOCRATS TO STAY AWAY FROM DEI POLICIES AFTER MIDTERM VICTORIES

Defund-the-police activists flooding the streets of Brooklyn, New York, in the summer of 2020. (Getty Images)

Criticizing policies in Democratic-led cities, Maher asked: ""Who benefited when you didn't enforce the laws against shoplifting? Who benefits when you give a homeless schizophrenic clean needles instead of forcing him into treatment?"

Maher also criticized what he characterized as White liberals' approach to racial issues, joking: "I talked to every Black person in America and it turns out they kind of don't give a s---. Yeah. Turns out they're not waking up every day saying, ‘What can I do today to make sure white people feel better about themselves?’"

Christian Toto, the editor of Hollywood in Toto, told Fox News Digital, "Bill Maher is the most refreshing, unexpected pundit on late-night TV. He calls balls and strikes while simultaneously copping to his liberal bona fides."

Toto added that Maher is "a pariah of sorts within his industry" and predicted that the "modern Left will happily ignore his wisdom, likely at their political peril."

Maher also criticized conservatives, arguing that Democrats won across several states in the midterms because voters have a history of shifting from one political extreme to another.

He first rejected what he characterized as Democratic moral superiority, then criticized what he described as Republicans' embrace of "cruelty."

"Republicans lost this election because no one wanted the pendulum to swing all the way to full a--hole, to cruelty," he said.

"Yes, liberal virtue signaling had become tiresome, but did we have to go to vice signaling?" he added.

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS

Then-Democratic Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico addresses supporters during a joint campaign rally with then-gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa in Austin, Texas, on Monday, Nov. 2. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Maher pointed to fatal shootings during immigration enforcement, cuts to the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and other incidents as examples of what he believed caused the political pendulum to swing back to the left.

"This is how you lose even Texas," he insisted, referring to wins for Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in the longtime red stronghold.

"Everything is a reaction to what went before," he added later.

Maher's comments come as Republicans review their midterm losses and reassess the party's strategy ahead of the 2028 elections.

Republican candidates suffered upsets in a handful of red and purple states, including South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi and Georgia earlier this month, leading to Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress.

Taylor Penley is an associate editor for Fox News Digital and contributor to FOX Business and Fox Nation who covers media, culture and Flash

articles.title: NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership

Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership

Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.

The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.

Exclusive analysis of official figures for the Guardian reveals the NHS would have to treat 2,850 additional patients on time each month to get back on track, assuming patient volumes remain consistent.

According to calculations by Radiotherapy UK, 24,400 cancer patients a month would need to start treatment on time to hit the 80% target in March. But the NHS is only treating about 21,500 cancer patients a month within the 62-day target, leaving a monthly shortfall of 2,850 and a cumulative shortfall of 9,490 patients, the charity found.

Prof Pat Price, the chair of Radiotherapy UK and a leading oncologist, said: “The government is going to miss its cancer treatment target because the NHS does not have enough staff or equipment to treat the number of patients coming through its doors. This lack of leadership means thousands more people could die because they don’t get their treatment on time.”

The analysis also found significant disparities between treatment of common cancer types. While more than two-thirds of patients with prostate and breast cancers were treated within two months ((70.1% and 68.8% respectively), only 60.9% of those with lung cancer and 60% of those with gynaecological cancers were treated on time. For head and neck cancers, barely half (56.5%) were. Regional inequalities were also stark, the research found. The Midlands had the lowest proportion treated on time, at 66.6%, compared with 77.3% in London.

Mark Lawler, a professor of digital health and chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, believes failures of accountability and focus are to blame. He said: “The whole system is being held together by goodwill glue alone. Lack of leadership is derailing efforts to improve cancer survival. Unless there is accountability for these failures by the NHS, a radical change in mindset and a focus on the basics, we will miss hitting treatment targets for another decade.”

The figures come as analysis of latest cancer diagnosis targets by Cancer Research UK shows that, over the last year, barely half (55.4%) of patients with cancer were diagnosed within 28 days of an urgent referral, against the faster diagnostic standard target of 80%, compared with 79.1% of patients who received the all-clear on time.

Naser Turabi, Cancer Research UK’s director of health policy and evidence, said hospital capacity was not able to keep pace with surging demand for cancer diagnosis – with urgent referrals in England up about 20% over the past four years alone. “While recent investment in diagnostic equipment is welcome, we’re not seeing enough progress to cut waiting times for the 6% of people who go on to receive a cancer diagnosis,” he said.

Dr Hilary Williams, the Royal College of Physicians clinical vice-president and a consultant in medical oncology, said crucial earlier diagnosis was only beneficial if patients could then be treated quickly.

“To close the gap, the NHS needs sufficient capacity across the whole cancer pathway,” Williams said. “That means more diagnostic capacity, including imaging, endoscopy and pathology, alongside the specialist workforce needed to deliver and interpret those tests. It also means enough treatment capacity in surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments so that diagnosing people more quickly doesn’t simply move the bottleneck further down the pathway.”

Dr Stephen Harden, the president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said “chronic shortages” of clinical radiologists and clinical oncologists, who diagnose, monitor and treat cancer, were “driving dangerous delays” in diagnosing and treating the disease.

“Perversely, NHS hiring freezes for these doctors have doubled in the last year, making it even harder to keep patients safe,” Harden said. “Technology and new ways of working can relieve pressure to an extent, but fundamentally, rising demand for cancer care has outpaced workforce capacity. The government must now step in to end recruitment freezes and ensure services have the doctors they need to diagnose and treat patients on time.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction, with all three cancer standards better than a year ago, and around 290,000 more people over the last year getting diagnosed on time or having cancer ruled out, compared to the year before the election.

“But we know there is much more to do. Our national cancer plan will help more people to get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner, giving them the best possible chances of recovery and survival.”

articles.title: 4 critical travel issues for those delayed and disrupted by FAA nationwide ground stop
articles.excerpt:
Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell analyzes the aging technology and router issues. He says the immediate issue has been resolved, but now it will take time to rebuild the schedule.

Travel...
articles.body_text:
Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell analyzes the aging technology and router issues. He says the immediate issue has been resolved, but now it will take time to rebuild the schedule.

Travel plans were ruined for hundreds of thousands of airline passengers following a nationwide FAA ground stop, which caused more than 15,000 flights to be canceled or delayed across Friday and Saturday.

Telecommunication issues that affected multiple air route traffic control centers led to the FAA issuing the ground stop for all U.S. airports on Friday afternoon at about 4 p.m. ET, the country’s largest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.

The ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET, but the ripple effect felt by airline crews and passengers is lasting, with residual delays continuing to impact airport operations, as Fox News Digital has been reporting.

FAA GROUND STOP LIFTED ON FRIDAY NIGHT, BUT SOME COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS STILL SCRAMBLING TO TRAVEL

People preparing to travel in the wake of this monumental event should be aware of a few key issues.

Here are important details and insights on four key areas.

A view from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) in California as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the U.S. due to a telecommunications and air traffic control communication outage affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers on Nov. 13, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a post on X this weekend.

Travelers should continue to check their flight status directly with their airline for real-time updates, he noted.

TRAVEL NIGHTMARE UNFOLDS AS MAJOR AIRLINE SCRAPS FLIGHT AFTER HARROWING 12-HOUR DELAY

"Check those, be in touch with your airline, check their websites, look at online monitoring tools," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From the Wing," told Fox News Digital.

"Don’t be surprised if there are aftereffects, but they should get under control soon," he added.

A line of passengers is shown above in Austin, Texas. The FAA ground stop issued on Friday, Nov. 13, has affected hundreds of thousands of travelers, and is still having ripple effects for many.  (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

"There are going to be planes that didn’t take off, which means the aircraft aren’t where they’re supposed to be for the next flight," Leff also said.

This means that "the crews are going to be out of position too."

He added, "And when planes and crews are not where they’re supposed to be, there are downline effects for all the flights that are supposed to be operated by those people."

The five biggest domestic airlines have shared guidelines for travelers looking for refunds or to rebook their trip after the ground stop.

American Airlines issued a travel waiver covering passengers with trips booked on or before Thursday, Nov. 12, for flights on Friday, Nov. 13, or Saturday, Nov. 14, Fox News Digital reported. Eligible flyers, including Basic Economy ticket holders, can rebook for no fee in the same cabin, provided their new ticket has the same departure point and destination.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Travelers can cancel their trip and request a refund, or they can book a new trip through Nov. 17, as long as they make the change by Saturday, Nov. 14.

They can also postpone their trip for up to a year without any fee, although fare differences may apply.

Delta has issued a waiver covering all trips scheduled for Friday Nov. 13 and Saturday Nov. 14. Passengers can change their flights and depart on or before Saturday, Nov. 21, at no extra charge.

The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

United Airlines is waiving flight change fees and fare differences for passengers scheduled to fly on Friday, Nov. 13 and Saturday, Nov. 14.

Eligible customers may rebook their flights departing through Friday, Nov. 20, free of charge, as long as they travel between the same origin and destination.

Southwest Airlines customers holding tickets from Friday, Nov. 13 through Monday, Nov. 16, can rebook their trips or fly standby within five days of their initial departure date for no extra fee, or they can request a full refund if their flight is significantly delayed or canceled.

JetBlue will waive fare differences, change fees and cancellation fees for passengers with flights scheduled on Friday, Nov. 13 and Saturday, Nov. 14.

Customers can rebook their trip through Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Transportation officials warn travelers to expect residual delays as airlines begin normal operations again after the FAA ground stop. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Transportation Department rules say that passengers with canceled flights are entitled to a full refund if they choose not to accept a voucher or other compensation from their airline.

For those who checked bags during their travels, there are guidelines set in place to ensure passengers are reunited with lost or delayed luggage.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If an airline unreasonably refuses to consider a bag lost after it has been missing for an unreasonable period of time, the airline could be subject to enforcement action by the DOT," the U.S. Department of Transportation website states.

Customers are entitled to a refund if they paid a baggage fee and their bag has been lost or significantly delayed, according to the website.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Pentagon's former UFO investigator offers simple theory for mysterious jellyfish-shaped object on video
articles.excerpt: Former Pentagon UFO investigator Sean Kirkpatrick says the strange object filmed near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson could have a much simpler explanation. (Credit: Peter & Sara Jane Osborn via Story...
articles.body_text:
Former Pentagon UFO investigator Sean Kirkpatrick says the strange object filmed near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson could have a much simpler explanation. (Credit: Peter & Sara Jane Osborn via Storyful)

A bizarre, jellyfish-shaped object filmed moving through the sky near a major U.S. military base in Anchorage, Alaska, has sparked online speculation, but the Pentagon's former top UFO investigator says there may be a much simpler explanation.

Video recorded June 15 shows a dark object appearing to hover along a mountainside near a rainbow, with several long strands dangling beneath it.

The object appears to pulse and shift in the air as the strands rise, fall and wave beneath it. As it moves toward the left side of the frame, the strands trail behind before the object moves back toward the right.

NEW PENTAGON UFO FILES DETAIL FBI AGENTS' SIGHTING OF SILENT TRIANGULAR OBJECT WITH NO VISIBLE ENGINES

Sara Jane Osborn recorded the unusual sighting and posted the video to Facebook the following day.

A dark, jellyfish-shaped object with strands hanging beneath it was captured on video in the sky near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on June 15, 2026. (Peter & Sara Jane Osborn via Storyful)

"It looks like a friggin alien. I don't like it," Osborn can be heard saying as she records the object.

"It's moving very weirdly," she says moments later.

Fox News Digital reached out to Osborn for additional details about the sighting.

Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson confirmed to Fox News Digital that officials are aware of the footage.

"We are aware of a video circulating on social media regarding a reported aerial sighting near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson from June 15, 2026, but have no additional information to provide at this time," the base's 673d Air Base Wing Public Affairs office said in a statement.

NEW TRUMP UFO FILE DUMP INCLUDES MILITARY FOOTAGE OF MYSTERIOUS STAR-SHAPED OBJECT

Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick, the director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, testified before the Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities on April 19, 2023. (U.S. Senate Committee on Armed Services)

Sean Kirkpatrick, who led the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), which investigates unidentified anomalous phenomena, or UAP, cautioned against relying on social media footage to assess unexplained sightings.

"I don't usually make any assessment from an online video," Kirkpatrick told Fox News Digital. "First, as I've said many times, social media is not a good source of data for anything, let alone UAP sightings."

NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS'

"The video, if authentic and not generated, is compressed and cannot be used for data analysis. It's too easy to make up video now and cover your signatures," he added.

Kirkpatrick said the footage alone does not provide enough information to determine the object's size, altitude, distance or actual movement.

He did, however, point to a possible explanation for what appears in the video.

"The motion is similar to a kite with streamers, particularly the waves," Kirkpatrick said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Historical weather observations show there was plenty of wind in Anchorage around the time of the reported sighting.

Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, is seen against the Chugach Range. (Getty Images/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Winds were blowing from the west at 16 mph at 9:55 p.m. on June 15 and from the west-southwest at 15 mph at 10:55 p.m., according to Weather Underground. The sighting was reportedly recorded at about 10:15 p.m.

The wind data alone does not establish that the object was a kite or moving with the wind, since the video does not make clear which direction the camera was facing or exactly where the object was located.

Despite the bright sky, the reported time of the sighting is not unusual for Anchorage in June, when daylight stretches late into the evening near the summer solstice.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

A sign marks the entrance to Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on Aug. 13, 2025. (Mark Thiessen/AP)

The base did not say whether the object was detected by military personnel or equipment, whether it entered military or restricted airspace or whether any known activity could account for what appears in the footage.

Kirkpatrick said determining what was actually in the sky would require more information than the video alone can provide.

"If it was a real video and not generated, I would add kite with streamers to the hypothesis category and then do some local research on whether there was any sort of celebration or party, what the wind patterns were, and whether or not there's any corroborating video from another angle," Kirkpatrick said.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
articles.excerpt:
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.

Among the dead were...
articles.body_text:
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.

Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.

The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.

Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.

Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.

Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.

So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:

The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.

The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.

However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.

Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”

However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.

A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.

The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.

The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.

About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.

Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.

After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.

Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.

Older men from poorer, often minority regions.

The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.

Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.

Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.

Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.

The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.

Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.

Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.

The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.

About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.

Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.

Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.

Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.

An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.

An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.

The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.

It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.

Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.

One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.

His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”

Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.

In Kenya, where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.

Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.

They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.

The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.

It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.

Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.

He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

articles.title: Torture survivors may have been sent to Sussex asylum camp unlawfully, documentary reveals
articles.excerpt:
Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East ...
articles.body_text:
Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East Sussex have been subjected to inadequate welfare checks, and torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully, a new undercover documentary for ITV has revealed.

Mass accommodation sites are central to the government’s plan to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers. For the documentary Inside The Asylum Camp, ITV’s undercover reporter got a job as a welfare officer at Crowborough and covertly filmed inside the former military training camp. The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers.

This May, the high court ruled that a Home Office policy change forcing torture survivors to share rooms was unlawful. The accommodation at Crowborough is in large dormitories.

The Home Office’s decision to accommodate asylum seekers on two former military sites – Crowborough, and Wethersfield in Essex – has triggered opposition from local residents. Plans to use three other sites – Bicester, Barnham and Linton-on-Ouse – have caused a similar outcry, mostly around fears about asylum seekers causing a rise in violent crime. However, very low levels of even minor crimes have been recorded by police at Wethersfield and Crowborough among asylum seekers at the two camps.

The Crowborough site is run by Clearsprings Ready Homes. According to its latest accounts, it is generating millions of pounds in income every day from its asylum accommodation contracts. Its boss, Graham King, has become the first asylum accommodation billionaire.

The documentary footage shows that, although two comprehensive welfare checks are supposed to be carried out each month by Clearsprings welfare officers, some staff appear to admit cutting corners and not asking all the questions they are required to ask of asylum seekers. On one occasion a welfare officer is filmed telling the undercover reporter “you don’t need to go in too deep”.

Staff appear to admit to falling behind on the 1,000 welfare checks they are supposed to carry out each month saying: “We’re so fucked.”

Concerns about an asylum seeker can be flagged on their file. A welfare officer is filmed telling the undercover reporter: “Those flags mean nothing” and that “nobody ever looks at them again”. When asked by the undercover reporter if some asylum seekers fall through the net due to brief welfare checks carried out, the welfare officer replies: “Oh, absolutely.”

The undercover reporter says he has identified four or five survivors of torture who should not have been sent to the military camp.

Louise Calvey, the executive director of the charity Asylum Matters, raised concerns about the findings of the undercover documentary. Her organisation has a campaign to accommodate asylum seekers in communities not camps. “The reports of torture survivors being accommodated on military barracks are appalling,” she said. “Brave survivors endure appalling experiences arriving to a country where they thought they’d be safe – a supposed civilised country, placing them in camps without the support they desperately need.

“People being held in isolation for prolonged periods of time without access to sufficient water demonstrate just how far we have fallen as a country. That government contractors can fail so resoundingly in their duty of care to people seeking safety in our country demonstrates how much our system dehumanises refugees.”

Calvey said the government needed to urgently review its use of the camps, which she described as “a choice to punish people for having the audacity to exercise their lawful right to seek asylum here”.

Clearsprings has been approached for comment. A spokesperson for the Home Office said it would “investigate any allegations thoroughly”, adding: “Welfare checks are a vital tool to assess wellbeing for all individuals on site, including those in medical isolation. We expect the highest standards from our staff and contractors and frequently assess the delivery of these to ensure compliance with contractual requirements.”

articles.title: Anti-Trump Republican courts other defectors as House weighs another vote against Iran war
articles.excerpt: Friction over foreign policy leads President Donald Trump to remove JD Vance from negotiating with the Iranian regime. Marc Thiessen tells Stuart Varney that Vance's failure to support key decisions l...
articles.body_text:
Friction over foreign policy leads President Donald Trump to remove JD Vance from negotiating with the Iranian regime. Marc Thiessen tells Stuart Varney that Vance's failure to support key decisions led to his swift dismissal as chief negotiator. The high-profile decision highlighting administrative divisions occurs two weeks after the midterms.

EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans and Democrats are preparing another effort to challenge President Donald Trump's military operations in Iran, with lawmakers signaling that additional Republicans could break with the president and support a War Powers resolution.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital that another Iran War Powers resolution could come to the House floor "in the next few legislative days" or around Christmas.

This would mark the fourth attempt this year to restrict Trump's military actions against Iran.

"I'm offering Republicans a life boat from MAGA," Massie told Fox News Digital, expressing optimism that more members of his party could join the effort.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

Three more House Republicans joined Democrats in backing a resolution aimed at reining in President Donald Trump’s war powers during the conflict with Iran. (Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)

House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital that he would oppose the resolution but acknowledged that "Massie has been having conversations with members" in an effort to secure additional Republican support.

Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., echoed Rogers' assessment, suggesting that "one or two" additional Republicans could join Massie and the Democrats who previously supported the measure.

SWING-DISTRICT REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, PUSHES LIMITS ON IRAN WAR

Reps. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., previously voted in favor of an Iran War Powers resolution.

Barrett told Fox News Digital on Thursday that he would maintain his support if the new resolution mirrors the previous legislation.

"My position would be consistent for it," Barrett said.

However, Barrett expressed skepticism that additional Republicans would join the effort, noting that few members appeared willing to shift their positions during the previous vote.

GOP HOLDS WITH TRUMP ON IRAN WAR, BUT CRACKS EMERGE AS DEADLINE NEARS

Rep. Thomas Massie speaks with supporters after his concession speech on May 19, 2026 in Hebron, Kentucky. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images)

Massie also acknowledged uncertainty over whether he could secure more Republican votes, criticizing his party's continued support for Trump's military operations.

"Congress is paralyzed," Massie told Fox News Digital, accusing Republicans of remaining "still in the suicide pact with this administration."

TRUMP SUFFERS RARE HOUSE DEFEAT AS BIPARTISAN VOTE MOVES TO WITHDRAW TROOPS FROM IRAN CONFLICT

House Democrats, meanwhile, expressed optimism that Republicans' losses in the 2026 midterm elections could encourage more GOP lawmakers to break with Trump's foreign policy agenda.

"If they're listening to the people that sent them here, yes," Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital when asked whether additional Republicans could support the effort. "That's what they should do."

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., also expressed confidence that more Republicans could join the effort, saying she "thinks they would."

Meanwhile, Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., suggested that Republicans may feel less pressure to remain aligned with Trump following the midterm elections — especially as many prepare to leave Congress and others hunker down to serve in the minority.

"The threat of Trump dumping a lot of money into Republican districts is over, perhaps more members of Congress we think represent their communities will listen to what constituents are saying about the war," Grijalva told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES

U.S. Navy E/A 18G electronic-warfare aircraft patrol the skies over the Middle East as the U.S. military is enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, according to CENTCOM. (CENTCOM)

The renewed effort comes as lawmakers continue debating Congress' constitutional authority over military operations and the president's ability to conduct sustained hostilities without congressional authorization.

Under the Constitution, Congress holds the power to declare war, while the president serves as commander in chief of the armed forces. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 establishes procedures and limits for military operations conducted without congressional authorization.

Despite growing discussions among lawmakers, no vote on an Iran War Powers resolution has been scheduled or confirmed.

articles.body_text:
Could Steve Maclin end up in AEW? Deonna Purrazzo weighs the possibility in an interview with OutKick.

Steve Maclin is one of the top free agents on the market when it comes to pro wrestling.

He parted ways with Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) at the top of his game and immediately made his presence known when he stepped up to the plate and put on an incredible match with All Elite Wrestling (AEW) star Adam Copeland at Maple Leaf Pro’s Northern Rising earlier this year.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Donna Purrazzo and Steve Maclin appear during a segment of "Good Night New York" on May 13, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

It makes any pro wrestling fan wonder where Maclin’s next home is going to be. Deonna Purrazzo, Maclin’s wife and Ring of Honor women’s pure champion, told OutKick Dropkick she could see Maclin in AEW if he wanted to be there.

"I definitely think there's a place for him here," she said in an interview earlier this week. "I'm Steve's biggest fan, obviously, right? We're talking today. It's our fourth wedding anniversary today, and so, obviously I wouldn't have married him if I didn't believe in him and I wasn't his biggest fan, but I think that he has to go where he's happy, right? And he has to go where he thinks he can contribute the best, and I do believe that there would be a spot for him on AEW. I do believe there's a spot, maybe versus Bandido for the Ring of Honor World Championship.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Pro wrestling stars Steve Maclin and Deonna Purrazzo were champions at TNA. (Provided to Fox News Digital)

"Steve is such a phenomenal wrestler, and I think there's so much of Steve that also while we're talking, it's the 251st Marine Corps birthday, and there's a piece of Steve that carries that and what it means to be a Marine with him everywhere he goes, especially in the ring. He's not just trying to engage the fans and engage the audience at home, but he's also trying to live fully for the brothers who didn't get to make it home. I think that intensity that he brings translates so much to where the best wrestle, which is AEW."

Copeland defeated Maclin at Northern Rising, even as Purrazzo came out to assist her husband.

But Maclin left little doubt that he can hang with one of the best wrestlers of this generation. For now, he’s tearing it up on the independent scene.

Adam Copeland hits Steve Maclin with a spear at Maple Leaf Pro Wrestling's Northern Rising on Oct. 3, 2026. (Geoffrey Cole/Maple Leaf Pro Wrestling)
