articles.title: Jayden Maiava and Josh Hoover face off as USC visits defending national champion Indiana
articles.excerpt: Sports attorney Dan Lust reacts to the College Football Playoff expanding to 24 teams. Lust also addresses criticism from Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the expansion a short-sighted move that will ero...
articles.body_text:
Sports attorney Dan Lust reacts to the College Football Playoff expanding to 24 teams. Lust also addresses criticism from Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the expansion a short-sighted move that will erode the sport's traditional appeal.

There has been some news about College Football recently about the idea that they are expanding to 24 teams in the College Football Playoffs. That won’t happen this year, but it will next season. If that were the case, it is likely that both of these teams would be part of that. There are a lot of people complaining because it likely will take away Conference Tournaments. Personally, I like the expansion. Before we get there, let’s take a look at today’s game between USC and Indiana.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

USC is 7-2 for the season, and they are 20th in the nation coming into this afternoon’s game. The Trojans' losses came against Oregon and Wisconsin this season. The Oregon loss is probably the most frustrating because they were at home, and the Ducks haven’t been consistently good this season. The loss on the road against Wisconsin was a bit confusing as well. The Trojans should’ve been plenty good to beat the Badgers, but they couldn’t get anything going on the ground to open things up. Their leading rusher in the game had 28 yards on the ground.

USC Trojan football fans cheer for their team at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Sept. 20, 2025, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Getty Images)

You can’t really blame the running game completely; I think we all know the Trojans will only go as far as quarterback Jayden Maiava will take them. He has completed about 67% of passes this year and thrown for 20 touchdowns. He only has five interceptions this season, so he has put together a good year. He had two interceptions against Wisconsin, which clearly didn’t help the USC cause. He also somehow had -57 rushing yards in the Wisconsin game.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL SELLS ANOTHER PIECE OF ITS SOUL WITH CFP OFFICIALLY EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS

Indiana is the defending National Champion, but the team that won last year is significantly different from this season’s team. Fernando Mendoza is obviously gone, and the team was going to have to adjust to him leaving for the NFL. They don’t have a bad quarterback – Josh Hoover – under center, it just is that he isn’t quite as elite as Mendoza. Hoover has fewer than 2,000 yards this season, but he does have 19 touchdown passes. Perhaps the best part is that he is taking care of the ball, throwing just two interceptions this season.

Indiana Hoosiers quarterback Josh Hoover drops back to pass during the second quarter of a college football game against the North Texas Mean Green on Sept. 5, 2026, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

The Hoosiers haven’t looked very good lately, either. Perhaps they are playing better competition than before, but they’ve had four consecutive close games. They won by just three against Nebraska. Then they lost by four to Ohio State, though they probably could’ve won that game if they could’ve stayed in bounds. Then they had to go into overtime to beat Michigan. The following week, they again needed overtime in order to beat Minnesota. Four straight weeks of close games, but the team went 3-1.

INDIANA SURVIVES MINNESOTA SCARE WITH SECOND STRAIGHT OVERTIME WIN TO KEEP NATIONAL TITLE DEFENSE ALIVE

Indiana head coach Curt Cignetti watches during warm ups before the College Football Playoff national championship game between Miami and Indiana, Monday, Jan. 19, 2026, in Miami Gardens, Florida. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)

This could be a great game between the two teams, and I find it very hard to trust Indiana right now. Both teams are coming off of bye weeks, so they have had plenty of time to prepare for this game. I think Indiana has the better defense, and I do think they likely took this time to get their team refocused. I’m going to take the Hoosiers here, but I’m going to play them at just -7 instead of them at -7.5.

For more sports betting information and plays, follow David on X/Twitter: @futureprez2024

articles.title: How does Iran view shift in US approach after JD Vance ordered away?
articles.excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the c...
articles.body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the chances of conflict between the two sides.

Vance has been the US’s chief negotiator in talks with Iran, but US President Donald Trump told him to direct his focus on alleged Democratic “corruption”, according to a post by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. He added that a deal with Iran was no longer a priority for the government.

The vice president is believed to be viewed by Tehran as one of the more pragmatic figures in the Trump administration since the US and Israel launched their surprise war on Iran on February 28.

Nasser Hadian, professor of international relations at the University of Tehran, said that by assigning Vance to the case of alleged domestic corruption, Trump was mainly signalling a confrontation with the Democrats after their sweeping victories against the governing Republican Party in the midterm elections.

But the move may also serve Israel, which is reportedly eager for Trump to launch new strikes against Iran, after Vance blamed the Republicans’ humiliating defeat in the midterms on the war.

“Another signal is to Iran, essentially saying reaching a deal now is not a priority, and that the person known to have a relatively softer stance on Iran was redirected to other issues,” Hadian said.

Vance is believed to have been in favour of a negotiated resolution to the war, due to its rising economic costs for US citizens and their opposition to the war suggested in opinion polls.

The vice president was backed by Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff when he negotiated the now-defunct memorandum of understanding with Iran in June, which briefly paused the war and resumed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio has, meanwhile, called Iranian authorities “insane” for their demands on ending the war. But he also acknowledged the cost of an all-out war and seeks to win via deepening economic pressure and isolation on all Iranians.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced an impeachment vote due to his role in the war, and Central Command chief Brad Cooper are reportedly in favour of renewed military action against Iran.

Vance wrote a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in late October, as regional mediators redoubled their efforts to bridge gaps between the two sides. Rezaei initially described the tone of the missive as positive, but by last week, he was addressing claims of progress and a possible direct meeting with Vance as “fake news about imaginary talks”.

“You lost the war and the election. Vance has conceded, Rubio is heading for the exit, Hegseth is about to be fired, and the CENTCOM commander is now a podcaster!” he wrote on X at the time.

Mediated contacts are ongoing between the two sides, but no breakthrough is expected. Tehran is demanding seven conditions and clear sequencing of concessions to end the war, but this is appearing to be unacceptable to the US.

Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies, pointed out that Trump has repeatedly highlighted alleged rifts within the Iranian negotiating team. But he said Iranian authorities were also questioning the reliability of another potential agreement with Washington.

“Even if you can imagine Mr Rezaei sitting down with Mr Vance, and reaching a deal? What guarantee is there that Trump will enforce it?” he told Al Jazeera.

The atmosphere of mistrust between the two sides is also complicating prospects of a deal, he added. This means that the ongoing US siege on Iran and harsh sanctions will continue, something that could cost Iran more than a relatively shorter military conflict with Washington, he added.

“The blockade and disruptions are significantly raising the costs for Iranian people. The current state of no war and no negotiated resolution is very dangerous,” Sedghian said.

Iranian reformist newspaper Shargh argued this week that Vance’s role concerning Iran is unresolved rather than definitely terminated, but also said the conflict could further escalate.

Conservative Farhikhtegan daily disputed the portrayal of Vance as genuinely antiwar, arguing that diplomacy, military force and economic pressure ultimately serve a common objective for the US in trying to coerce Iran to accept its conditions.

For now, the two sides are continuing to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, with retaliatory attacks on shipping and military installations.

On Friday and Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and regular army separately claimed several new incidents of vessels either hitting naval mines or being struck by projectiles after attempting “unauthorised” routes in the critical waterway.

The latest weekly report by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported eight incidents in and around the strait, mostly in the southern route near Oman.

UKMTO also recorded 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the strait during the week, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels.

Hadian believes that Iranian decision-makers will not tolerate the current situation indefinitely.

“The authorities will either go after their warships, their vessels, or their military bases,” he added. “The stronger the blockade becomes, including through maritime pressure and disruptions for overland borders and air travel, war becomes more probable.”

But Trump’s sidelining of Vance on the Iran issue will not radically alter the current situation, Hadian said, since Washington believes its tactic of economic pressure on Tehran can force it to make concessions.

“The US would have done this with or without Vance, and I believe it will continue to do this,” he said.

articles.title: College football legend Brian Bosworth says he supports the controversial 24-team expanded playoff
articles.excerpt:
Oklahoma legend Brian Bosworth tells OutKick in a recent interview that the expanded playoff gives more programs an opportunity to shine.

College football legend Brian Bosworth is a fan of the contro...
articles.body_text:
Oklahoma legend Brian Bosworth tells OutKick in a recent interview that the expanded playoff gives more programs an opportunity to shine.

College football legend Brian Bosworth is a fan of the controversially expanded playoff format.

The 24-team format will begin in the 2027–28 season and run for five seasons, but fans don’t like it because it dilutes the impact of the regular season. However, Bosworth likes the new format because it gives more programs opportunities to compete on bigger stages.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"It just gets bigger and better, and it deserves to be bigger and better because there's so many college programs that deserve the opportunity to show who they are," Bosworth told OutKick in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Brian Bosworth speaks onstage during weekend two, day one of the Austin City Limits Music Festival at Zilker Park on Oct. 8, 2021, in Austin, Texas. (Rick Kern/WireImage)

The Oklahoma football legend talked about the incredible parity in college football and how top teams lose nearly every weekend . Bosworth also said the expanded playoff gives more fans a reason to stay invested later into the season.

"To expand to include colleges that otherwise would be forgotten. They're on the edge and you say, ‘Oh, maybe next year, maybe next year.’ It gives the fans some more hope. It gives them a dream. It gives them a destination and it keeps their passion alive," Bosworth said.

When asked whether 24 teams realistically have a chance to win the national championship each season, Bosworth said not to discount the longshots.

"There could be 10 or 12 really good teams, but there could be another 10 teams behind them that are just hungry and want an opportunity. So, yeah, it extends the season and it gives more teams an opportunity, but there's something to be said about the long shot or the hungry dog," Bosworth said.

RAVENS STAR KYLE HAMILTON SAYS HE HATES WHERE COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS GOING AMID 24-TEAM PLAYOFF, NIL CHAOS

Former Seattle Seahawks linebacker Brian Bosworth visits with fans during the AdvoCare Texas Kickoff football game between the Oklahoma Sooners and the Houston Cougars at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas, on Sept. 3, 2016. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor is returning to the Bulldogs next season on a $7.5 million deal that could reach $9 million with incentives, according to multiple reports. Bosworth has said the exorbitant amounts of money involved in some of these contracts are a "head-scratcher."

"The money has gotten to a point where it's just a head scratcher. I'm a firm believer of putting some fences around it and controlling the fact that not every school is going to have the deep pockets in which to go deep into," Bosworth said.

"I think the fairness of it should be across the board that every team has the same pool so that they can manage the team across the board. Everybody's doing the same thing on the same page and you don't have somebody that's funneling money into it and then you can have these crazy contracts the way they're going about it now."

Bosworth noted that Taylor is an amazing player, but football isn’t a one-man show. If the team doesn’t invest in the players around him, it will struggle to play well.

"But it's not a one-man show (because) great quarterbacks can fail based upon their offensive scheme, the play calling, the injuries on the offensive line. If you've got a defense that's super porous, you know. It really does take a team to be an elite team to get into the conversation to be a championship in the conference and then maybe get to the playoffs," Bosworth said.

Bosworth knows what it takes to have a winning team, as he won the 1985 national championship and three Big Eight titles. He won the Butkus Award as the nation’s top linebacker in both 1985 and 1986. He was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2015.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In addition to being a star linebacker during his playing days, Bosworth has also brought the iconic "Sheriff Boz" to life in Dr Pepper commercials. In Norman, Oklahoma, Dr Pepper is bringing Fansville to life with the Dr Pepper Water Tower Park.

More than a landmark, the park gives fans a new gathering place to connect, celebrate gameday traditions and experience a piece of Fansville . Bosworth, who knows the passion of Oklahoma fans well, said bringing Fansville to life is a dream come true.

Head coach Brent Venables of the Oklahoma Sooners greets former star linebacker Brian Bosworth before the team's spring game at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium in Norman, Okla., on April 23, 2022. (Getty Images)

"It's really a dream come true," Bosworth, who spoke on behalf of Dr Pepper said. "College football is perpetual. It's been with us, it's here now and it will always be with us. And to be part of that is really an honor. And to have Fansville come here and then put up their iconic water tower in a spot, it's just cherry. You couldn't ask for anything better."

articles.title: Ben Shapiro warns Democrats have 'strong incentive' to crater the economy and blame Trump
articles.excerpt: The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro joins Sean Hannity to break down the seismic political shifts under President Trump, the alarming rise of global antisemitism, and what the 2028 presidential landscape loo...
articles.body_text:
The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro joins Sean Hannity to break down the seismic political shifts under President Trump, the alarming rise of global antisemitism, and what the 2028 presidential landscape looks like.

Democrats could be gearing up to undermine the economy and leave President Donald Trump to shoulder the blame, Daily Wire co-founder Ben Shapiro warned this week, raising concerns about the party's agenda following its 2026 midterm victories.

"I think that the Democrats right now have a strong incentive to basically crater the American economy over the course of the next two years and blame President Trump for it," Shapiro told Sean Hannity on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast.

Shapiro predicted that Democrats would introduce "affordability bills" that "aren't actually about affordability" and seek to "destroy" the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, as part of what he characterized as a broader effort to undermine Trump's presidency.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

Daily Wire co-founder & "The Ben Shapiro Show" host Ben Shapiro takes part in the panel "Future of News: How Creators and Influencers Are Reshaping Journalism," at the Reuters NEXT conference, in New York City on Dec. 3, 2025. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

"[The AI industry] is responsible for the vast majority of economic growth in the country right now," Shapiro said.

The warning comes after Democrats' midterm victories, which Shapiro suggested could embolden the party to pursue a more aggressive legislative agenda.

"And they'll do it in the name of populism," he said.

During Thursday's podcast episode, Shapiro also discussed his evolving views on Trump, the rise of antisemitism, the personal security threats he says have affected his family and his outlook on the 2028 presidential race.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

Fox News Channel's Sean Hannity welcomed Ben Shapiro to the latest episode of his podcast, "Hang Out with Sean Hannity." (FOX News Media)

"The only hope that Republicans have is that Democrats will do what Democrats typically do, which is misread the moment, see this as a mandate for radical change..." Shapiro said, discussing Republicans' prospects following the midterm elections.

"You and I have been in this game for a long time, and we've seen a lot of these cycles," he told Hannity.

"And whenever I hear Republicans go, 'Oh, we'll never win again,' I'm old enough to remember when Barack Obama won re-election and then four years later, Donald Trump was taking his seat in the Oval Office," he added.

articles.title: Milder weekend forecast in UK as autumn freeze eases off
articles.excerpt:
Met Office says overnight frost to give way on Saturday to ‘fine day with some sunshine’ in most regions

The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after cold health ...
articles.body_text:
Met Office says overnight frost to give way on Saturday to ‘fine day with some sunshine’ in most regions

The UK should have a milder weekend as the unusual autumn freeze eases off, after cold health alerts were issued and temperatures plummeted overnight, forecasters have said.

After frost on Saturday morning, most of the UK should enjoy a “fine day with some sunshine”, the Met Office said. However, it will not be blue skies for everyone, as torrential rain and showers are predicted to move in from the west, bringing patchy rain and strong winds across the north and far west of the UK.

Snow is also on the cards for north-west Scotland, the Met Office said. Temperatures on Saturday morning were expected to vary between 5C (41F) in Norwich and Manchester and 11C in Plymouth

The mild reprieve will be welcome to many Britons after temperatures on Friday night fell as low as -6.6C in Sennybridge, near Bannau Brycheiniog in south Wales, and -6.5C in Shap, a village near Penrith in Cumbria.

The first yellow cold health alerts of the season were issued this week by the UK Health Security Agency for the West Midlands and the north-west, and remained in place until midday on Saturday.

These alerts indicated the weather was “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life to vulnerable people, the agency said.

Eastern parts of England should have drier conditions on Saturday evening, with clear spells and some frost. But other parts of the UK would be cloudy, with passing showers, the forecaster said.

On Sunday, temperatures are expected to stay above freezing in the morning. Sunshine is expected to brighten things up in the east, and the UK’s far north and west will also be treated to a bit of sunshine later in the day.

However, people elsewhere should expect plenty of cloud and wind, as well as rain, some heavy, and potential hill snow in Scotland and the north of England.

WWE champion Ethan Page explains to OutKick why he has no interest in competing in the John Cena Classic.

John Cena’s namesake pro wrestling showcase will feature some of the best WWE has to offer and give the fans a voice in who takes home a championship belt next month.

Ethan Page, who won the Intercontinental Championship earlier this month over Chad Gable, said he wants no part in it – at least for right now.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Ethan Page celebrates his win during RAW at Barclays Center in New York City on Nov. 2, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

"I think it's silly for you to think that I, as the smartest wrestler in the WWE, would put me in a position that even if I defeat my opponent, I could not win because of the voting fans, who boo me out of every single building that I walk into, and now I'm gonna put the power of my success, on a device where no one has to look me in the eye and tell me that they don't appreciate what I offer," Page told OutKick Dropkick in a recent interview.

"They get to hide in a bathroom stall, or even worse, surround themselves with like-minded idiots. They will all decide that I am not worthy of their vote and then, at the end of this event, some pathetic crybaby who went on a political tour on social media for seven weeks straight, gets voted into victory and my talents are completely ignored. Never mind my talents, my more than likely victory, over some poor schmuck from NXT, will go unrewarded."

WWE fans will get the power to vote for the winner of the John Cena Classic via Club WWE. The winner will get to take home the John Cena Classic Championship.

And, yes, the wrestlers in the competition don’t necessarily have to win their match to win the title.

John Cena debuts the John Cena Classic Championship during RAW at Barclays Center in New York City on Nov. 2, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Page did clarify, saying he’s happy those in the competition could get an accolade they could be proud of and if he was invited, maybe he would reconsider.

"Now let me answer politically correct. I'm happy that people will get the opportunity to have something in their career they can be proud of," he added. "The only issue is I already do. I am the intercontinental champion, and I am not going to rush to get in line for a free watch and a jacket with another man's name on it, so I can enter a tournament that I will be voted to lose, no matter what.

"Now if I get invited, we'll talk about it then and I will reassess my decisions, but at this very moment, that is my clear-cut stance on the John Cena Classic, and I wish everybody luck. And I hope they manipulate the fan base enough to vote for them, so that they can win and be happy."

The John Cena Classic will take place at the ESPN Wide World of Sports Complex at Disney World on Dec. 14. It will be a part of a special double episode of "Monday Night Raw" – the first of which is taking place in Australia following Wrestlepalooza: Perth.

On "Friday Night SmackDown," he invited Charlotte Flair, Jacy Jayne, Fallon Henley and Lainey Reid to the competition.

articles.title: Spain vs England: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
articles.excerpt:
Who: Spain vs England
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A3
Where: Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain
When: Sunday, November 15, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you a...
articles.body_text:
Who: Spain vs England
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A3
Where: Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain
When: Sunday, November 15, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.

England have the chance to avenge their defeat and end Spain’s 43-match unbeaten record when they face the reigning world champions in Sunday’s final Nations League group encounter.

Spain staged a 3-2 comeback victory at London’s Wembley Stadium in late September, as Lamine Yamal scored an early opener and Mikel Oyarzabal finished the job.

Spain and England have both sealed their berth in the competition’s quaterfinals, with La Roja assured of the top spot should they avoid defeat on Sunday. England, meanwhile, will finish second if they fail to beat the two-time World Cup winners.

Teenage sensation Yamal, with four goals, and Mikel Merino, with three, have headlined Spain’s attacking charge, while newly-crowned Ballon d’Or recipient Harry Kane leads England.

Before Spain vs England, here’s everything you need to know:

Spain have a perfect record and lead Group A3 with 15 points.

They beat England 3-2 in the first game, an away trip, and followed it with a 4-1 rout of Croatia at home.

Then, they beat Czechia 3-1 at home, followed by a 2-1 away win over Croatia and a 2-0 away win over Czechia.

England are second in Group A3 with 12 points from five games, having won four times and lost once.

Their Nations League campaign started with a 3-2 home defeat to Spain before Thomas Tuchel’s side beat Czechia 2-0 and thrashed Croatia 7-0 in back-to-back away fixtures.

Later, they beat Czechia 3-0 at home and Croatia 2-1.

Tuchel believes England are ready to end Spain’s unbeaten record when they face the world and European champions in Madrid.

While victory offers little more than the prospect of a more favourable Nations League quarterfinal in March, it would be a landmark moment for England if they could end Spain’s run of 43 matches without defeat.

“It (Spain) is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so of course it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost,” said Tuchel.

“I think we’re there, and I think we’re ready to win on Sunday.

“I know what it takes, and no one can ever guarantee it, but I think it’s the moment to check how far we are and to push our limit and proof of concept,” the German added.

“It’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength.”

De la Fuente said their unbeaten record provided his players with extra motivation.

“We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” he explained.

“None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.”

Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter on September 26, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit.

Yamal put Spain ahead in the second minute, but Anthony Gordon equalised, and Kane added another as England ended the first half with a 2-1 lead.

The Three Lions captain missed a penalty in the second half, though, allowing Spain to bounce back, as Alex Baena found the equaliser before Oyarzabal sealed victory in the 74th minute.

Opta’s supercomputer favours Spain for victory. They have a 59.6 percent probability of winning, while England’s odds of victory are 19.3 percent.

There is a 21.1 percent chance the game ends in a draw.

Yamal is expected to face England after missing the last game with a knee problem. Nico Williams and Aymeric Laporte are doubtful

Probable Spain XI: Unai Simon; Marc Pubill, Pau Cubarsi, Dean Huijsen, Marc Cucurella; Dani Olmo, Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Mikel Oyarzabal, Alex Baena

Myles Lewis-Skelly returns from his suspension, while Ezri Konsa is also expected to return after missing the last game due to a knee injury.

Djed Spence (muscle) is doubtful, and Marc Guehi (muscle) remains out with injury.

Probable England XI: Jordan Pickford; Trent Alexander-Arnold, Ezri Konsa, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall; Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice; Morgan Rogers, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon; Harry Kane

You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official broadcaster listing.

articles.title: Ford privacy promise raises questions about your car data
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Norway's confirmation that Chinese-owned rental cars recorded military data on 'Fox Report.'

Your car probably knows more ab...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Norway's confirmation that Chinese-owned rental cars recorded military data on 'Fox Report.'

Your car probably knows more about you than you realize. It can track where you drive, how fast you go and whether something under the hood needs attention. Depending on the vehicle, that information may also travel back to the manufacturer. And chances are, you haven't spent much time thinking about who gets to see it.

Now, Ford wants to put those privacy concerns in the spotlight. On Nov. 2, the automaker announced a new Ford privacy promise designed to give drivers more transparency and control over their personal information. The company also says it won't sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

That sounds encouraging. But there's a catch worth understanding. Turning off certain data-sharing settings could also mean losing some of the connected features you've come to rely on. So how much privacy can you get without giving up the technology you paid for?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

Ford's new privacy promise gives drivers more information about how their vehicles collect and share personal data, but disabling certain settings could limit connected features. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Ford says its new privacy initiative will make it easier for drivers to understand what information their vehicles collect and how the company uses it. The automaker has also launched a dedicated data and privacy website where owners can learn about their options. The announcement centers on several commitments. Ford says it designs its products with privacy in mind and wants customers to have clearer information about their choices. It also promises to respect the privacy settings drivers select. Perhaps the biggest commitment involves what happens to driving information. Ford specifically says it does not sell data about how customers drive to insurance companies or data brokers.

However, that promise does not mean Ford stops collecting connected vehicle data altogether. The company still uses information from equipped vehicles to operate services and improve its technology. Ford's chief privacy officer, Kristin Jones, explained to TechCrunch that the company wants to build greater trust by helping customers understand its data practices. The effort comes as Ford prepares to introduce more connected vehicles, including models built on its upcoming universal electric vehicle platform. Importantly, many of Ford's privacy controls already existed. The new initiative focuses on making those controls easier to understand and find.

Modern Ford vehicles can generate a surprising amount of information. Exactly what gets collected depends on your model, its connected features and the privacy settings you select.

For example, Ford says equipped connected vehicles may share information about:

There are practical benefits to some of this sharing. Vehicle diagnostics can help identify maintenance problems earlier. Location information can support roadside assistance or help you find your parked car. Ford also says it may use connected vehicle data to improve future technologies. With your consent, certain information can support personalization and relevant offers. Still, your driving habits can reveal personal details about your daily routine. That's why understanding which settings are enabled deserves your attention.

Ford's announcement follows increased scrutiny of how automakers handle customer information. On Oct. 29, a coalition of 36 attorneys general announced a $220 million settlement with General Motors over allegations involving drivers' personal information. The states alleged that GM collected and sold driving behavior and location data to third parties, including data brokers that supplied information to insurance companies.

According to the state attorneys general, some insurers used that information when calculating insurance rates. The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative, express consent before collecting or disclosing covered driving and location data. GM previously discontinued its Smart Driver program. The case shows why vehicle privacy has become such a sensitive issue. Drivers may agree to connected features without fully understanding how much information those systems collect.

We've explored similar concerns in our CyberGuy article, Is it worth saving money to let a car insurance company track your every move? Insurance monitoring programs can offer savings, but drivers should understand what information they are agreeing to share. Against that backdrop, Ford's public commitment could help set expectations for how automakers handle sensitive driving information.

Ford says customers can turn off connected vehicle data sharing. However, doing so may affect some of the features that make newer vehicles convenient. Depending on your Ford model, equipment and which settings you disable, you could lose access to:

The exact impact depends on which settings you disable and the technology installed in your vehicle. Turning off all vehicle connectivity can affect more features than changing individual data-sharing preferences. Some features can continue working even when connected vehicle data sharing is disabled. Ford says features such as Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility can continue working without sharing connected vehicle data with Ford. Local Bluetooth connections and regular radio playback can also remain available.

Of course, availability depends on your vehicle's equipment and software. Before turning anything off, check which services your particular Ford needs. Disabling one optional sharing preference does not automatically disable every connected feature. And remember, Apple CarPlay and Android Auto use smartphone technology. Your phone and its apps may have their own data collection settings that you'll want to review separately.

Ford gives owners several ways to review their data-sharing preferences. You can manage vehicle connectivity through the car's touchscreen. The Ford app and your online Ford account provide additional controls for certain uses of your information.

Start with the vehicle parked safely. Ford recommends that owners of vehicles built in 2018 or later review their connected vehicle settings.

Menu names and available controls vary by Ford model and infotainment system. If you want to stop sharing connected vehicle data with Ford, the company says to find Vehicle Connectivity in your vehicle's settings and turn it off. However, this broader change can limit connected services and other features. Ford provides additional guidance through its official privacy settings page.

GM WANTS DRIVERS TO TAKE THEIR EYES OFF THE ROAD BY 2028

Ford says it does not sell customers' driving behavior data to insurance companies or data brokers as it introduces a new vehicle privacy initiative. (Photo by John Keeble/Getty Images)

You can also adjust certain information-sharing preferences through the Ford app on your smartphone.

Ford also provides controls related to Google Maps in the app and certain preferred dealer notifications. Keep in mind that the app's personalization and marketing controls are separate from the vehicle's main connectivity controls. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. If you own more than one Ford, review each vehicle's settings separately.

You may also want to find out what personal information Ford already holds. The company provides options to request access to personal data and seek corrections or deletion, subject to applicable privacy laws and exceptions. You can find those options through Ford's privacy notice.

If you're selling or trading in your Ford, perform a factory reset to remove stored personal information from the vehicle. Ford says this can erase saved addresses, connected accounts and programmed garage door opener codes. You should also make sure the vehicle is disconnected from your Ford account. Depending on its connectivity equipment, you may need to remove the vehicle's VIN from your account as well. Simply deleting the Ford app will not stop vehicle data sharing. However, that reset will not erase data the company already received. Any request to delete that information must be handled separately.

There's an important point worth keeping in mind. Ford's commitment about selling driving behavior data to brokers and insurers is specific. It does not prohibit every form of data collection or disclosure. Ford's privacy notice describes circumstances in which information may be shared with service providers or other parties. It also addresses disclosures made in response to valid legal requests. Meanwhile, Ford offers personalization and marketing settings that deserve a separate review. And even though Ford says it doesn't sell driving behavior data to insurance companies, that doesn't mean an insurer can't collect information about how you drive through a separate smartphone app or a voluntary insurance monitoring program.

There are also exceptions to Ford's privacy controls. The company says it may collect vehicle location data in certain circumstances even when location sharing is turned off. These can include legal requirements, emergencies and protection of property. Vehicles equipped with the Ford Security Package may also share location information when a Theft Alert is triggered.

So even with Ford's new promise, I would still encourage drivers to examine their individual settings. A company can make a meaningful privacy commitment while continuing to collect information needed for its services. And if you're shopping for a new vehicle, consider privacy before making the purchase.

If you own a newer Ford, this announcement gives you a good reason to check your privacy settings. You may discover that your vehicle shares more information than you expected. You might also find settings you can disable without affecting the features you enjoy. However, you should understand the tradeoff before switching off all connectivity. Losing remote access or other useful services could be inconvenient, especially if you rely on them regularly.

The same advice applies if you drive another brand. Take a few minutes to find your manufacturer's privacy settings and learn what information your vehicle shares. You can explore the broader privacy concerns in our article, What your car knows about you and could be telling the world. Ultimately, knowing what your car collects gives you a better chance of controlling your personal information.

DATA BROKERS DON'T JUST COLLECT FACTS. THEY GUESS ABOUT YOU

Ford owners can adjust vehicle data-sharing settings to protect their privacy, though turning off connectivity may affect remote start, navigation and other features. (Photo by Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images)

I like seeing Ford make a public commitment about protecting driving data. Especially after what we've learned about how vehicle information can end up in the hands of insurance companies. But here's what I keep coming back to. When you spend tens of thousands of dollars on a vehicle, how much of your personal information should you have to share to enjoy the features you already paid for? I understand why Ford needs certain data to make connected technology work. Real-time traffic updates can be useful. So can getting an alert before a mechanical problem leaves you stranded. But I also think automakers need to make privacy choices much easier to understand. Drivers shouldn't have to dig through complicated menus to figure out what's happening with their information. Ford's promise is encouraging, and I hope other manufacturers pay attention. The real test will be how well these commitments hold up as vehicles become even more connected.

Would you sacrifice features like remote start or live navigation to keep your driving data private, or should automakers be required to offer those conveniences without collecting so much personal information? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson is an award-winning tech journalist who has a deep love of technology, gear and gadgets that make life better with his contributions for Fox News & FOX Business beginning mornings on "FOX & Friends." Got a tech question? Get Kurt’s free CyberGuy Newsletter, share your voice, a story idea or comment at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’
articles.excerpt:
Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence

Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanista...
articles.body_text:
Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence

Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days.

Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence.

A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported. And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight.

As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts.

Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government.

Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all.

Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved.

Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others.

“In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.”

VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition”.

Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.

Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said.

Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban.

Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers.

Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US.

The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation.

The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled, according to the AP.

The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice.

Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture.

The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return.

More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated.

In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue.

The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater.

“We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?”

One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife.

Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan.

The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide.

Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back.

Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.”

articles.title: Underwater salt mine closure in Ohio raises safety and supply concerns for winter
articles.excerpt:
Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter

When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton S...
articles.body_text:
Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter

When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good.

For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos.

On top of that, in the weeks since the mine’s closure what’s been concerning mining experts and residents alike across the Great Lakes region is the mine’s location – about 2,000ft (610 meters) underneath Lake Erie. And that is sending broader warning signals across the region among activists and environmentalists, as to whether the issue could eventually hit other mines underneath the Great Lakes.

At the Fairport Harbor facility, one of 12 rock salt mines that Morton Salt runs around the world, around 1.3 million tons of rock salt were mined from underneath the lake every year.

Last winter’s colder and snowier than average weather ate into road salt stockpiles at hundreds of municipalities across the region.

Situated 30 miles (48km) from the now-shuttered mine, Trumbull county’s 200,000 residents relied entirely on the Fairport Harbor mine for road salt.

Trumbull county’s location downwind of Lake Erie means its roads and highways are particularly affected by lake-effect snowstorms and the freeze-thaw process for up to five months a year.

“We get about 30,000 tons [of salt] a year from the mine. But we have a stockpile of around 14,000 tons,” says David DeChristofaro, the Trumbull county engineer.

“We are waiting for the Ohio department of transportation [to see about acquiring additional road salt supplies]. If necessary, we will mix salt with aggregate, one to one, as was typically done 15 years ago, to stretch our supply of salt. But that adds to cost because it needs to be swept up at the end of winter.” Trumbull county gets around 4.5ft (1.4 meters) of snowfall every winter.

Authorities in a township in a neighboring county have had to issue a warning to motorists about potentially hazardous driving conditions this winter because of the salt shortage.

While the mine closure could mean transportation problems for more than a million residents in a region of Ohio that experiences especially harsh winter conditions, the water intrusion has also raised safety questions.

With five salt mines situated partly or entirely underneath Great Lakes waterways – in Fairport Harbor, Detroit and Cleveland, and two over the Canadian border in Ontario – a growing concern is that weeks later, Morton Salt officials say they still can’t find the source of the water intrusion.

The salt is extracted by drilling and using explosives, and while the distance between the bed of Lake Erie and Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine is in excess of 1,000ft (305 meters), decades of blasting and the presence of underground aquifers could contribute to significant subterranean rock movement, say experts.

“Blasting can fracture rock near an excavation, and removing rock changes the stresses carried by the roof, pillars and surrounding layers. For water to enter, there must also be a connected pathway from a water source to the mine,” says Xiong “Bill” Yu, a professor of engineering at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

“A nearby aquifer could supply that water through a fault, connected fractures, or a compromised shaft or seal. More than 1,000ft of rock is meaningful separation, but the engineering question is whether the layers provide a continuous barrier and whether anything crosses it.”

While the likelihood that the lake is the source of the water entering the Morton salt mine appears to be remote, local voices have begun calling for an investigation into just how safe salt mines carved out from under large bodies of water are and whether drinking water resources may be affected.

“Could the rock roof be breached, creating saline water swamps in a Lake Erie that’s the source of drinking water for millions in both the US and Canada?” an editorial in the Cleveland Plain Dealer asked this month.

In 2017, the much larger Cargill-run Whiskey Island salt mine 30 miles (48km) west of Fairport Harbor experienced a water intrusion event that also saw dangerous levels of hydrogen sulfide gas released. That facility, which is one of the largest of its kind in the world, producing up to 4m tons a year and supplying road salt for states across the Great Lakes and midwest, spreads out 16 sq miles (41 sq km) beneath Lake Erie. More than 200 employees work 12-hour shifts there every day.

In 1994, one of the largest salt mines in the world, located in western New York, was inundated with aquifer water and collapsed. And in 1980, Lake Peigneur in Louisiana was accidentally drained when an oil rig breached the roof of an underwater salt mine 1,300ft (396 moeters) under the surface of the lake. No salt miners were injured in either incident.

The Mine Safety and Health Administration, a federal agency, oversees health and safety operations in US mines. But under the Trump administration, a deregulation drive has been enacted that includes, among other measures, eliminating diesel particle matter exposure levels in mines.

In 2022, under the Biden administration, a Morton Salt mine in Louisiana was placed on the Department of Labor’s pattern-of-violations notice for “a high number of significant and substantial violations and other safety and health compliance problems”. That notice was lifted in April 2025.

Emails sent and calls made by the Guardian to Morton Salt asking how often the Fairport Harbor mine underwent a full perimeter inspection for water intrusion before its closure, whether the company knows the source of the water intrusion, and if it is scheduling any new or improved safety measures at other mines it operates were not responded to.

Emails sent to Cargill inquiring about any potential additional safety steps it may be taking at its Whiskey Island mine, in light of the Morton Salt mine closure, were also not responded to. In 2020, two miners at a Cargill salt mine in Louisiana died while trying to prevent water from flooding the mine, according to lawsuits filed by family members.

Miners employed at the Fairport Harbor mine contacted by the Guardian declined to be interviewed, citing restrictions in a non-disclosure agreement.

For industry observers, the almost immediate decision to close Morton’s Fairport Harbor mine means that it might be time for monitoring authorities to step in.

“I would support a targeted, regulator-led review of water-intrusion risks at operating salt mines beneath the Great Lakes,” says Yu.

“[The Morton mine] incident is reason to check how each mine detects and responds to unusual seepage, and to review the condition of shafts and seals, the stability of roofs and pillars, and any known pathways from water-bearing rock.”

articles.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
articles.excerpt:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the de...
articles.body_text:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia 
  As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.

Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain 
  The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.

Devastating floods across much of the world 
  In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.

World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly 
  The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.

Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan 
   
 At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.

Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia 
  At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.

Ocean heat enters uncharted territory 
  Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.

Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth 
  Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.

West African deluge takes heavy toll 
  Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.

Fires choke Canada and Europe 
  Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.

Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup 
  Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.

At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.

Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 
  Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.

Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown
 
 The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.

Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia 
  Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.

Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño 
  The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.

Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires 
  Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.

Roads turn to rivers in Chile 
  After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.

Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest 
  Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.

2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history

Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

articles.title: GOP midterm bloodbath exposes cracks in Vance's 2028 White House ambitions
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump said he was fine with Vice President JD Vance's post-midterm critique on the political unpopularity of the Iran conflict, but he would have wanted to hear Vance add that if they...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump said he was fine with Vice President JD Vance's post-midterm critique on the political unpopularity of the Iran conflict, but he would have wanted to hear Vance add that if they had to do it again, they would.

Vice President JD Vance has long been viewed as President Donald Trump's heir apparent, but a string of developments following Republicans' bruising midterm losses is raising new questions about his potential path to the White House in 2028.

Vance is facing criticism from some Republicans over his explanation for the party's election defeats, particularly his decision to blame the Iran war. Meanwhile, other prominent Republicans are beginning to draw support for potential 2028 bids, complicating the political picture for the vice president.

The political debate follows a devastating election for Republicans, who lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress beginning next year, with at least 30 GOP House members losing their races. The losses have prompted competing explanations from within the party over what went wrong and what Republicans should do differently.

Some of Vance's allies have reportedly urged him to consider sitting out the 2028 race following the midterm losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Nov. 7. However, others close to the vice president still expect him to run, The Washington Post reported Friday, underscoring the uncertainty surrounding his political future.

TRUMP SAYS HE DOESN’T DISAGREE WITH VANCE THAT IRAN WAR FUELED GOP LOSSES

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a press briefing at the White House in Washington D.C. on Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

A Vance ally pushed back on suggestions that the midterm losses have diminished his 2028 prospects, saying the vice president will decide whether to run on his own timeline. The ally also argued that Vance would be better served by winning a competitive Republican primary than being handed the nomination, expressing confidence in his ability to prevail if he runs.

In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance identified several concerns among voters who abandoned Republicans, including inflation, America First priorities and the U.S. relationship with Israel, but singled out the Iran war as the main reason for the party's defeats.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote, adding that Republicans needed to acknowledge the political cost of the conflict as they consider where to go next.

The post drew sharp criticism from Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., who told Fox' LiveNOW in a Nov. 8 interview that he would not support Vance in a potential 2028 presidential primary.

PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES

"I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest," Fine said, comparing Vance's remarks to rhetoric from "1932 Germany."

Fine, who is Jewish, accused Vance of blaming Jewish people for the Republican losses, pointing to his criticism of the war and the pollster's finding that some voters wanted a change in America's relationship with Israel.

Vance did not explicitly blame Jewish people in his post, and his office previously declined to respond to Fine's characterization.

Vice President JD Vance walks to board Air Force Two at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY

Some Republicans are already expressing support for possible alternatives to Vance. Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital after the midterms that he was "all in" for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, describing him as a potential unifying figure for Republicans following their election losses.

Rubio is among several prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced as possible 2028 presidential contenders, along with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas.

From left to right: Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida (Alex Brandon/Pool via REUTERS; Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Former Vice President Mike Pence also disputed Vance's explanation for Republicans' midterm losses, arguing in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview Thursday that voters had grown frustrated not because Trump launched the Iran war, but because his administration failed to finish it.

"There's no question that the war in Iran became a frustration for millions of Americans, but it wasn't because President Trump started the war or took on Iran. It's because we stopped short and didn't finish it," Pence said. "As Americans saw the politics of appeasement that the administration embraced, one negotiation after another, I think people became ... frustrated with the lack of progress, frustrated with the price of fuel at the pump."

Trump, meanwhile, has publicly defended Vance's assessment of the midterms, rejecting suggestions that the remarks damaged their relationship.

"No, not at all," Trump told reporters Sunday when asked whether Vance's comments had strained their relationship, according to The Hill.

But the president also stood by his decision to launch the war, arguing that he would make the same choice again despite the political fallout.

Donald Trump Jr. also backed Vance's assessment, writing "Every word of this is [100 emojis]" in response to his Nov. 4 post on X.

On Thursday, Trump directed Vance to focus his attention on alleged corruption and crime in Democratic-led cities and states rather than pursuing negotiations with Iran, declaring that the United States no longer needed a deal with Tehran.

Vance had played a central role in diplomatic efforts involving Iran, including negotiations over a short-lived truce earlier this year.

Vice President JD Vance praised President Donald Trump's leadership style and work ethic during the interview. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"The Blue States, such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, and many more, are all poorly run, corrupt disasters," Trump wrote in the post. "Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month. Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!"

"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" the president continued.

VANCE ‘PRIVATELY’ BLASTS NETANYAHU AS IRAN WAR DIVIDES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND 2028 AMBITIONS LOOM

Trump has previously signaled support for Vance as his potential successor, telling donors during an Oval Office meeting over the summer that Republicans needed to elect the vice president in 2028, Fox News Digital reported at the time.

But Trump has stopped short of publicly endorsing Vance, and the president has continued to leave open the possibility of other Republicans entering the race.

When asked on Nov. 4 whether he had talked about a prospective 2028 White House run with Vance, Trump replied that the two discuss "a lot of things," Axios reported. Trump added: "Maybe he [Vance] won't run. I don't know who's going to run."

Still, Vance told Mark Halperin in an October interview that he believes Trump would back him if he jumps into the presidential race, ABC 7 reported.

"I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven't focused on it. We, you, and I have talked about that. Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me," Vance said during the interview.

Fox News Digital's Ashley DiMella and Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this story.
