articles.title: Stroke survivors get FDA-approved daily pill shown to cut repeat risk by 26%
articles.excerpt: Dr. Richard Kovacs, a cardiologist at Indiana University School of Medicine and chief medical officer of the American College of Cardiology, spoke to Fox News Digital about a newly approved drug desig...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Richard Kovacs, a cardiologist at Indiana University School of Medicine and chief medical officer of the American College of Cardiology, spoke to Fox News Digital about a newly approved drug designed to prevent repeat strokes.

The FDA has approved Sunharbo (asundexian) to reduce the risks of a recurring stroke in some adults.

The medication is taken as one 50-mg pill each day, along with standard blood-clot-preventing medicine, such as aspirin.

It is designed to lower the risk of another stroke in adults who recently had a stroke caused by a blood clot (not a heart-related clot) or a mini-stroke (transient ischemic attack, or TIA), which is a temporary interruption of blood flow to the brain, according to the FDA release.

HEALTHY RUNNER SUFFERS SUDDEN STROKE AT 27 AS DOCTORS DISCOVER POSSIBLE CAUSE

Sunharbo is the first medication of its kind to block a specific protein in the blood (factor XIa) that helps blood clots form.

"This blocks a very specific protein that’s part of the cascade of blood clotting," Dr. Richard Kovacs, a cardiologist at Indiana University School of Medicine and chief medical officer of the American College of Cardiology, told Fox News Digital.

The FDA has approved Sunharbo (asundexian) to reduce the risks of a recurring stroke in some adults. (iStock)

Approval followed a phase 3 randomized trial involving 12,327 patients across 37 countries, all of whom had a recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA.

Among those who took 50 mg of asundexian orally once daily plus antiplatelet therapy for a period of 14.2 months, there was a 26% relative reduction in ischemic stroke compared to groups who took a placebo along with antiplatelet therapy.

COMMON HEART PILL UNDER SCRUTINY FOR OLDER PATIENTS AS STUDY WEIGHS RISKS OF STOPPING

Although there was not a significant overall increase in major bleeding, the risk of that side effect was higher in certain subgroups. However, gastrointestinal bleeding was more common with asundexian, and major bleeding was increased among patients older than 75 during the first 90 days.

Patients who took asundexian also had a lower risk of stroke, heart attack or death compared with those who received a placebo.

The medication is designed to lower the risk of another stroke in adults who recently had a stroke caused by a blood clot or a mini-stroke (transient ischemic attack, or TIA), which is a temporary interruption of blood flow to the brain. (iStock)

About 6.6% of patients taking asundexian experienced a stroke, compared with 8.8% in the placebo group.

"So it doesn’t completely eliminate the risk of a second stroke," Kovacs said.

EVEN OCCASIONAL MARIJUANA USE LINKED TO HIGHER STROKE RISK, STUDY FINDS

The risk of death from heart-related causes, heart attack or stroke was also lower among patients taking asundexian (9.2% versus 11.1%).

Similarly, 10.5% of patients taking the medication experienced death from any cause, compared with 12.3% of those receiving a placebo.

"This drug is not for patients who have had strokes due to atrial fibrillation or due to a valve problem in their heart."

The findings were published in The New England Journal of Medicine on Nov. 9.

The trial, which was funded by Bayer, the manufacturer of asundexian, had several limitations.

Because patients were treated for an average of about 14 months, long-term safety and effectiveness of the medication are unclear.

The study also excluded patients with certain heart conditions and those with more severe strokes.

About 6.6% of patients taking asundexian experienced a stroke, compared with 8.8% in the placebo group. (iStock)

"Importantly, this drug is not for patients who have had strokes due to atrial fibrillation or due to a valve problem in their heart," Kovacs said.

Longer-term studies are needed to identify safety and effectiveness among older patients, underrepresented populations and patients with greater stroke severity, the researchers noted.

Kovacs emphasized that patients should discuss the medication with their care team soon after a stroke.

"In the clinical trial that approved this drug, this drug was given very soon after the stroke – within 72 hours," he said. "So it’s important to have that conversation about whether this is a drug for the patient early on, often in the hospital."

The medication is taken as one 50-mg pill each day, along with standard blood-clot-preventing medicine, such as aspirin. (iStock)

Medication is only one part of preventing another stroke, the cardiologist emphasized.

"The cause of the stroke in many of these patients was atherosclerosis," he said, describing the condition as "plaque buildup that can cause circulation problems and the lack of blood flow to the brain."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So it’s important for any stroke patient to do all the other things that you can do in addition to this medicine to prevent a second stroke – like stopping smoking, keeping your cholesterol low, eating healthy, and most importantly, getting exercise."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

More than 795,000 people in the U.S. have a stroke each year, including about 185,000 who have had one before, according to the CDC.

About one in four stroke survivors experiences another within five years.

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

articles.title: THAD ROTHROCK: Bible reminds us to keep serving God even after we retire
articles.excerpt:
Fairfield University associate professor T.C. Schmidt joins ‘Saturday in America’ to discuss new research supporting the authenticity of Josephus’ 2,000-year-old account of Jesus Christ.

Culture may ...
articles.body_text:
Fairfield University associate professor T.C. Schmidt joins ‘Saturday in America’ to discuss new research supporting the authenticity of Josephus’ 2,000-year-old account of Jesus Christ.

Culture may see retirement as a time to step back, but Scripture never suggests that our calling retires with us.

In fact, the psalmist prayed, "Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, my God, till I declare your power to the next generation, your mighty acts to all who are to come." (Psalm 71:18 NIV)

Even in his old age, the psalmist petitioned God for more time on earth to continue living out the calling set before him and to declare the truths of God to the generations who will follow.

WHO IS RAISING AMERICA'S CHILDREN? MENTOR WARNS KIDS ARE SEEKING ROLE MODELS ONLINE AS COMMUNITIES FADE

Contrary to what culture says, one’s role in the community becomes most urgent in his later years. Paul told Titus the same thing and instructed older believers to teach what is good and train those younger than them. Neither the psalmist nor the Apostle Paul considered age as a legitimate reason to pull back; rather, both considered it the qualification for stepping further in.

A church group holds hands and prays in a circle. Younger churchgoers say they want mentorship at their places of worship. (iStock)

It can be easy to treat retirement from a career as retirement from the church as well, as though stepping down from a job also means stepping away from service. The transition is gentle. A person might move from active participation in ministry to being on its prayer list, from teaching a class to sitting in the back row.

JUDGE JUDY CREDITS HER HONOR PROGRAM WITH MAKING HER 'HOPEFUL' FOR THE NEXT GENERATION

While the shift away from a lifetime of active service in the community is well-intentioned, treating retirement as a phasing out opposes what Scripture prescribes for older churchgoers, which is to draw even closer to the younger generations.

When elder believers draw from deep reservoirs of life experience and Spirit-led sanctification to counsel younger or more immature believers, they’re faithful to the charge by the Apostle Paul to see to it that all can be presented mature in Christ (Colossians 1:28-29). In fact, the church has benefited from and treasured this kind of discipleship for centuries.

GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM

The practical case follows directly from the theological one. A congregation losing its younger members to another church or to religious disaffiliation may not be because of a lack of programming. It may be that folks leave because of a lack of engaged older mentors.

The generation now entering retirement has spent decades leading households, raising children, weathering seasons of doubt and staying in the church through it all. They don’t lack wisdom. They just lack the opportunity to extend it to the rest of the congregation.

THE CRISIS FACING AMERICAN BOYS MIGHT TRACE BACK TO ONE ESSENTIAL PROBLEM

Barna Group found that 77% of adults 55 and older have a close relationship with someone younger, but only 19% of Christians say their church provides opportunities for people from different generations to connect. Yet, young adults say the top social reason they come to church is to build deeper relationships with other Christians.

So, what would it look like for aged wisdom to be championed within a community?

EX-PRISONER WHO BECAME MAYOR AND PASTOR CREDITS FAITH-BASED PROGRAM WITH GIVING HIM SECOND CHANCE

Senior living communities like ours offer a glimpse of what this can look like lived out. Residents lead the choirs at their life plan communities rather than simply attending them. They volunteer in chaplaincy work alongside our caregivers, sitting with residents who are further along in illness or grief than they are. They chair resident associations and continue serving in leadership roles at their home churches. None of this is unusual for them. It is simply what continues when nobody has told them their season of contribution is over.

A congregation losing its younger members to another church or to religious disaffiliation may not be because of a lack of programming. It may be that folks leave because of a lack of engaged older mentors.

Congregations bear fruit when they deliberately recognize this opportunity, rather than assume it will happen on its own. Mentorship can be built into structure, rather than left to whoever happens to volunteer. A church that wants its retirees mentoring its twentysomethings will bear new fruit when it asks for it directly, pairs people intentionally and treats that pairing as real ministry work rather than a nice idea.

EXCLUSIVE: NEW CHURCH CAMPAIGN SAYS AMERICA'S FAMILY CRISIS WON'T BE SOLVED BY POLITICS, BUT BY PASTORS

This can look as simple as an established deacon walking a new one through a hard pastoral visit, or a retired teacher counseling a young couple through their first year of marriage. The alternative — leaving it informal — can easily become the same thing as not asking at all.

Scripture never frames old age as a countdown to irrelevance. It frames it as the season with the most to declare and the least time left to declare it in, which makes this time of life more urgent, not less. The picture of retirement that most congregations envision, a quiet transition into rest and gratitude, was never the biblical picture. Even in the psalmist's telling, old age comes with an assignment, not a discharge from one.

Our retired churchgoers don’t just have time on their hands, but — what’s even more beneficial to their congregations — plenty left to give, and no shortage of people who need their wisdom and experience. The question now becomes: Will the church call on its older members to step into this crucial role?

Thad Rothrock is CEO of Homewood Living Ministries.

articles.title: Media can’t muster any outrage or coverage of violent comments from the left
articles.excerpt: Dave Chappelle faces backlash over a controversial joke about Charlie Kirk during a stand-up performance. Political commentator Alexa Henning joins to discuss the implications of the comedian's commen...
articles.body_text:
Dave Chappelle faces backlash over a controversial joke about Charlie Kirk during a stand-up performance. Political commentator Alexa Henning joins to discuss the implications of the comedian's comments.

In spite of all the thrills traveling up the legs of the broadcast news veterans over the "blue tsunami" of the midterms, not everyone on the left is celebrating the victories with class and civility. But when leftists engage in the nastiest speech, they know that their liberal friends will carefully edit that out.

The elitist networks will pretend that kindness, compassion and decency are hallmarks of their progressive movement. That’s why the nastiest speech must be hidden. None of the broadcast networks touched any of this.

The conservative media exploded in outrage over podcaster Jennifer Welch and her sidekick Angie "Pumps" Sullivan when they laughed uproariously over a joke about the Charlie Kirk assassination. Welch and Sullivan starred in a Bravo reality series called "Sweet Home Oklahoma." Their podcast is called "I’ve Had It," and conservatives have definitely had it with their ugly speech. But their YouTube channel has over 1.8 million subscribers.

WELCH DOUBLES DOWN ON TPUSA FEUD, CALLS GROUP 'LOSERS' AFTER LAUGHING AT JOKE ABOUT KILLING CHARLIE KIRK AGAIN

On Nov. 5, they were reading comments from their fans in an episode titled "Drinking MAGA Tears." Welch announced: "Dead Moroz says, ‘we’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again.’" They bowed their heads in laughter for 10 seconds. Sullivan felt it necessary to add, "Other than he was shot by somebody that was super-MAGA," and Welch echoed, "He was shot by a MAGA person." Late night host Jimmy Kimmel’s lie keeps getting repeated.

Co-hosts of the "I’ve Had It" podcast, Jennifer Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan spoke on their show.

Collin Rugg’s clip of this bilge on X has more than 7 million views and more than 19,000 likes.

CHARLAMAGNE THA GOD CALLS OUT DAVE CHAPPELLE'S KIRK COMMENTS, WOULDN'T WISH THEM 'ON MY WORST ENEMY'

Welch is a popular figure, not only on her podcast, but on other liberal podcasts, where hosts think her nastiness is a balm. On Instagram, former CNN anchor Don Lemon touted her appearance on his show with the question: "In need of a political detox?" In Lemon’s head, it’s a purging of toxins to be toxic.

Two days after the Welch giggles, comedian Dave Chappelle seconded that nasty emotion on the stage of his "Karmageddon" tour stop at Madison Square Garden: "It’s scary being a public speaker. Ever since that guy Charlie Kirk got murdered, and I shouldn’t say this publicly but … I feel better." There were laughs and scattered applause. "I know I shouldn’t say that, but it’s just a feeling," he added. "I just be driving around, like, ‘Why am I in such a good mood … oh!"

A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH

Then Chappelle concluded with the vision of Kirk in hell: "I’m sure Charlie Kirk is looking up at us right now, laughing so hard he can’t breathe." Comedian Tony Hinchcliffe delivered a nearly identical punchline about George Floyd in May at a roast for Kevin Hart.

Back in April, National Public Radio celebrated Chappelle in a long "Newsmakers" interview for YouTube – in large part because he donated a cool $5 million to the NPR station in Dayton, Ohio. Chappelle boasted about comedians: "We're like a nation's kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts but feelings around facts or ideas." Is that what the dead Charlie Kirk jokes do? Purify the body politic?

TURNING POINT USA SPOX ANDREW KOLVET SPEAKS OUT AS JENNIFER WELCH, DAVE CHAPPELLE MOCK CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER

Charlie’s widow Erika Kirk responded bluntly on X: "To see leftist podcasters, comedians, and commentators laugh about political assassination as though it’s entertainment and the destruction of a human life is a punchline, is beyond disgusting. … A culture that laughs at assassination is one of profound moral decay."

But most people didn’t see the leftists laugh. The same broadcast networks that routinely treat the president’s Truth Social posts as overwrought and uncivil couldn’t locate these clips. It's not "newsworthy" when the left is vicious.

CHAPPELLE, JENNIFER WELCH JOKES ABOUT KIRK'S MURDER PART OF PATTERN OF LEFTISTS FINDING HUMOR IN VIOLENCE

So, there’s assassination commentary, and then there’s execution commentary. Scott Galloway, a prominent multi-millionaire New York University professor and podcaster, acidly expressed that Elon Musk should be executed as a "traitor to the West." Why? Because his company Space X restricted Starlink satellite internet speeds in Ukraine last month. Musk said using Starlink "for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed."

The elitist networks will pretend that kindness, compassion and decency are hallmarks of their progressive movement. That’s why the nastiest speech must be hidden. None of the broadcast networks touched any of this.

Galloway argued this led to Ukrainian civilian deaths and proclaimed on his "Prof G" podcast: "And my question is, or my thesis is, we took the Rosenbergs and put them up against a wall and executed them for being traitors. And I realize this is an incendiary statement, but I’ll make it, and I believe it."

On a recent episode of the "Pivot" podcast with co-host Kara Swisher, Galloway repeated it: "We lined up the Rosenbergs against a wall. This is a traitor to the West, and he should be held to the same standards as every other traitor in the West."

Shortly after this, Galloway claimed that he hated Musk so much that he sold his Tesla, but not before defecating in the passenger seat. These unhinged haters are the people that media elites would like you to consider the enlightened voices of a brighter future.

articles.title: Natalee Holloway's confessed killer caught trying to extort $250K from grieving mother in FBI sting video
articles.excerpt:
Beth Holloway believes that Joran van der Sloot's confession to murdering his daughter in Aruba is corroborated.

Joran van der Sloot spent years tormenting Natalee Holloway's family with a tangled we...
articles.body_text:
Beth Holloway believes that Joran van der Sloot's confession to murdering his daughter in Aruba is corroborated.

Joran van der Sloot spent years tormenting Natalee Holloway's family with a tangled web of lies. But behind closed doors, the convicted killer was playing an even more sinister game.

Now, previously unseen video from an FBI sting reveals just how far he was willing to go to exploit a grieving mother's desperate search for answers. The Netflix true crime docuseries "Taken: Natalee Holloway," co-directed by Dani Sloane and Matthew Galkin, features video of the 2010 sting operation showing the Dutch national attempting to extort money from Holloway's family.

"His brazenness stood out to me, the fact that he's sitting across from lawyer John Q. Kelly, and he's going 'Can I have a soda? It's so hot outside, I had to wait for a cab,'" Sloane told Fox News Digital. "He's having a casual conversation while he's extorting the mother of his victim for money, for information that only he knows. It's astonishing. You really don't often get to look at a perpetrator like that. He feels really cavalier and he's just casual about the whole thing."

SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED

Joran van der Sloot is currently imprisoned in Peru, where he is serving time for the 2010 murder of 21-year-old Stephany Flores Ramírez. In October 2023, he confessed to killing Alabama teenager Natalee Holloway in Aruba in 2005 as part of a plea agreement in a federal extortion and wire fraud case involving her family. He has never been charged in connection with Holloway's murder. (REUTERS)

"It’s pretty haunting to see," Sloane added.

Holloway, 18, disappeared on May 30, 2005, while she was on a graduation trip in Aruba with her high school classmates. She was last seen leaving a bar with van der Sloot, a student at an international school on the Caribbean island where he grew up.

Natalee Holloway (left) was a straight-A student who earned a full scholarship to the University of Alabama and dreamed of becoming a doctor. Friends remembered her as a driven teenager who was focused on her future before she disappeared in Aruba in 2005. (Netflix)

Van der Sloot, long suspected in connection with her disappearance, was never charged with her murder. A judge declared Holloway dead in 2012, but her body was never found.

Natalee Holloway disappeared on May 30, 2005, while on a high school graduation trip to Aruba. The 18-year-old Alabama teenager was last seen leaving a nightclub with Joran van der Sloot and two other young men. Her body has never been found. (Netflix)

Nearly five years after Holloway's disappearance, van der Sloot emailed Kelly, an attorney for Holloway's mother, Beth Holloway, the film revealed. For $250,000, he offered to provide information about Holloway's death and the whereabouts of her remains.

Kelly and van der Sloot agreed to meet at a hotel in Aruba in May 2010, where Kelly would hand over a $25,000 deposit in exchange for the information, starting with $10,000 in cash. By then, according to the documentary, van der Sloot had changed his story about what happened to the Alabama teen roughly 40 times.

Joran van der Sloot takes a walk to a local supermarket near his parents' house in Oranjestad, Aruba, just after he was released from prison on Dec. 7, 2007. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Joran went on TV countless times and continued to tell slightly different fabricated stories," Sloane said.

Dutch citizen Joran Van der Sloot looks on at the end of his trial at Lurigancho prison in Lima on Jan. 6, 2012. Van der Sloot went on trial in the killing of Stephany Flores Ramirez in 2010, five years to the day after Natalee Holloway vanished on Aruba after spending time with him. (Reuters)

"I think it's probably an even higher number than that. We did our own approximations and it's a pretty staggering number of different stories he told, even just small details he changed within the storytelling about what happened that night. It's astonishing. I've been doing this for a really long time, but I personally have never seen anything like this where it's very clear who did this."

"He is so masterful at evading law enforcement and evading consequences by just outright lying," Sloane added.

According to former Aruban police official Gerold Dompig, Joran van der Sloot changed his story an estimated 40 times during the initial investigation into Natalee Holloway's disappearance. (Netflix)

According to the film, Beth agreed to give van der Sloot $25,000 because she believed it was her chance to finally learn what happened to her daughter from the man she had long suspected of killing her. She was on standby at an Alabama bank, ready to wire the remaining $15,000 as soon as van der Sloot signed their agreement.

Beth subsequently wired the remaining $15,000 to van der Sloot's bank account, bringing the initial payment to $25,000.

Beth Holloway appears in Netflix's "Taken: Natalee Holloway," which is now available for streaming. (Netflix)

Before the meeting, Kelly had contacted the FBI, which worked with police in Aruba to secretly record the exchange in hopes of building a criminal case against van der Sloot.

The previously unreleased video of the exchange shows Kelly handing over $10,000.

Joran van der Sloot has a daughter with his Peruvian wife, Leidy Figueroa. The couple married in 2014 while he was serving a prison sentence in Peru for the murder of Stephany Flores Ramírez. (Netflix)

"To be completely honest, for me, the biggest deal is the 225 afterwards," van der Sloot tells Kelly in the recording. "Did you put in the contract that that would be paid within a month?"

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"The piece that's worth highlighting is this extortion tape that we got access to that has never been seen before," director Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. (Reuters)

Kelly said yes and van der Sloot signed the agreement.

In the docuseries, Kelly explained that van der Sloot was never going to receive the remaining $225,000.

Natalee Holloway is seen here with her mother Beth Holloway. (Netflix)

"If he disclosed Natalee's whereabouts then he was going to be arrested for it," Kelly explained. "And if he didn't disclose what happened to Natalee, he was going to get arrested anyway for extortion or fraud."

Dutch national Joran Van der Sloot is seen in Lima in this June 11, 2010 handout taken by Peruvian police. (Reuters)

Van der Sloot then took Kelly to a nearby house, claiming Holloway's body had been buried in the foundation while the home was under construction.

Beth Holloway participates in the launch of the Natalee Holloway Resource Center on June 8, 2010, in Washington, D.C. The nonprofit resource center was founded by Holloway and the National Museum of Crime & Punishment to assist families of missing persons. (Getty Images)

"It's honestly a horrific thing to watch," Sloane said. "Just to see how that conversation played out is really stunning."

"Beth Holloway was the one who was on this the longest," director Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. "She was the one who rallied the investigators in the end, the FBI, to become involved again. And it was her dogged pursuit that really made the confession happen in the end." (Netflix)

Investigators determined the information was false. But before U.S. authorities could file charges against van der Sloot, he left Aruba for Peru.

A man holds posters of Dutch citizen Joran Van der Sloot and Peruvian girl Stephany Flores Ramirez outside Lurigancho prison in Lima on Jan. 13, 2012. (Reuters)

Van der Sloot's trail of lies was about to take an even deadlier turn. On May 30, 2010, exactly five years after Holloway's disappearance, van der Sloot murdered 21-year-old Stephany Flores Ramírez in his hotel room in Lima, Peru.

Joran Andreas Petrus van der Sloot is escorted by Peruvian police as he arrives at the DIRINCRI (Criminal Investigation Direction) offices in Lima on June 5, 2010. Van der Sloot was the main suspect in the killing of Stephany Flores Ramirez, 21, daughter of Peruvian businessman and race car driver Ricardo Flores Chipoco. (AFP via Getty Images)

According to the film, van der Sloot told investigators he attacked Flores Ramírez after she discovered information about Holloway's disappearance on his laptop. He beat and strangled her.

In July 2014, van der Sloot married Leidy Figueroa, a Peruvian woman. They later had a daughter.

Ricardo Flores, whose daughter Stephany Flores was murdered by Dutch citizen Joran Van der Sloot, listens to the reading of the sentence in Van der Sloot's murder trial in Lurigancho prison in Lima, Peru, on Jan. 13, 2012. (Reuters)

In the film, retired FBI special agent Alexandra Montilla recalled an encounter in which the "charismatic" van der Sloot told her about a pet rabbit he shared with his daughter. According to Montilla's account, the rabbit scratched his daughter while she was petting it. Montilla said van der Sloot told her that he grabbed the animal and "ripped his head off."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Alexandra Montilla is a retired FBI agent who was involved in bringing Joran van der Sloot from Peru to the United States in 2023 to face federal extortion and wire fraud charges involving Natalee Holloway's family. (Netflix)

"I've dealt with a lot of criminals and, as a female, I thought this is probably one of the most dangerous ones," Montilla said.

Sloane said Montilla still vividly remembers the encounter.

Joran van der Sloot was convicted of murdering 21-year-old Stephany Flores Ramírez in Peru in 2010. He claimed he killed her after she discovered information about his connection to Natalee Holloway's disappearance, but investigators disputed his account. (AFP via Getty Images)

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

"He was good at spinning a story," Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital about Joran van der Sloot. (Netflix)

"It really lives in her memory," Sloane said. "It's something that stands out to her out of all the offenders and perpetrators she has spent time with. It counts a lot when a seasoned member of the FBI is horrified by something."

In June 2023, van der Sloot was temporarily transferred from Peru to the United States to face federal extortion and wire fraud charges stemming from his 2010 scheme targeting Beth. On Oct. 18, 2023, he pleaded guilty to both charges in federal court in Alabama and was sentenced to 20 years in prison, to be served concurrently with his Peruvian prison sentence.

Natalee Holloway poses with her mother at home before her graduation ceremony at Mountain Brook High School in Mountain Brook, Alabama, on May 24, 2005. (Alamy)

If van der Sloot is released from prison in Peru before completing his U.S. sentence, he would serve the remaining time in the United States.

"Beth says closure isn't not missing somebody that you love," Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. "Closure is learning to live with it and learning to find peace and learning to open up to a next chapter." (Netflix)

As part of his plea agreement, van der Sloot also confessed to killing Holloway in 2005. The convicted killer said he struck her in the head with a cinder block after she rejected his sexual advances, then disposed of her body in the ocean. This time, Beth said she believed he was telling the truth.

"This case was difficult to solve," Sloane said. "There were no forensics to speak of. Natalee’s remains were never found and have never been found to this day. All of this hinged on dealing with Joran. It was incredibly difficult for anyone that was interrogating him to pin him down. He was good at spinning a story. This was someone who told years of stories, one more outlandish than the next about what happened to Natalee."

Natalee Holloway shared a close bond with her mother, Beth, who kissed her goodbye before the teenager departed for a high school graduation trip to Aruba in May 2005. It would be the last time Beth saw her daughter. In the years that followed, the grieving mother refused to give up her search for answers. (Netflix)

Beth spent nearly two decades seeking answers about her daughter's disappearance and now advocates for other families of missing people. Sloane said that while Beth finally has answers about Holloway's death, she continues to live with the loss of her daughter every day.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Beth Holloway has become an advocate for other families dealing with missing loved ones and high-profile criminal cases. (Netflix)

"I think Natalee would be proud of all of us," Beth says in the film. "I think Joran tangled with the wrong girl."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

"He is so masterful at evading law enforcement and evading consequences by just outright lying," Sloane added.

According to former Aruban police official Gerold Dompig, Joran van der Sloot changed his story an estimated 40 times during the initial investigation into Natalee Holloway's disappearance. (Netflix)

According to the film, Beth agreed to give van der Sloot $25,000 because she believed it was her chance to finally learn what happened to her daughter from the man she had long suspected of killing her. She was on standby at an Alabama bank, ready to wire the remaining $15,000 as soon as van der Sloot signed their agreement.

Beth subsequently wired the remaining $15,000 to van der Sloot's bank account, bringing the initial payment to $25,000.

Beth Holloway appears in Netflix's "Taken: Natalee Holloway," which is now available for streaming. (Netflix)

Before the meeting, Kelly had contacted the FBI, which worked with police in Aruba to secretly record the exchange in hopes of building a criminal case against van der Sloot.

The previously unreleased video of the exchange shows Kelly handing over $10,000.

Joran van der Sloot has a daughter with his Peruvian wife, Leidy Figueroa. The couple married in 2014 while he was serving a prison sentence in Peru for the murder of Stephany Flores Ramírez. (Netflix)

"To be completely honest, for me, the biggest deal is the 225 afterwards," van der Sloot tells Kelly in the recording. "Did you put in the contract that that would be paid within a month?"

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"The piece that's worth highlighting is this extortion tape that we got access to that has never been seen before," director Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. (Reuters)

Kelly said yes and van der Sloot signed the agreement.

In the docuseries, Kelly explained that van der Sloot was never going to receive the remaining $225,000.

Natalee Holloway is seen here with her mother Beth Holloway. (Netflix)

"If he disclosed Natalee's whereabouts then he was going to be arrested for it," Kelly explained. "And if he didn't disclose what happened to Natalee, he was going to get arrested anyway for extortion or fraud."

Dutch national Joran Van der Sloot is seen in Lima in this June 11, 2010 handout taken by Peruvian police. (Reuters)

Van der Sloot then took Kelly to a nearby house, claiming Holloway's body had been buried in the foundation while the home was under construction.

Beth Holloway participates in the launch of the Natalee Holloway Resource Center on June 8, 2010, in Washington, D.C. The nonprofit resource center was founded by Holloway and the National Museum of Crime & Punishment to assist families of missing persons. (Getty Images)

"It's honestly a horrific thing to watch," Sloane said. "Just to see how that conversation played out is really stunning."

"Beth Holloway was the one who was on this the longest," director Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. "She was the one who rallied the investigators in the end, the FBI, to become involved again. And it was her dogged pursuit that really made the confession happen in the end." (Netflix)

Investigators determined the information was false. But before U.S. authorities could file charges against van der Sloot, he left Aruba for Peru.

A man holds posters of Dutch citizen Joran Van der Sloot and Peruvian girl Stephany Flores Ramirez outside Lurigancho prison in Lima on Jan. 13, 2012. (Reuters)

Van der Sloot's trail of lies was about to take an even deadlier turn. On May 30, 2010, exactly five years after Holloway's disappearance, van der Sloot murdered 21-year-old Stephany Flores Ramírez in his hotel room in Lima, Peru.

Joran Andreas Petrus van der Sloot is escorted by Peruvian police as he arrives at the DIRINCRI (Criminal Investigation Direction) offices in Lima on June 5, 2010. Van der Sloot was the main suspect in the killing of Stephany Flores Ramirez, 21, daughter of Peruvian businessman and race car driver Ricardo Flores Chipoco. (AFP via Getty Images)

According to the film, van der Sloot told investigators he attacked Flores Ramírez after she discovered information about Holloway's disappearance on his laptop. He beat and strangled her.

In July 2014, van der Sloot married Leidy Figueroa, a Peruvian woman. They later had a daughter.

Ricardo Flores, whose daughter Stephany Flores was murdered by Dutch citizen Joran Van der Sloot, listens to the reading of the sentence in Van der Sloot's murder trial in Lurigancho prison in Lima, Peru, on Jan. 13, 2012. (Reuters)

In the film, retired FBI special agent Alexandra Montilla recalled an encounter in which the "charismatic" van der Sloot told her about a pet rabbit he shared with his daughter. According to Montilla's account, the rabbit scratched his daughter while she was petting it. Montilla said van der Sloot told her that he grabbed the animal and "ripped his head off."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Alexandra Montilla is a retired FBI agent who was involved in bringing Joran van der Sloot from Peru to the United States in 2023 to face federal extortion and wire fraud charges involving Natalee Holloway's family. (Netflix)

"I've dealt with a lot of criminals and, as a female, I thought this is probably one of the most dangerous ones," Montilla said.

Sloane said Montilla still vividly remembers the encounter.

Joran van der Sloot was convicted of murdering 21-year-old Stephany Flores Ramírez in Peru in 2010. He claimed he killed her after she discovered information about his connection to Natalee Holloway's disappearance, but investigators disputed his account. (AFP via Getty Images)

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

"He was good at spinning a story," Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital about Joran van der Sloot. (Netflix)

"It really lives in her memory," Sloane said. "It's something that stands out to her out of all the offenders and perpetrators she has spent time with. It counts a lot when a seasoned member of the FBI is horrified by something."

In June 2023, van der Sloot was temporarily transferred from Peru to the United States to face federal extortion and wire fraud charges stemming from his 2010 scheme targeting Beth. On Oct. 18, 2023, he pleaded guilty to both charges in federal court in Alabama and was sentenced to 20 years in prison, to be served concurrently with his Peruvian prison sentence.

Natalee Holloway poses with her mother at home before her graduation ceremony at Mountain Brook High School in Mountain Brook, Alabama, on May 24, 2005. (Alamy)

If van der Sloot is released from prison in Peru before completing his U.S. sentence, he would serve the remaining time in the United States.

"Beth says closure isn't not missing somebody that you love," Dani Sloane told Fox News Digital. "Closure is learning to live with it and learning to find peace and learning to open up to a next chapter." (Netflix)

As part of his plea agreement, van der Sloot also confessed to killing Holloway in 2005. The convicted killer said he struck her in the head with a cinder block after she rejected his sexual advances, then disposed of her body in the ocean. This time, Beth said she believed he was telling the truth.

"This case was difficult to solve," Sloane said. "There were no forensics to speak of. Natalee’s remains were never found and have never been found to this day. All of this hinged on dealing with Joran. It was incredibly difficult for anyone that was interrogating him to pin him down. He was good at spinning a story. This was someone who told years of stories, one more outlandish than the next about what happened to Natalee."

Natalee Holloway shared a close bond with her mother, Beth, who kissed her goodbye before the teenager departed for a high school graduation trip to Aruba in May 2005. It would be the last time Beth saw her daughter. In the years that followed, the grieving mother refused to give up her search for answers. (Netflix)

Beth spent nearly two decades seeking answers about her daughter's disappearance and now advocates for other families of missing people. Sloane said that while Beth finally has answers about Holloway's death, she continues to live with the loss of her daughter every day.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Beth Holloway has become an advocate for other families dealing with missing loved ones and high-profile criminal cases. (Netflix)

"I think Natalee would be proud of all of us," Beth says in the film. "I think Joran tangled with the wrong girl."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.
