Green turtles move from ‘endangered’ to ‘least concern’ status

Green turtles have been reclassified from endangered to ‘least concern’ in global conservation rankings after decades of protection efforts. In Malaysia’s Turtle Islands, nesting has tripled since the 1970s, but threats from hunting, fishing nets and pollution remain.

articles.title: Southeast Asian leaders to meet as Trump visit highlights trade disruption
articles.excerpt: Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Southeast Asian leaders are preparing to hold their flagship annual summit as US President Donald Trump embarks on an Asia Pacific trip that will focus attention on his upendi...
articles.body_text:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Southeast Asian leaders are preparing to hold their flagship annual summit as US President Donald Trump embarks on an Asia Pacific trip that will focus attention on his upending of trade and traditional alliances.

Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are gathering in Manila, the Philippines, for a series of multilateral and bilateral meetings running from Sunday until Tuesday.

Trump is scheduled to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr during a brief stop in Manila on Tuesday, before heading to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, where he will have his fourth face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in just over a year.

It will also be the first time that Trump, Xi and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will meet for trilateral talks, the White House has confirmed.

Trump’s visit to Southeast Asia – his second since his return to the White House after his attendance at the 2025 ASEAN summit in Malaysia – comes after his administration announced new tariffs on dozens of trade partners, including most of the region’s economies, in July.

Trump’s administration announced the duties of between 10 and 12.5 percent after the US Supreme Court struck down his steeper “reciprocal” tariffs in February.

The Office of the US Trade Representative said it was imposing the tariffs on 60 trade partners over their alleged failure to clamp down on forced labour.

The Trump administration is also conducting trade probes over alleged national security and “excess” manufacturing concerns that could result in yet more tariffs for Southeast Asian trade partners.

Southeast Asia has weathered Trump’s trade salvoes relatively unscathed until now, in part as a result of the diversion of billions of dollars of Chinese trade through the region.

US imports from ASEAN rose more than 29 percent to $453.6bn in 2025, expanding the trade deficit between the sides to $327.4bn, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, said, however, that Southeast Asian countries cannot guarantee that their luck will continue.

“ASEAN has had mixed success in navigating US tariffs. Overall exports are up. But this is primarily driven by shipments of electronics which are largely exempt from tariffs,” Elms told Al Jazeera.

“These shipments are also strongly tied to the AI buildout. If that falters, ASEAN will feel it,” she said.

While ASEAN leaders have provided few details about the summit agenda, trade is likely to be among the main topics of discussion.

For a bloc that often faces accusations of being a talking shop, one of the most anticipated tangible outcomes is the signing of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, a pact aimed at easing cross-border data transfers and electronic payments.

Initiated in 2023, the framework has been billed as a step towards building an ASEAN digital economy worth $2 trillion by 2030.

Jayant Menon, a senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, said Southeast Asian leaders will be concerned about “what comes next” from Trump on trade.

“So far, the recent tariffs appear to have had a limited impact on competitiveness of ASEAN exports. But this may change in the future, with more sectoral tariffs, in particular, or other measures such as export controls,” Menon told Al Jazeera.

“Trump still retains significant autonomous authority over trade policy despite losing control of both houses, and could double down rather than back off,” Menon said, referring to the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3.

Phar Kim Beng, a professor of ASEAN studies at the International Islamic University of Malaysia, said Southeast Asian leaders are likely to reiterate calls for increased trade within the region, a goal that has lagged aspirations despite decades of trade liberalisation in the bloc.

“Whether measured from 1970 or 2025, intraregional trade remains paltry at 23 percent. In contrast, the European Union can cross intraregional trade of 67 percent easily,” Phar told Al Jazeera.

Phar said he does not expect ASEAN to announce any significant measures to spur trade within the bloc, but its leaders will continue to “mouth the mantra of better and bigger” trade volumes.

“Regardless of the tariffs intended by President Donald Trump, ASEAN will continue to muddle through by speaking of the importance of trade and more trade,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine is running out of options, and Russia knows it
articles.excerpt:
Leonid Ragozin is a freelance journalist based in Riga.

The trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that took place in Abu Dhabi this week may not lead to a rapid breakthrough,...
articles.body_text:
Leonid Ragozin is a freelance journalist based in Riga.

The trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that took place in Abu Dhabi this week may not lead to a rapid breakthrough, but they clearly outline the trajectory of a conflict that might, after all, be nearing its end.

If anything illustrates the political and emotional rift the two sides are yet to bridge, it is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s remarks in Copenhagen this week, in which he lamented that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was still alive. Ukraine’s harsh reality, however, is pushing him towards an unsavoury compromise with his arch-enemy.

Kyiv was compelled to enter the talks at the most disadvantageous moment, when it has few means to counter devastating Russian air strikes that damage its key industries and cripple essential infrastructure in major cities. One of Ukraine’s top negotiators, David Arakhamia, who leads Zelenskyy’s parliamentary faction, described the negotiations as among the most difficult he had participated in since 2022. He said the Russians had arrived with very strict instructions and that it had been difficult to soften the tone of the discussions. His assessment confirms that Russia sees itself as well equipped to negotiate from a position of force.

Moscow, meanwhile, expressed optimism about the outcome. Putin’s aide, Vladimir Medinsky, said the talks had brought the two countries closer to peace. Even Arakhamia said there was momentum towards reaching a solution before the end of the year. That optimism, it needs to be noted, comes without any signs of Russia changing its position on the contours of the agreement. Just as it has for years, the Kremlin insists on a genuinely neutral, demilitarised Ukraine which honours the rights of its Russian-speaking population.

If all this comes as a nasty surprise to many in the West, that’s because for most of this year, Western politicians and the mainstream media kept insisting that the tide of war was turning and that Ukraine was getting the upper hand. Their optimism was fuelled by Ukrainian long-range strikes targeting Russian oil refineries as well as by the snail’s pace of Russian advances on the battlefield.

As late as September, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that “in all but name, Russia has already lost the war”. Around the same time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia was not doing well in Ukraine.

When NATO leaders convened for the Ankara summit in July, it seemed that even US President Donald Trump had bought into the idea that Ukraine had the battlefield advantage.

But Russia responded to Ukraine’s surge, backed up by European funds and US intelligence-sharing, with round-the-clock air strikes that are bringing Ukraine close to its pain barrier. Moscow’s message was cruel: any damage Ukraine and the West might inflict on Russia would be met with epic devastation in Ukraine, from which it would take decades to recover.

The coming winter spells nationwide humanitarian disaster. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure have disrupted electricity and central heating supplies. Millions of Ukrainians, particularly in major cities, live in apartment blocks dependent on central heating, without which their homes can become virtually unliveable. Generators can provide temporary power, but their use is making the cost of war enormous for Ukraine and Western taxpayers who fund its war effort.

It is these dire circumstances, rather than pressure from Trump’s administration, that have forced Ukraine to enter the talks. Zelenskyy would have waited at least until the spring had he not felt so pressed.

Ukraine’s surge has failed to shift Moscow’s peace conditions one inch. Meanwhile, the Western perception of this war’s realities has undergone a considerable transformation. There are two major signs of the shifting landscape which directly affect the agenda of the Abu Dhabi negotiations.

For the first time since the start of the war, a larger part of the Western establishment appears to be ready to discuss Europe’s post-war security architecture. The subject was first broached by US negotiator Jared Kushner, causing outrage in the warmongering camp. But Medinsky said after the Abu Dhabi talks that it was the central issue on the agenda.

This topic harks back to the agenda which Moscow brought to the table in December 2021, a few months before the all-out invasion. It did so after the US and Ukraine signed a charter on strategic partnership which may have served as the decisive trigger for Putin’s decision to invade. The very idea of discussing Europe’s security architecture with Moscow became a strict taboo in the West for over four years, but clearly it is not any more.

Curiously, this broad and vital topic was not the main sticking point at the talks, according to Kushner, who said the territorial issue was the hardest. Moscow has long insisted that Ukrainian forces should withdraw from the remaining part of the Donetsk region for talks to succeed.

But Moscow’s opposition to territorial compromise might be an act of deception aimed at achieving maximum gain on overarching geopolitical issues it considers really vital. At the end of the day, it is only propagandist symbolism that prompts the Kremlin to claim Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

The other sign of change is European governments trying to jump on the bandwagon of peace talks even as this exposes a rift between hardliners, like the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, and pragmatists who believe compromise is unavoidable. The latter most prominently include Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who held a lengthy telephone call with Putin on October 27, ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks, with discreet consent from parts of the EU leadership.

Both the US and Ukraine suggested in recent days that Europeans should nominate a single envoy to be at the table during the next round. US envoy Steve Witkoff said on November 12 that Putin had agreed to let European representatives join the next round of talks. Russia didn’t confirm it, while Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov linked the possibility of EU’s inclusion to the personality of its chosen envoy.

Perhaps the most remarkable shift on display in Abu Dhabi was the appearance of NATO’s supreme commander in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, especially as it was hailed by the Kremlin which tends to see the war as a proxy conflict with NATO.

But even the staunchest of hardliners, like the German and British governments, are visibly changing tack. Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested he could talk to Putin during the next G20 summit. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting unexpectedly called for opening communication channels with Russia.

Others, like Kallas or Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, are finding themselves increasingly isolated and unable to influence rapid developments. So is Zelenskyy, who has sounded extremely bitter about the perceived lack of Western support in his latest appearances. But he is going ahead with the US-brokered peace process because there isn’t much of a choice.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier
articles.excerpt:
Mohamed Salah scored twice in Egypt’s 5-0 thrashing of Malawi in the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers on Friday, becoming the country’s leading all-time scorer with 70 goals.

The 34-year-old former L...
articles.body_text:
Mohamed Salah scored twice in Egypt’s 5-0 thrashing of Malawi in the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers on Friday, becoming the country’s leading all-time scorer with 70 goals.

The 34-year-old former Liverpool star left it late in Cairo to overtake Hossam Hassan, scoring with a far-post header in the 84th minute and from a penalty five minutes into added time.

Hassan was fired as Egypt coach last week, and replacement Ali Maher made a perfect start with goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany building a 3-0 lead by half-time.

Egypt have seven points in Group B after three matches, three more than Angola, who host South Sudan on Saturday.

Achraf Hakimi, favourite to win a second successive African Footballer of the Year award next month, also bagged a brace as Group A pacesetters Morocco crushed Niger 5-1 in Casablanca.

Substitute Tolu Arokodaro scored twice within eight minutes as Nigeria beat Tanzania 3-1 in Uyo to get their campaign back on track.

Tunisia suffered a shock home 2-0 loss to Libya, and Kenya scored in the final minute to snatch a surprise 2-2 draw away to South Africa.

Alhassan Yusuf put Nigeria ahead after just 103 seconds and Alphonce Msanga equalised on 32 minutes following a rare Tanzanian attack.

Arokodaro, scorer of six goals in his last five matches for Ajax Amsterdam, came off the bench for the second half and quickly made an impact.

His near-post back heel off a low cross put Nigeria ahead for the second time after 52 minutes, and as the match reached the hour mark, he struck again from close range.

An ultimately comfortable victory lifted the Super Eagles to six points after three rounds in Group L, one point behind Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Although bottom of the table with just one point, Tanzania are guaranteed a place at the 2027 AFCON as cohosts with Kenya and Uganda.

That means Guinea-Bissau, Nigeria and Madagascar must fight for one place at the 24-nation tournament, the first to be staged in East Africa since Ethiopia were the 1976 hosts.

Nigeria were in trouble after a 3-0 hammering in Guinea-Bissau two months ago, but now have a clear path to a tournament they have won three times.

Away wins over Tanzania on Tuesday and Madagascar in March, and a home win over Guinea-Bissau, also in March, will assure qualification.

Tunisia are in Group H, which includes cohosts and automatic qualifiers Uganda, and their record of reaching every AFCON tournament since 1994 is in peril.

A 2-0 defeat at home to neighbours Libya leaves them bottom of the table with just two points, and a venue switch two months ago means their remaining three fixtures are all away.

Ali Youssef converted a 44th-minute penalty for Libya, and Hamdou Elhouni, who once played for leading Tunisian club Esperance, doubled the lead in the 62nd minute.

Victory lifted Libya from last place to a share of the lead on four points with Uganda. Botswana and Tunisia have two each. Uganda host Botswana in Kampala on Saturday.

The Group D clash between South Africa and Kenya pitted two South African coaches against each other. Pitso Mosimane handles Bafana Bafana and Benni McCarthy guides the Harambee Stars.

Former Manchester United coaching staffer McCarthy was the happier at full-time after Ryan Ogam equalised in the final minute of regular time.

From a South African perspective, this was two points lost, although they remain on top with seven. Guinea have six, automatic qualifiers; Kenya, two; and Eritrea, one.

articles.title: Philippine court orders arrest of jailed, US-wanted celebrity preacher
articles.excerpt: A Philippine court has ordered the arrest of jailed celebrity preacher Apollo Quiboloy, who is wanted in the US on child sex trafficking charges, in a step towards his possible extradition, according ...
articles.body_text:
A Philippine court has ordered the arrest of jailed celebrity preacher Apollo Quiboloy, who is wanted in the US on child sex trafficking charges, in a step towards his possible extradition, according to the country’s Justice Department.

The department’s spokesman Polo Martinez told the AFP news agency on Saturday that the Makati Regional Trial Court issued the warrant of arrest and a hold-departure on Thursday after finding probable cause that he committed the offences charged.

The Philippine government filed its petition with a lower court on Monday, three months after Washington formally requested his extradition in August. Under Philippine law, the court must now hold hearings before deciding whether or not to hand him over.

The court issued the same orders against two co-accused, Teresita Dandan and Helen Panilag, both officers of Quiboloy’s Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) sect. The two women are still at large, according to local media reports.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, speaking on behalf of the Office of the President, denied that the warrant was timed to coincide with US President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila on November 17 for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

“No, it was probably just a coincidence,” she said, according to the Philippines News Agency.

Quiboloy, who calls himself the “appointed son of God”, is being held without bail while on trial for human trafficking in Pasig, which carries life in prison if convicted, AFP reported.

He also faces a child abuse trial in Quezon City, according to local media. He has denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to the Philippine charges.

A US grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for conspiracy to engage in sex trafficking by force, fraud and coercion, sex trafficking of children and bulk cash smuggling, AFP reported.

The FBI identified Dandan as the “international administrator” of a fake charity operation, and Panilag as a former top church administrator in the US, according to local media reports.

Police said after his 2024 arrest that alleged victims were told they were having sex with the “spirit of God” and were threatened that “angels of death” would hunt them down if they told anyone, AFP reported.

The church said at the time that members had “freedom of choice”.

Quiboloy’s sect claims to have millions of followers and owns a television network.

He is a close ally of former President Rodrigo Duterte. He ran for Senate last year from prison and received 5.6 million votes, but lost, AFP reported.

articles.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global outage that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
articles.excerpt:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Microsoft outag...
articles.body_text:
Experts say outage exposes ‘Australia’s reliance on foreign technology’ as software giant says services being restored

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.

The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.

Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.

Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.

“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.

Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.

“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.

The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.

“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.

Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.

Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.

Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.

Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

articles.title: Siege fuels disease fears in Yemen’s Taiz
articles.excerpt:
Taiz, Yemen – The woman held the body of a young baby girl wrapped in a white shroud.

“Our children are dying because of the siege. We have no open road, no medics and no medicines,” the woman said.
...
articles.body_text:
Taiz, Yemen – The woman held the body of a young baby girl wrapped in a white shroud.

“Our children are dying because of the siege. We have no open road, no medics and no medicines,” the woman said.

Wearing the traditional clothing of women from Jabal Sabir, the mountain that overlooks the city of Taiz and is one of its most famous symbols, she appeared in a short video widely circulated on social media on November 10.

In her arms was the body of an infant from her family, identified as Gaza Ali Abdulmughni al-Shaqab, who had fallen ill and died after her family was unable to get her emergency medical care. The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms said the vehicle carrying the baby to the hospital was attacked by Houthi forces as it travelled through mountain roads.

“She died, and we couldn’t get her emergency treatment because of the siege,” the woman said, referring to the ongoing Houthi siege of al-Shaqab, which lies on a front line between the rebel group and Yemeni government forces.

The siege of Taiz and the surrounding areas such as al-Shaqab intensified in early October, when the Houthis advanced around the city and cut off the last major supply route into government-held areas.

Fighting between the Iran-backed group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government intensified over the summer, before the Houthis captured substantial territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September and then made further advances in Taiz governorate.

Government counteroffensives have only had limited success so far, and the siege of the city of Taiz continues.

The Yemeni government has accused the Houthis of tightening their siege on nearly two million people living in Taiz for more than a month, preventing the entry of food, safe drinking water, medicines and fuel.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) said in a statement on October 29 that the siege imposed by the Houthis on civilians in Taiz “may amount to the war crime of using starvation as a method of warfare”.

The Houthis have denied responsibility for the road closures, instead blaming Yemeni government forces.

But HRW said that residents, aid workers and United Nations officials had all reported that the Houthis were to blame.

International bodies have repeatedly warned of the crisis now facing Taiz.

On October 14, the World Food Programme (WFP) said that it had been unable to reach more than 600,000 people in Taiz dependent on humanitarian assistance.

The WFP described the situation as “especially alarming”, noting that most districts in Taiz were classified as facing emergency levels of hunger.

For its part, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that health services in Taiz were failing because of a shortage of supplies.

Nearly 250,000 people had lost access to essential healthcare, including more than 186,000 children younger than five years old, the agency said.

It added that more than 1,400 cases of acute diarrhoea and suspected cholera were reported in just one week.

“Twelve hospitals are at risk of closing or have had to reduce services due to a lack of fuel and critical supplies,” OCHA added.

According to figures obtained by Al Jazeera from the Epidemiological Surveillance Department at Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office, 5,642 cases across three disease categories were recorded during the latest four-week reporting period.

The vast majority – 5,228 cases – were of acute watery diarrhoea. There were also 232 suspected dengue fever cases and 182 suspected cholera cases.

The number of watery diarrhoea cases decreased compared with the previous reporting period, but Dr Yasin Abdulmalik, the director of the department, said that was likely the result of residents finding it increasingly difficult to reach health facilities because of road closures between the city and surrounding rural areas.

“The siege has led to a shortage of petroleum products, including fuel, whose prices have risen on the black market,” Abdulmalik said. “This has created an additional difficulty in travelling to hospitals and health centres for treatment because of higher transport fares.”

“In reality, more than twice this number of cases were unable to reach [health facilities] because of the siege and its various consequences,” he said.

Taysir al-Samiei, a health communications official at Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office, told Al Jazeera that patients’ ability to reach hospitals had fallen by between 60 and 70 percent by the end of the second week of the siege.

Dr Fares al-Absi, a consultant in diabetes, endocrinology and obesity, said the reported high number of acute watery diarrhoea and cholera cases was down to the use of unsafe water sources.

Al-Absi said the situation had worsened “after the Houthis prevented safe drinking water from entering the city, except for limited quantities sold at high prices, which have risen dramatically because of the shortage of diesel”.

“Recently, access to the al-Dhabab water basin, a major source of water transported by trucks, has been restricted,” al-Absi added. “Only about 8 percent of Taiz’s water needs are currently being met, while most local wells are unfit for consumption.”

Al-Absi also explained that dengue fever was spreading because of the conditions in the city.

The disease is transmitted by mosquitoes that breed in stagnant water, while accumulated rubbish can also create conditions that favour mosquito breeding.

Al-Absi said that tonnes of waste had accumulated in Taiz’s streets because of insufficient diesel to transport the rubbish. He also accused the Houthis of preventing sanitation trucks from reaching the landfill in the west of the city.

“Both stagnant water and rubbish have increased significantly as a result of the siege, as streets and residential neighbourhoods have turned into open rubbish dumps,” he said.

articles.title: Could one daily pill narrow the diabetes treatment gap in the Global South?
articles.excerpt: Medication that has been a lifeline for patients with uncontrollable diabetes is now slowly shifting from injections to pills, a move that could fundamentally alter treatment for the disease – and who...
articles.body_text:
Medication that has been a lifeline for patients with uncontrollable diabetes is now slowly shifting from injections to pills, a move that could fundamentally alter treatment for the disease – and who can access it.

This shift could also affect the treatment of obesity, a long misunderstood condition once associated with overeating and laziness, rather than the metabolic disorder it is now recognised as.

GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists therapy isn’t new. The first FDA-approved drug, Exenatide, hit the market in 2005 and was followed by Liraglutide in 2009, which was seen as a revolutionary alternative to insulin.

But the market has until recently been dominated by weekly injections like Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide), and Mounjaro (tirzepatide). These drugs have also proved successful for weight loss.

Now, once-daily oral GLP pills are emerging as an alternative, especially for the diabetes-stricken Global South.

Oral once-daily pills of the same wonder drug could make access more affordable, and less reliant on the cold chain that GLP-1 injections and insulin depend on – and that are harder to secure in emerging economies.

One in nine people in the world between the ages of 20-79 lives with diabetes, and one in eight people globally is obese.

The GLP injections come with a high price tag and are often not covered by insurance companies, which treat them as an elective drug.

In the United States, Eli Lily’s Mounjaro costs about $500 for a month’s worth of doses; in the UK, about 199 pounds ($264); and in Saudi Arabia, 1,261 riyals ($336). In India, the brand is locally manufactured and available at 14,766 rupees ($157). In Pakistan, the imported Mounjaro is a whopping 220,000 rupees ($723), while the locally manufactured Tirzepatide from Getz Pharma costs 17,000 rupees ($61).

While pills are usually taken once a day, injections are once per week.

Pakistan has the highest diabetes prevalence in the world – 31.4 percent of its population suffer from the disease – followed by the Marshall Islands (25.7 percent) and Kuwait (25.6 percent).

Many other Middle Eastern countries rank among nations with the highest diabetes prevalence.

For many countries in the Global South, the relative affordability of oral GLP drugs, where the locally manufactured oral semaglutide is about $18 for a 30-day supply, could make them more accessible for diabetes and obesity patients, remove the need for refrigeration and make rural distribution easier.

Dr Zakir Alavi is an endocrinologist in Karachi, Pakistan and has been treating patients with diabetes and obesity for nearly 30 years.

“Pakistan is a country of contrast. We have, on one hand, childhood malnutrition, underweight, and stunted growth. On the other hand, we have childhood and adult obesity,” said Alavi. “And surprisingly, there is at least some element in the adult and childhood obesity which can be linked to a malnourished mother, and an underweight, premature baby.”

Malnutrition during pregnancy can lead to low birth weight, and babies born small who gain weight rapidly in infancy face a higher risk of childhood obesity, according to doctors.

Alavi said GLP drugs – whether the injectables or pills – have revolutionised the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. They not only help type 2 diabetes patients manage their weight, but can also help non-diabetics tackle obesity, improving cardiac and renal outcomes, liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea and osteoarthritis.

“They can be used for management of all these things when weight reduction is important, or sugar control is important, or both,” he said.

Rayaz Malik is a professor of medicine at Weill Cornell Medica College Qatar, and a senior consultant at Hamad Medical Corporation in Doha. Malik has been at the front line of helping patients with diabetes and obesity, and he echoed Alavi’s views.

“We looked at how much weight you need to lose to cure diabetes, the magic number seemed to come in at around 15kg, at least,” he said, speaking of research on the subject.

With the wider availability of GLP medication in oral pill form, a cure for diabetes is closer than ever for many more people.

Jens Juul Holst is one of the central scientists behind the GLP revolution that has given millions around the world a way to live with diabetes and, for those struggling with obesity, a chance to reclaim their bodies.

A professor, physician and physiologist, Holst lives in Copenhagen and began his journey with gut hormones in the 1970s.

“When we discovered this, what we found was an insulin-releasing peptide from the gut,” Holst told Al Jazeera. “We were interested in what regulates insulin secretion, and that was as a physiological mechanism because we had some people who were developing too low blood glucose levels, [which is called] hypoglycemia, and we were looking for a peptide that could create insulin release stimulation and then be responsible for the low glucose levels.”

He says reactive hypoglycemia, which patients experience after certain operations like bariatric surgery, explains how the GLP molecule works.

Eventually, his team discovered that the molecule plays a role not only in insulin release and secretion, but also helps regulate appetite and food intake.

“The discovery of that was actually perhaps even more exciting than the discovery of its insulin-releasing activities,” Holst said, the excitement in his voice rising. “And then, the big day really was when we were able to infuse people with diabetes with this new peptide and see what happened.”

They found that an intravenous infusion of GLP-1 “would normalise blood glucose levels completely in people with long-standing, problematic type 2 diabetes and this happened in the course of four hours,” he said. “From then on, we knew that we were really onto something big.”

Holst and his team’s discovery led to what is now known as semaglutide, which paved the way for another drug, tirzepatide, and a third drug called retatrutide that is currently undergoing trials with a potential release in 2027.

Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two of the primary manufacturers, expect the GLP market to jump from $80bn per year to $135bn by 2030.

Obesity alone was responsible for 3.7 million deaths worldwide in 2024.

In December 2025, the World Health Organization issued guidelines recommending GLP-1 medicines as a long-term treatment for obesity, which affects more than 1 billion people globally.

“As we realised that it was a very good anti-diabetic therapy, it was obvious that millions could benefit from this,” Holst said.

“Because now you have a population which is 40 percent of the globe who would be interested in regulating body weight and the amount of interest would be huge,” he said, referring to the WHO’s 2016 estimate that 39 percent of adults worldwide are overweight. In 2024, WHO revised this estimate to 45 percent.

Injectable GLP medicines, particularly tirzepatide and semaglutide, remain the most effective treatments because they provide the strongest evidence for long-term weight loss and cardiovascular benefits.

The human gut releases a hormone called GLP-1 when we eat. As blood sugar rises, GLP-1 instructs your pancreas to release insulin. GIP is a gut hormone also released when we eat. Like GLP-1, it tells the pancreas to release insulin as blood sugar rises.

GLP-1 also slows how quickly food leaves your stomach, helping you feel full. GLP-1 medicines, therefore, mimic the hormone’s effects to lower blood sugar and reduce appetite.

Imagine a six-way traffic light when the lights aren’t working, leading to chaos over who can pass the intersection and who can’t.

Semaglutide, a GLP-1 drug, works on one receptor. This is like having a single-lane underpass at this intersection, meaning there is a guaranteed flow of traffic, albeit limited.

Tirzepatide is a GLP and a GIP, meaning it works on two receptors. That’s like having a signal-free overhead bridge, traffic lights at the intersection and an underpass making traffic much smoother. In effect, the organs and cells are rerouted to work the way they are supposed to.

Oral GLP-1 medicines promise the convenience of a pill without sacrificing much of the weight-loss effect, but they still face one major hurdle: the stomach.

Unlike injections, which deliver the drug directly into the body, oral semaglutide must survive digestion before a small fraction is absorbed.

That is why it must be taken on an empty stomach and at a higher dose.

Newer oral GLP-1 drugs such as orforglipron, however, are designed to overcome those limits and can be taken without fasting.

While oral drugs appear capable of delivering similar results for many patients, there are still few head-to-head trials comparing pills directly with injections, experts say.

The biggest winners may be people in countries already carrying the world’s heaviest diabetes burden.

If future versions become available as tablets and prices fall after patent expiry, the impact in South Asia and the Middle East could be enormous.

Malik said once-a-week GLP oral medication isn’t that far from being a reality.

Meanwhile, he added, efforts are also under way to develop formulations of the current drugs that are much longer-acting – once-a-month doses might work.

What makes the GLP-1 drugs work is their ability to mimic what the body naturally does, Malik said.

“The clever way for treatment is to do what your human body is doing,” he said. “And it’s transforming people’s lives.”

articles.title: Democrat flips Alaska governor's mansion after Trump-backed GOP infighting
articles.excerpt: After a midterm rally in Alaska, President Donald Trump told Fox News' Matt Finn "we are looking into" Dan Sullivan, an independent challenger who goes by the same name as the Republican incumbent, Se...
articles.body_text:
After a midterm rally in Alaska, President Donald Trump told Fox News' Matt Finn "we are looking into" Dan Sullivan, an independent challenger who goes by the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won Alaska's gubernatorial election, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson and flipping the governor's mansion.

The Associated Press called the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, Friday evening local time. He is the first Democratic governor in Alaska since 1998.

Alaska's gubernatorial election became an unusual contest as Republicans battled among themselves over who should succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred from seeking a third consecutive term.

A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS

Former State Representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat from Alaska, during the What's Next conference in Denver, Colorado, on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Wilson, a conservative activist and former political operative, received President Donald Trump's endorsement during a campaign in which multiple Republicans competed for the governor's office.

Trump publicly criticized fellow Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, accusing them of dividing conservative voters and potentially jeopardizing the party's hold on the governorship.

Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor, and Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, remained part of the Republican field, creating a complicated general-election contest.

ALASKAN POLITICAL SCION HOPES TO HOLD ONTO STATE'S SINGLE HOUSE SEAT

Alaska gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson was the only Trump-endorsed candidate in the race, despite being one of three Republican options. (Courtesy: Bernadette Wilson for Governor)

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, emerged as the Democratic contender, seeking to return his party to the governor's mansion after Dunleavy's two terms.

The election unfolded under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.

If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and those ballots are redistributed according to voters' next preferences. The process continues until a candidate secures a majority among continuing ballots.

The system has added an unusual dynamic to Alaska politics, allowing multiple candidates from the same party to compete in the general election without a traditional partisan runoff.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy speaks at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, in October 2026. President Trump endorsed GOP gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson at this rally, but Dunleavy did not offer an endorsement for any candidate. (Nathaniel Wilder/Getty Images)

The contest also came as Alaska remained a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, despite occasionally electing Democrats and independents to statewide office.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.
