“Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine. We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side.”

Meanwhile, the EU is planning to approve new sanctions on Russia on Monday, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said.

“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against Russia, on 150 additional entities, 50 ⁠banks and it’s France which proposed the bulk of the entities to add,” Haddad told LCI ⁠television, as reported by Reuters.

“We will continue to put economic pressure on Russia ​and of course support Ukraine,” ‌he added.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Moscow this morning, where they are expected to meet Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to advance some of the issues discussed at trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi over the last two days.

The meeting is expected to get under way around 9am GMT, with Russia’s deputy foreign minister Sergei Rybakov trying to manage everyone’s expectations by saying it was too early to say that necessary trust had been restored between Russia and Ukraine.

The US envoys are then expected to fly to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the margins of the European Political Community summit, which is being attended by more than 40 leaders from Ukraine’s allied countries.

The EPC – set up on the initiative of France’s Emmanuel Macron – offers a rare chance to discuss key European issues with non-EU allies, including Britain’s Andy Burnham and Canada’s Mark Carney.

For Burnham, it’s also an opportunity to dot the i’s and cross the t’s ahead of next week’s EU-UK summit, which is a key part of his proposed reset in relationship with the bloc. Let’s see what we are going to hear on this today.

For Dublin, the meeting comes with a massive security operation, particularly after some past concerns about drones, particularly around Zelenskyy’s visit to Ireland last December.

I will keep an eye on both of these events and bring you all the latest here.

It’s Thursday, 12 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years
articles.excerpt:
GDP ‘grew robustly’ by 0.7% in third quarter and by 0.2% month on month in September despite high oil prices

The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half ...
articles.body_text:
GDP ‘grew robustly’ by 0.7% in third quarter and by 0.2% month on month in September despite high oil prices

The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, as the rollout of AI services increased activity.

The Office for National Statistics reported that the economy “grew robustly” in the July to September quarter, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in the services sector, led by the IT sector.

The quarterly growth rate matched economists’ expectations, and was the fastest recorded since the first three months of 2024, when GDP also rose by 0.7%.

In a boost to the chancellor, John Healey, the ONS also said the economy grew by 0.2% in September, though the ONS revised down the growth rate in August from 0.1% to zero. September’s data beat forecasts of zero growth in the month.

The UK’s information and communication sector grew by 2.1% in the quarter, mainly driven by increases in computer programming, consultancy and related activities. This industry has been the largest driver of GDP growth across 2026, the ONS reported, adding that the businesses related to AI and cloud computing have been reporting the largest increases in turnover.

Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the investment platform AJ Bell, said AI continued to do “a significant portion of the heavy lifting” in the last quarter.

“Since the start of the year, it’s the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth. These areas are benefiting from the increasing adoption of AI,” Coles said.

Healey said the UK was showing “standout resilience”.

The chancellor added that the economy was growing at the fastest rate in almost 10 years, excluding the time of the Covid-19 pandemic – when lockdown restrictions distorted economic growth.

“GDP is up 1.8% so far this year, and pushing at an annualised pace of just above 2.5% – marking the best first three quarters since the pandemic rebound. Strip out the pandemic years and you have to go back to 2017 to find the economy running this hot,” Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said.

“Compared to its G7 peers, the UK has relinquished its title as the fastest-growing economy this year to the US, but only just,” Raja added.

The services sector proved to be the most important engine of growth over the third quarter of 2026, rising by 0.9%. There was also a positive contribution from the production sector, which grew by 0.1%. It was a sharp drop in construction that dragged down economic growth, even though it only accounts for about 6% of economic activity.

Construction work on new projects has fallen more than 7% from mid-2025 while private housebuilding has fallen 30% from its 2022 high.

Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the accountancy body ICAEW, said the figures confirmed a “strikingly strong” third quarter as the UK remained resilient to the economic fallout from US-Iran hostilities”.

He said it was becoming clear that investments in artificial intelligence were driving the expansion of services sector activity.

“The third quarter showcased the continued resilience of households and firms. Businesses ramped up investment amid an AI boom, while stronger consumer spending suggests households continued to draw on savings to support consumption despite rising inflation,” he added.

James Smith, an economist at ING, said much of the rise in investment and growth can be traced back to IT and professional services – sectors that have grown rapidly this year despite shedding staff.

“IT is very clearly a datacentre story,” he said. “The UK is one of the leading destinations for investment in Europe. And while output here actually fell through August and September, we expect this to remain an area of outperformance in 2027.”

The Office for Budget Responsibility said at the time of the budget at the end of October that it expected the economy to expand by 1.2% this year, which already looks out of date as growth continues to exceed expectations.

Policymakers at the Bank of England voted last week to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% to cool inflationary pressures in the economy.

Inflation has risen this year mostly in response to higher motor fuel prices, which in the UK have pushed the cost of petrol above £1.70 a litre and diesel towards an average of £2 a litre.

The ONS said wholesale electricity prices were about double the level of a year ago.

“Automotive fuel prices also remained elevated following increases in recent months, reflecting continued pressures in global energy markets,” it added.

Analysts said the strength of the economy could persuade the Bank of England to raise rates when policymakers meet again in December.

“These robust figures help keep a December interest rate rise firmly on the table by reinforcing policymakers’ view that the economy remains resilient enough to cope with another rise in borrowing costs,” Thiru said.

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research went further and urged the central bank to raise rates.

Further rate rises are needed to keep inflation contained and protect the economy from a costlier correction later,” said Fergus Jimenez-England, an economist at the institute.

Other analysts were more sceptical that the momentum could be sustained into the new year.

Simon Pittaway, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said the UK’s resilience “will be severely tested” over the coming months by rising inflation and interest rates.

Unions said a rise in energy bills in the new year could put a break on household spending, which had played a significant part in boosting growth this year.

TUC general secretary Paul Nowak said: “Despite the good news, working people across the country are still up against it today as they face spiralling energy bills as a result of Trump’s illegal war in Iran.”

articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly meets to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s future as chip giant’s share price plunges – follow live
articles.excerpt:
Nvidia shares plunge in extended trading, sending Asian markets lower

Nvidia board reportedly deciding whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang

Nvidia’s board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen...
articles.body_text:
Nvidia shares plunge in extended trading, sending Asian markets lower

Nvidia board reportedly deciding whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang

Nvidia’s board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told the Reuters news agency, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with reports of two extramarital affairs involving its longtime ⁠leader.

The reports mark a sharp escalation in a controversy that began with revelations about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence has said was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

In a memo to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took “full responsibility,” but gave no details about the relationship.

Huang, 63, has ⁠no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.

The company’s shares slid about 8% in ​after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal first reported that Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang. ‌Including Wednesday’s after-hours selloff, Nvidia has lost about $600bn ‌in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman.

Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had ‌an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

US stock futures are down, pointing to a lower open on Wall Street later.

The S&P 500 is seen opening 0.4% lower while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is set to fell 0.85%, and Dow futures are flat.

Nvidia shares are now down about 7% in Frankfurt. About $600bn have been wiped off the US chipmaker’s market value since the board announced an investigation into longtime boss Jensen Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. On Sunday, he admitted to cheating on his wife with the mysterious Shanghai executive.

Under the company’s bylaws, Jensen Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

Meanwhile, the US news website Axios is reporting that Donald Trump on Thursday authorised a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — and he even consulted Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.

But one administration official repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, Axios reported.

The Nvidia board met last night after the second revelation about Jensen Huang.

In a sharp shift from Sunday when it expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, the board met to discuss his future after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee called Kimberly Powell.

She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

Farewell Jensen, said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.

double quotation markOne of the most impressive careers is set to end. Huang might have been able somehow to cling on at Nvidia after one revelation (though news about chip shipments made that doubtful), but after two, one of which involving a direct report, his fate is sealed.

Nvidia’s shares are moving rapidly to price in a post-Jensen world, and this is weighing on tech stocks globally. Nvidia is much bigger than one man now, but this isn’t the way anyone thought it would happen, and denies the company the chance to set up an orderly transition. The question is now whether this news torpedoes the renewed tech rally.

Germany’s Dax also reached a new all-time high, climbing more than 1% in early trading.

The Frankfurt exchange surged 283 points to 26,944, up 1.06%.

Nvidia shares have fallen nearly 6% in Frankfurt, after reports that its board has met to decide whether to oust its longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

However, European shares hit a record high, lifted by strong financial results from companies for the third quarter, and the recent sharp drop in energy prices.

While Brent crude is up slightly today at $93.27 a barrel, 0.55% higher on the day, it’s well off the highs seen in recent weeks above $100 a barrel.

The Stoxx 600 index rose 0.3% to hit a fresh all-time high, beating its previous record set in August.

In London, the FTSE 100 index is 28 points ahead at 10,863, up 0.26%.

Jensen Huang has led Nvidia since it was founded in 1993, but with the CEO now unexpectedly on the backfoot, and with no known successor in the wings, the field is wide open should the board decide to oust Huang.

Agence France-Presse has looked at some of the names being suggested most frequently as Huang’s potential successor.

With more than 40,000 employees, Nvidia could opt to go with an in-house pick to take the helm, including one of Huang’s dozens of direct reports.

Tech publications frequently cited Nvidia’s chief financial officer Colette Kress as an easy choice. Another longtime Nvidia executive is Ian Buck, who oversees the company’s datacentre clients.

Business magazine Inc. also lists Nvidia’s vice-president of applied deep learning research, Bryan Catanzano, as a possible pick.

Huang could also try to position a member of his own family as his replacement. His daughter Madison Huang is currently the senior director of product marketing at Nvidia and is among the names most suggested by analysts.

His son Spencer Huang could also be a potential successor. He currently works at Nvidia as the director of product management in the company’s robotics division.

Huang’s cousin, Lisa Su, could also be a viable candidate for selection; she is the longtime CEO of semiconductor giant AMD.

Su is not the only tech chief being bandied around as a possible replacement for Huang.

Rene Haas, CEO of UK chip design firm Arm, is another candidate being suggested by the tech press.

Speculation runs wide in Silicon Valley: former Apple CEO Tim Cook – who stepped down from leading the tech company in August after 15 years at the helm – is another person insiders say could be tapped.

Global stocks are in decline, as a near-9% plunge in Nvidia shares in extended trading sent waves across Asian markets, on news that its board may oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia shares fell as much as 8.8% in pre-market trading in New York, wiping another $360bn off the company’s value. That takes losses this week to $640bn, a 14% decline.

Asian stock markets are a sea of red. Japan’s Nikkei is down 0.7%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 1.3% and South Korea’s Kospi fell nearly 0.6%, while Taiwan’s benchmark index tumbled 2.6%.

In China, the Shenzhen Composite slid 1.6% and the CSI 300 dropped 0.87%.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore, said:

double quotation markNvidia sits at the centre of an increasingly interconnected AI ecosystem. Its turmoil comes when financing, hyperscaler capex, valuations and ⁠returns on AI investment were already under scrutiny.

Nvidia’s board reportedly met late Wednesday to decide whether to oust Huang, after he admitted to an affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Beijing has rejected the spying allegations.

The New York Times has reported that Huang also had an affair with a company executive who reported to ‌him.

Jake Dollarhide, chief executive at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma, told Reuters:

double quotation markIt looks bad from every single angle. I believe the board won’t oust him until they have an all-star, a known entity in the tech sector, to replace him.

At the end of the day, let’s not forget that the Nvidia chip is the centrepiece of the AI story.

It’s not yet clear who might replace Huang as CEO. In the meantime, Chinese domestic GPU makers surged on Thursday amid expectations that Nvidia’s troubles could help local chip suppliers win greater market share.

Chinese AI firms ‌are reportedly rushing to secure Nvidia chip capacity, fearing that the US could cut them off in the wake of the scandal.

Good morning, readers. Julia Kollewe in London is now taking over from Jonathan Yerushalmy in Sydney.

A Chinese university with close ties to the country’s defence bodies recently bought advanced AI chips made by Nvidia, procurement notices show, despite stringent US controls.

Agence France-Presse reported that Northwestern Polytechnical University in the city of Xi’an purchased two Nvidia H200 chips from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology – not Nvidia directly – for $131,200), according to a procurement notice dated 21 October.

H200 chips are subject to US export controls that limit direct shipments to China and apply certain restrictions on their resale globally.

The spotlight is already on Nvidia’s relationship with China this week after the news of Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for Beijing.

China and the United States are locked in a fierce competition for supremacy in the AI field, and Nvidia’s market-leading products have become a major point of contention.

We’re pausing our live coverage now – but you can read the latest report on Nvidia and Jensen Huang’s future as CEO here.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said that it would “be an honour” to hire Jensen Huang, in a response to a poster making the suggestion on X.

Musk has been among the more prominent supporters of the embattled Nvidia CEO, after it was revealed he was facing an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

On Wednesday he indicated that he agreed with a suggestion from AI investor Gavin Baker that Nvidia’s board should “wait for the results of the investigation before ousting Jensen.”

More now on the call from two Democratic Senators for the Trump administration to preserve all documents tied to Nvidia’s chip ⁠exports to China.

As first reported by the Wall Street Journal, Elizabeth Warren ⁠and Chris Coons wrote in a letter to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, secretary of state Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller:

double quotation markThis ‌incident raises significant ‌concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export ‌controls and protect our national security.”

double quotation markQuestions also remain ⁠regarding whether or not prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken ​or national security ​recommendations were overruled.”

Warren and Coons also requested a congressional ​briefing on the national ‌security risks ​posed by ​the suspected intelligence operation.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been one of the poster boys for the AI revolution, because his company’s chips are essential for the technology. But the $4tn company had more humble beginnings.

Huang was born in Taiwan and then spent some time in Thailand because his father moved the family there for work. His parents then sent him to live with an uncle in the US when he was 9, along with his older brother. Huang’s parents later came to the US and the family reunited in Oregon, where he attended high school, graduating early after skipping two grades.

At Oregon State University, Huang studied electrical engineering in a class that had about 250 students, only three of whom were women, including his future wife, Lori, who was on his lab team.

The couple went on to work as chip designers in Silicon Valley, with Huang earning his graduate degree from Stanford University in 1992.

Nvidia got its start when three engineers – Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem – gathered in 1993 at a Denny’s diner in San Jose, California, in what is now the heart of Silicon Valley.

Huang worked at a Denny’s restaurant when he was young and has spoken about how working there helped him overcome his shyness and to learn the value of hard work. On his LinkedIn profile he lists only two work experiences – as Nvidia’s founder and CEO, and as a dishwasher, busboy and waiter at Denny’s.

At that first meeting, the three men discussed building a computer chip that would make graphics for video games faster and more realistic. That conversation, and ones that followed, led to the founding of Nvidia.

Nvidia’s specialised graphics processing units (GPUs) were designed to rapidly process computer graphics for video games, but are now also widely used to power the booming spread of artificial intelligence systems.

Huang is now one of the world’s wealthiest people, with a personal fortune that Forbes estimates at more than $150bn.

Alice Huang – the woman accused of spying for Beijing during an affair with Jensen Huang – visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, a Taiwanese government minister said Thursday.

Chiu Chui-cheng, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) minister, made the remarks in parliament in response to lawmakers’ questions about a New York Times report that the US had advised Taiwan as early as 2024 to monitor her movements.

Taiwan, a dominant player in the global semiconductor industry, sits at the centre of strategic competition between the US and China, which claims the self-ruled island as part of its territory.

Huang has admitted to having an extramarital affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the spying allegations.

Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, used a Hong Kong passport to enter Taiwan “under a standard business visitor status” and there were “no special flags” about her at the time, Chiu said.

“At least we at the Mainland Affairs Council did not receive any relevant information,” Chiu said.

double quotation markIf we had, we definitely would have stepped up our entry screening and border flow management. If we had any of the kind of critical intelligence … we would have definitely flagged her for heightened review,” Chiu said.

The government has said Taiwan’s security agencies are investigating the incident.

articles.title: Argentina threatens UK oil firm CEO with jail over Falklands drilling
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Legal notice comes as Buenos Aires ramps up rhetoric over UK territory and seeks to halt Sea Lion project

The Argentinian government threatened a British businessman involved in an offshor...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Legal notice comes as Buenos Aires ramps up rhetoric over UK territory and seeks to halt Sea Lion project

The Argentinian government threatened a British businessman involved in an offshore Falkland Islands oil project with jail, the Guardian can reveal.

Sam Moody, the chief executive of Rockhopper Exploration, and his company’s chief financial officer received the correspondence this autumn as Buenos Aires began ramping up its rhetoric over the British overseas territory.

“As recently as 1 September 2026, Argentina wrote to me and Rockhopper’s chief financial officer personally threatening us with criminal prosecution, imprisonment and fines under its domestic legislation,” Moody said.

The disclosure was made in a witness statement submitted by the UK to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) before two days of hearings that were held this week. The sealed document was made available for viewing after an application by the Guardian.

Argentina is seeking an order from Itlos for the urgent suspension of drilling at the Sea Lion off-shore oil project north of the Falklands, which is being led by Rockhopper, a British firm, and Navitas, an Israeli company.

Buenos Aires has passed domestic legislation criminalising the project and in Moody’s statement to the tribunal, the oil executive also said he believed there was a risk in him engaging with the hearing in Hamburg.

“I also want the tribunal to be aware that I, in common with others, [am] taking some personal risk by preparing the statement as I have repeatedly been under threat of criminal prosecution and a custodial sentence in Argentina,” he wrote.

Moody’s submission listed a series of other actions taken by Buenos Aires that he said had made it increasingly difficult to finance Sea Lion. They included Argentina banning Navitas from operating in the country for 20 years.

It is also claimed that Argentinian officials wrote to Standard Chartered bank, which has a branch in Port Stanley, the capital on the Falklands, urging it to “refrain from participating in oil and gas development in the Falkland Islands to avoid falling within the terms of certain Argentine domestic legislation”.

In a further submission to the tribunal, it emerged that Navitas and Rockhopper had not named their partners in court documents for fear that they would be subject to Argentinian retribution.

“The names of the contractors engaged by Navitas UK have been witheld to preserve their confidentiality in light of the ongoing scrutiny by Argentine authorities and their ongoing efforts to frustrate the project, including through purported actions directed at contractors and partners involved in the project,” according to a submission made by Ian Ramsay, chief executive of Navitas Petroleum Development and Production.

The US firm Halliburton recently issued a statement in which it said it would not conduct any work on the Sea Lion project after discussions with Argentina.

Last month, the Guardian revealed that the UK government had written to Interpol seeking reassurance that the international law enforcement agency would not act on any Argentinian “red notices” requesting the arrest of those deemed criminal by Buenos Aires for their involvement in the Falklands economy.

Argentina’s application for suspension of the Sea Lion project is based on the claim that Britain’s agreement to drilling is illegal as the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands is a matter of dispute between the UK and Argentina.

In 1976, a UN resolution called for the two countries to settle their rival sovereignty claims and to refrain from acting unilaterally to modify the situation in the Falklands. Argentina seeks a temporary suspension of the project before further arbitration, claiming that the oil drilling is “aggravating” the sovereignty dispute.

In response, the UK claimed this week that the tribunal did not have jurisdiction in the dispute and that the UN resolution cited was not legally binding. Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, further told the tribunal that the oil project’s suspension would be terminal to its hopes of success with “devastating consequences” for the people on the islands.

The Sea Lion project is expected to double the island’s GDP, providing an £8bn uplift in revenues of the Falkland government over the oilfield’s active lifetime.

In a further submission to Itlos, Jack Ford, a member and the current chair of the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly, told the tribunal that the impact of the collapse of the Sea Lion project would “not just be economic but also social, and felt across the whole of the Falkland Islands”.

In September, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, told the UN’s general assembly that reclaiming the sovereignty of the Falklands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, was a national cause and that Buenos Aires was taking “matters into our own hands” through peaceful means.

Argentina invaded the Falklands in 1982. The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentinian military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.

A ruling by Itlos on Argentina’s application is expected on 28 November.

articles.title: Florida city says new GOP-backed DEI law blocks St. Patrick’s parade, Pride event
articles.excerpt:
Delray Beach officials said a new Florida anti-DEI law prevents the city from organizing or promoting its annual St. Patrick’s Day parade and Pride event in 2027.

A Florida city says it cannot host i...
articles.body_text:
Delray Beach officials said a new Florida anti-DEI law prevents the city from organizing or promoting its annual St. Patrick’s Day parade and Pride event in 2027.

A Florida city says it cannot host its annual St. Patrick's Day Parade or Pride event in 2027 because of a new Republican-backed state law restricting local governments from funding, promoting or taking official action related to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.

Officials in Delray Beach announced the decision Tuesday, citing restrictions on "certain programming and activities designed or implemented with reference to ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity."

"Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, or promoting these events in 2027," the city said in a statement.

"The City recognizes that these annual events have provided opportunities for members of the community to gather, celebrate, and connect. We appreciate the residents, participants, volunteers, and community partners who have contributed to these events over the years," the statement added.

RED-STATE SENATOR DROPS HAMMER ON DEM MAYOR OVER NEW 'WOKE' DEI ORDINANCE WHILE VIOLENT CRIME SURGES

A Florida city canceled its annual St. Patrick’s Day Parade for 2027 over a new state law banning government-funded DEI initiatives. (City of Delray Beach)

Florida Senate Bill 1134, which passed both chambers of the Republican-controlled state Legislature largely along party lines before being signed by GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis in April, is scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

The law prohibits counties and municipalities from funding or promoting DEI initiatives, directly or indirectly, or taking certain official actions related to them, including adopting ordinances, resolutions, rules, regulations, programs or policies.

It also establishes potential consequences for local officials who violate the restrictions, classifying violations as misfeasance or malfeasance in office. The measure further restricts the use of local government funds by employees, contractors and others to promote DEI initiatives.

GAVIN NEWSOM SIGNS EID AL-FITR AND EID AL-ADHA INTO LAW AS NEW CALIFORNIA STATE HOLIDAYS

Delray Beach officials said the law's restrictions include "certain programming and activities designed or implemented with reference to ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity." (City of Delray Beach)

The measure also restricts cities from funding, hosting or officially promoting heritage events that celebrate heritage, culture and ethnicity.

But the legislation carves out exceptions for holidays designated by federal law, including New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday, Presidents’ Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas Day.

Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney said he has received numerous messages and seen social media posts criticizing the decision to cancel the St. Patrick’s Day Parade, adding that "it is clear that the parade means as much to you in the community as it does to me."

"This bill puts severe restrictions on how cities can pay for community events such as the St. Patrick’s Day Parade along with potentially other city-sponsored events," he explained in a Facebook post.

The legislation carves out exceptions for holidays designated by federal law. (City of Delray Beach)

"The St. Patrick’s Day Parade isn’t just another parade. It’s engrained in the DNA of the Delray Beach community," the mayor continued, noting that the city is "working feverishly with multiple entities to ensure the 2027 St. Patrick’s Day parade goes on as scheduled!"

"For those who live, work & play in Delray, we want the Delray Beach St. Patrick’s Day parade to stay!" Carney added.

Fox News Digital has reached out to DeSantis' office for comment.

"For those who live, work & play in Delray, we want the Delray Beach St. Patrick’s Day parade to stay!" Carney added.

Fox News Digital has reached out to DeSantis' office for comment.

articles.title: US envoys arrive in Moscow for Russia-Ukraine talks with Putin
articles.excerpt:
United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have ⁠arrived in ⁠Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in their latest push for a peace deal ⁠in Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin...
articles.body_text:
United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have ⁠arrived in ⁠Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in their latest push for a peace deal ⁠in Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, met Kushner and Witkoff at their plane on Thursday morning and accompanied them to central Moscow.

The meeting comes on the heels of two days of trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates that concluded in the capital, Abu Dhabi, on Wednesday with news of another planned major prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year war.

The US said differences remained on major issues, including territory, but some progress had been made on post-war security guarantees.

Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin’s demands to surrender all of its eastern region of Donbas in ⁠return for peace.

The Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in nine months.

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said one of the goals of Thursday’s visit would be for the US team to persuade Putin to invite Europeans to the negotiation process.

“Ukraine and the US want the European partners to be involved while Moscow is adamant about talks without the Europeans, and that’s why they’ve been largely excluded from the process,” she said.

Shapovalova added that the US delegation would bring Putin an updated proposal for a peace plan and the presence of Dmitriev in the talks was an indication that they would address some of the more complex issues.

During the US-backed effort to revive talks, leaders from more than 40 European countries gathered in Dublin on Thursday for a summit focused on the continent’s security.

The meeting of the European Political Community (EPC) brought together heads of state and government from the European Union and other European countries, including the United Kingdom. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also attended.

The EPC was established in 2022 as a forum for countries both inside and outside the 27-nation EU.

Zelenskyy and his European allies are expected to discuss this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, and Witkoff are scheduled to meet Zelenskyy in Dublin on Friday after talking to Putin.

Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Ukrainians do not believe the talks in Moscow will yield results. “Over the past two days, we saw just another prisoner exchange, which has been the case in previous talks,” the correspondent said.

“When it comes to the negotiations, not much has changed in terms of where these two sides stand,” Macalpine added. “Perhaps the biggest thing of note [in the talks] was that they took place at all.”

Meanwhile, French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad on Thursday ‌said the ⁠EU will approve more sanctions ⁠against Russia.

“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against ⁠Russia on 150 additional ⁠entities, 50 banks, and it’s ⁠France which proposed the ⁠bulk ⁠of the entities to add,” Haddad ‌told LCI television.

articles.title: India bypasses own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking tech
articles.excerpt: New Delhi, India – India has exempted an Israeli phone-hacking company from New Delhi’s own rules, allowing it to sell phone-extraction products and surveillance technology to government agencies and ...
articles.body_text:
New Delhi, India – India has exempted an Israeli phone-hacking company from New Delhi’s own rules, allowing it to sell phone-extraction products and surveillance technology to government agencies and sparking concerns and criticism from rights groups and activists.

An investigation by the digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, a close confidante of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, signed off on exemptions from “make in India” procurement rules, clearing the way for government forensic institutions to buy at least 422 items of foreign technology, including products made by the Israeli firm Cellebrite.

Modi’s federal government and state governments ruled by his Bharatiya Janata Party are not the only ones who bought this Israeli technology. States governed by the opposition Indian National Congress party, including Himachal Pradesh, Keralam and Karnataka, also purchased similar phone-extraction and cloning tools.

A review of documents revealed that India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend far beyond just cloning phones and extracting data without passwords to accessing cloud-based data from social media platforms – such as Instagram, X and Tinder – as well as data from connected devices such as Amazon’s Alexa and Google Home.

Experts argued that India’s current laws offer no guardrails against overreaching surveillance and the data extractions happen in a legal grey zone.

“It is clear that there is an expansion of India’s surveillance capabilities and it is becoming both wider and deeper,” said Vrinda Bhandari, a lawyer in the Supreme Court who works on digital rights and privacy issues.

“It’s now easier to conduct mass surveillance rather than targeted, specific surveillance and also possible to do more intrusive surveillance,” she told Al Jazeera. “[Today,] surveillance gives you a richer picture of an individual’s life.”

The IFF reviewed a letter also seen by Al Jazeera from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs dated January 7 in which Shah signed off on a wide-ranging, one-year waiver of “make in India” rules to clear a path for buying at least 422 forensic items.

Under “make in India” procurement rules, preference must be given to eligible Indian manufacturers over foreign suppliers in awarding government contracts. However, the rules allow exemptions with the approval of the minister in charge of the procuring department.

Another letter by the ministry dated January 20 showed Shah permitted the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to buy Israeli company Cellebrite’s Premium Tool on a three-year licence for about 50 million rupees ($529,947).

In specifications demanded by the government that were revealed in a review of tender bids, “solution” software must be capable of using login tokens recovered from seized phones or computers to access more than 100 cloud services. Login tokens are in effect digital keys that keep users signed in to online accounts.

Although an exemption for a company does not confirm whether a certain product was purchased by any government agency, it points to the range of forensic capabilities that opened up for procurement by Indian agencies.

From the 422-item exemption list, the IFF identified 118 items under digital and multimedia forensics, including Israeli company Cellebrite’s Pathfinder, Inseyets On-Prem Pro and Inseyets Offline.

Cellebrite’s tools have been used against journalists and activists in countries like Serbia, Jordan, Kenya and Russia.

Other products included tools from foreign digital-forensics companies like Magnet, MSAB, Oxygen Forensics and Belkasoft as well as software for open-source intelligence, dark-web monitoring and cryptocurrency investigations.

Al Jazeera reviewed a request for a bid proposal by the Delhi Police for software for its National Cyber Forensic Laboratory, which comes under the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre, an initiative of the Home Ministry.

Consider the capabilities the police department was seeking in its request: software that bypasses passwords on Apple’s macOS, Microsoft Windows and Linux operating systems; recovers internet activity, browser histories, deleted files and identifies traces of VPNs; bypasses screen locks; performs full file system extractions; decrypts backups; and extracts information from messaging applications.

The Delhi Police demanded another “all-in-one” system to access more than 100 cloud services, including Google, Apple, WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram, Discord and dating platforms such as Tinder, Grindr and OkCupid or platforms like Slack and OnlyFans using account credentials or login tokens recovered from devices. Its specifications also sought the extraction of data from drones, wearable devices and devices like Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Al Jazeera reached out to officials at the NIA, the Home Ministry and home departments of opposition-ruled states of Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka and Keralam for comments. The Delhi Police reports to Shah’s mInistry.

None of them had responded to Al Jazeera by the time of publication.

For some, the lack of transparency in the surveillance capabilities of India’s security agencies is not just a theoretical concern.

Last month, when Modi’s government faced street protests demanding the election chief resign, popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, a Modi critic, landed in New Delhi to participate in the demonstrations.

On the morning of the protest, he was detained by Delhi Police while still at home. His phone was taken from him. Speaking on a podcast later, Rathee said he believed police had tried to clone his iPhone using Israeli company Cellebrite’s tools but the attempt may have failed because his device was running a newer version of the iOS operating system than what the tool was capable of tricking.

Al Jazeera could not verify Rathee’s account, but Rathee is not alone in this suspicion.

Mohammad Aslam Hussain, a reporter with the newspaper Siasat Daily, told Al Jazeera that he was detained with a cameraperson on October 10 in New Delhi and his phone was confiscated at the scene.

“When I got my device later in the evening, all recorded footage of our reporting had been selectively deleted from the device,” Hussain said. The reporter uses Samsung’s Android-operated Galaxy S24 secured with a pattern lock and fingerprint authentication.

Hussain added that he cannot say conclusively what tools the police used to bypass his phone’s authentication requirement. “But it raises several questions with no one willing to respond to them,” he added. “How did they get inside my phone?”

The Indian government has faced accusations that it has used sophisticated spyware against journalists, activists, lawyers and political opponents during Modi’s years in power.

In 2019, WhatsApp disclosed that the Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group, had been used to target Indian journalists and human rights defenders. Forensic examinations by Amnesty International later confirmed Pegasus infections on the phones of journalists Siddharth Varadarajan and Anand Mangnale. The government has denied allegations of unauthorised surveillance.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that another problem in holding overarching surveillance to account is identifying the affected party. Often, she pointed out, the person placed under surveillance “does not know about it, so what does one do?”

The central legal gap identified by digital rights group IFF is that India has no statute or protocol that specifically authorises or regulates the forced unlocking and full extraction of data from a mobile phone seized by law enforcement agencies.

Existing seizure powers under criminal law do not explicitly address bypassing passcodes, copying an entire file system, harvesting login tokens to access cloud accounts or establishing rules for the retention and deletion of extracted data.

The Supreme Court in a 2017 judgement recognised privacy as a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. The judgement established that any state intrusion into privacy must have a legal basis, pursue a legitimate state aim and be proportionate to that aim.

Bhandari told Al Jazeera that when the government agencies “deploy these capabilities without any proper meaningful oversight, the net of surveillance is cast wider and deeper and a lot more people are affected without either legislative, parliamentary or judicial oversight”.

Bhandari noted that while some countries like the United Kingdom or Germany “have some element of either parliamentary oversight or judicial oversight, India only has an internal review mechanism in executive oversight”.

“The whole point of having any oversight is to create a friction for surveillance,” she said, “so that it’s not easy for the government to just target everybody.”

“The current legal framework fails in this safeguard,” Bhandari said.

articles.title: Ten police officers, 18 fighters killed in northwest Pakistan attack
articles.excerpt:
Gunmen have attacked police officers conducting an operation against illegal gold mining in northwestern Pakistan, with 10 officers and 18 fighters killed in the ensuing violence.

A statement by prov...
articles.body_text:
Gunmen have attacked police officers conducting an operation against illegal gold mining in northwestern Pakistan, with 10 officers and 18 fighters killed in the ensuing violence.

A statement by provincial police in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa said officers were returning from a mine in the Gumbat area of Kohat district on Wednesday when armed men opened fire on them.

In addition to the dozens killed, 12 police personnel were wounded, the statement said.

Hours later, the Pakistani Taliban issued a statement claiming the attack.

Earlier, a senior administrative official in Kohat told the AFP news agency that fighters had set two police vehicles on fire during the assault, while two other police vehicles and one private vehicle were missing.

Another senior administrative official in the Orakzai area of Kohat said that 10 fighters belonging to the Pakistan Taliban were killed during a separate operation in the district.

A large quantity of weapons was also recovered from the fighters, the official said.

A spokesman for a local emergency service said earlier on Wednesday that there had been a “firing incident involving police personnel” in Kohat district, adding that rescue workers were treating a dozen wounded officers.

Security forces are battling intensifying violence in the border province that they say emanates from Afghanistan, an accusation the Taliban government in Kabul rejects.

The Pakistan Taliban, formerly known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, have stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.

Pakistan has seen a surge in violence in recent years, much of it blamed on the TTP.

The group is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in neighbouring Afghanistan in 2021.

Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Afghan Taliban retook power, and worsened after deadly border clashes in October last year that led to near-total closure of the border.

Pakistan frequently accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of sheltering TTP fighters, an allegation Kabul denies.

Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries in the last year, according to figures from the United Nations mission in Afghanistan.

articles.title: ‘Tourists hate themselves’ – which is why Tasmania is telling them to stay away
articles.excerpt:
Island state declares it ‘is not really for tourists’ – but is the marketing strategy just a cheeky piece of reverse psychology?

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Research ...
articles.body_text:
Island state declares it ‘is not really for tourists’ – but is the marketing strategy just a cheeky piece of reverse psychology?

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Research shows “tourists hate themselves” – which is exactly why the marketing flacks at Tourism Tasmania are telling them to stay away from the island state.

Its new campaign declares Tasmania is “not really for tourists”, enlisting former SBS newsreader Lee Lin Chin to help sell the tongue-in-cheek campaign, based on the idea that Australians prefer identifying as a “traveller” rather than a “tourist”.

Its centrepiece is a short video of a man being pointed to the back of an endless queue for a “world famous” pastry. He eventually abandons the line to find solitude in the Tasmanian outdoors.

Chin, who lives mostly offline without a mobile phone, also fronts videos exploring the state’s walking trails on her visit.

Tourism Tasmania’s CEO, Sarah Kingston Clark, said the campaign was deliberately wry rather than anti-visitor, to reflect the “tensions” of modern travel.

Those tensions play out in the research, Prof Can-Seng Ooi, the professor of cultural and heritage tourism at the University of Tasmania, suggested.

“Studies have shown that tourists hate themselves,” he said. “They want to avoid each other.”

Ooi identified stressed people yearning for “quietness” as the campaign’s target audience, especially those living in urban cities on the mainland.

“It taps into the type of tourist people want to be,” Ooi said. He added that people prefer to view themselves as “travellers” because of the negative connotation of “tourist”.

Ooi spent 20 years living in Scandinavia, researching how tourism, culture and heritage contributes to the development of regional destinations.

“The message is very Scandinavian, even the imagery: the sauna, the vinyl records, the books and so on,” Ooi said. “Instead of the cold north, we are talking about the cold south … it’s a quiet place, time slows down.”

Char-lee McLennan, an associate professor from QUT’s school of management, said the campaign used “an element of reverse psychology” that could benefit regional economies by steering visitors beyond established hotspots.

Prof David Waller, a marketing expert with UTS, said Tasmania’s “Come down for air” theme was less “anti-tourist” and “more anti-overcrowded, line-joining, tourist destinations”.

“Lee Lin Chin is adding humour to the message,” he said. “Lee Lin Chin is an icon – intelligent, avant garde and [she has a] dry sense of humour.”

But, McLennan said, the campaign’s success depends on whether the real experience of visiting Tasmania lives up to its promise as well as delivering meaningful economic benefits to regional communities.

Hundreds of thou...
articles.body_text:
Sporadic clashes broke out in Madrid and Barcelona after protests were held across Spain over housing affordability and purchasing power, just weeks before an early general election.

Hundreds of thousands of protesters turned out on Wednesday during Spain’s first nationwide 24-hour strike since 2012.

Authorities estimate about 120,000 demonstrators marched through the capital and more than 50,000 rallied in Barcelona.

In Madrid and Barcelona, groups of hooded and masked demonstrators hurled projectiles at police and sparked fires. Police, meanwhile, used rubber bullets and tear gas to disperse protesters.

Police forces reported at least 73 arrests nationwide by 21:00 GMT on Wednesday from at least 1,044 incidents linked to the general strike, including blockades of offices and industrial estates, and the burning of rubbish containers.

articles.title: Water industry bonus ban to be tightened as Ofwat warns of ‘damage to public trust’
articles.excerpt:
Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses

The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industr...
articles.body_text:
Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses

The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules.

Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for chief executive Mark Thurston despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said she wanted to “close loopholes” so that “failure doesn’t pay”.

Nine water companies in England and Wales – including Thames Water and Yorkshire Water – were banned from paying bonuses for the 2025-26 financial year, the regulator Ofwat said on Thursday. Seven of the bans related to environmental pollution.

The Labour government introduced the bonus ban last year amid public outrage over sewage leaking into Britain’s rivers and seas. Yet water company bosses’ pay has risen in the past two years despite the ban, according to Guardian analysis.

Campaigners and opposition politicians have argued that companies are circumventing the ban through a variety of payments which are not “performance-related” – but which effectively replace the banned bonuses.

Ofwat on Thursday said it would accelerate a review into the rules, over concerns that companies were deliberately “undermining” the ban. It is understood that ministers will also consider whether payments from water companies’ parent companies could be included in the ban.

The regulator said: “The growing use of fixed so-called ‘retention payments’ and substantial increases in base pay without sufficient explanation or supporting evidence risks damaging public trust and creating a perception that companies are circumventing the rule.”

Anglian’s payments to Thurston “could give the impression the company had prioritised offering executive directors a cash award in a way that would not technically breach the rule and would in practice replace the loss of PRP [performance-related pay] prohibited by it,” Ofwat said.

As well as Anglian, Ofwat highlighted potential retention payments of £1m for Thames Water’s chief financial officer, £1.5m for Northumbrian Water chief executive Heidi Mottram, and £1.7m for Louise Beardmore, the chief executive of United Utilities.

Andy Burnham is under pressure to clamp down on the water industry. He has said he wants to exert “more public control” over the water industry, although he is yet to give details. He is yet to make a decision on whether to move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement, months after suggesting he might do so.

Thames Water paid its chief executive, Chris Weston, a previously deferred bonus of £99,000 during the year, despite the ban. Ofwat said that Thames Water’s future owners would have to pay for the bonus, rather than the money coming from customer bills. Thames was also criticised for raising executives’ base pay.

The other companies banned from paying bonuses were Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, South West Water, Wessex Water and Dŵr Cymru (Welsh Water). Ofwat said they would have paid out another £6.5m to executives during the year had the ban not been in place.

Eagle said: “People are sick of seeing water bosses profit while rivers are polluted and customers are repeatedly let down. A wide-ranging review launching today will ensure that failure doesn’t pay, whatever name the payment goes by.

“The bonus ban was the first step. Where there are loopholes, I want them closed.”

South East Water was not subject to the ban, but Ofwat said the company’s shareholders will have to pay for future bonuses after huge supply failures left tens of thousands of households without water during the financial year.

Helen Campbell, the interim executive director for delivery at Ofwat, said: “It is disappointing that so many companies continue to trigger the rule through serious performance failures which has seen £10m in payments blocked in the past two years.

“Public trust in the water sector remains low, and executive bonuses which do not reflect performance, use of retention payments and poorly explained increases in base pay contribute to that low trust. That is why we are accelerating our review to ensure the rule better delivers the outcomes customers rightly expect.”

Ofwat also criticised the paucity of information on pay reported by South Staffs Water.

articles.title: GOP senator says Republicans can 'forget 2028' as party looks to reclaim Upper Chamber
articles.excerpt: Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume discusses the results of the 2026 midterm elections as Mississippi turns blue, examining the political implications of the Democratic gains, shifting voter s...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume discusses the results of the 2026 midterm elections as Mississippi turns blue, examining the political implications of the Democratic gains, shifting voter sentiment and what the election results could mean for the future of the Republican Party on 'Special Report.'

Sen. Jim Justice, R-W. Va., said the GOP can "forget" about taking back the Senate majority in 2028 after Democrats' blue wave secured the majority in both chambers of Congress following last week's midterm elections.

Eight Republican-held Senate seats were flipped, bringing the Democratic caucus to 55 seats after Democrat Scott Colom was projected on Wednesday to win Mississippi’s Senate race. The caucus could gain another seat if Democrat Mary Peltola holds onto her narrow lead in Alaska.

"You can forget 2028. Absolutely," Justice told the Washington Examiner of the next federal election.

"I hope and pray we don’t lose the presidency. But this is such a colossal blow that it is beyond belief how colossal this is to America," he continued.

GOP EYES SENATE COMEBACK AFTER DEMOCRATIC BLOODBATH, BUT ANOTHER POLITICAL NIGHTMARE COULD AWAIT

Sen. Jim Justice said the GOP can "forget" about taking back the Senate majority in 2028 after the Democrats' blue wave. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Justice joined President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other Republicans in partially attributing the party's midterm losses to the war in Iran, which led to surging fuel prices.

Gas prices are nearly 90 cents per gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA, which listed the national average at about $3.94 per gallon on Wednesday, compared with $3.07 a year earlier.

This is the most Senate seats a party has secured in an election in 18 years. (ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)

"Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for," Thune told reporters earlier this week. "But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us."

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who was chosen to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, Republicans' Senate campaign arm for the 2028 cycle, said the GOP must learn from their disastrous showing in the midterms.

"I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it," he said.

Sen. Jim Justice joined President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other Republicans in partially attributing the midterm losses to the war in Iran. (Leon Neal/Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Similar to the 2006 midterms, Republicans suffered significant losses and huge upsets in midterm elections shaped largely by voter anger over a Middle East war and scrutiny of a GOP president’s leadership.

In 2006, Democrats gained 31 House seats and six Senate seats to retake both chambers of Congress under then-President George W. Bush. Two years later, Democrats further added to their majorities and elected former President Barack Obama.

articles.title: Ugandan police investigate deaths of four pupils in suspected school poisoning
articles.excerpt:
The school's head teacher has been arrested to assist with investigations

Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the r...
articles.body_text:
The school's head teacher has been arrested to assist with investigations

Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.

The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.

The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.

According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.

Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.

Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.

A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.

The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.

Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.

The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.

The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.

Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.

The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly deciding whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang as stock price plunges
articles.excerpt:
Meeting comes after CEO admitted to having a relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy

Nvidia’s board of directors met on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang as CEO of...
articles.body_text:
Meeting comes after CEO admitted to having a relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy

Nvidia’s board of directors met on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang as CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, according to multiple reports, after a tumultuous week in which the executive and co-founder of the company admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The meeting marks ⁠a sharp shift from Sunday, when Nvidia’s board ​expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team. However, Huang’s position became more tenuous late on Wednesday after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

The company’s stock slid more than 8% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal reported that ⁠the company was preparing to fire Huang.

If those losses hold, Nvidia will have lost about $685bn (£516bn) in market value since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is accused of being a Chinese spy.

“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not ‌a tail risk,” said Armina Rosenberg, a portfolio manager and the co-founder ‌of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares.

Dan Ives, a US tech analyst, said the company “likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm”.

Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

The board’s independent directors this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship. The firm directed Huang to continue to helm Nvidia as the investigation was ongoing.

Huang is seen as the ambitious and visionary leader of Nvidia, a company he co-founded in 1993. His exit would leave a leadership vacuum at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex.

He has no obvious successor, and personally owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, making him the world’s 13th richest person according to Bloomberg. Unlike many of his contemporaries at other big tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire artificial intelligence ecosphere relies on the company, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. It is also one of the most valuable companies on earth, with a market cap of more than $4tn. Huang himself is one of the world’s richest people, with an estimated net worth of $148bn.

While Huang admitted to having an affair – without naming Alice Huang directly – he denied any knowledge that the woman allegedly worked for the Chinese government, according to Trump.

The Nvidia CEO and the Chinese businesswoman, an Nvidia customer, were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is an executive at the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, which uses Nvidia chips.

On Thursday a Taiwanese government minister said Alice Huang had visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, as he responded to questions about a New York Times report that claimed the US had advised Taiwan as early as 2024 to monitor her movements.

Chiu Chui-cheng, Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council minister, said there were “no special flags” about her at the time, Chiu said, adding that “if we had any of the kind of critical intelligence … we would have definitely flagged her for heightened review.”

Jensen Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Donald Trump has backed Huang, saying he had done “an incredible job” and is “an honorable guy”. Leading tech industry players, including Elon Musk, have also thrown their support behind Huang.

Musk was asked on X early on Thursday if he would hire a jobless Huang. He replied: “That would be an honour”.

Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren ⁠and Chris Coons have asked the Trump administration to preserve all documents tied to Nvidia’s chip ⁠exports to China, it was revealed late on Wednesday.

“This ‌incident raises significant ‌concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export ‌controls and protect our national security,” the senators said in the letter sent to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, secretary of state Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Nvidia did not immediately return a request for comment.
