articles.title: Horny bull elk keeps attacking cars, forces Missouri wildlife park to close indefinitely
articles.excerpt: Country music star Chris Janson tells OutKick OutDoors about his challenging elk hunt in Colorado, where he finally harvested a bull in the final 30 minutes of his trip. The "Buy Me a Boat" singer als...
articles.body_text:
Country music star Chris Janson tells OutKick OutDoors about his challenging elk hunt in Colorado, where he finally harvested a bull in the final 30 minutes of his trip. The "Buy Me a Boat" singer also explains why he takes the sport so seriously.

A wildlife park in Missouri has been forced to close indefinitely because one particularly aggressive bull elk won't stop attacking visitors' cars.

Lone Elk Park, located just outside St. Louis, closed Monday after officials decided the animal had become too much of a safety risk. Apparently, the problem is that he's young, he's horny, and he's new to this whole being-in-charge thing.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

According to St. Louis Public Radio, the bull recently replaced his own father as the dominant male in the herd. This is his first mating season running the show, and he's not exactly handling his newfound responsibilities gracefully.

A bull elk flicks his tongue as part of the mating ritual while watching over his harem of cow elk on the Lake Estes Golf Course. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"We have a younger, more inexperienced herd bull this year," Eric Johnson, acting director of St. Louis County Parks and Recreation, said. "It's his first year, and he's acting a little bit like a teenager."

One visitor, Theresa Hammer, learned that the hard way.

Hammer told St. Louis Public Radio she was sitting in her Ford Fusion last week when the bull approached her vehicle. She looked away briefly, and when she looked back, he was ramming his antlers into the front of her car.

"I looked back up, and he hit the front of my car with his horns," she said. "He scratched up the whole side of my car, my hood and put a big dent in the rear quarter panel."

A bull elk stands in Colorado during rutting season. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Despite the damage, Hammer said she doesn't blame the elk. After all, she's the one driving through his home.

Lone Elk Park is a 546-acre drive-through wildlife park where visitors can observe elk, bison and other animals from their vehicles. Officials had posted warnings about keeping a safe distance from the elk, but visitors weren't always following them.

And with the bull becoming increasingly aggressive, the county decided it was safer to close the park until he settles down.

BULL ELK IN COLORADO NICKNAMED 'SMASH' IS CHASING OFF TRUCKS AND GOLF CARTS

For what it's worth, this kind of behavior isn't unusual during the elk rut, which is the annual breeding season. Bull elk experience a surge in testosterone and become more territorial as they compete for females. That can make them particularly dangerous to people who get too close.

But even by elk standards, this guy is apparently a handful.

Johnson, who has worked for the parks department for 32 years, said it's been roughly a decade since they've dealt with a bull quite this worked up.

"Some of [the bulls] have it figured out and they calmly go about their business, and sometimes it's like this," he said.

A bull elk wanders across Moraine Park in Rocky Mountain National Park on Wednesday, Sept. 14, 2022. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Officials haven't announced a reopening date, but they're monitoring the bull's behavior daily and hope to reopen the park within the next several days.

So, for now, an entire wildlife park is closed because one young elk can't get his hormones under control.

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube!

articles.title: Russian Ambassador to US Alexander Darchiev dies suddenly at 66
articles.excerpt:
Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on the arrest of a senior U.S. Army officer in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia following a joint U.S.-U.K. investigation.

Russia's Ambassador to the United ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on the arrest of a senior U.S. Army officer in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia following a joint U.S.-U.K. investigation.

Russia's Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev, 66, died suddenly Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced.

"The leadership and staff of the Russian Foreign Ministry report with deep sorrow that on Nov. 11, at the age of 66, the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Russian Federation to the United States of America, Alexander Nikitich Darchiev, passed away suddenly," Russia's statement, as translated to English, said. "A distinguished diplomat, experienced leader, kind colleague, and mentor has departed this life. A consummate professional and brilliant Americanist, A.N. Darchiev served on one of the most critical and demanding fronts of Russian foreign policy."

"We express our deepest and most sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of Alexander Nikitich Darchiev," the statement added. "The cherished memory of our untimely departed colleague will forever remain in our hearts."

Fox News confirmed the death came in Russia and not the U.S.

MELANIA TRUMP HAILS OLESHKY CEASEFIRE AS POTENTIAL ‘SPARK’ FOR PROGRESS AMID UKRAINE-RUSSIA WAR

Alexander Darchiyev, head of the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America Department and a candidate for the position of ambassador to the United States, poses for a picture before a session of the Federation Council's committee on foreign affairs in Moscow, Russia, on Nov. 25, 2024. (Kommersant Photo/Dmitry Dukhanin via Reuters)

Russia's Vladimir Putin appointed Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known in the past for his public denunciations of the West, as ambassador to Washington in March 2025 to lead a rapprochement with the Trump administration that has rattled Ukraine, the European Union and NATO.

His death comes less than a week after a White House news conference hailing a temporary ceasefire in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia.

First lady Melania Trump and envoys from both Russia and Ukraine hailed the ceasefire in the Oleshky region.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

Shortly after being tapped as ambassador, Darchiev met with Trump administration officials and delivered a message of hope for peace.

"Russia and the United States are destined, as great powers, to have non-confrontational peaceful existence," Darchiev said during a June 10, 2025, Russia Day reception at the Russian Embassy in Washington after delivering his credentials to the White House, adding, "our discussion was very constructive."

Before taking the helm of the Russian Embassy in Washington, Darchiev played a role as the Kremlin’s point man for high-stakes bilateral negotiations, most notably during the delicate discussions that led to prisoner swaps involving imprisoned arms dealer Viktor Bout and detained Americans Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan.

EVAN GERSHKOVICH DETAILS RUSSIAN ARREST, REVEALS MOMENT THAT NEARLY BROKE HIM DURING WRONGFUL DETENTION

In August 2022, while serving as the director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s North American Department, Darchiev provided the first on-the-record Russian confirmation that Moscow and Washington were actively discussing those situations.

"This quite sensitive issue of the swap of convicted Russian and U.S. citizens is being pursued along the channels designated by our presidents," Darchiev told the Russian state news agency TASS. "The individuals are, indeed, being discussed. The Russian side has long been seeking the release of Viktor Bout. The negotiations are bearing fruit."

An empty table for the Russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev is visible during a Senate Appropriations Subcommittee hearing on "The Abduction of Ukrainian Children by the Russian Federation" on Capitol Hill on December 3, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

His comments marked a breakthrough moment in months of backchannel diplomacy, which ultimately culminated in December 2022 when the U.S. and Russia completed a one-for-one swap of Griner for Bout at an airport in Abu Dhabi.

Fox News' Gillian Turner, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
articles.excerpt:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from ...
articles.body_text:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.

On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks between 1969 and 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.

Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.

A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.

The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.

Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.

Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

articles.title: Teen charged with murder in fatal shooting of 15-year-old NYC student Javits Frimpong
articles.excerpt: President Donald Trump exits the stage to the parents of Jacob Freytes, a Bronx boy who was killed by a repeat criminal's stray bullet. Trump was on Long Island, N.Y., Friday addressing law enforcemen...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump exits the stage to the parents of Jacob Freytes, a Bronx boy who was killed by a repeat criminal's stray bullet. Trump was on Long Island, N.Y., Friday addressing law enforcement about his administration's crackdown on crime.

A 17-year-old boy has been arrested after a teenager was fatally shot while walking to school in New York City last month, police announced Wednesday.

The teen suspect, who has not been publicly identified, faces a murder charge in the Oct. 29 death of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, according to the New York City Police Department (NYPD).

"The NYPD will be relentless in our efforts to get dangerous people out of our communities, especially when it involves the murder of a 15-year-old boy," the department wrote in a post on X.

Members of the community visit and maintain a memorial for Javits Frimpong Nov. 7 in the Bronx borough of New York City. Frimpong, a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana, was shot to death more than a week earlier. He was being bullied at school, and a 17-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of the killing. (Corbis via Getty Images)

Javits, a Ghanaian immigrant, was fatally shot in the stomach in the Bronx. His father believes the killing may be linked to ongoing bullying his son experienced at school.

Just two days before the tragedy, the school’s principal had called Thomas Frimpong to report that his son was being targeted and that two students had been suspended as a result.

The tragic killing sparked local protests and urgent calls from community members to end youth violence and bullying.

Last week, NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny noted that investigators were exploring multiple angles.

"The alleged bullying is one aspect that we’re looking at, as well as some others," Kenny told the New York Post.

"All three gave chase," Kenny added. "And these cowards shot him in the back. If their intention was to rob him, he dropped his backpack."

PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION'

Members of the community visit and maintain a memorial for Javits Frimpong on Nov. 7, 2026, in the Bronx borough of New York City. Frimpong, a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana, was shot to death more than a week earlier. Frimpong was being bullied at school, but the reasons for his murder remain unclear. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"As of right now, all indications are that he was trying to live the American dream," the chief said. "He was trying to get ahead by going to school. We have nothing in our investigation to indicate he was involved in any gang activity. Seems like he was just a very good kid."

The tragedy also prompted federal intervention to support the grieving family. President Donald Trump agreed to grant Javits’ mother an emergency visa so she could travel to the United States from Ghana to lay her son to rest.

"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 2 post on X.

"Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
articles.excerpt:
It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll

Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’

A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for...
articles.body_text:
It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll

Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’

A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.

The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.

The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”

The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.

Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.

“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”

In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

articles.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.excerpt:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we kn...
articles.body_text:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms

Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.

She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.

“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.

“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.

“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.

“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.

“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”

Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.

Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title: Trump planning new military assault or tighter sanctions, say Iranian officials
articles.excerpt:
Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening ec...
articles.body_text:
Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action.

The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response.

If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.

Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.”

He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait.

For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.

Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.

On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.

Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.

In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.

A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”.

Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.

A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.

articles.title: Biden ripped for ‘totally delusional’ claim about debate that preceded his 2024 exit
articles.excerpt:
Former President Joe Biden told People Magazine in an interview released Wednesday that his June 2024 presidential debate against then-candidate Donald Trump was not "consequential."

Former President...
articles.body_text:
Former President Joe Biden told People Magazine in an interview released Wednesday that his June 2024 presidential debate against then-candidate Donald Trump was not "consequential."

Former President Joe Biden is facing sharp backlash after dismissing his disastrous 2024 debate performance against President Donald Trump as "not very consequential" — despite dropping out of the presidential race just 24 days later.

When asked about what his "perspective" on the June 27, 2024 debate is now in an interview with People Magazine released Wednesday, Biden suggested he felt his debate performance was inconsequential.

"Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate," Biden told People Magazine. "To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t."

JILL BIDEN SAYS SHE THOUGHT JOE WAS HAVING A STROKE DURING HIS DISASTROUS 2024 DEBATE PERFORMANCE

Former President Joe Biden speaks with moderator Jake Tapper as former first lady Dr. Jill Biden looks on after a presidential debate with Donald Trump in Atlanta, Ga., on June 27, 2024. (Brian Snyder/Reuters)

"But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential," he added.

Biden's comments drew swift criticism on social media on Wednesday.

SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALS SHE WAS 'FRIGHTENED' WATCHING JOE'S DISASTROUS DEBATE

"Joe Biden now claims his 2024 presidential debate against President Trump, which forced him to drop out of the race, was not very consequential," former Trump campaign operative Steve Cortes wrote Wednesday in an X post.

"Just 24 days after the 'not very consequential' presidential debate, Joe Biden ended his campaign for President," Cortes added.

Conservative commentator Steve Guest wrote on X that Biden "is TOTALLY delusional."

Meanwhile, former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser Matt Whitlock asserted in a Wednesday post on X that it was actually "the most consequential" presidential debate of all time.

"It was without question the most consequential Presidential debate in history - he [Biden] likely would have stayed the nominee without it," Whitlock said. "But I’m definitely excited for the other hot takes in the book now."

"It was the most lopsided debate in history. C’mon, man!" Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis quipped.

Former U.S. First Lady Dr. Jill Biden revealed that she thought then-President Joe Biden had had a stroke during his 2024 debate with then-candidate Donald Trump. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images)

During the presidential debate, Biden stumbled over his words, paused for long periods of time and displayed confused facial expressions.

The Office of Joe and Jill Biden did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says
articles.excerpt: Nearly a quarter of Lebanon’s population, or more than one million people, is facing acute food shortages due to two consecutive conflicts in less than two years and a dire economic situation, accordi...
articles.body_text:
Nearly a quarter of Lebanon’s population, or more than one million people, is facing acute food shortages due to two consecutive conflicts in less than two years and a dire economic situation, according to the United Nations.

The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme (WFP) and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture warned in a joint statement published on Wednesday that the number is expected to rise to 1.15 million by the middle of next year.

“Employment opportunities remain limited, savings have been depleted, and debt remains high, while the cost of food, fuel and other essentials continues to strain household budgets,” the joint statement said.

“Some households can still draw on savings, borrow, cut expenses or find other ways to put food on the table. For others, those options are being exhausted. When families have nothing left to fall back on, even a small additional shock can push them deeper into crisis,” Allison Oman Lawi, WFP representative and country director in Lebanon, said.

Lebanon’s Agriculture Minister Nizar Hani said: “These findings call for a coordinated national response that addresses urgent food needs while protecting livelihoods and restoring productive capacity.”

Lebanon’s authorities estimate that the cost of two wars between Israel and the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah since October 2023 amounts to about $27bn.

The last war, launched in March, displaced more than one million people in Lebanon. That number has fallen to about 300,000 since violence subsided in June.

Despite a United States-brokered framework deal signed between Israel and Lebanon’s government in June to bring fighting to an end, Israel is still occupying land in Lebanon.

Under the terms, Israeli forces were to withdraw, and Lebanon’s army was to take up positions in vacated territory.

Lebanon was meant to disarm Hezbollah, which is not a party to the agreement.

The fighting broke out as Lebanon struggled to recover from its worst-ever economic crisis, which began in 2019.

Beirut has been seeking a bailout from the International Monetary Fund but has yet to implement reforms demanded by the institution to release the aid.

articles.title: Spain’s first general strike in 14 years begins
articles.excerpt:
Millions of workers across Spain are striking to demand government action over the country’s housing crisis, less than three weeks before a national election that could bring the far right to power.

...
articles.body_text:
Millions of workers across Spain are striking to demand government action over the country’s housing crisis, less than three weeks before a national election that could bring the far right to power.

The 24-hour walkout, which began at midnight on Wednesday, disrupted public transport and forced businesses, factories and shops to scale back operations or close entirely across the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy. It’s Spain’s first general strike in 14 years.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours, including roadblocks with burning tyres in Barcelona, the second-largest city in the country. There were also scuffles between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market on the outskirts of the capital, Madrid.

The two main unions that called the strike, UGT and CCOO, reported widespread participation in the early hours “with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors”, including 90 percent in the automotive and port sectors, according to a statement posted on social media.

The CEOE organisation, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.

The UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner who died several days later.

The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

Spain’s socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election for November 29 after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.

“This is not a strike against anyone, but rather one in favour of a common response from all levels of government to a real problem, which is access to housing,” he said in an interview published Sunday in the daily newspaper La Vanguardia.

The strike has been rejected by business groups, which have described it as an election-related protest, and criticised by the conservative opposition Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike in the run-up to the election.

Feijoo, whose party leads opinion polls, said going ahead with the strike was a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.

Spain’s average gross monthly salary is about 2,460 euros, while renting a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid cost an average of 1,170 euros a month in October, according to property portal Idealista.

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, and 98.7 percent of the average young person’s income, according to the Youth Council of Spain. It’s well above the 30 percent share commonly recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

Alison Quinn, president of Dinova, tells Fox News Digital how participating restaurants are showing appreciation for America's military community through complimentary menu items and promotional offers, including incentives for future visits.

Veterans and active-duty military members can find free food and other promotions at restaurants across the country on Veterans Day, Nov. 11. Some offers also give customers a reason to return for another deal later.

About 30 restaurant brands are included in Dinova's 2026 Veterans Day Dining Guide, according to Alison Quinn, the company's Florida-based president.

The guide is in its fifth year and includes national and regional chains like Bonefish Grill, Carrabba's Italian Grill, Hooters, Outback Steakhouse and Red Lobster.

102-YEAR-OLD NAVY VETERAN STILL CRAVES HOT WINGS AFTER 102 COMBAT MISSIONS IN KOREA: 'I MIGHT MAKE IT TO 115'

"What we're starting to see now is it's going beyond Veterans Day, to try to give back to the vets in a way that is more meaningful," Quinn told Fox News Digital. "Just not about one day but come back, and we'll give you something again."

Quinn pointed to California-based Hofman Hospitality Group, which is offering select meals to veterans and a $10 bonus card for a future visit. Lucille's Smokehouse Bar-B-Que is among the group's brands.

The Veterans Day Dining Guide is a compilation of restaurants offering free meals and discounts to veterans and active-duty military. (iStock)

Outback Steakhouse is offering a complimentary Bloomin' Onion and soft drink, along with a meal offer for a return visit, she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Other deals listed in the guide include 10 free boneless wings and fries at Buffalo Wild Wings, a complimentary Red's Big Tavern Burger at Red Robin, free shrimp at Red Lobster and a free All-American Smash at Smashburger.

Lucille's Smokehouse Bar-B-Que is among the restaurants offering certain meals for free to veterans on Nov. 11. (Noah Graham/NBAE via Getty Images)

Dinova started the guide to share offers with veterans and, in some cases, active-duty military personnel, Quinn said. The company's business dining network includes about 25,000 restaurants and 600 corporate partners, she said.

Downloads of the guide have increased over the years, Quinn said, and the promotions may be useful for veterans or active-duty personnel who are struggling or "living under a tight budget."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Asked which deal she would choose, Quinn singled out Eddie Merlot's complimentary cheeseburger. Her father is an 85-year-old veteran, she said, and she plans to tell him about it.

Veterans and active-duty military members should bring identification and check with their local restaurant before visiting, Quinn said. Participation and ID requirements can vary by location and offer.

articles.title: Washington AG's office indicates it will defend girls' sports ballot measure after ACLU sues to block it
articles.excerpt:

Washi...
articles.body_text:
Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports. (Credit: Seattle Public Schools)

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown’s office indicated it will fight to uphold a new voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports, after the ACLU of Washington and other groups announced a lawsuit to block the measure.

"When a new law is passed by the people or the Legislature, our role is to ensure it is defended regardless of our personal views about the policy. We will review court filings as they come and discuss next steps," Brown’s office told OutKick.

However, the lawsuit to challenge the initiative involves Brown’s former law firm, a teachers union that supported his campaign and the former employer of his policy director. His office reiterated its position when OutKick asked follow-up questions about those connections and how the defense would be handled.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

Supporters of Initiative 638, a Nov. 3 ballot measure in Washington state that would require K-12 athletes to compete according to their sex at birth speak at a pre-meet rally.  (OutKick)

"We’re discussing next steps and do not have more to add to the previous comment at this time. Again, when a new law is passed by the people or the Legislature, our role is to ensure it is defended regardless of our personal views about the policy," the office said.

The responses did not identify who would lead the defense or say whether the office had evaluated recusal or screening measures concerning those relationships.

Pacifica Law Group, where Brown previously served as a partner, is representing the Washington Education Association in the challenge, according to the Northwest Progressive Institute’s account of the filing.

Brown worked as a Pacifica partner from 2017 to 2021 before accepting President Joe Biden’s appointment as U.S. attorney for Western Washington, according to the firm. He returned in June 2023, and Pacifica identified him as a partner when it announced his election as attorney general in November 2024.

The Washington Education Association endorsed Brown’s 2024 campaign, according to Transparency USA.

The union’s political action committee was also among Brown’s campaign donors, according to The Spokesman-Review’s 2024 candidate profile, which cited Washington Public Disclosure Commission information. The profile did not specify the contribution amount.

Brown’s policy director, Enoka Herat, previously served as the ACLU of Washington’s policing and immigration policy program director.

Brown, a Democrat, also has a record of supporting transgender students’ participation in girls’ sports.

On Oct. 31, 2025, he led a coalition of attorneys general in filing an amicus brief supporting Minnesota’s policy in Female Athletes United v. Keith Ellison. The coalition urged the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to deny an emergency injunction that would have barred transgender students from most girls’ sports.

"I believe strongly in protecting the rights of all Washington kids—including transgender youth," Brown said in his office’s announcement of that amicus brief.

JACKSON THOMPSON: SEATTLE SCHOOL BOARD AUTHORIZES LEGAL CHALLENGE TO BALLOT MEASURE PROTECTING GIRLS' SPORTS

He argued that sports participation benefits children’s physical and emotional well-being and that excluding students based on gender identity perpetuates discrimination.

The lawsuit challenging Washington’s initiative was filed Monday in King County Superior Court. Plaintiffs include TransFamilies, the Washington Education Association and parents of transgender and nontransgender students who participate in girls’ sports.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The challengers argue the initiative violates state constitutional privacy protections and anti-discrimination law.

"Initiative 638 seeks to deny transgender girls equal opportunities simply because of who they are. It is discrimination, and it threatens all girls who play sports at school," the ACLU said in its announcement.

Let’s Go Washington, the organization behind the initiative, disputed the lawsuit’s claims Tuesday and argued existing sports physicals could satisfy the medical verification requirement.

Brown’s office also said it does not serve as legal counsel to the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association or local school districts.

"We don’t speculate on hypothetical events. Also, we only provide legal guidance to our state agency clients, which do not include WIAA or local school districts. We advise the state Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and any such conversations would be attorney-client privileged," the office said.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: Romanian servers targeted by Russian hackers to scoop up emails about NATO, EU
articles.excerpt: VIENNA — Hackers linked to Russia’s FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has ...
articles.body_text:
VIENNA — Hackers linked to Russia’s FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.

Using an advanced suite of tools that the researchers dubbed Cereal, a pun on the technology of serialization, emails going through Romanian government servers were scanned for a relation to NATO and the European Union. If this was discovered, the malicious software would create a copy for its Russian spymasters.

In particular, one component, CerealBox, targeted messages involving NATO and EU institutional addresses, the cybersecurity form ESET said. The module selected emails with Word or PDF attachments using predefined filters, then compressed and encrypted copies for later retrieval by the attackers.

The hack was discovered by the Bratislava-based  company and made public on Nov. 10. ESET had first discovered the tool being used against Kazakhstan in November 2025, and found the infiltration of Romania’s Microsoft Exchange servers a month later.

In a blog post and press release, the company attributed the attack to the known hacking group Turla, which it said was generally considered to be affiliated with Russia’s FSB, the country’s domestic intelligence agency. Turla has also been involved in attacks against high-profile Ukrainian targets, and the researchers said 70% of countries the group targeted were post-Soviet or post-communist states in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The APT – a term designating an “Advanced Persistent Threat,” or known hacking group – primarily attacks government institutions.

ESET attributed the toolset to Turla with high confidence, citing the simultaneous use of another component publicly linked to the group and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware.

The researchers also noted a surge in activity in Kazakhstan on Jan. 15, 2026, the day after Old New Year, an informal holiday observed in Russia and some neighboring countries. “While malware does not celebrate holidays, its operators do,” the company wrote.

Romanian servers were compromised on Dec. 23, 2025, ESET researchers said; roughly a month after the cybersecurity firm first detected the same malicious code on the server of a Kazakh government agency. That discovery was the first time this tool had been seen, which the researchers described as “a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages.”

The tool was unusual for its “combination of novel techniques requiring deep knowledge of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods,” ESET wrote.

The tool was designed to be especially stealthy, meant to allow it to spy undetected at length. While malware commonly communicates with an external command-and-control server, which can lead to detection and help cybersecurity professionals trace the origin, Cereal used the target organization’s own Microsoft servers as its infrastructure.

Romania is an eastern flank member of NATO and has faced physical and digital spillover of the confrontation between Russia and the West, particularly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Airspace violations, drone shootdowns and even the strike of commercial vessels in its exclusive economic zone have been among the consequences.

The country  has also been targeted by cyber warfare. In May 2025, another known Russian APT actor attacked arms makers involved in supporting Ukraine, including those located in Romania; and just months after the war broke out, government websites were hit by a crude distributed denial-of-service attack, making Romanian public-authority and financial-sector websites unavailable for several hours.

Linus Höller is Defense News’ Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

articles.title: Poultry and captive birds must be kept inside in England and Scotland because of bird flu
articles.excerpt:

Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the secon...
articles.body_text:
Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds

Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu.

The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. A similar designation was made across the whole of Scotland on Tuesday.

Birdkeepers must also follow enhanced biosecurity measures including reporting changes in egg production and reporting suspected disease immediately to the Animal and Plant Health Agency.

The government said the declaration followed an increased risk and escalating number of confirmations of the highly pathogenic avian influenza, or bird flu, in kept and wild birds.

A prevention zone was also declared across all of England, Scotland and Wales in 2025.

Since 2014, the disease has been spreading rapidly and has devastated UK wild bird populations since the summer of 2021. It has also spread across an unusually broad range of species around the world, with four of the five main southern elephant seal populations reporting the disease. In some south Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.

The disease has also been detected in humans, with 11 deaths recorded globally between 1 January and 4 August 2025.

This strain of bird flu causes illness and high death rates in birds, as well as flu-like symptoms and conjunctivitis in humans who come into close contact with infected animals.

The British government said the current risk to human health from bird flu remained very low.

The government says it does not anticipate an impact on the availability of Christmas turkeys or other seasonal poultry for consumers. The Food Safety Authority said properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, were safe to eat.

The UK chief veterinary officer, Christine Middlemiss, said: “Having avian influenza confirmed in your flock can be devastating. I understand the impact this disease can have on the poultry sector and am extremely grateful for the continued cooperation of the industry.”

articles.title: Burnham faces Badenoch at PMQs following huge windfarm approval – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
PM to face leader of opposition before leaving for the Cop31 climate crisis summit

Good morning. Andy Burnham has got PMQs today, and after that he will leave for what looks like a rather hectic Turk...
articles.body_text:
PM to face leader of opposition before leaving for the Cop31 climate crisis summit

Good morning. Andy Burnham has got PMQs today, and after that he will leave for what looks like a rather hectic Turkey/Ireland trip which tomorrow will see him address the Cop31 climate summit in the morning, before attending his first major summit with EU leaders (and some other European leaders – it’s a European Political Community event) in Dublin later in the day.

Of the two events, the EPC is probably the more important for Burnham because it will give him the chance to clear the air ahead of the UK-EU summit next week, and because Burnham has made renegotiating the relationship with the EU a key aim of his premiership.

But Cop31 is important too because Burnham wants to show that he remains committed to the net zero climate agenda but that he is also “pragmatic” about pursuing this in a way that helps with cost of living pressures. This morning he has an announcement that will help in this respect; Downing Street has announced the next stage in two huge offshore wind projects.

One relates to the Vanguard East and Vanguard West projects. No 10 says:

double quotation markEnergy company RWE, together with global investment firm KKR, have announced a total investment of £12bn, believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history to date. It will give the green light to its Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms, set to be operational by 2030 and delivering clean, secure, homegrown power to homes and businesses that will protect families from global fossil fuel price shocks …

On top of bolstering the UK’s green energy future, the investment will support more than 2,400 jobs during construction and operation, and once operational, the wind farms will have the capacity to supply the equivalent of around three million UK homes …

The decision marks a major milestone for the project, with the developers now making their final investment commitment to deliver the projects. Onshore works are already well advanced, with construction offshore set to begin in early 2027.

The other relates to Berwick Bank B. No 10 says:

double quotation markOn top of this, Scottish-headquartered SSE has announced that the latest phase of its major offshore wind farm, Berwick Bank B, will back 2,677 skilled jobs in manufacturing, engineering and project delivery across the north of England and Scotland, with the company contracting Siemens Energy for the manufacturing of wind turbines and substation platforms. This includes the creation of 130 new project delivery roles in Glasgow and Montrose.

At its full capacity, Berwick Bank, off the east coast of Scotland, could become the world’s largest offshore wind farm, capable of meeting more than 6% of current UK electricity demand.

Welcoming these announcements, Burnham said:

double quotation markThis major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain. And it is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

Ajit Niranjan has a separate live blog covering Cop31.

10am: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, gives evidence to the Commons housing committee.

10.50am: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, gives a speech to the Association of Colleges annual conference in Birmingham.

11am: Louise Casey gives a speech at the National Children and Adult Services conference in Liverpool.

Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.

Noon: Morgan McSweeney, Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff, gives evidence to the Lords constitution committee about constitutional safeguards.

1pm: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, gives a speech to the annual airlines’ conference in London.

2.15pm: John Healey, the chancellor, gives evidence to the Commons Treasury committee about the budget.

Afternoon: Burnham leaves London to fly to the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

Badenoch says the government is legislating to ban drilling off Scotland. That is ludicrous, she says.

Burnham says the Jackdaw gas field has been approved. And the new windfarms are going ahead. He goes on:

double quotation markIf she wants to,address energy policy in this house, perhaps we can talk about why energy bills went up and up under the party opposite. Perhaps we can discuss how they lost public control and lost control of people’s bills and left people paying more and more.

Badenoch says Rosebank has not been approved because Ed Miliband was not in favour when he was energy secretary,

double quotation markHe called Rosebank climate vandalism. But then he also thought cosying up to Russell Brand would make him prime minister. So I don’t think we need to trust his judgement.

Burnham says Rosebank would have been approved if it had not been for the last goverment messing up the licensing process. He says it is a quasi-judicial matter now. But he highlights the windfarm projects announced today. (See 8.55am.)

Badenoch jokes about Andy Burnham being in the audience for a speech by the cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, last night.

double quotation markHe’s supposed to be telling her his plan, not sat in the audience while she tells him hers.

She asks why the plan for the Rosebank oil field was in the budget calculations when it has not been approved.

Burnham says Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision.

Referring to the Tory plans for welfare cuts announced yesterday, he says:

double quotation markDoes she accept that so many of the people affected by what she announced are working people, people whose incomes will be hit hard in a cost of living crisis? I think the honourable lady needs to answer as to why she is making the cost of living crisis harder for people by the cuts she’s just announced.

Badenoch references a Guardian story about Labour MPs being concerned about the lack of ambition in the 10-year plan and she jokes about reports that it will include merging the DVLA with the DVSA. “Exciting stuff,” she says.

Burnham picks up on Badenoch mentioning the budget, and he says it was the most popular budget for years. On issues like social care and Neets, the government is taking big decisions, he says.

Kemi Badenoch asks if it is true that Andy Burnham is so short of ideas for his 10-year plan for Britain that he has asked the Boston Consulting Group to help.

Burnham says he will present his 10-year plans to MPs before the Christmas recess.

(Last week he said it might not come until January.)

Claire Hanna, the SDLP leader, says MPs would not let one party at Westminster to stop the Commons operating. But that is what is happening at Stormont, she says, because of the conduct of the DUP. Stormont is in its “dying days” without reform, she says.

Burnham says all MPs want to see Stormont up and running and delivering. He says the Northern Ireland is working with the parties to agree a budget, and he is considering further options for reform.

Andy Burnham starts by saying all MP remember the sacrifice of all those who have served their country.

No veterans should have to sleep on the streets, he says. He says he has written to councils asking him to help him end rough sleeping for veterans.

Here is the list of MPs who have got a question.

Back to Labour’s EU policy, and Stuart Ingham, head of the policy unit in No 10 when Keir Starmer was PM, has written a long and subtle article in the New Statesman arguing that, rather than focus on trying to rejoin the EU fully, or just the single market, Andy Burnham would be better off focusing for now on goals around which Labour could unite.

double quotation markWhere does Rejoin fit into this? If there was a referendum tomorrow, I’d vote to undo a mistake. Perhaps for some, saying so is the first necessary step of a longer journey. But I fear divisions about questions we don’t have to answer at the moment will be a barrier to unity over the questions that we do. The soft Euroscepticism inherent in Labour may harden at just the wrong moment …

Then there are the voters. The Prime Minister speaks with them when he says that Brexit has been a failure and the status quo isn’t good enough. There is scope to sell an economic and security partnership, and leave Reform and the Tories to fight over a tiny pool of voters that think it’s been a success. The arguments against Rejoin are stronger: they allow the populist right to avoid defending the Brexit it has delivered and go straight to its home territory – emotional arguments about democracy, betrayal and elites.

The reset should be promoted on its own terms. It can be a stepping stone for those with a destination in mind and a leap forward to a better deal for those that don’t. Labour, for now, is a party with Rejoiners in it rather than a Rejoiner party.

When Ingham was in Downing Street, he was working on the deals on food exports, energy policy and youth mobility that are due to be presented as a reset moment at the UK-EU summit next week. The EU regularly says it will not allow cherry picking, and that to gain the all the advantages of the single market, states have to accept all the obligations (including free movement). Ingham points out that, in practice, it is not that straightword, which is why there are opportunities for Britain that don’t involve full membership or full single market membership. He explains:

double quotation markThe government I advised on Europe policy made headway in getting the UK included in both the Made in Europe and European defence programmes. The EU has agreed that Britain can participate in the Ukraine loan scheme – so Kyiv can buy weapons and munitions from British firms with European capital. The UK is within the scope of draft clauses of the Industrial Accelerator Act, meaning its companies may be able to bid for large procurement contracts. The emissions trading agreement, expected to be signed this month, paves the way for British manufacturers to be exempt from Europe’s carbon import taxes, without which reindustrialisation cannot happen. Although the EU will not want it presented this way, that emissions agreement is Britain being allowed access and rights within the parts of the single market where it follows the rules. The food and drink and electricity deals, pitched to the EU as about food security and energy security, are the same. Cherries can be picked when it’s in everyone’s common security interest.

In a Bluesky thread on the Joe Martin story (see 11.04am), Will Hayward, the Welsh political commentator, says he thinks Martin may soon defect from Reform UK to Restore Britain. “Mr Martin has been making kissy faces at Restore for a while,” Hayward says. “Reform sources within that group tell me the party are deeply concerned at Restore eating into their vote and potential defections.”

Hayward points out that Rupert Lowe, the Restore Britain MP and party leader, has been tweeting in support of Martin. In one message, Lowe said:

double quotation markIf the Welsh Parliament is going to shut down legitimate debate around demographic security and immigration, the Restore Britain answer is quite straightforward...

Roll back devolution and shut down the Welsh parliament.

The leader of Reform in Wales has said her party stands with a member who was banned from speaking in the Welsh parliament after claiming white British people were being replaced in the UK, the Press Association reports.

Reform’s Joe Martin was handed the ban yesterday after his comments were described as “discriminatory” and “offensive” by the Llywydd (presiding officer), Huw Irranca-Davies.

Helen Jenner, the Reform UK leader in the Senedd, posted a message on social media this morning saying:

double quotation markReform stands with Joe Martin.

Freedom of speech must be protected at all costs.

Speaking in the Senedd yesterday, Martin, the MS for Caerdydd Penarth, said:

double quotation markCan I have a statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place in the UK? Because the scale of change has been breathtaking. Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years’ time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country. That change has already taken place in London, Birmingham, Leicester, Slough, Luton and Manchester, and I don’t want it to happen here.

Indeed, at every opportunity, the majority of the electorate have wanted less immigration so that their nation can be preserved. A nation is not an economic zone, it’s not a hotel, and neither is it a charity. It’s a family, which is capable of absorbing people of all races if done at a sensible rate, but not if it’s replaced altogether.

Welsh minister Heledd Fychan responded by asking for a ruling on whether the comments were in line with Senedd rules, adding:

double quotation markWe have a duty for every single member of our communities that we represent. I reject division and hate. We had a question earlier to the prif weinidog (first minister) around antisemitism. We cannot differentiate between people of different religions, different sexuality, different skin colour. We are a government for everyone here in Wales, we are supposed to be a Senedd for everyone here in Wales. I reject wholeheartedly the division that is spouted by those members.

Later in the afternoon, Irranca-Davies said he considered the comments made by Martin to be “unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive”. He said:

double quotation markWhilst it is always possible to raise legitimate policy matters in relation to immigration in this siambr [chamber], the focus of that contribution on race and ethnicity was clearly discriminatory, offensive, and detracted from the dignity of the Senedd.

This is not the first time the member has pushed the boundaries in his contributions, and I have previously warned him about his conduct.

Until I receive a clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises to the siambr, we will not be calling the member to speak.

Reform is the largest opposition group to the Plaid Cymru-led government.

articles.title: Slain New Jersey mom’s bedroom furniture removed by investigators months after unsolved stabbing
articles.excerpt:
A former FBI agent and private investigator Robert Strang analyzes law enforcement's return to the property after five months of investigation into Hanlon's death.

CHESTER, N.J. – A neighbor confirme...
articles.body_text:
A former FBI agent and private investigator Robert Strang analyzes law enforcement's return to the property after five months of investigation into Hanlon's death.

CHESTER, N.J. – A neighbor confirmed investigators removed what appeared to be a headboard, hamper and possible comforter or quilt from the property where Brooke Hanlon, 35, was found stabbed to death earlier this year.

Fox News Digital was on the scene outside the home on Pottersville Road in Chester, New Jersey last week and witnessed investigators carrying scads of those items wrapped in brown paper and marked with evidence tape out of the Hanlon home.

Hanlon, a psychotherapist and mother, was found fatally stabbed in the home on June 6. Her husband, James "Conor" Hanlon, had called 911 from the home after his wife was found stabbed there. No arrests have been made.

He was seen speaking with police on Wednesday afternoon, his neighbors said.

Law enforcement personnel remove evidence from the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Hanlon's wife, Brooke Hanlon, was found dead in their home in June. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

COPS RETURN TO NEW JERSEY MOTHER'S HOME MONTHS AFTER SHE WAS FOUND STABBED AND HUSBAND CALLED 911

On Thursday, Fox News Digital witnessed officers remove what appeared to be a large comforter from a second-story window at the house.

Brooke Hanlon was found stabbed to death inside her Morris County, New Jersey home. Police have yet to name a possible suspect. (LinkedIn, Facebook/Meta)

It's a two-bedroom, two-bathroom home with few windows on the second floor.

Law enforcement officers seize evidence from the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Several neighbors expressed concern to Fox News Digital over the lack of new information in the case.

SLAIN NJ MOTHER 911 CALL MADE BY HER HUSBAND HAS FORENSIC EXPERT WARNING ONE MISTAKE COULD DERAIL FOCUS

Law enforcement officers remove evidence from the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026.  (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Investigators returning to the property had some residents hopeful for an arrest, neighbors said.

NEW JERSEY MOM’S SLAYING HAS NEIGHBORS ON EDGE WITH EVERY 'STRANGE NOISE’ NEARLY 7 WEEKS LATER

Investigators remove evidence from Conor Hanlon's home in Chester, N.J., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

One neighbor said, "I just want them to resolve this as soon as possible." She said seeing law enforcement return to the street on Wednesday, Nov. 4, brought tears to her eyes.

Police remove evidence from the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Hanlon's wife, Brooke Hanlon, was found dead in their home in June.  (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Robert Strang, a former FBI agent and private investigator, said law enforcement's return to the home months after the homicide could mean investigators have developed new leads and are looking for specific evidence, including DNA.

JONBENET RAMSEY MYSTERY REIGNITED BY LAB SCANDAL THAT ADDS PRESSURE TO UNLEASH DNA HELP DAD IS ‘BEGGING’ FOR

Investigators take evidence from Conor Hanlon's house in Chester, N.J., Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Strang – who is not affiliated with the case – said "the more people they talk to, the more information they get, the more reason they have to go back to try to identify DNA."

📩 Send me a story idea: kelsie.cairns@fox.com

Law enforcement personnel remove evidence from the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Several neighbors previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Conor Hanlon has been spending nights at the home.

"How do you sleep in that house?" one neighbor said.

'THAT WAS THE LAST I HEARD FROM HIM': SLAIN NJ THERAPIST’S NEIGHBOR RECALLS LAST CONTACT WITH HUSBAND

Investigators' vehicles sit along Pottersville Road in Chester, New Jersey, near the home where Brooke Hanlon was found stabbed to death. Her husband, Conor Hanlon, was seen speaking with officers Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, and has denied any involvement in her death. (Fox News Digital)

Hanlon has not been accused of any crime or wrongdoing, and has publicly denied any involvement in his wife's death. The Morris County Prosecutor's Office previously confirmed to Fox News Digital he has hired a private attorney.

SLAIN N.J. WOMAN, MISSING BAHAMAS BOATER'S SPOUSES LAWYER UP; ONE DISAPPEARS WHILE OTHER RECENTLY SPOTTED

One neighbor said she has seen Hanlon doing yard work, like cutting the grass and weed-whacking.

"Recently he’s been sitting outside quite a bit on that front porch," she said.

EXCLUSIVE PHOTOS, TIMELINE TRACE BROOKE HANLON'S LIFE AS FRIEND SAYS CASE IS 'SO UNUSUAL EVEN FOR A MURDER'

James "Conor" Hanlon's home, where his wife was murdered. A police cruiser parked in the driveway. New Jersey, Nov 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

"You would think, knowing that everybody drives by gawking at your house, that you’d sit in the back where people aren’t looking at you," the neighbor said.

Law enforcement personnel from multiple agencies arrive outside the home of Conor Hanlon in Chester, N.J., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

Neighbors confirmed that people frequently drive past the home, snapping photos and videos now that it has been the center of a murder mystery with national news coverage.

NJ HUSBAND BEGS FOR CPR HELP IN 911 CALL AFTER WIFE FOUND DEAD WITH STAB WOUNDS: AUDIO

A police cruiser parked in the driveway of the Hanlons' home in New Jersey, Nov 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

One resident who drives past the home on Pottersville Road during her commute to work said she has seen Conor Hanlon in a white SUV drive past her from time to time.

A police cruiser parked in the driveway of Conor Hanlon's home in New Jersey, Nov 5, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

DNA may not be the only thing that investigators are after at the house. Describing how investigators can use phone data, Strang said, "We have towers throughout New Jersey that can tell you what vicinity you were in at what time."

James "Conor" Hanlon's home, where his wife was murdered, is searched by police in New Jersey, Nov. 4, 2026.  (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

He explained that investigators may also examine the Hanlons' relationship and digital footprint.

"They are going to look at what the relationship was like. They are going to have their cellphones. They will have all their social media. They’ll look very deeply into their lifestyle. They talk to friends," he said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

There is an abundance of tools that investigators can use to pinpoint what may have motivated an alleged crime.

No arrests have been made in the killing of Brooke Hanlon at her Chester, New Jersey, home. (Fox News Digital)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

In gathering this information, he said it is not out of the ordinary that the prosecutor's office has been instructed to keep quiet – and shut media out.

The Morris County Prosecutor's Office has been investigating the Brooke Hanlon homicide case. (Google Maps)

Why? Strang predicts it's possible the unsolved homicide could "involve a grand jury." He went on to say, "This is a case where they don't want to make a mistake."A spokesperson for New Jersey Courts confirmed to Fox News Digital that "matters of a grand jury are kept secret unless and until there is a return of an indictment."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

WATCH: Conor Hanlon witnessed getting into white pickup truck in Boston.

Law enforcement has previously noted that there is no threat to the public – however a $1, 000 reward is still being offered to anyone who has information that could lead to an arrest.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Hanlon on numerous occasions but calls have not been returned.
