articles.title: New Orleans attorney fined $400,000 after exposing abusive priest says it was ‘worth it’
articles.excerpt:
Richard Trahant says accusers have been vindicated after Catholic church officially classifies Paul Hart as sex abuser

An attorney who was fined more than $400,000 after getting an abusive Roman Cath...
articles.body_text:
Richard Trahant says accusers have been vindicated after Catholic church officially classifies Paul Hart as sex abuser

An attorney who was fined more than $400,000 after getting an abusive Roman Catholic priest removed as a New Orleans high school’s chaplain says it was “worth it” now that the church has officially classified the cleric as a clergy molester.

That remark from Richard Trahant came days after the archdiocese of New Orleans, having waited years, added Paul Hart on 6 November to a list of Catholic priests and deacons faced with credible claims of clergy abuse while serving in the area.

The late Hart had previously dismissed news coverage of his admitted but largely unpunished sexual misconduct with a 17-year-old girl he met in the course of his ministry as “bogus” and “made-up”. But, while continuing to implement the terms of an agreement to settle a bankruptcy protection case that it filed amid the fallout of the Catholic church’s worldwide clergy abuse scandal, the New Orleans archdiocese ultimately included Hart on a list of more than 100 credibly accused priests and deacons – vindicating those who spoke out against him and his religious superiors.

“This is the very definition of a Pyrrhic victory,” Trahant said, invoking a phrase for something achieved at a high cost. “Sure, it’s exoneration – yet only after I paid a fortune.

“But if the question is: was it worth it? The answer is yes, and I would do it again tomorrow.”

Hart and Trahant were at the center of one of the most contentious chapters of the New Orleans archdiocese’s bankruptcy, which the institution filed in 2020.

Trahant’s work representing clergy abuse claimants whose cases became ensnared in the archdiocesan bankruptcy gave him access to documents chronicling how Hart had secretly admitted to his supervisors that he had sexual contact with a 17-year-old girl in the early 1990s after meeting her through his role as a priest.

In 2012, she reported Hart to the church for that behavior and confessed to it during a confidential internal investigation, according to hundreds of legal documents obtained and reviewed by the Guardian.

An advisory board working with New Orleans’s archbishop at the time, Gregory Aymond, recommended removing Hart from public ministry, saying the case victimized someone who was considered a minor under canon – or church – law since 2002.

But Aymond let Hart continue his ministry because in the early 1990s the age of consent under canon law was 16. And Louisiana law sets the age of consent at 17.

Aymond then appointed Hart to serve as chaplain at Brother Martin after the New Orleans Catholic high school asked for one in 2017.

“Please know that I not only appreciate your ministry but will pray for you that God will use you to be a sign of pastoral care to our young people,” Aymond wrote to Hart after appointing him to Brother Martin, an all boys’ school where there are activities that girls can participate in.

Hart was still in that role toward the end of 2021 when Trahant became aware of his past. He notified Brother Martin’s principal – coincidentally, Trahant’s cousin – that Hart had “a credible allegation from [his] past that involved a minor”.

Also, Trahant emailed this journalist to keep Hart on his “radar”. But he would not elaborate to either Gallagher or this journalist, citing a bankruptcy court confidentiality order, according to the legal documents stemming from the case.

Aymond and the archdiocese soon provided Brother Martin with the details about Hart’s past misconduct. And he retired in January 2022, nine months before his death, after Brother Martin requested that Aymond remove him from its campus.

Meanwhile, using methods and sources exclusive of Trahant, this journalist wrote an article in New Orleans’s Times-Picayune newspaper detailing the circumstances of Hart’s departure – though the archdiocese insisted the priest had retired because of “struggles with treatment for brain cancer”.

The federal judge in charge of the archdiocese’s bankruptcy, Meredith Grabill, later ruled what Trahant had done set off a chain of events that was enough to constitute a confidentiality order violation. She fined him $400,000 – which eventually grew by $60,000 because of interest. And she expelled four of Trahant’s clients from a committee of clergy abuse survivors helping negotiate an archdiocesan bankruptcy settlement, contending that it would aid the group’s functioning.

Grabill so acted despite a court investigation which she ordered having determined that Brother Martin got the specifics about what Hart had done from the archdiocese – not Trahant, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.

Court investigators also conceded there was evidence supporting Trahant’s denial that he ever provided any confidential information to this journalist.

Trahant unsuccessfully appealed his fine from Grabill up to the US supreme court. But the supreme court declined to hear his case in June, months after Aymond’s retirement as New Orleans archbishop – so he paid the levy.

Aymond’s successor, archbishop James Checchio, on 6 November then added 27 priests and deacons to a list of credibly accused clergymen which the New Orleans archdiocese first released in 2018, calling it a step toward “accountability and healing”. The list now had 106 names after the update – a key provision of an agreement announced in December 2025 requiring the archdiocese and its insurers to eventually pay $305m to hundreds of clergy abuse survivors to resolve the bankruptcy.

Hart’s name being listed immediately leapt out at Trahant, he said.

The archdiocese said that records associated with Hart and all others on the credibly accused list would be kept at a public archive hosted by Louisiana State University. A release of such records for Hart would mean none of the information in them was ever confidential, according to Trahant.

Trahant also said he interpreted Hart’s inclusion on the credibly accused list – and a notation that he had three claims filed against him in the bankruptcy – as an admission that archdiocese and court officials had mishandled his case. Furthermore, he said it was perhaps the ultimate repudiation of one of Hart’s last known statements – telling bankruptcy court investigators that news media reporting on his departure from Brother Martin was “so bogus that it looked … almost made up”.

“He was lying,” said Trahant, mentioning that he is contemplating seeking further legal action out of principle to attempt to recoup his fine and the costs he incurred fighting it. “And … now they’ve admitted [it].”

Separately, one of the Trahant clients who was ousted from the bankruptcy settlement committee said Checchio could “truly” promote accountability by apologizing to the advocate and returning the fine money to him.

“At least [now], everyone knows that we were wrongly removed,” James Adams said. “The court sanctioned an innocent lawyer and his clients.”

articles.title: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
articles.excerpt:
181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report

Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying ga...
articles.body_text:
181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report

Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.

Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.

The report was published on Wednesday as global leaders gathered in Turkey for the 31st UN climate summit, where increasing electrification – ideally from clean sources – is a central part of discussions. However, a number of key European leaders, including from France and Germany, will not be at Cop31, instead heading to Dublin where EU leaders will hold their first dedicated AI summit on Friday.

Mark Daly, the head of datacentres and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said: “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on datacentre developers.

“The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”

By 2035, the electricity demand of AI datacentres was predicted to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours – equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand – the report said.

AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cool equipment, and to run facility systems.

Daly said while the developers of the future datacentres claimed their gas-fired power supplies would be temporary while they waited for grid connections, once they were online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk.

The report said ensuring new datacentres were connected to the grid was the more sustainable option. Faster grid connections were crucial to limiting emissions impacts and locking in fossil fuel risk, it said.

UK planned datacentres made more than 100 inquiries in 2024-5 to connect to gas as a result of delays in securing access to the electricity grid, according to Future Energy Networks, the representative body for the UK gas networks.

For example, Wapseys Wood, Buckinghamshire and Quest Park, Bedfordshire are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations because of the long wait to connect to the grid. The datacentres are among the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project regime, which allows developers to rapidly deliver major infrastructure, bypassing locally elected planning authorities.

But the use of fossil fuel power generation on site is likely to be repeated by many more UK sites after the chancellor, John Healey, gave the green light for datacentres to build and run temporary on-site fossil fuel power stations while they wait for connections to the grid, as part of a so-called datacentre covenant.

Oliver Hayes, the head of policy and campaigns at Global Action Plan , said: “Private gas power stations for datacentres should be a red line for any government serious about climate action, so it’s shocking to see the chancellor give them his explicit backing.

“No one seriously believes these gas power stations will be temporary – once they’re built, they’ll lock in high emissions for years.”

articles.title: ELI FEDERMAN: A boycott backfired when Philadelphia showed up for Jewish businesses
articles.excerpt:
Mac Mart Cart owner Marti Lieberman discusses the community support her business received after being named in a Philadelphia anti-Israel protest flyer on 'America's Newsroom.'

The best response to a...
articles.body_text:
Mac Mart Cart owner Marti Lieberman discusses the community support her business received after being named in a Philadelphia anti-Israel protest flyer on 'America's Newsroom.'

The best response to antisemitism isn’t censorship. It’s philosemitism and exposing the truth.

I learned about the protests targeting Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia on Nov. 8 when my friend Ari Engel posted on social media about going out to eat to support those establishments.

In Philadelphia, anti-Israel protesters organized a bicycle demonstration targeting six Jewish-owned restaurants and calling for a boycott. They wanted to discourage people from patronizing these businesses.

PHILLY DSA DECRIES BACKLASH OVER BOYCOTT TARGETING JEWISH EATERIES

Instead, the community turned their boycott upside down with a deluge of support and patronage for those Jewish-owned businesses.

Demonstrators and counter-protesters confront each other during a protest ride organized by Philly Bike on Your Left around Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia, Pa., Nov. 8. (Bastiaan Slabbers/Reuters)

The timing of the protest was chilling as it took place on the eve of the 88th anniversary of Kristallnacht, when Nazis attacked Jewish businesses, shattered storefronts and terrorized Jewish communities across Germany and Austria.

ANTI-ISRAEL SOCIALIST SILENT ON JEWISH BUSINESS BOYCOTT IN DISTRICT HE'S SET TO REPRESENT

Jewish organizations mobilized supporters in Philadelphia. The ADL encouraged people to eat at the targeted restaurants. JewBelong erected billboards urging residents to boycott the boycott. Hundreds of people showed up, packed restaurants and formed lines around city blocks. One restaurant worried it wouldn’t have enough food to serve everyone.

The protesters wanted to drive customers away. Instead, they drove customers in.

I’M AN ARAB MUSLIM — I STILL DON’T UNDERSTAND THE ANTISEMITIC BDS MOVEMENT

There’s a profound lesson here about the power of free expression. The protesters exercised their freedom to call for a boycott. The community exercised its freedom to reject it. Rather than demand censorship, ordinary citizens used their voices, their presence and their purchasing power to challenge prejudice.

That’s how a free society should work. We don’t need to silence hateful ideas to defeat them. We can expose them, challenge them and let them lose in the marketplace of public opinion. Censorship can turn extremists into martyrs. Public rejection can reveal just how little support their ideas command.

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

And when non-Jewish neighbors stand alongside Jewish neighbors, antisemitism loses something essential: the illusion that it speaks for the majority.

Of course, criticizing Israel or advocating a political boycott isn’t inherently antisemitic. But targeting Jews because of their identity or holding them collectively responsible for Israel crosses a moral line. We can defend the right to peaceful protest while vigorously confronting prejudice.

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

We need more than opposition to antisemitism. We need proactive philosemitism: people of every background celebrating Jewish culture, supporting Jewish neighbors and embracing Jewish life.

There’s a profound lesson here about the power of free expression. The protesters exercised their freedom to call for a boycott. The community exercised its freedom to reject it. Rather than demand censorship, ordinary citizens used their voices, their presence and their purchasing power to challenge prejudice.

And solidarity shouldn’t end when the protesters go home. Keep visiting those restaurants. Build friendships. Learn about one another. Turn a moment of outrage into lasting relationships.

The answer to people who want Jewish businesses to disappear isn’t to silence the protesters. It’s to fill those businesses with customers.

They organized a boycott. Philadelphia organized a food crawl.

That’s how you turn hatred into solidarity and let antisemitism defeat itself.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ELI FEDERMAN

Eli Federman has written at the Wall Street Journal, New York Times, USA Today, New York Post, Reuters, and others on society and religion. X: @elifederman

articles.title: Common heart pill under scrutiny for older patients as study weighs risks of stopping
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan when deciding whether to continue statin use.

Some older adults may...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan when deciding whether to continue statin use.

Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety.

That’s according to a randomized clinical trial that was presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago, and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. They are known to help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.

COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The study – conducted by researchers from the University of Bern in Switzerland, the University of California, San Francisco, and other institutions – included 1,880 adults aged 70 years and older, all of whom were taking statins to prevent a first heart attack or stroke.

Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety. (iStock)

All participants had at least two chronic medical conditions, but did not have established cardiovascular disease or previous cardiovascular events. Half of the participants stopped taking statins, and the other half continued.

After two years, the added risk from stopping statins was small enough to fall within the limits researchers had set for the study. However, that did not mean stopping carried no added risk.

5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON

Over the full follow-up, which lasted about two years for the typical participant and up to four years for some, about 13% of those assigned to stop statins had a heart attack, an ischemic stroke or died from any cause, compared with 9% assigned to continue treatment.

The study’s safety monitoring board also recommended that participants who were assigned to stop statins discuss restarting treatment with their healthcare team, according to the American College of Cardiology.

Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. (iStock)

For other outcomes, the researchers found no meaningful differences between the two groups in reported quality of life, muscle pain, falls, or loss of muscle mass and strength.

Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized that continuing statins did not worsen reported muscle pain or quality of life in the trial.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Although guidelines support lowering high cholesterol earlier in life, the benefits of continuing statins in older age are less certain, said study author Dr. Rita F. Redberg, a cardiology professor at the University of California, San Francisco, in a press release.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population."

Earlier studies found no difference in mortality after adults 70 and older stopped statins for primary prevention, she noted.

"One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins," Redberg said, adding that her team explored whether stopping was safe for older adults taking the drugs to prevent a first cardiovascular event.

The study had several limitations. About 14% of participants did not stick with their assigned treatment plan. Some who were told to stop taking statins resumed them, while others assigned to continue treatment stopped taking the drugs, according to the researchers.

The findings also may not apply to all older adults, as the study was limited to people aged 70 and older who had multiple chronic health conditions but no history of heart disease or stroke.

Although some participants were followed for up to four years, the study primarily assessed outcomes over about two years. Longer follow-up is needed to determine how stopping statins affects patients over many years.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," Redberg said.

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication," the researcher said. (iStock)

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Kelly, who was not involved in the study, noted that a healthy 70-year-old could live another 20 years, leaving questions about the effects of stopping treatment over that longer period.

The doctor also emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan, noting that he "errs on the side of caution" with his own patients.

"I typically recommend that they continue taking it unless they have specific concerns about that medication, such as side effects, or if they are taking a lot of medicines, and they're just really eager to stop taking one of them."

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

articles.title: The election is over: It's time for young Jews to step up and lead
articles.excerpt:
Jewish Student Union leaders, educators and student activists equip high schoolers with the tools to face antisemitism, defend their identity and stay proudly Jewish on campus.

A week has passed sinc...
articles.body_text:
Jewish Student Union leaders, educators and student activists equip high schoolers with the tools to face antisemitism, defend their identity and stay proudly Jewish on campus.

A week has passed since Election Day. The votes have been counted. But no election can decide how proudly we live as Jews, how we support one another or what kind of leaders we become. Those decisions belong to us.

As the former student body president at the University of California, Santa Barbara, I know what it means to lead while your Jewish identity becomes a target.

My experience, featured in the documentary "October 8," taught me how urgently institutions need to confront antisemitism — and how much courage it can take to speak up when they fail. It also taught me that we cannot put our lives or our leadership on hold until someone else finds that courage.

JEWISH TEENS PREPARE TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM ON CAMPUS WITH HISTORY, HUMOR AND COURAGE

Jewish students at El Camino Real Charter High School during a walkout protesting antisemitic incidents at the Woodland Hills school in 2024. (Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images)

Recently at the Jewish Student Union Presidents Conference in Stamford, Connecticut, I saw hundreds of Jewish high school students putting that principle into practice.

They had gathered as the country headed into Election Day. But their leadership did not depend on who would win.

They were already building Jewish communities in their schools. Already taking responsibility for something larger than themselves. Already choosing to show up.

I recognized myself in them. I am a Jewish Student Union alumna. Before I became a student body president, I needed opportunities to understand my Jewish identity, develop my voice and discover that I had something worth contributing.

BACK TO SCHOOL SHOULD NOT MEAN BACK TO FEAR FOR JEWISH STUDENTS

Demonstrators draped in Israeli and US flags at a rally for tolerance. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Returning to speak with these students reminded me why that early investment matters. Leadership grows through practice: inviting someone to a first meeting, organizing a program, asking a difficult question or standing beside a classmate who feels alone. Those actions can seem small. For the person on the receiving end, they can change everything.

Too often, we talk about young Jews only in terms of what is happening to them. The harassment they face. The friendships they lose. The pressure they feel to distance themselves from Israel or explain away a part of who they are.

Those experiences deserve attention. Antisemitism must be exposed and confronted. But young Jews also deserve to be seen for what they are creating.

CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS

Students at Columbia University participate in an anti-Israel protest. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

In Stamford, I saw students developing the skills and relationships that will shape their schools now and their college campuses later. They were learning to lead before a crisis demanded it of them.

That preparation matters. A strong Jewish identity gives us something to draw on when others challenge our belonging. A community gives us people to turn to. The experience of speaking up once can help us do it again. We should be giving more young Jews those opportunities. We should also make room for the joy that makes Jewish life worth building in the first place.

A student who encounters the Jewish community through music, sports or a celebration may discover a connection that a discussion about antisemitism could never provide. Those experiences give us friendships, memories and reasons to keep showing up for one another.

People waiting in a line to vote. (Rawpixel/Getty Images)

Last week’s Omer Adam concert at Barclays Center offered a powerful example: thousands of people gathering around Hebrew music, Jewish pride and a shared connection to Israel. Among those celebrating were wounded Israeli warriors. Their presence brought another dimension to that joy: the opportunity to stand alongside people who have sacrificed so much and welcome them into a shared celebration.

That is why I want to thank Warriors of Israel, which supports Israel’s wounded warriors. Its work reminds us that building a Jewish community means taking responsibility for one another, including helping those living with the consequences of their service find support, connection and joy.

For young Jewish leaders, there is a lesson in that kind of commitment. We can build communities that celebrate who we are while making sure people who need us feel included and supported. That spirit belongs in our schools and on our campuses, too.

Jewish advocate Tessa Veksler talks to a high school student at the Jewish Student Union's annual Presidents Convention in November 2026. (Warren Cohn)

We need Jewish life that welcomes people in. We need students who know how to organize, build friendships across differences and explain what they believe. We need leaders who can confront hatred without allowing it to consume their entire sense of purpose.

None of this releases elected officials or university administrators from their responsibilities. They must enforce rules against threats and harassment. They must confront antisemitism within their own political circles. Jewish students have every right to demand accountability from the institutions that serve them.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Pro-Israel activist Naftoli Sherman records a video during a pro-Palestine rally at UCLA to protest ICE's detention of Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil, in Los Angeles, California, on March 11, 2025. (Juliana Yamada / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

And we can make those demands while taking responsibility for the communities we want to build. Run for student government. Start the club your school is missing. Invite the student who is hesitant to join. Learn enough about your history to speak about it with confidence — and enough about someone else’s experience to listen with care.

You do not need a title to begin. You need a willingness to act and the humility to keep learning. The students I met in Stamford will enter a world full of challenges. They will also enter it with ideas, conviction and the ability to make a difference.

My message to them, and to young Jews across this country, is simple: Become the leaders you want to see in the world, regardless of who holds political office.

Tessa Veksler is an advocate and national spokesperson for NCSY’s Jewish Student Union.

articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Supreme Court justices confront what it will take to keep America's founding freedoms alive
articles.excerpt: Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett reflect on America's founding principles and urge Americans to embrace civic education and engagement to preserve the nation's freedoms for...
articles.body_text:
Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett reflect on America's founding principles and urge Americans to embrace civic education and engagement to preserve the nation's freedoms for future generations. (Federalist Society)

FIRST ON FOX: As America celebrates 250 years of independence this year, three conservative Supreme Court justices are warning that preserving the nation's founding freedoms for future generations depends on Americans understanding their history, embracing civic education and actively participating in their system of government.

Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett each implored Americans to familiarize themselves with their system of government and the history behind it to ensure that the nation’s legacy is preserved.

Though the three conservative justices were united in their call for civic education, they each approached the topic differently in a series of interviews filmed by the Federalist Society and obtained by Fox News Digital. The videos come ahead of the Federalist Society's 2026 National Lawyers Convention this week, which spotlights "250 Years of American Exceptionalism."

Gorsuch, for instance, struck a distinctly religious tone.

GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK

Supreme Court Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch discussing America's 250th anniversary. (Federalist Society)

"I think it's very easy to take the rights granted in our Constitution and the ideals expressed in the Declaration for granted," he said. "They are, for us, a little bit like the air we breathe and the water a fish might swim in. They seem natural to us, but they weren't in 1776. The ideas in the Declaration of Independence that all of us are created equal, that every one of us has God-given rights — they don't come from government, they come from God."

Gorsuch, who was appointed to the court by President Donald Trump in 2017 following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, went on to describe the importance of historical study to the preservation of the American way of life.

THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER

Chief Justice of the Supreme Court John Roberts, Justice Elena Kagan, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, Justice Amy Coney Barrett and retired Justice Anthony Kennedy attend President Donald Trump's address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Pool via REUTERS)

"Our country is a blessing from God, and that we owe great thanks for it, and we have great responsibility for it," he went on. "The reason why our Constitution and Declaration have survived is because people choose it anew in every generation. You need to know its history. You need to know what you're preserving. Daniel Webster said it took 6,000 years for us to generate a system of government like this. Don't expect that to happen easily or again."

Kavanaugh, similarly, emphasized the importance of education.

"I think our education system is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that in the next 250 years, we preserve this republic and improve upon this republic. So, teaching American history, teaching the values of this country, the history of this country, why this country exists, how this country has been preserved, how this country has been improved over time, for example, by our constitutional amendment process and otherwise," the justice, appointed to the bench following a tumultuous confirmation process in 2018, said.

"And I think all of us should be constantly striving to ensure civics education, not only for our youth, but for all of us, and that we constantly are learning and participating in our system of government," he continued.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

John Roberts, chief justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, from left, Elena Kagan, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, Brett Kavanaugh, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, and Amy Coney Barrett, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, during a State of the Union address in the House chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Federalist Society filmed its interviews ahead of its National Lawyers Convention, which will bring together minds from across the conservative legal movement to discuss matters deemed pressing.

While not interviewed by the Federalist Society, Justice Sonia Sotomayor shared her thoughts on America's 250th anniversary during an event at Mount Vernon's Washington Library, taking a slightly darker tone than her conservative colleagues.

During her talk, which centered primarily on civic engagement, Sotomayor argued that the United States is in a rough place at the moment and that it would take "some hard work" for it to get back on an "even keel."

"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

Barrett, meanwhile, focused on the Declaration of Independence and how she believes it should inspire civic participation today.

"We're not passive observers in the American project. We're participants in it. It is our project," she said. "I might suggest that people look at the last line of the Declaration of Independence. It ends with a mutual pledge in which the signatories to the document mutually pledge their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor to the success of the American project. And they made good on that promise. Some lost their fortune, lost their property to loyalists ... and they pledged with their honor not to deviate from the commitments that they had made in signing the Declaration of Independence."

"Surely that's the kind of commitment that it takes to have it keep going forward," said Barrett.

Gorsuch, who was appointed to the court by President Donald Trump in 2017 following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, went on to describe the importance of historical study to the preservation of the American way of life.

THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER

Chief Justice of the Supreme Court John Roberts, Justice Elena Kagan, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, Justice Amy Coney Barrett and retired Justice Anthony Kennedy attend President Donald Trump's address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Pool via REUTERS)

"Our country is a blessing from God, and that we owe great thanks for it, and we have great responsibility for it," he went on. "The reason why our Constitution and Declaration have survived is because people choose it anew in every generation. You need to know its history. You need to know what you're preserving. Daniel Webster said it took 6,000 years for us to generate a system of government like this. Don't expect that to happen easily or again."

Kavanaugh, similarly, emphasized the importance of education.

"I think our education system is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that in the next 250 years, we preserve this republic and improve upon this republic. So, teaching American history, teaching the values of this country, the history of this country, why this country exists, how this country has been preserved, how this country has been improved over time, for example, by our constitutional amendment process and otherwise," the justice, appointed to the bench following a tumultuous confirmation process in 2018, said.

"And I think all of us should be constantly striving to ensure civics education, not only for our youth, but for all of us, and that we constantly are learning and participating in our system of government," he continued.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

John Roberts, chief justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, from left, Elena Kagan, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, Brett Kavanaugh, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, and Amy Coney Barrett, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, during a State of the Union address in the House chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Federalist Society filmed its interviews ahead of its National Lawyers Convention, which will bring together minds from across the conservative legal movement to discuss matters deemed pressing.

While not interviewed by the Federalist Society, Justice Sonia Sotomayor shared her thoughts on America's 250th anniversary during an event at Mount Vernon's Washington Library, taking a slightly darker tone than her conservative colleagues.

During her talk, which centered primarily on civic engagement, Sotomayor argued that the United States is in a rough place at the moment and that it would take "some hard work" for it to get back on an "even keel."

"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

Barrett, meanwhile, focused on the Declaration of Independence and how she believes it should inspire civic participation today.

"We're not passive observers in the American project. We're participants in it. It is our project," she said. "I might suggest that people look at the last line of the Declaration of Independence. It ends with a mutual pledge in which the signatories to the document mutually pledge their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor to the success of the American project. And they made good on that promise. Some lost their fortune, lost their property to loyalists ... and they pledged with their honor not to deviate from the commitments that they had made in signing the Declaration of Independence."

"Surely that's the kind of commitment that it takes to have it keep going forward," said Barrett.

articles.title: Ukraine-Russia talks end with deal on prisoner swap, but Moscow remains cool on European involvement – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
US negotiators to meet Putin in Moscow, Zelenskyy in Dublin next

Russia’s chief negotiator ⁠at Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi Vladimir ⁠Medinsky said ​after their conclusion that mutual understandi...
articles.body_text:
US negotiators to meet Putin in Moscow, Zelenskyy in Dublin next

Russia’s chief negotiator ⁠at Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi Vladimir ⁠Medinsky said ​after their conclusion that mutual understanding ⁠had been achieved on some issues and that more ⁠talks would be held.

Medinsky, ​in ‌remarks broadcast ‌on Russian state television, said that ‌Russia and Ukraine had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap, the latest in a long line of ‌such exchanges.

He was cool however on the ​prospect of European countries joining the talks and said it was unclear what ⁠there was for Russia and the ​European ​Union to ​discuss, given what he ​said ‌was a lack ​of ​proposals from the European side, Reuters reported.

Meanwhile, just a quick update on Italy: the country’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the email bomb alerts sent to school (11:36) pose no danger, but police and other public bodies were monitoring the situation.

“These reports appear to be part of a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern – a matter that is currently under thorough investigation,” she said.

Meloni will chair a meeting on the situation later today to assess what may need to be done after “hundreds” of schools saw their plans for today disrupted by the alarm.

A large number of schools in Northern Ireland were also ​sent a threatening email, the Northern Ireland ‌Education Authority said, via Reuters, but have been advised to stay open as the authority said police did not regard it as ‌a credible threat.

Kushner also said he thought “it would be great” for Zelenskyy and Putin to meet in person to hold further talks, but acknowledged “the Russians have said they would like to see more progress made before that happens.”

“Clearly, there’s not great trust or love between the leaders,m so I think that if we can find a pathway to arrange…I will say this, … these deals do take time.”

Kushner also acknowledged that there is “no trust between the sides and that’s to be expected after a conflict like this,” but he hoped he could make progress on that.

He said it is important to have Europe at the table for any discussions on Ukraine and postwar security as “it’s a discussion where they have to be involved,” and pointedly praised his engagement with top Europeans so far.

He said he hoped Putin would “give his blessing” to expanding the format during their meeting in Moscow.

Speaking after today’s talks, US negotiator (and Donald Trump’s son-in-law) Jared Kushner described the discussions as “very substantive,” even if “pretty tough … after almost eight months of not being together.”

He said he and peace envoy Steve Witkoff would meet Putin in Moscow on Thursday to “go over what was discussed today and try to make progress on some of the issues that we discussed.”

Afterwards, they will fly to Dublin to meet with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy “to debrief with him and further explore some of the ideas that we came up with today,” he said.

Zelenskyy will be in Dublin at the European Political Community summit, alongside other EU leaders.

Kushner said he also hoped to “finalise the humanitarian relief” and “the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners” during tomorrow’s meeting with Putin.

He said the US was also working to “try and see if we can get the Europeans added to the format so that we can make this a multilateral format,” praising already existing discussions with European partners, including the EU, Nato, France, Germany, Italy, and the UK.

Kushner said the key issues revolve around “postwar security” and “security guarantees,” as well as “deconfliction” and monitoring any future ceasefire.

But he acknowledged that “the territorial issues … will be the hardest.”

Meanwhile, David Arakhamia, a close ally ‌of president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and ​the head of his faction ⁠in parliament, said he hoped to keep up “good momentum” in the talks with a view of reaching a solution by the end of the year.

Russia’s chief negotiator ⁠at Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi Vladimir ⁠Medinsky said ​after their conclusion that mutual understanding ⁠had been achieved on some issues and that more ⁠talks would be held.

Medinsky, ​in ‌remarks broadcast ‌on Russian state television, said that ‌Russia and Ukraine had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap, the latest in a long line of ‌such exchanges.

He was cool however on the ​prospect of European countries joining the talks and said it was unclear what ⁠there was for Russia and the ​European ​Union to ​discuss, given what he ​said ‌was a lack ​of ​proposals from the European side, Reuters reported.

Meanwhile, we are getting some lines from those present at the Abu Dhabi talks participating in the Ukrainian, Russian, and US delegations.

Zelenskyy also turns to Russia’s demands for security guarantees.

He points out that is not obvious given “no one has attacked Russia for many decades,” and yet “since the second world war, Russia has not gone through even one decade without starting a war or using military force against another country.”

“So when the Russians now talk about a security architecture for themselves, or about security guarantees for Russia, they are hardly talking about real security and peace.

What they really want is to freely interfere in the affairs of other countries, and to use force whenever they want, and to make sure that no one can support liberty inside Russia, because Putin wants to keep his personal power forever and pass on his imperialist and in many ways, simply fascist views to the next generations.”

He also says clearly that Europe “must be at the table” of any talks on ending the war in Ukraine, warning that “whenever Europe does not believe in its own strength, others try to impose their decisions on us.”

He gets warm applause and a standing ovation at the end of his speech.

Zelenskyy also talks about the need for Europe to develop “its own anti-ballistic defence programme,” Freyja to become independent of deliveries from overseas (mostly the US).

He also mentions the importance of drone technologies and learning from Ukraine’s real-life experience.

Zelenskyy brings up the Abu Dhabi discussions, but in quite general terms.

“Yesterday and today our Ukrainian team together with American team has been talking to the Russians in Abu Dhabi.

Putin started this war thinking he could break Ukraine in just days or few weeks. But here we are in the fifth year of the full scale war. The Russians have to sit across from our representatives and have to listen to Ukraine and to talk to us as equals about what comes next. They wanted to decide Ukraine’s future without us, without Ukrainian people, but they failed.”

Zelenskyy says the strait of Hormuz crisis creates a dangerous precedent, asking “what if Russia tries to do the same in Baltic Sea”?

“What if someone tries to repeat what happened in the Strait of Hormuz, this time in other major shipping routes and straits around the world? And who will protect European interests?”

He says the Iran crisis also has an effect on Ukraine, as is experiencing “the shortages of weapons we need for our defence.”

“Today, everyone in the world can see just how connected everything is in our world. Nothing stays local. Nothing. Especially wars and injustice,” he warns.

Zelenskyy then begins his speech proper, with a much more sombre point about the war in Ukraine.

He says that on 11 November, “people in many European countries remember those who lost their lives in war on the anniversary of the end of the first world war.”

“This is not just some distant history, unfortunately. What is happening in the world today brings our thoughts, our feelings, our fears back to those times when Europe and the whole world were turned upside down.”

He says “Russia has fallen for the same illusion as back then more than a hundred years ago. The illusion that it could simply grab more land, a few more colonies, more power and influence at the cost of Ukrainians independence.”

He also points to the events in the Middle East as an additional destabilising element, warning against “rising energy prices” and “one of the worst cost of living crises.”

Zelenskyy also jokes that given the warm relations between Denmark and Ukraine, he regrets the two countries “do not share a border.”

“You have much better neighbours,” he says in a swipe at Russia.

“After all, we have Russia as our neighbour and having a neighbour like Denmark is something any country would dream of right now.”

He then lands another joke about the US and Donald Trump:

“Maybe when someone in America wanted Greenland, he didn’t even realise that what he really wanted was not the land, but to become a little more Danish. And who knows, maybe that was exactly what he needed.”

Zelenskyy begins with words of thanks to PM Frederiksen and to Denmark on behalf of the Ukrainian people.

He opens with an interesting US-themed dig, as he notes he is the first foreign leader to address the Folketinget.

“I‘ve heard that many leaders wanted to be here, to speak here. One of them was even the president of the United States.

That was back in 1997. In the end, the American president spoke to the Danish people in the different place.”

Zelenskyy is now getting ready to address the Danish parliament.

I will bring you the key lines here, or you can watch along:

Back in Abu Dhabi, the Ukrainian negotiating team is now meeting with the European and US envoys for a debrief after the earlier trilateral meeting, a Kyiv delegation source told AFP.

articles.title: Senate Republicans plan 54-day blitz to push Trump's agenda before Democrats seize power
articles.excerpt:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune discusses lessons he’s taking from the midterms and his future as the GOP’s leader in the U.S. Senate on ‘Special Report.’

With their leadership elections settled, S...
articles.body_text:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune discusses lessons he’s taking from the midterms and his future as the GOP’s leader in the U.S. Senate on ‘Special Report.’

With their leadership elections settled, Senate Republicans are gearing up to "maximize" their remaining time in power before Senate Democrats take over next year.

All eyes are again on Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who was re-elected to another term as the Republican leader. Shortly after winning, Thune declared that he and the Senate GOP were "committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can."

"That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we're here, the number of hours we're here, the number of votes we may end up taking," Thune said. "But we are going to finish this legislative session strong."

SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., conducts a news conference in the U.S. Capitol after winning the minority leader position for the 120th Congress in Senate Republican leadership elections on Nov. 10, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

The Senate was initially set to be in roughly 20 days from Tuesday until the changing of the guard, but Republicans are now squeezing the juice out of every last minute to ram through must-pass legislation, dozens of President Donald Trump’s nominees and more.

And Republicans agreed to hold themselves to that sprint until the end of the year at the tail end of their marathon closed-door meeting on Tuesday.

Lawmakers plan to "maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3," according to a resolution agreed to in the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital.

Another crack at budget reconciliation could be the trickiest part of their ambitious year-end gauntlet, particularly depending on what lawmakers try to cram into the process.

GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS

"I think we've got to keep it realistic to probably have any chance of passing, pretty narrow," Thune told Fox News Digital.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who chairs the Senate Budget Committee responsible for developing the scaffolding around the process, told Fox News Digital that he intended to present his plan to Republicans during their lunchtime meeting on Wednesday.

It’s also where Republicans are considering one last attempt at getting the SAVE America Act, or a version of it that could pass muster with the Senate rules referee.

"Oh yeah, that'd be part of it, you know, to provide funding for states for election integrity type of measures," Johnson said.

Defense funding will be another major task for Republicans, given that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats are determined to use Congress’ power over the nation’s purse strings as a way to choke off spending on the Iran war.

SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., conducts a news conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee about Democrats taking control of the House and Senate in the midterm election on Nov. 4, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Thune acknowledged that reconciliation could be another landing spot for Pentagon dollars to flow, but hoped Democrats would choose a different route.

"It's going to depend on whether or not they have any of their members who are persuaded that making sure that we have enough munitions and ammo and weaponry to be able to defend the country is a priority," Thune said. "I hope they do, in which case maybe we won't have to go down that path, but we're scoping it out right now."

One of the White House’s top priorities, and at the top of Thune’s to-do list, is confirming a slate of judicial and executive branch nominees. As of Tuesday, there were 23 judicial nominees, many of whom still needed to go through committee, and nearly 100 executive branch nominees that need confirmation.

There is a slew of other high-priority items that were punted to the lame duck, like the National Defense Authorization Act, a bipartisan permitting reform package and keeping the government funded.

Preventing another shutdown, or at least hammering out a deal, could be tricky given how the political winds shifted after the election.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., who serves on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Fox News Digital that "where we can clear the decks, the better," to fund the government.

"I know that prior to the election that was the thought of some of our Democratic colleagues as well, but we have to be able to work together to get some of that done," Britt said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: CFP reaction: Alabama feels the love, Indiana gets the shaft and Big 12 gets relief as committee confuses us
articles.excerpt:
"They're not keeping them out. And you look at their schedule, they've got SMU, Boston College, and Syracuse in the season. Their toughest game out of that three is going to be SMU."

The second week ...
articles.body_text:
"They're not keeping them out. And you look at their schedule, they've got SMU, Boston College, and Syracuse in the season. Their toughest game out of that three is going to be SMU."

The second week of the College Football Playoff rankings have been released, and controversy once again reigns around the CFP committee thanks to Big Ten and SEC placement.

What was going to happen to teams like Ole Miss and Kentucky, who both suffered bad losses this past weekend against Georgia and Tennessee respectively?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL SELLS ANOTHER PIECE OF ITS SOUL WITH CFP OFFICIALLY EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS

Now, with former No. 1 ranked Miami taking its first loss of the season and dropping to No. 7 in the latest poll, Georgia was the obvious choice to take over the top spot this week, though Utah could have made a strong case as well after beating a Top-10 BYU team at home.

But, as the regular season comes to an end over the next three weeks, there are plenty of valid concerns coming from conferences like the Big Ten and Big 12.

LSU head coach Lane Kiffin reacts during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Mississippi State in Baton Rouge, La., on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Matthew Hinton)

And then we have the SEC, which currently has five teams ranked within the top-12, led by No. 1 Georgia, No. 3 Alabama, No. 6 Texas, No. 8 Tennessee and No. 11 Kentucky.

If the Wildcats were to catch another loss this season, the arguments are going to be made about the margin of defeat, and that's one kerfuffle. I don't know if Kentucky could win against other conference teams.

As for the Tennessee versus Alabama argument, I think we can put a pin in that one for now. The CFP committee is not going to rank the Vols ahead of the Tide, based off the number of quality wins Alabama has compared to Tennessee.

And yes, the Vols defeated Alabama by sixteen points last month.

"Alabama was in that first pool, Tennessee was not in that first pool ... If you look at their schedule compared to Alabama's schedule, the committee feels like Alabama has a stronger schedule," CFP's Hunter Yurachek noted.

What happens with a team like No. 19 Ole Miss, who has wins against two top-25 opponents?

They are essentially eliminated from the postseason, unless a miracle happens. The lopsided losses to Georgia and Florida, with the close loss against Texas has them needing help from others with a trip to Oklahoma this weekend, followed by games against Wofford and Mississippi State.

13TH-RANKED TENNESSEE DISMANTLES SIXTH-RANKED KENTUCKY TO STAY ALIVE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RACE

What about No. 21 LSU? After the loss to Alabama this past weekend, Lane Kiffin's squad is barely hanging onto CFP hope. If the Tigers were to win out (Texas, Tennessee, Arkansas), that would mean two wins against what should be Top-10 teams to wrap the season.

Would the Tigers deserve a spot over a two-loss team? The new ranking on Tuesday night is deserved. Sure, if they were to win out, which would include wins against two Top-10 teams, maybe the conversation changes in the last week.

Indiana head coach Curt Cignetti paces the sideline as his team plays Nebraska during the first half of an NCAA college football game Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, in Lincoln, Neb. (AP Photo/Rebecca S. Gratz)

The bigger questions now turn to how many teams can the Big Ten get into the postseason over the next three weeks, with No. 20 Ohio State essentially being eliminated after their loss to now No. 16 Oregon. And, what happens this weekend if No. 18 USC were to stroll into Bloomington and beat No. 9 Indiana?

There is also No. 4 UCLA, which remains undefeated but has a weak strength of schedule that could hurt its playoff chances if it loses to Illinois on Friday night. UCLA also has a showdown against USC looming to close out the regular season.

OHIO STATE'S COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF HOPES TAKE BIG HIT WITH LOSS TO OREGON, JEREMIAH SMITH SHOWS FRUSTRATION

On top of that, the committee felt strong enough about Alabama's SOS to put them ahead of an undefeated Big Ten team, even with two losses on the season.

In addition to that conundrum, Indiana dropped all the way from 4th to 9th in this week's CFP rankings, and the Hoosiers were on a bye-week. Why? Teams that Indiana had already beaten this season that helped its case took losses this past weekend.

"Indiana was probably victim of having a bye-week at the wrong time ... Every team that they had played within the Big Ten lost," CFP's Yurachek noted about Indiana dropping during a bye-week.

In reality, this is probably where the Hoosiers deserved to be ranked last week, but the committee must have needed a little bit of anticipation for this reveal, which still does not make much sense.

If CFP members thought Indiana was the 9th best team in the country this week, then they should have had them around this spot in their first rankings.

Again, questions we are still having a hard time grasping.

BYU head coach Kalani Sitake talks with defensive tackle Keanu Tanuvasa during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Central Florida on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Orlando, Fla. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

Two weeks ago, most would've thought No. 10 BYU would find themselves in the postseason following their win over now No. 5 Notre Dame.

Now? After a very bad loss to UCF on the road, followed by the loss to No. 2 Utah last weekend, it's the Cougars who are hanging on for dear life in terms of making the CFP. There was a strong chance that if BYU would not have lost that game to UCF, they could’ve found themselves playing for a conference title, and most likely getting into the postseason.

Not any longer. It's No. 12 Texas Tech that now finds itself in a great spot moving forward, with wins over Arizona and Houston to bolster their resume, even with the loss to Cincinnati.

If the Red Raiders were to make the Big 12 title game to face Utah, they could find themselves potentially earning a CFP spot.

Unfortunately for the Big 12, who are hoping to get at least two teams in, No. 12 Texas Tech still has to face Oklahoma State and Baylor to close out the regular season. If they lose one of those games, the chances of representing the Big 12 are over, outside of whichever team could potentially knock off Utah in the conference title game.

But, Houston coming in at No. 14 could create an avenue that still gets the Big 12 at least two teams in. They will need some help, though.

Three weeks ago, there was a scenario in which the Big 12 potentially saw three of its teams make the postseason.

Now, this could turn into a one-bid league if Utah takes care of business and the Big 12 continues to devour itself.

Here ya go, the latest college football playoff rankings that were released on Tuesday night.

First round, on-campus, matchups if they were to take place today.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Oregon head coach Dan Lanning stands on the field during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Southern California on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill)

The Oregon Ducks find themselves back in the conversation after thrashing Ohio State this past weekend in Columbus. Dan Lanning really needs USC to keep winning, given they won the matchup earlier this season in Los Angeles.

But, the Ducks might also prosper with the Trojans catching a loss to UCLA at the end of this November run, which could open up an additional spot in the Big Ten.

With South Carolina and USC moving up in the rankings, the next three weeks just got a whole lot more interesting for those two teams. The Gamecocks still host No. 1 Georgia, while USC will face No. 9 Indiana and No. 4 UCLA.

So, we've obviously got a wild few weeks ahead, and the committee is clearly not worried about shaking things up every Tuesday night throughout November.

Buckle up ... this is going to get interesting.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

Trump hails ‘exoneration of a Great American Patriot’ as moves against his defense secretary fail for now

House Republicans block effort to impeach Hegseth

Hello and welcome to the US politics live ...
articles.body_text:
Trump hails ‘exoneration of a Great American Patriot’ as moves against his defense secretary fail for now

House Republicans block effort to impeach Hegseth

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Republican representative Thomas Massie compared the GOP with passengers content to go down with the Titanic after colleagues thwarted his effort to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.

articles.title: Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
articles.excerpt:
Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation in...
articles.body_text:
Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy.

The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. Wachtell’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management.

Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”.

The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer.

The US ambassador to China, David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent.

“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television.

Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang.

On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. The scandal has wiped $430bn off Nvidia’s value as shareholders gauge the potential impact of the scandal on a company and an executive who are synonymous with the AI boom.

Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers.

Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval.

The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won.

In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis.

The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings.

From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime, and tax offences.

That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner, who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor.

He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran.

Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo.

One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%.

“Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, has put Huang’s survival chances at “about 50-50”.

articles.title: Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England and Wales
articles.excerpt:
Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences

Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England and Wales will be targeted in a police crackdo...
articles.body_text:
Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences

Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England and Wales will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding.

Tactics will include the expanded use of criminal behaviour orders – where repeat offenders are banned from high streets and town centres – GPS tagging and intensive supervision courts, where perpetrators must attend regular judicial hearings.

Those who do not comply or breach conditions will face imprisonment in the most serious cases, and foreign offenders could face deportation.

Mahmood said the government wanted to target people “who are causing so much harm to our communities”. She said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.”

The government said it wanted to replicate the success of Operation Kelleher, a targeted crackdown on 10 shoplifters in Bromley in 2025 that reduced recorded retail crime in the area by 70%, according to Metropolitan police data.

The number of shoplifting offences recorded by police in England and Wales rose to the highest on record in 2024, surpassing half a million offences. Last year there was a 2% decline.

The Metropolitan police said 104 repeat offenders were responsible for more than 5,300 shoplifting crimes over the past two years.

Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s, said retail crime was a “national emergency which requires a national response”. He said: “The number of incidents of theft, abuse, aggression and violence happening in stores right across the country has an unacceptable impact every single day.

“We now need to see more arrests and prosecutions of those who target UK retailers without fear of consequences and we look forward to working closely with authorities as these measures are put into action.”

Former shoplifters have spoken about how drug addiction and mental health problems are one of the main drivers of this type of crime, and charities have called for more funding for support services.

The government said the police crackdown would also be tough on the causes of crime by tackling drug and alcohol addiction “to break the cycle”.

Revolving Doors, a charity that helps to rehabilitate repeat offenders, said the scheme was a chance to “follow the evidence on what works, combining focused enforcement with sustained support to address the addiction, mental ill health and homelessness that can drive repeat offending. Success should mean fewer repeat offences and safer communities, alongside more people able to recover, contribute and realise their potential.”

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said dealing with the small group of repeat offenders responsible for a disproportionate amount of crime was crucial. “Combining robust enforcement with targeted support to tackle the root causes could make a real difference to our high streets and communities,” she said.

Former Celtics All-Star Jaylen Brown confronted ex-running mate Jayson Tatum at a dinner table in France last June over their future in Boston, and that bad blood finally resurfaced on the hardwood Tuesday night.

According to ESPN insider Shams Charania, that awkward European sit-down marked the last time the two stars spoke face-to-face.

GIANNIS ANTETOKOUNMPO ERA TO END IN MILWAUKEE AS BUCKS WILL SEND TWO-TIME MVP TO MIAMI HEAT FOR YOUNG CORE

Boston had just struck out on Giannis Antetokounmpo, who ended up in Miami instead. Celtics brass had put Brown on the table in those talks. Once Brown caught wind he was being shopped, he went straight to Tatum to find out where he stood and whether Tatum still wanted him in Boston.

Jaylen Brown #7 of the Philadelphia 76ers dribbles the ball during a game against the Boston Celtics on Nov. 10, 2026, at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pa. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Jaylen Brown #7 of the Philadelphia 76ers and Jayson Tatum #0 of the Boston Celtics look on during an NBA game on Nov. 10, 2026, at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pa. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Charania reported that Brown approached and confronted Tatum at the dinner table specifically to address their future as a tandem and gauge where Tatum stood on the entire situation.

Boston traded Brown to Philadelphia days later, effectively ending communication between the two. Tatum called and texted, but Brown never answered.

JAYLEN BROWN SOUNDS LIKE A 'SORE LOSER' AFTER BLAMING EMBIID FOR CELTICS' COLLAPSE

Seconds before tip-off Tuesday night in Philly, Tatum walked over and tapped Brown on the chest to say hello. Brown gave him absolute zero back. Eyes locked dead ahead, Brown didn't flinch, didn't dap him up, and blew right past him like Tatum wasn't there.

Jayson Tatum of the Boston Celtics looks on against Jaylen Brown of the Philadelphia 76ers in the second quarter at Xfinity Mobile Arena on Nov. 10, 2026, in Philadelphia, Pa. (Getty Images)

Asked before Tuesday's tip if he planned to clear the air, Brown said, "There's nothing to talk about." Brown then dropped the first on-court faceoff between the two, as Philadelphia fell 123-101 to Boston.

After the final buzzer, Brown hugged several of his former teammates before heading back to the locker room, leaving the floor without saying a word to Tatum.

Brown had 13 points against his former team. Tatum had 21 on 8-for-17 shooting.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

When Tatum claimed on video last month that the trade caught him off guard, Brown hit back on Instagram with a blue cap emoji. Tatum tried shutting down the drama to reporters: "This ain't no f---ing Shaq and Kobe. There's no beef."

Brown countered on camera: "I saw that he said it's no beef and I think he's right. There's no beef. Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef. But it might be a little lambchops and some gravy."

Jaylen Brown of the Philadelphia 76ers guards Jayson Tatum of the Boston Celtics in the first quarter at Xfinity Mobile Arena on Nov. 10, 2026, in Philadelphia, Pa. (Getty Images)

Drafted third overall in back-to-back drafts (Brown in 2016, Tatum in 2017), the duo reached five conference finals, two NBA Finals and won the 2024 NBA title.

Debates over franchise ownership followed. Tatum earned First Team All-NBA nods, while Brown won the 2024 Eastern Conference Finals MVP and Finals MVP awards.
