articles.title: First-ever Collaborative Combat Aircraft fly in formation, demonstrate air combat maneuvers
articles.excerpt:
For the first time, the U.S. Air Force’s semi-autonomous drones flew in formation and executed air combat maneuvers.

Shield’s Hivemind, the autonomy software that “runs” Collaborative Combat Aircraft...
articles.body_text:
For the first time, the U.S. Air Force’s semi-autonomous drones flew in formation and executed air combat maneuvers.

Shield’s Hivemind, the autonomy software that “runs” Collaborative Combat Aircraft flights, helped multiple CCAs fly in a “multi-ship” formation and execute beyond-visual-range counter-air tactics, according to a recent company release.

The release did not specify how many aircraft flew in formation or which CCA participated in the Oct. 26 exercise.

“We are excited that the aircraft and mission systems are reaching a level of integration to start showing what Hivemind can really do,” Todd Wesley, vice president of Hivemind engineering at Shield, said in the announcement.

Each flight generates data that contributes to a software release, per the statement, which supports decisions on testing and fielding.

“The combined Hivemind and aircraft software release process is nearing the point where the Air Force can fly a sortie, update the software overnight and fly again the next day,” Wesley said. “I’m grateful to the Air Force operators, engineers and test teams who fly with us and help us build trust on every flight.”

The demonstration comes as the Air Force announced its intention to have 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet size of 1,000. For the CCA program, the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request included $996.5 million in procurement funding, as well as $150 million in advanced procurement for the following fiscal year and $1.37 billion in continued research and development, for a total program request of $2.37 billion.

The new Shield milestone in the CCA program comes after a F-22 raptor completed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A last month, serving as a “quarterback” and giving high-level directives to the Anduril-made CCA.

Meanwhile, Shield AI announced last week its decision to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction to expand the contractor’s drone-warfare capabilities.

The move to absorb Echodyne — which can produce next-generation, solid-state radar systems — was said to support Shield’s expansion into different areas of unmanned systems.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Judge who sentenced Russell Brand praised for dispelling rape myths
articles.excerpt:
Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hail Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering remarks with ‘piercing clarity’

The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with...
articles.body_text:
Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hail Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering remarks with ‘piercing clarity’

The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with “piercing clarity”.

Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks were particularly welcomed given that rape myths had played a part in the trial. He was also lauded for calling out “enablers” who witnessed sexual assaults by the comedian.

Sentencing Brand to 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, Bennathan said: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

Andrew Thomas KC, the chair of the Criminal Bar Association, and Kama Melly KC, its vice-chair, said: “We welcome the piercing clarity of the judge’s statement. Myths about rape and sexual assault must play no part in our culture or in our courtrooms. Raping or sexually assaulting someone is a crime, and blame lies entirely with the perpetrator.

“Victims of sexual violence should know that when they go to the prosecution authorities, their evidence will be judged fairly and properly. As the verdicts in Russell Brand’s case show, a properly directed jury will not be put off by a defendant’s appeal to rape myths.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, said Bennathan’s remarks were “hugely important” at the end of such a high-profile trial. “We’re pleased he emphasised and upheld women’s rights and freedoms, and recognised the profound courage of the women who came forward, and what they endured during the trial, too,” she said.

“This recognition stands in stark contrast to the appalling accusations made by Brand’s defence barrister, who perpetuated myths, misconceptions and conceptions about rape, such as needing to have fought, screamed or reported immediately for it to be considered a credible allegation. Of course this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault and all of them are valid.”

Deniz Uğur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said rape myths should be prohibited. “The judge’s comments are welcome given the significant role that rape myths played in this trial, which in turn have influenced public discussions about the case,” she said. “This will be having a profound effect not only on the women involved in this case, but on survivors exposed to victim-blaming and misconceptions online and in their daily lives.”

On Tuesday, Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, praised Bennathan’s “incredibly powerful” sentencing remarks, contrasting them with the “depressing” nature of the cross-examination of Brand’s victims by his barrister, Ian Winter KC.

The judge also took aim at Brand’s “enablers” who witnessed Brand sexually assault women in front of them at a radio station and TV studio. He said of the former incident: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with. It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”

Bennathan told Brand the assault at the TV studio showed “your staggering arrogance, and it shows how your entourage indulged your dreadful behaviour”.

Bergman described the comments as “crucial”, adding: “This case and the national response to it is about more than just one man, it is about everyone who laughed along, didn’t speak up and/or looked away, even when it was happening right in front of them. They may not have committed Brand’s crimes, but they contributed to the culture that meant he went on harming other women with impunity for so long.”

Uğur similarly welcomed Bennathan’s remarks, saying it was “critically important to look at the many institutions and individuals that enabled [Brand’s] behaviour”.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Woman jailed for posing as man to dupe partner into sex found guilty of similar deception
articles.excerpt:
Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and du...
articles.body_text:
Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and duping a woman into a physical relationship has been found guilty of tricking another woman into a similar abusive partnership.

In both cases, Blade Silvano, 44, met the women on an online dating site and falsely claimed she was a man who had served in the armed forces before meeting them in person and sexually assaulting them.

Both women said Silvano tricked them into believing she was male and neither had any idea they were being deceived.

Silvano was jailed in 2023 in Cambridge after a jury heard she carried out the deception using a blindfold, sex toy and a “wholly fake persona”. Silvano and her victim even became engaged as a man and woman.

On Tuesday, a jury at Caernarfon crown court in north Wales found her guilty of six counts of sexual assault by penetration between November 2022 and the following June after being told she had carried out the same sort of deception on another woman.

Using the alias “Hunter”, Silvano began messaging the victim on the Plenty of Fish site before meeting her for sex, always keeping the lights very low and not allowing herself to be touched intimately.

Silvano claimed to be a captain and surgeon in the army and on one occasion claimed “his” condom had broken as they had sex. Silvano assured the alleged victim it was “very unlikely” she would get pregnant and told her: “Trust me, I’m a doctor.”

The jury was told the woman noticed her partner sounded a “little feminine” and began to have doubts about their “odd” sex life.

Eventually, the victim received a call from Silvano’s long-term partner, a woman, who said the person she’d known as “Hunter” was female, the court heard.

The victim told police she felt sick when she learned of the deception, saying: “I thought it was some sort of joke.” In court, she said: “I believed I was in a relationship with a straight, heterosexual man. I would never go out with a woman.”

Philip Clemo, prosecuting, told the jury Silvano was a gifted con artist and suggested she was inspired by the myth of Zeus turning into a bull.

The Cambridgeshire offences took place in 2016 and 2017. Using the fake name Blade Mendez, Silvano presented herself as a male army veteran throughout a two-year relationship.

She would send the victim photos of herself apparently shaving her face and would pretend to urinate standing up.

Silvano, of Shropshire, would not allow the victim to touch her genitals, claiming to be “body conscious due to injuries sustained in the army”. Silvano and the woman got engaged and she was encouraged to try on wedding dresses and book a registrar.

The victim accidentally uncovered Silvano’s deception after coming across her on Facebook in September 2018 “in a completely different living situation”. Silvano was found guilty of two counts of assault by penetration.

Silvano will be sentenced for the six sexual assaults next month. Judge Jones ordered a pre-sentence report so that the risk she posed could be assessed.

articles.excerpt: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, co-hosts of the 'I've Had It' podcast, address the backlash after apologizing for laughing at a joke about digging up Kirk’s body. (Credit: I've Had it Podcast - Nov...
articles.body_text:
Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, co-hosts of the 'I've Had It' podcast, address the backlash after apologizing for laughing at a joke about digging up Kirk’s body. (Credit: I've Had it Podcast - Nov. 8)

A source in the office of a prominent nationally elected Democrat called "I've Had It" podcast host Jennifer Welch a "sicko" after she allegedly sought help managing backlash over a joke about digging up Charlie Kirk 's body. Welch denied the source's account as she and co-host Angie Sullivan renewed their attacks on Turning Point USA , with Sullivan telling the conservative organization to "f— all the way off" despite the hosts' earlier apology.

The controversy has also cost the podcast advertisers. Cash App announced it was ending its sponsorship, saying on social media: "We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast." Luxury bedding company Boll & Branch also reportedly dropped its sponsorship, while Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet claimed on X that several other advertisers had withdrawn their support.

The hosts apologized over the weekend, but Sullivan subsequently told TPUSA to "f--- off" while Welch said her apology was motivated by her own convictions rather than pressure from the conservative organization.

"Alright there's a huge online, cancellation campaign from all the titty babies over at Turning Point who want the 'I've Had It' podcast cancelled," Welch said in a video posted to the podcast's YouTube channel. She accused Turning Point USA of "spearheading" the campaign because they're "losers and they lost" and "want to prove to their donors we can cancel libs."

SOCIAL MEDIA HORRIFIED BY DAVE CHAPPELLE’S SICK ‘JOKE’ ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK’S MURDER

Co-hosts of the "I’ve Had It" podcast, Jennifer Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan spoke on their show. ("I've Had It" YouTube channel)

"When we apologize for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn't for you. That was for us," Welch continued. "Because someone I loved very much died from gun violence two years ago and I just didn't feel good about that. And that apology was so that when I advocate for common sense gun reform that I'm doing it clean and clear. I don't expect you to understand this because at Turning Point y'all laugh at violence all the time."

FAR-LEFT PODCASTER CALLS FOR 'PISTOLS FIRING' TOWARD JD VANCE, DEFEATING HIM IN 2028

A Democratic source told Fox News Digital that Welch called them while seeking advice on how to manage the fallout from her comments. According to the source, Welch blamed Turning Point USA for the controversy rather than expressing remorse.

"I am not Turning Point. I'm a national Dem and we don't need people like her in this party because it is exactly what we don’t like about the hard right," the source said. The source also called Welch a "sicko" and estimated that the podcast had lost "tens of thousands" of dollars in sponsorships over the weekend. The source further alleged that Welch's team used ChatGPT to help formulate a response to the controversy and identify "ways out of this."

A supporter attends a vigil in memory of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk who was fatally shot during an event at Utah Valley University, outside the headquarters of Turning Point USA in Phoenix, Ariz., Sept.19, 2025.

Welch denied the claims in a text message to Fox News Digital, saying she had not spoken with a top Democrat and that the podcast had not used ChatGPT. "Those are both wholly untrue," she said.

A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH

"We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it, and we apologized," Welch said. She added that the podcast had removed the segment and donated to Everytown for Gun Safety, a gun-control advocacy organization.

"Turning Point, the group leading the cancellation against us, mocks violence and never apologizes," Welch added. "We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren’t going anywhere."

Jennifer Welch, co-host of the "I've Had It" podcast was an Oklahoma City-based interior designer who starred in the short-lived Bravo reality show "Sweet Home Oklahoma" from 2017-2018. ("I've Had It" YouTube channel)

While discussing their apology, Welch called TPUSA a "hateful organization," and Sullivan said she was "not going to be lectured by these people."

"These people support Representatives to Congress that protect pedophiles and sex traffickers. They're completely fine with American citizens being gunned down on the streets of Minnesota. They're fine with putting people in cages and treating them like animals," she continued. "And for those of you at Turning Point who are worried that I don't talk enough, but yet, you don't believe in universal human rights, I want you to hear me: F— off. F— all the way off."

TURNING POINT USA TURNS THE TABLES ON 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' AFTER LATE-NIGHT SKETCH MOCKS CAMPUS RECRUITERS

The controversy began during an episode last week in which Welch and Sullivan read social media posts celebrating Democratic victories in the midterm elections. Both laughed after Welch read one post saying, "We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." The hosts also suggested, without presenting evidence, that Kirk's accused killer supported President Donald Trump. Voter records, however, showed that he was unaffiliated and had not voted in the previous two general elections.

After the episode sparked backlash, Welch and Sullivan posted an apology Saturday saying they had laughed at an "insensitive joke" and "should not have laughed." They said there was "nothing funny about gun violence."

The hosts' remarks also drew criticism from Democrats, including strategist Kaivan Shroff. "They are not helping Democrats," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "They are hijacking the attention Democrats actually earned at the ballot box."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

articles.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
articles.excerpt:
The victory comes after an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones

A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the ...
articles.body_text:
The victory comes after an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones

A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

articles.title: Trump defends Pentagon chief as Massie targets him: 'Hegseth should be praised, not impeached'
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump calls out Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., amid the congressman’s push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as outgoi...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump calls out Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., amid the congressman’s push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

President Donald Trump is defending War Secretary Pete Hegseth as outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targets the Pentagon chief for impeachment.

The president issued a Truth Social post on Monday slamming the congressman as "a total loser" while asserting that the war secretary "should be praised, not impeached."

"Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth," Trump declared Monday on Truth Social.

HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., speaks on impeaching U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!" he added.

Massie did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday.

Hegseth shared a screenshot of the president's post and thanked him.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH

President Donald Trump speaks with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit at U.S. Army War College on July 15, 2026, in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"Thank you Mr. President. Like you, we will never back down," Hegseth wrote.

Massie, who has served in the House of Representatives since late 2012, lost the GOP primary earlier this year in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL who went on to win the seat during the general election.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said, according to a press release. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate."

WHY THE HOUSE LET OUT EARLY IS A MATTER OF DEBATE AFTER JOHNSON SAYS CHAMBER HAS 'DONE ITS WORK'

Hegseth said Monday there will be a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday morning.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Khor Mor drone attack raises fears over Iraq’s energy security
articles.excerpt: A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has drawn attention to the security challenges facing the country’s energy sector, amid escalating region...
articles.body_text:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has drawn attention to the security challenges facing the country’s energy sector, amid escalating regional tensions and domestic political disagreements over restricting weapons to state control.

The attack in Sulaimaniyah governorate late on Sunday sparked a fire and forced the suspension of gas supplies to several power stations, initially reducing electricity generation in areas administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) by between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts, according to regional officials.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the formation of a joint investigative committee with KRG authorities to determine who was behind the attack.

No group has claimed responsibility, but the attack comes as regional tensions are heightened due to the US-Israel war on Iran, with Baghdad facing pressure to bring weapons held by predominantly pro-Iranian Shia armed factions under state control. KRG authorities have blamed Iran-backed groups in Iraq for previous attacks on the field in recent years.

The attack also comes days after the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) announced its withdrawal from the KRG, deepening a political crisis with its rival, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).

Mohammed Amer, a political science academic and a member of the KDP, said the Khor Mor attack represents a genuine test of the Iraqi state’s sovereignty and its ability to rein in armed groups operating outside its control, and protect its territory and vital facilities.

“The [federal Iraqi] government bears responsibility for protecting Iraqi territory and airspace,” Amer told Al Jazeera. “The repeated targeting of energy sources in the Kurdistan Region also requires it to hold accountable the parties and factions behind these attacks, and to question the authorities responsible for the areas from which they are launched.”

Amer urged the Iraqi government to accelerate efforts to bring weapons under state control, warning that repeated attacks coud deter foreign investment in Iraq’s energy industry.

“These strikes target foreign investment in Iraq’s energy sector, particularly as the Khor Mor field has been targeted many times using drones and missiles,” he said. “There are factions that declare their loyalty to Iran and not to the Iraqi state, and this raises questions about the government’s ability to impose its authority and sovereignty over all Iraqi territory.”

Strategic affairs researcher Kadhim Yawer also linked the attack to regional tensions, with fears continuing that the war between the United States and Iran may escalate once again in the coming days and weeks.

“The strategic purpose of targeting the Khor Mor field at this time is primarily due to external factors linked to the escalation of the conflict between Iran and the US, as well as the desire to inflict economic damage on the Kurdistan Region and Iraq in general,” Yawer said.

He said that the dispute over disarming militias, combined with worsening divisions between the KDP and the PUK, could add to the economic pressure on the region. That comes at a time when, according to Yawer, the field’s importance could grow as the KRG seeks to expand gas production and potentially reach new markets.

Yawer argued that the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq had created additional security challenges, particularly as some political forces – including parliamentarians – continue to not support the full disarmament of militias, allowing them more freedom to operate.

Political researcher Ghanem al-Abed pointed to the timing of the attack, which came as the political dispute between the KDP and the PUK intensified and Baghdad faced resistance from armed groups over its disarmament plans.

“The notable point about the timing of the targeting of the Khor Mor field is that it coincides with political disagreements between the KDP and the PUK, as well as the escalating disagreements between the Iraqi prime minister and some armed factions over handing their weapons to the state,” he said.

The Reuters news agency has reported that the attack originated from the Tuz Khurmatu area of Salah al-Din governorate, outside of northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region – although neither the launch location nor the perpetrators have been officially established so far. Al-Abed called on the Iraqi central government to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

Al-Abed said the economic consequences of further attacks could extend beyond areas administered by the KRG, given the field’s role in electricity generation in the neighbouring governorates of Kirkuk and Nineveh.

“The Iraqi government must announce the identity of the parties seeking to destroy the country’s economy and hold them accountable,” he said. “The situation in Iraq could explode at any moment because some armed factions are not complying with the demand to hand over their weapons to the state. If war breaks out again between Iran and the US, these factions may intervene in the confrontation, and Iraq could then turn into a battlefield.”

articles.title: PAUL MAURO: Sanctuary states have a DMV problem — and Trump can demand answers
articles.excerpt:
‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss Hunter Biden’s criticism of former Vice President Kamala Harris as a politician.

The Democrats have captured both houses of Congress and are gleefully announcing, "woke is...
articles.body_text:
‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss Hunter Biden’s criticism of former Vice President Kamala Harris as a politician.

The Democrats have captured both houses of Congress and are gleefully announcing, "woke is back." But there’s one inconvenient detail: President Donald Trump still controls the executive branch.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER

On October 16, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea, a University of New Haven hockey captain studying criminal justice, was driving home from a game when a pickup truck traveling the wrong way on Connecticut’s Interstate 91 slammed head-on into his car. Ryan was killed instantly.

Police say the other driver was Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who is a Mexican national who DHS says had already been removed from the United States twice. Somehow, he was back.

ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

The story circulated widely on social media, but received limited mainstream coverage. One needn’t wonder why. Ryan was not a member of any of our media’s preferred victim classes, he wanted to go into law enforcement, and he was allegedly killed by someone who the feds say shouldn’t have been here.

But his death raises a larger question: How is it possible that so many foreign drivers are permitted — or even assisted — in getting licensed to drive on our roads? Is there more going on here?

Examples similar to Ryan’s are legion. In July, Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who had entered the U.S. legally, allegedly killed 21-year-old college soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe when his tractor-trailer slammed into the young man’s car. Asrarov, who held an Ohio CDL, reportedly couldn’t communicate with police without Google Translate, failed an English-proficiency test and allegedly attempted to conceal evidence, including his electronic driving logs.

Then, on September 2, Indian national Manjit Singh, whom DHS identified as illegal, was involved in another fatal Ohio crash that killed 50-year-old Brenda Watson. Singh held a California CDL and has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide.

We could go on. Ohio has at least moved to tighten the loopholes that allowed this. Too late for two Americans.

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

But that’s more than blue states are willing to do. So in September 2025, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced emergency restrictions on CDLs issued to foreign drivers after a nationwide audit uncovered widespread fraud.

In New York alone, Duffy’s audit found that over half of commercial trucking licenses went to illegal drivers — and those drivers hit the roads across the country. In one case, investigators found that a Chinese national accused of causing a fatal highway pileup in Tennessee was illegally issued a New York State driver’s license.

In California, the audit found that 25% of CDLs were unlawfully issued — with a stated policy that California will not enforce federal English proficiency rules.

So this year, Duffy began the process of cracking down on the practice nationwide. He withheld $73 million from New York State, which refuses to comply (and is suing in response).

But more significantly, the feds announced "Joint Task Force Crossroads of America," a nationwide initiative targeting fraud and criminal activity regarding CDLs.

DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR

How widespread is the problem? The task force started with more than 1,000 leads and inspected more than 200 driving schools across 23 states. Multiple criminal investigations have already been opened.

It’s a start. But let’s recall: Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who allegedly killed Ryan O’Shea, did not have a CDL.

DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

So limiting the task force to just CDL enforcement is a mistake. Because somewhere in the DMV systems of our states there are officials issuing licenses to applicants who not only likely couldn’t pass the driver’s tests we’ve all taken — they cannot even read the exam. Or our road signs.

And someone is recruiting these drivers, getting them here, corrupting the DMVs and facilitating their placement onto our roads.

This is activity squarely within the province of the federal executive. Our newly woke Congress can bemoan investigating it… but Congress cannot stop it. And targeting the scheme also has the advantage of opening another front on immigration enforcement that doesn’t involve highly visible ICE sweeps. The Trump administration just got some good news on this front. In a major November 6 federal court ruling, Judge Lewis Kaplan ordered New York City to comply with an ICE subpoena seeking information about migrants with serious criminal histories at a Bronx shelter.

The administration can now build on that reasoning by pursuing targeted, court-enforced subpoenas for New York DMV records to identify criminal aliens who have obtained driver’s licenses — and then deporting them.

The administration should go all-in on this over the next two years. Because there’s also this: At least 17 states, plus Washington, D.C., both permit illegals to obtain driver’s licenses or driving-privilege cards, while also operating automatic voter-registration systems for license holders.

The administration has received little credit for recognizing the illegal driving problem (arguably, another failure in messaging on good policy that has plagued Trump 2.0). And the standing up of the Crossroads of America task force is a good start. But this initiative could go further. Successfully enforced, it would serve as one of the ways red states demonstrate the superiority of a little common sense. So, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has gleefully announced that "75% of Americans will be governed by DEM Govs." Fair enough — the electorate spoke.

Now the other 25% should demonstrate what makes them different by cooperating with the feds to keep illegals off the roads, penetrate the criminal networks running this trafficking and disincentivize others from accessing this pipeline to enter the country illegally.

While the new task force uses this recent federal judge’s decision to issue subpoenas, identify illegals in our DMV systems and bring sanctuary jurisdictions back in line with the Constitution.

Then maybe at least some of today’s left, so intent on resurrecting our open border madness, will recognize that young men like Ryan O’Shea are not just collateral damage for their Woke 3.0 ambitions.

Paul Mauro is a contributor for FOX News Media providing legal and criminal justice analysis across FOX News Channel and FOX Business Network programming. He joined the network in 2024.

articles.title: ‘Double amputees run marathons,’ says Badenoch as she proposes £36bn cuts to disability and other benefits – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Conservative leader launches Welfare That Works policy document

Good morning. It is quite easy for politicians to declare that they will cut the welfare bill by X amount – but much harder when they h...
articles.body_text:
Conservative leader launches Welfare That Works policy document

Good morning. It is quite easy for politicians to declare that they will cut the welfare bill by X amount – but much harder when they have to explain exactly who will lose out. This is summed up by a good anecdote about a former chancellor (Ken Clarke, according to some versions, but it could have been any of them), who gave this reply when asked for cuts that would save £1bn:

Here is a page from the document summarising where the cuts would fall.

People with serious illnesses and disabilities. People who need time to recover. We must have a safety net for those people.

10.30am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech on her plan to cut benefits by £36bn.

11am: Michael Marra gives what is being billed as his first major speech since becoming Scottish Labour leader.

11.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

Q: [From Katie Harris from the Express] Are you worried that you won’t be able to implement these plans because the polls suggest Andy Burnham has done a good job uniting the left, while the right is still split?

She said a year ago people said the Tories might cease to exist. But the person who left was Keir Starmer. She went on:

double quotation markThe fact is, no one can predict what is going to happen. I remember the election I came in, in 2017, we were 20 points ahead at the beginning of that election and we went backwards.

The idea that the polls now are exactly what’s going to happen for an election, which could be early – but why would the prime minister be calling one only to raise taxes? – or in three years’ time [is wrong].

What we are doing is making sure that we are ready, not just for an election, but ready to govern.

Until recently Badenoch was predicting that Andy Burnham would call an early election.

Q: [From Bethany Dawson from the LBC] How will you change the way Pip (personal independence payments) assessments are carried out? And who will sign people off sick for the long term under your plan if it is not longer GPs?

Whately said the Tories would redesign the Pip assessment process, including “a higher expectation of medical evidence, which is something that is missing from the system at the moment”.

On sick notes, she said it did not make sense for GPs too have to do this. It would be better for an occupational health professional to do this, she said.

In response to another question about Russell Brand, and whether the BBC was at fault, Badenoch said:

double quotation markWhat I do know is that we have sexual predators all around. But celebrities do find it easier. They find victims more easily. They have the resources to cover up what it is that they do.

And so organisations like the BBC need to take extra care.

Q: [From David Maddox from the Independent] We have heard the story this week of Eivie White, a 13-year-old with special educational needs who killed herself because she was not getting enough support. Won’t your cuts just make things worth for people facing similar problems?

Badenoch accepts that is a serious question. But she says there is a problem with children being told they are disabled, and then being on a path to getting Pip and being Neet as an adult.

Q: [From Jason Groves from the Mail] We heard Lucy Powell squirming this morning when asked about Russell Brand, and Ed Miliband’s interview with him in 2015. (See 10.27am.) Should Miliband apologise?

Badenoch starts by joking that Labour should apologise for everything.

double quotation markI’m sure if it was Ed Miliband sitting in this chair, he’d be very happy to attack us for guilt by association.

But I don’t know that they knew the extent of what he had done.

Conservatives believe in the principle of you’re innocent until you’re proven guilty. And he has now been proven guilty.

Badenoch says she remembers the Guardian journalist Owen Jones saying Russell Brand endorsing Labour in 2015 would be bad for the Tories. She says she just thought it was “embarrassing” that Labour wanted celebrity endorsements.

Politicians are supposed to be serious, she says, not “wanting to be on Gogglebox or whatever”.

double quotation markLet Labour chase the celebrity status and the TikToks. We’re going to focus on getting Britain working again.

Badenoch says the Tories are against mandatory national service.

And she veers off into an attack on the SNP over the Scottish Government’s Remembrance Day tweet. She claims they were “tweeting something that had nothing to do with Remembrance [Sunday], basically to thumb their noses at everybody else.”

double quotation markWhen Reform is coming out with all these random plans, they haven’t done the homework, they haven’t looked at the impact. They’re just randomly ripping out a contract with the EU settled citizens here … We are doing things the right way.

Q: [From Nomia Iqbal from the BBC] If you spend money to get people into work, aren’t you just spending money to get them off the unemployment register.

Whately does not accept that. She says it can make sense to support people into work.

Q: Do you still think the government is not doing enough to help the US in its war against Iran?

And she says it is “very concerning” that the Americans are withdrawing aircraft from bases in the UK.

double quotation markAnd our government has got absolutely nothing to say about it. So we need to focus on what is actually happening right now. Whately says the Tory plan would involve intensive support for young people to get them into work. But it would be stricter than Labour’s version, because young people will lose their benefits if they don’t show up.

Whately says the government will publish Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle youth unemployment next week.

But this will involve higher spending upfront, she says (because the government wants to invest in support to get people off benefits into work).

She says the Tory approach would be different; they would help more young people into work by cutting employer national insurance for under-25s, and getting rid of some of the measures in the Employment Rights Act that make hiring people more expensive.

She starts by describing a mum, Nicky, who came to see her because her son, who has autism and ADHD, had now incentive to get a job because he was getting benefits.

Whately claims stories like this were increasingly common.

She says that, since becoming shadow work and pensions secretary, she had spoken to many people – jobcentre coaches, tribunal judges, Pip assessors. psychiatrists, GPs, charity workers and government insiders – all frustrated by the way the system works.

She claims that Labour had made made benefits “more generous and easier to claim”.

Kemi Badenoch is now delivering her speech at the launch of the Conservative paper giving details of its proposed £36bn welfare cuts.

It’s more than we spend on our army, our schools and our police combined. It is more than £4,000 for every taxpayer in the UK. It is more than the entire GDP of Ukraine.

The weight of this welfare burden is crushing our economy and plunging us deeper and deeper into debt. There is no world in which the current system is sustainable and not just because of the cost.

And she criticises Andy Burnham for suggesting in a recent interview that welfare cuts could lead to people committing more crime. She says:

double quotation markLabour think that, if someone is struggling, the answer is always to give them more money. The prime minister even said that unless we give people benefits, they will commit to crime. This is a terrible view of human nature.

In that interview, Andy Burnham criticised all £36bn of savings. That is because he lacks the imagination, he lacks the will and he lacks the support of his party to even try to cut welfare.

Badenoch was referring to an interview Burnham gave to ITV where he said:

double quotation markIf [the Tories] were to do that, there’d be another big number over here for the utter chaos that they cause in people’s lives. If you just go to brutal cuts, you will leave people in absolute crisis and then they will be going into other services in a chaotic way.

If you come at it from a numbers game, you’ll just make those cuts and you’ll throw people into crisis, so the £36bn won’t be a number that will hold because you’ll be spending money on people in A&E and the police, [the] criminal justice system.

In an interview this morning, Lucy Powell defended her role in arranging for Ed Miliband to do an interview with Russell Brand during the election campaign in 2015, when Miliband was Labour leader. Powell was vice chair of the election campaign and was said to be one of those encouraging Miliband doing the interview with Brand, who was already controversial at the time but was also seen as being influential with younger voters.

Powell told Sky News that Brand at the time had a “powerful platform” with his online show, The Trews.

double quotation markIt was a long time ago, obviously and had I or Ed Miliband or anybody at the time had any sense at all that this was someone who was a sexual predator, who was involved in these sorts of crimes.

I think like anybody who would have paid to go to his show, would have watched him on TV, who was his employer at the time, who had interactions with him – anybody, including those of us who were involved in that at the time – would look back and really regret that, knowing today what we now know.

As the Press Association reports, by the time the interview took place, Brand had already lost his BBC Radio 2 show for leaving a series of lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs’ answerphone about a romantic liaison with his granddaughter, been fired from XFM for reading pornography on air and detailed his womanising in his autobiography.

Asked about her role in setting up the interview, Powell said:

double quotation markLook, we were in very different times. We weren’t in the social media age at the time, so where you could maybe search things up and see allegations or things about somebody at the time.

And, as I say, if there was any suggestion at all, we were dealing with someone who was a known sexual predator at the time then, of course, no one would have done that.

But as I say, he was a well-known public figure. Lots of people, from Hollywood to the BBC to many others, gave this person a very, very powerful platform.

We didn’t know at the time and unfortunately, maybe had people come forward or felt able to … it was a different era.

Here are pictures of some of the ministers arriving for cabinet this morning.

Lucy Powell was giving interviews this morning in part to publicise an announcement from the Department for Education beefing up guidance on mobile phones in schools in England. As the BBC reports, schools are already supposed to be phone-free, but in many places this just means they operate a “not seen, not heard” policy, allowing pupils to retain their phones in their bags.

The new guidance, which will come into force in September next year, will require schools to adopt a tougher approach. The DfE said:

While most schools set out that phones should be not seen and not heard, only 16% of secondary pupils say phone rules are followed all of the time, and with the rapid increase in technology take-up and emerging evidence, pupils, schools and parents need more clarity.

Some schools are already putting stronger whole-school approaches into practice through lockable pouches, collection at the start of the day, secure storage or prohibiting phones onsite altogether.

The strengthened guidance will build on this leadership, giving every school clearer backing to keep phones inaccessible and helping parents and pupils understand what a truly phone-free school day means.

Caroline Voaden, the Lib Dem schools spokesperson, said the new guidance was “a positive step”, but that the government should ensure schools had the funding to implement it properly.

The US military has reportedly evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in ⁠Britain after a threat from Iran, Jamie Grierson and Dan Sabbagh report.

double quotation markI can’t comment on those sort of live operations, as you know.

But we’re constantly keeping the security of our bases under review and, as we’ve seen with other cases recently, we take firm and quick action where we need to.

articles.title: Cop31 live: host Turkey celebrates new oilfields as climate summit enters second day
articles.excerpt:
UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries as scientists find global carbon emissions flatlined this year

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that s...
articles.body_text:
UN climate summit prepares to host world leaders from more than 90 countries as scientists find global carbon emissions flatlined this year

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night.

“We have discovered oil in two further fields in the region. Production began in October at the fields we have named Gaziler and Çardaklı. According to our initial assessments, these two new fields hold an in-situ oil potential of 135m barrels.”

The new fields and further wells should increase oil production by 30% in the Gabar region, which has “virtually become the capital of oil”, Erdoğan said in separate comments made after a cabinet meeting yesterday.

Burning fossil fuels is the main driver of carbon pollution and the resultant heating of the planet, and roadmaps to a clean economy require steep, immediate cuts to the supply of coal, oil and gas.

Turkey is far from alone in expanding fossil fuel infrastructure while promising climate action. In recent weeks, co-host Australia granted a licence to restart production at an offshore gasfield, the UK gave the green light to the already-licenced Jackdaw gasfield, and Norway announced a new oil and gas discovery in the North Sea.

Now the former US secretary of state, John Kerry, has joined the calls for Cop31 to pick up the mantle of building support to transition away from fossil fuels.

“We are going to have to draw on ourselves and find the courage to speak the truth to powerful interests that seem intent to ignore the basic science.

“We know clean power is cheaper than fossil power. That argument is over except amongst those people who keep wanting to hold on to the past.”

Then the UN secretary general is excused from the stage to attend another meeting, and the room gives him a raucous standing ovation as he walks out.

We’ve just heard from Patricia Espinosa, the former UN climate boss (succeeded by Simon Stiell) and now we are hearing from former US secretary of state and climate ambassador, John Kerry.

Kerry has congratulated Brazil for keeping the fossil fuel transition issue alive, and the room has erupted in cheers.

We’re in the plenary that’s promoting Brazil’s new roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, and the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, has backed up the comments of the UN secretary general a few moments ago. Perhaps not unexpected, given Guterres is his boss. But he said:

“Antalya must accelerate delivery [of a transition away from fossil fuels]. This roadmap can help us do that.”.

The UN secretary-general, António Guterres, has just issued a challenge to Turkey and Australia to carry on the work to develop a roadmap for the plan to transition away from fossil fuels.

Remember that this roadmap, promoted by last year’s Cop president, Brazil, is not even on the official agenda here at Cop31.

We might see this as an intervention. Guterres said:

“Now, here at Cop31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it. I thank the Presidency for its leadership.

“Let us leave Antalya with clear next steps to advance this Roadmap. I encourage the current and future Cop Presidencies to carry this work forward. We must give the world reason to believe in the commitment made at Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels.”

This will need a response from Australia and Turkey.

The president of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil, the veteran Brazilian diplomat André Aranha Corrêa do Lago, is presenting his roadmap for “Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Energy Systems” on a stage here in Antalya.

Alongside him is the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, former US secretary of state, John Kerry, and British conservative politician, Lord Alok Sharma, who was the president of Cop26 in Glasgow.

A pretty remarkable lineup. The very large plenary room is packed.

A short update on our Cop31 bus journey from hell.

We have arrived. It only took three and a half hours. And it turned out I had the key for our Guardian Cop31 media cubicle, which meant my colleagues had to do some wrangling to get inside.

But to show they bore no grudges and, as a testament to the collegiate and supportive spirit that exists within the Guardian’s Cop31 reporting team, here is what greeted me at my desk after my odyssey.

As Turkey convenes world leaders to forge agreements that stop climate breakdown, its own leader is celebrating new fossil fuel exploration.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who is expected at Cop31 in Antalya later today, announced the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields in the Gabar mountains in a post on X last night.

“We have discovered oil in two further fields in the region. Production began in October at the fields we have named Gaziler and Çardaklı. According to our initial assessments, these two new fields hold an in-situ oil potential of 135m barrels.”

The new fields and further wells should increase oil production by 30% in the Gabar region, which has “virtually become the capital of oil”, Erdoğan said in separate comments made after a cabinet meeting yesterday.

Burning fossil fuels is the main driver of carbon pollution and the resultant heating of the planet, and roadmaps to a clean economy require steep, immediate cuts to the supply of coal, oil and gas.

Turkey is far from alone in expanding fossil fuel infrastructure while promising climate action. In recent weeks, co-host Australia granted a licence to restart production at an offshore gasfield, the UK gave the green light to the already-licenced Jackdaw gasfield, and Norway announced a new oil and gas discovery in the North Sea.

Bus horror update. So I am still on the bus and it has been three hours. We think we are still half an hour away (I said that an hour ago).

Some people got off and tried the tram. Splitters. We watched a packed tram go past and leave a few of the splitters on the platform.

Some people are walking. We are now a forming a community forged in bus hell. Philippa has some Simit – like a Turkish bagel. Here’s a picture of us.

Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.

Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.

The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.

Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.

Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.

In an attempt to get to the venue a bit early, I decided to ditch the tram and try the special Cop31 buses. This was a bad decision.

We have just reached the two-and-a-half-hour mark on the bus and are still crawling through Antalya traffic. New friendships are being spawned in here. We are starting to eat each other’s food.

I want to thank Philippa Bayley from Groundwork for the walnut and chocolate biscuits she snaffled from her hotel buffet.

Exceptional, which is more than I can say for the traffic.

Good morning from Turkey and welcome to the second day of Cop31, the UN gathering that is taking place, again, to help prod indolent countries clear of catastrophic planetary heating.

A lot of angst was vented on the first day of the summit over whether this goal is being achieved, and even if Cop is the best forum in which to achieve it. Perhaps sensing the fractured, distracted geopolitical mood, Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and Cop negotiations chief, plaintively urged countries to “show the world that multilateralism works. Let’s show the world we are equal to the challenge.”

Further evidence, if it was needed, was unveiled yesterday showing the world is failing rather badly in this challenge to stem its growing fever. But research published this morning shows carbon emissions from fossil fuels are falling slightly, and there is still hope here in Antalya that things can change. If not then, well, what are we all doing here? Right?

About 100,000 delegates crammed into the well-tended conference venue yesterday and the long queues for registration badges led the UN to plead for people to return for them today if attendance on Monday wasn’t compulsory.

Tuesday will lay the groundwork for the arrival tomorrow of leaders from more than 90 countries, with notable absentees including the heads of the US and China. Today’s theme is “energy and transport, touching on a key goal of this Cop to get the world to agree to greatly increase the share of energy used via electricity”. That power will, hopefully, be clean.

Let’s see how close to consensus the world will be on that. At the very least, the Turkish baked goods promise to be delicious and there is some tasteful art constructed of discarded waste to look at. Onwards.

articles.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo

articles.body_text:
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.

The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.

A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.

The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.

Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."

Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.

While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.

"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.

The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.

A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.

A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect.

Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion.

"Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.

Spanish opposition leader and President of the People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "What happened in Oviedo is heartbreaking.

"My condolences to the family of the officer who died and my best wishes for the recovery of the one who was seriously injured.

articles.title: Kushner enters Ukraine peace talks as Trump eyes securing safeguards against another Russian invasion
articles.excerpt: Negotiations to end the war could resume after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy tells Brian Kilmeade he is open to freezing f...
articles.body_text:
Negotiations to end the war could resume after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy tells Brian Kilmeade he is open to freezing front lines in exchange for security guarantees. American Military Project director Will Thibeau provides his analysis on the developments during 'Fox & Friends First.'

Russia and Ukraine will finally return to the negotiating table Tuesday for their first trilateral peace talks with the U.S. in nine months.

Ahead of the talks, officials said both Moscow and Kyiv have shown "a little bit of flexibility privately" on territorial disputes that have long stood in the way of reaching an agreement.

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will sit down with Ukrainian intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Putin aide and veteran negotiator Vladimir Medinsky in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The Trump administration has asked Russia to accept an "Article Four and an Article Five-like security guarantee" for Ukraine that would be "effectively very similar to NATO," a U.S. official said Monday on a background call previewing the negotiations.

President Donald Trump has not yet decided what security guarantee the U.S. itself would provide, the official said, describing an American guarantee as a "really, really big deal" that would ultimately have to be worked out between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, center, and U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner, right, and Steve Witkoff, left, walk prior to their talks in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

A lot has happened on the geopolitical stage since the latest trilateral talks happened in Geneva, Switzerland, in February. The first being the inception of a new conflict between the U.S. and Iran — and the second being the 2026 midterm elections, which saw a sweeping rebuke of Republicans with a blue wave taking the country by storm.

The latest round of talks will also mark the beginning of structured negotiations over territory.

Russia continues publicly to demand all of Donetsk, while Ukraine has pushed for freezing the conflict along the current line of contact. But behind closed doors, "both sides have shown a little bit of flexibility privately," the official said.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA

Trump also suggested in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Ukraine’s borders could ultimately change under a peace agreement, saying the country could emerge from the war with "a little bit different shape."

U.S. negotiators do not expect to resolve the territorial dispute in Abu Dhabi. Instead, officials say the goal is to clarify where each side stands, identify the remaining gaps and begin exploring potential compromises that can ultimately be taken back to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy.

The administration increasingly views the territorial question and postwar security arrangements as inseparable.

Officials believe neither Russia nor Ukraine will make the concessions needed to settle the territorial dispute until each understands what the security landscape will look like after the fighting stops.

INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL

Before sitting down with Russia and Ukraine, U.S. negotiators will meet with national security officials from Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, along with NATO, the European Union and Ukraine, to discuss security guarantees and a broader postwar security architecture.

Washington then hopes to persuade Russia to join a broader multilateral negotiating process involving European governments.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin meets with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Federal Acquisition Service Commissioner Josh Gruenbaum at the Kremlin in Moscow on Jan. 22, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"We need Europe at the table," a U.S. official said, arguing that direct negotiations between Russia and European countries will ultimately be necessary for a durable settlement.

Among the ideas under consideration is reviving the NATO-Russia Council, which the administration wants to make a more robust forum for communication, de-escalation and resolving future disputes.

Officials are also exploring crisis communications, greater military transparency and reciprocal measures intended to reduce the risk of another conflict.

The administration's goal in Abu Dhabi is not a final agreement. Officials instead hope the talks can establish a framework for more frequent negotiations and eventually move the process from a U.S.-Russia-Ukraine format to broader multilateral talks involving Europe.

The administration also sees sanctions as potential leverage in enforcing an eventual agreement. A U.S. official suggested sanctions on Russia could potentially be eased over time while retaining the ability to "spring back in place" if Moscow violates a peace deal.

Witkoff and Kushner, the son-in-law of the president, are also considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks.

"This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish," the official said.

But officials acknowledged the negotiations remain highly uncertain, with deep distrust between Moscow and Kyiv and major decisions on territory and security still unresolved.

The immediate test in Abu Dhabi will be whether the private flexibility U.S. negotiators say they are seeing can translate into something concrete once Russia and Ukraine are back in the same room.

But the Abu Dhabi talks could also set the stage for higher-level diplomacy.

President Donald Trump, right, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

U.S. officials said Witkoff and Kushner are considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the two-day negotiations.

Trump is also preparing to travel to China for the APEC summit next week, where he said Sunday he expects to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Discussions about a potential three-way meeting are underway, though no summit has been finalized.

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
articles.excerpt:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war be...
articles.body_text:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks are the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.

Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Before the trilateral talks, European officials held separate discussions on Tuesday with representatives from Ukraine and the US, where they agreed “any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine”, according to a joint statement.

European leaders are not convinced Russia intends to negotiate in good faith. “So far they have just been pretending that they negotiate because we haven’t seen any ⁠goodwill from the Russian side,” the EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, told Reuters on Monday.

European countries want to be involved in discussions, although there are signs of unease about the proliferating strands of peace talks. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, last week complained about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls that she argued weakened Europe’s ability to speak with one voice.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protects member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.

“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the US, described a potential new framework for Europe in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the UK, Italy and the EU will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kallas at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”

Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape”.

After meeting the Kremlin adviser Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

At that time, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal, and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

The US administration official said: “We have to build something new that works today … Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war.”

The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.

“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

articles.title: Israeli forces kill Palestinian boy in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.excerpt:
Israeli forces carried out a raid in the Old City of Nablus, near Burqa, on Sunday

Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestini...
articles.body_text:
Israeli forces carried out a raid in the Old City of Nablus, near Burqa, on Sunday

Israeli forces have shot dead a 14-year-old Palestinian boy during an operation in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say.

Moataz Daghlas was killed on Monday evening in the village of Burqa, north-west of Nablus, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

The Israeli military said soldiers identified "several terrorists who intended to hurl stones" in an area where stones had previously been thrown at Israeli vehicles. The soldiers fired towards them "to remove the threat", it added.

The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds, but that Israeli forces blocked their access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Moataz Daghlas's relatives said Israeli authorities were withholding his body.

Meanwhile, Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the two Palestinians wounded during the raid as a 17-year-old child, who it said was shot in the abdomen and pelvis, and a 19-year-old man, who was shot in the hand.

According to the UN, at least 98 Palestinians, including 22 children, have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year.

Six Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians in the West Bank over the same period, it says.

The rules of engagement for Israeli forces were reportedly broadened after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, allowing soldiers increased discretion to use lethal force against a perceived threat.

In June, the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory said it had verified the killing of 241 Palestinian children by Israeli security forces and settlers in the West Bank since then.

Most of the children were teenage boys and, in many cases, Israeli authorities accused them of having engaged in stone-throwing as justification, it found.

The UN office said its assessment was that none of the children killed while involved in confrontations with Israeli forces had posed an imminent threat to life, which it said was the only legal justification for the use of lethal force in the West Bank under international law.
