articles.title: Pete Hegseth to hold news briefing as he faces possible impeachment – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie pursuing measures against defense secretary as Iran war blamed for party’s sweeping midterm losses

Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Hegseth
...
articles.body_text:
Anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie pursuing measures against defense secretary as Iran war blamed for party’s sweeping midterm losses

Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Hegseth

On their first day back in the Capitol after comprehensive defeats in last week’s midterm elections, Republicans were divided into two camps: those who saw the catastrophe coming, and those who did not.

“I told you exactly what was going to happen. Over and over and over, I told you,” said West Virginia senator Jim Justice. “I said really and truly, if you weren’t concerned and you were a Republican, you were living in a cave. That was my exact words.”

“No one anticipated the magnitude,” said congressman Warren Davidson of Ohio. “I mean, you can’t tell me that the guy that ran as a Democrat for senator in Mississippi thought he was going to win.”

While Scott Colom hasn’t officially been declared the winner in Mississippi’s knife-edge US Senate race – a state that has not sent a Democratic to the chamber since 1982 – there was indeed plenty of evidence before the Tuesday vote that Republicans were in for it.

Not only does the party in power historically suffer defeats in midterm elections, but Donald Trump’s approval ratings had cratered with voters, even on issues that he had previously polled well on, while Democrats had surged in both special and off-year elections.

Nonetheless, few pollsters or political analysts were publicly forecasting the 54-seat Senate majority and 254-seat House majority Democrats won – both of which may expand even further as ballot counting continues.

“People are mad, and they have a right to be mad. They’re disappointed, and they feel like we haven’t delivered, and we deserve exactly what we got,” said Senator John Curtis of Utah. His state is deeply red, but last Tuesday Democrats managed to break the Republican supermajority in the state house of representatives by gaining at least 14 seats – a feat repeated in legislatures across the country.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Defense secretary Pete Hegseth is set to hold a rare news conference later today as he pushes back against congressional efforts to remove him from office for alleged misconduct.

Under pressure after President Donald Trump and Vice-president JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican party’s sweeping losses in midterm elections, Hegseth now faces impeachment proceedings in the House of Representatives.

“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who... may have substantial policy disagreements but their disagreements are with success,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday when asked about efforts to remove him.

“I couldn’t be more proud of what our president has done, the decisions that he’s made, the courageous calls that he’s made, the bold nature of our... military leadership, the skill and courage of the troops on the ground,” he said.

The impeachment efforts are being spearheaded by representative Thomas Massie, an anti-Trump Republican lawmaker who is leaving office after losing a primary contest to a candidate backed by the president, AFP reported.

Several of the articles of impeachment – which Massie introduced on Monday – relate to the Iran war, accusing Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution, which requires congressional consultation on and oversight of US military interventions.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Massie accused Hegseth of using “our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America” and derided the Trump administration’s refusal to acknowledge the bombing of a school in Iran.

“I mean, obviously we hit it, and you can determine what kind of missiles from the range and the kind of destruction there was. I don’t think they’re going to get out of that article of impeachment by saying, ‘oh, we don’t know who bombed that school’ – although I think the president tried that for a day or two,” Massie said.

It comes as the president said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.

During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed.

Donald Trump was joined by Dana White, the CEO of UFC, at a press conference. At the conference, Trump defended Hegseth, saying his defense secretary “won two wars”, and called Massie “a stone cold loser” and “sick”.

After saying that his deportation policy was “too tough” and offering to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in an interview on 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Donald Trump on Monday said his administration’s deportation policy was “very strong.” “Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No, but— they came in. They knew the law,” Trump told reporters during a press conference today. He added that he had not spoken with incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller about any changes.

In its first major move since last week’s elections, the Senate has advanced bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects. The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which would shorten the timeline for approving both clean and fossil fuel energy projects.

A Utah judge scheduled the trial of the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk for June 2028. District Judge Tony Graf allocated 105 days for the trial. Graf said the 2028 date balances the defense’s right to prepare with the Kirk family’s desire for a speedy resolution.

The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas. The majority paused a lower court’s decision as the case plays out. The Trump administration had filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in the region.

After initially saying he would accept the results of the midterm elections, Trump has begun to cast doubt Democrats’ electoral wins. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. Democratic senator Chuck Schumer responded to Trump’s statement, saying that the president’s “return to election denialism was inevitable”.

articles.title: Malaysian court clears former PM Najib Razak for house arrest transfer
articles.excerpt:
A Malaysian court has cleared the way for jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak to be transferred to house arrest after an earlier directive was disputed.

“In accordance with the order of conditio...
articles.body_text:
A Malaysian court has cleared the way for jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak to be transferred to house arrest after an earlier directive was disputed.

“In accordance with the order of conditional pardon, the accused shall serve the remainder of the reduced sentence of six years’ imprisonment under house arrest,” Kuala Lumpur High Court Judge Aslam Zainuddin said on Tuesday.

Najib, 73, was jailed for his role in one of the largest thefts of public funds ever recorded from the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) and was granted a conditional pardon in September.

On Friday, Najib’s political party paid the ⁠$12m fine as part of the terms of ⁠the royal pardon, and he was due to leave prison. However in a last-minute intervention, the attorney general postponed his transfer to house arrest after raising questions over the legal interpretation of the ⁠royal pardon and the court order allowing Najib to leave jail.

King Sultan Ibrahim has warned that any attempt to challenge his order to ‌let ‌Najib leave jail and move to house arrest could amount to defiance against his decree.

The king, a position held in rotation by Malaysia’s nine regional sultans, plays a largely ceremonial role but has the authority to grant pardons ‌under ‌discretionary powers granted by Malaysia’s Constitution.

Reporting from outside the court in Kuala Lumpur, Al Jazeera’s Rob McBride said: “This has caused all manner of political and constitutional controversy in Malaysia. The king made it plain he wasn’t happy with the interference of the attorney general over the weekend, and that it set a very difficult precedent.” He said it underlines the complicated, delicate relationship between the monarchy, the courts and the government.

The house arrest order applies only to Najib’s first conviction.

He faces ⁠an additional 15 years in prison after being found guilty last year in another 1MDB-linked case with the sentence set to begin after his stint under ⁠house arrest ends.

Najib has appealed the case, and his lawyers requested that the jail term and fines be halted, citing his poor health and inability to pay the fine.

articles.title: Who moves first in Iran-US diplomacy?
articles.excerpt: For nearly two decades, one question has haunted Iran-US diplomacy: Who should move first? Since the early 2000s, Washington and Tehran have repeatedly faced the same dilemma: Should Iran limit its nu...
articles.body_text:
For nearly two decades, one question has haunted Iran-US diplomacy: Who should move first? Since the early 2000s, Washington and Tehran have repeatedly faced the same dilemma: Should Iran limit its nuclear activities before receiving economic relief, or should the United States ease pressure before expecting Iranian concessions? Yet the latest diplomatic crisis suggests that these may no longer be the right questions.

The real challenge is not who moves first. It is whether both sides can move together.

This question has become urgent again amid the latest dispute over the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has proposed reopening the waterway if Washington meets a series of conditions, including lifting the naval blockade, easing sanctions and providing guarantees against renewed attacks. Tehran argues that negotiations cannot begin under conditions of pressure and confrontation. Washington, however, insists that any renewed diplomatic process must address the nuclear issue from the beginning.

This disagreement represents the central problem of the current negotiations: both sides are demanding confidence-building measures before taking the first step. History shows that this dilemma has been addressed before through mechanisms based on reciprocal action.

The 2013 Joint Plan of Action between Iran and the P5+1 – the five permanent United Nations Security Council members and Germany – was built around an interim approach in which both sides accepted limited and reversible measures. Iran agreed to restrictions on parts of its nuclear programme, including limits on enrichment levels and enhanced monitoring, while the US and its partners provided limited sanctions relief.

This approach later evolved into the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). The agreement established strict limits on Iran’s uranium enrichment, with a 3.67 percent cap, while expanding International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) monitoring and providing sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear restrictions.

The implementation of the JCPOA followed a phased process. First came the agreement in July 2015, followed by Adoption Day in October, then Implementation Day in January 2016 after the IAEA verified Iran’s initial nuclear commitments. Only after verification did major sanctions relief begin.

The lesson from this experience is not that agreements based on sequencing always fail. Rather, it is that sequencing without durable political guarantees is vulnerable.

When the US withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018 and restored sanctions, Iran concluded that technical commitments alone were insufficient. From the Iranian perspective, the central problem became the absence of guarantees that a future agreement would survive political changes in Washington.

The US, however, has its own concerns. US policymakers argue that sanctions relief must be linked to verifiable Iranian commitments, especially regarding the nuclear programme. They fear that providing economic benefits too early could reduce Washington’s leverage.

This is the strongest argument against synchronised steps: critics argue that deep mistrust makes simultaneous implementation unrealistic. They warn that Iran could use economic relief to rebuild its capabilities, while Washington worries that it could lose its negotiating advantage.

But the answer is not to abandon reciprocity. The answer is to design stronger verification mechanisms. A workable model would not rely on trust alone. It would rely on verification.

For example, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz could be linked to a phased easing of restrictions, with each stage monitored by a third party. Qatar, given its role as a mediator, could help facilitate communication, while technical nuclear issues could remain under international verification through the IAEA.

The principle would be simple: every Iranian action would have a clearly defined US response, and every US step would have a measurable Iranian obligation.

This approach is more realistic than demanding unilateral concessions because it gives both governments political space at home. Neither side would appear to be surrendering under pressure; both could argue that they are receiving something in return.

Recent diplomacy has already moved partially in this direction. The June memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, supported by Qatar and other mediators, attempted to create mechanisms for reducing tensions, including issues related to military operations and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Later discussions included technical committees and monitoring mechanisms designed to manage implementation.

Qatar’s mediation has also become increasingly significant. Doha has attempted to bridge the gap between Tehran’s demand for confidence-building measures before negotiations and Washington’s insistence that nuclear issues remain central.

The recent message from US Vice President JD Vance to Iranian officials also reflected this dilemma. Washington signalled willingness to explore renewed negotiations, but insisted that the nuclear issue remain part of the discussion. Tehran, meanwhile, has continued to argue that pressure must be reduced before broader talks can succeed.

The question facing both capitals is therefore not whether compromise is possible. It is whether they can design a process in which compromise becomes politically survivable.

The Middle East has already paid a high price for the belief that pressure alone can produce strategic outcomes. Military escalation, economic disruption and energy uncertainty have demonstrated the limits of confrontation.

The next diplomatic test will not be whether Iran or the US is willing to make the first concession. It will be whether both sides are prepared to accept a more difficult but more practical formula: not trust before action, but verified action that gradually creates trust.

The future of Iran-US diplomacy may depend on replacing the politics of the first move with the discipline of the synchronised move.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: France orders military Earth-observation satellites for more than €1.5 billion
articles.excerpt: PARIS — France ordered two military Earth-observation satellites from Airbus and Thales Alenia Space for more than €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) to replace three existing orbiters, and to maintain a s...
articles.body_text:
PARIS — France ordered two military Earth-observation satellites from Airbus and Thales Alenia Space for more than €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) to replace three existing orbiters, and to maintain a space-based image-intelligence capability beyond 2035.

The new satellites in the IRIS system will have an improved operational performance in terms of quality and the speed of making images available compared to the current CSO satellites, France’s Directorate General of Armament said on Monday. They’ll be able to take extremely high resolution images day and night in both the visible and the infrared spectrum around the world, the DGA said.

France is one of the few European NATO members with a sovereign constellation of high-end optical spy satellites, with many allies relying on lower-resolution assets and intelligence supplied by the United States. French President Emmanuel Macron said in January that France was providing two thirds of the intelligence capabilities supplied to Ukraine.

“The IRIS program aims to ensure the continuity of this capability while improving performance to meet the needs of the forces in a rapidly evolving strategic environment,” the DGA said.

The contract represents a value of more than €1.5 billion for the entire consortium, Airbus said in a separate statement. Airbus said it will provide the satellite platforms, a “significant share” of the payload on the first satellite and be responsible for the ground segment, while Thales Alenia Space will develop the second payload, provide critical elements of the first and contribute to the ground segment.

The new system, called IRIS after the French abbreviation of Instruments for Space Intelligence and Imaging, will be operated by the Space Command within the French Air and Space Force, though the DGA said the program is “resolutely open to cooperation” to allow partner countries to access the system.

The first of the new satellites is planned to become operational in 2033, with both in orbit around 2035, according to the DGA. The three satellites in the existing CSO system, for Composante Spatiale Optique, were launched in 2018, 2020 and 2025, respectively.

The DGA said it notified Airbus Defence and Space and Thales Alenia Space of the satellite order on Nov. 5. Subcontractors include Lynred, Pyxalis, Sodern, Safran Reosc and Air Liquide Advanced Technologies, according to the DGA.

The first IRIS satellite will replace the existing CSO-1 and CSO-2 satellites to ensure continuity of France’s space-based imagery intelligence capability, Thales said in a separate statement. After the end of the operational life of the last CSO satellite, the second IRIS satellite will “significantly enhance” image-resolution performance, it said.

Technologies developed for the IRIS system include a “hyper-stable” telescope with active optics, ultra-sensitive high-speed digital sensors and AI-based image processing, according to Thales, which owns 67% of Thales Alenia Space, with the remainder held by Italy’s Leonardo.

IRIS will integrate “the most advanced optical instrument ever built in Europe,” Thales Alenia Space CEO Hervé Derrey said in the statement.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

articles.title: Moroccan trio make African Player of Year shortlist as Salah absent
articles.excerpt: Achraf Hakimi will hope to defend his title of African Footballer of the Year on December 2 as he leads a trio of Moroccan players on the shortlist, which does not feature Egyptian star and former win...
articles.body_text:
Achraf Hakimi will hope to defend his title of African Footballer of the Year on December 2 as he leads a trio of Moroccan players on the shortlist, which does not feature Egyptian star and former winner Mohamed Salah.

Morocco captain Hakimi is joined by Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari on the 10-man shortlist released by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) last week.

The trio led Morocco to a controversial Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title in January. Although Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in the final, Morocco were subsequently awarded the title after Senegal walked off the pitch over a disputed penalty. A decision on Senegal’s appeal over being stripped of the title will be made ⁠⁠at the end of ⁠⁠November.

The three players also helped Morocco reach the quarterfinals of the World Cup, where Saibari was the country’s top scorer with three goals while Hakimi scored one.

At the club level, Saibari shone with Bayern Munich after they signed him for a hefty 50-million-euro ($56m) transfer fee this summer while Diaz continued to prove his worth with Real Madrid.

Hakimi, meanwhile, helped Paris Saint-Germain to their second consecutive Champions League title.

In 2025, he became the first Moroccan since 1998 and the first defender since 1973 to win Africa’s most prestigious award, finishing ahead of Salah and Nigeria striker Victor Osimhen, the 2023 winner.

The other players on the African Footballer of the Year shortlist are Amad Diallo (Ivory Coast); Yoane Wissa (Democratic Republic of the Congo); Antoine Semenyo (Ghana); Ismaila Sarr, Pape Gueye and Sadio Mane (Senegal); and Teboho Mokoena (South Africa).

Salah’s absence from the list has raised eyebrows because the Egyptian forward is widely recognised as a generational talent and one of Africa’s top players.

The former Liverpool star, now with the Turkish side Trabzonspor, took home the award in 2017 and 2018. Mane won the subsequent two awards.

Notable names in the coach category are Egypt’s Hossam Hassan, who was subsequently sacked by the national team over a marital scandal, and DR Congo’s Sebastien Desabre, both of whom led their side to historic runs to the World Cup round of 16.

The Moroccan duo of Mohamed Ouahbi, who led the team during the World Cup, and Walid Regragui, who was the coach during qualification, were also nominated for their country’s success at the tournament while Cabo Verde’s coach Pedro Leitao Brito has made the shortlist for helping the island nation make its World Cup debut.

Goalkeeper Vonzinha, who became an overnight global sensation due to his World Cup heroics, is among the 10 nominees for goalkeeper of the year alongside Egyptian pair El-Mahdi Soliman and Mostafa Shobeir.

Morocco’s Yassine Bonou remains a leading contender after his performances at the World Cup and AFCON.

The World Cup also saw several young stars shine on the international stage, earning them places on the shortlist for Young Player of the Year. Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenky scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner against Panama in the Black Stars’ opening match while Morocco’s Ayoub Bouaddi starred as a breakout defensive midfielder.

Bouaddi became the first African teenager to make five World Cup appearances and was signed by Manchester City in August. He is accompanied by compatriot Abdellah Ouazane on the shortlist.

Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) winners Cameroon have dominated every award category on the women’s side.

Midfielder Monique Ngock, 22, was named player of the tournament while Michaely Bihina was recognised as best goalkeeper. Marie Ngah Manga scored twice in Cameroon’s 3-0 final victory over Malawi.

Her brace tied her for most goals at a WAFCON (five) alongside Zambia’s Barbra Banda, 2024 winner of CAF Women’s Footballer of the Year, and Malawi’s Temwa Chawinga. All three along with Chawinga’s sister Tabitha feature on this year’s shortlist.

South Africa’s Thembi Kgatlana, who scored four WAFCON goals, is also a top contender for the accolade.

Standing out in the goalkeeper shortlist is Cameroon’s Michaely Bihina, who won the Golden Glove at WAFCON, and Malawi’s Mercy Sikelo.

Competition is also stiff for the women’s Young Player of the Year, which includes Cameroon’s Maeva Nyadjou, a breakout defender at the tournament.

Malawi’s Rose Kadzere scored in her side’s quarterfinal victory over Ghana to reach the semis and help secure qualification for the women’s World Cup.

articles.title: Russia launched deadly Ukraine attacks hours before start of Abu Dhabi talks – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
US-led talks in Abu Dhabi are first substantive negotiations in months focusing on ending the conflict which has raged for more than four years

US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as ...
articles.body_text:
US-led talks in Abu Dhabi are first substantive negotiations in months focusing on ending the conflict which has raged for more than four years

US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as talks begin

Russia ⁠attacked 10 ⁠Ukrainian ⁠regions overnight, hitting ​five major ⁠energy substations that ⁠transmit electricity ​between ‌regions, ‌Ukrainian prime ‌minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said.

The substations ‌that were hit ​were in the ⁠Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia ​and Kirovohrad ​regions, ​Koretskyi ​said. Russian attacks killed at least nine people and injured 39 others across Ukraine over the past day, according to a report in the Kyiv Independent.

The attacks came after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine, accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at the Abu Dhabi talks (see this post for more details).

Hungarian authorities have detained the brother of Viktor Orbán as part of a people-smuggling ⁠investigation, the prime minister, Péter Magyar, has said.

The Hungarian anti-graft body, the national asset protection and recovery office (NVVH), said in ⁠a statement it and ⁠police had ​detained four people and searched homes in Budapest and Pest county.

“Three ex-ministers of Orbán are already in custody,” Magyar said in Berlin, where he was giving a speech. “Already his brother today ⁠went to custody,” he added, referring to the former prime minister’s sibling, Aron, ​49.

Writing on Facebook, Orbán dismissed ‌his brother’s detention as a case of political revenge. “In this dirty game, the aim is the elimination of ‌the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system. I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool,” the former prime minister wrote.

The NVVH ‌was set up by Magyar to investigate allegations of corruption during Orbán’s 16-year rule. The latter has denied the claims.

Magyar ​ousted Orbán in an April election and the NVVH is central to his government’s anti-graft campaign which he has dubbed “Operation Purgatory”. You can read more here:

Here are some of the latest images being sent to us from Abu Dhabi, where trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war are under way:

Russia ⁠attacked 10 ⁠Ukrainian ⁠regions overnight, hitting ​five major ⁠energy substations that ⁠transmit electricity ​between ‌regions, ‌Ukrainian prime ‌minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said.

The substations ‌that were hit ​were in the ⁠Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia ​and Kirovohrad ​regions, ​Koretskyi ​said. Russian attacks killed at least nine people and injured 39 others across Ukraine over the past day, according to a report in the Kyiv Independent.

The attacks came after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine, accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at the Abu Dhabi talks (see this post for more details).

A police officer from Spain’s canine unit was killed ⁠and an expert from the explosives disposal unit was seriously injured in ⁠a backpack explosion in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo, according to authorities.

The officers had been deployed to an address in the Villafría neighbourhood after a previous alert about a shooting in which a 17-year-old girl was injured, according to the Spanish outlet El Mundo.

When the officers arrived, they saw a partially opened backpack with a flashlight, prompting them to call the bomb squad (Tedax) for assistance, El Mundo reports.

An officer from the canine unit approached the bag to inspect it, but it reportedly then exploded, killing him, and injuring the bomb disposal expert that was with him. The bomb disposal expert has been taken for treatment at the Central university hospital of Asturias in a serious condition, according to the report.

Spanish police paid tribute to Juan José following his death. “Our heartfelt love and support go out to his family and friends during these difficult times, the Guardia Civil wrote in a post on X.

“And we wish the TEDAX-NRBQ officer a speedy recovery. Rest in peace, colleague.”

At least 10 people died ⁠in a traffic accident involving about 50 vehicles on both ⁠sides of a foggy ⁠stretch ​of highway in southeastern Bulgaria this morning, the BTA ⁠news agency reported, citing the Yambol regional governor, Georgi Chalakov.

Ch Insp Todor Mishinev from ​the Yambol regional directorate of the ministry of internal affairs told Nova TV that some people were still trapped ⁠in their cars.

“Right now, the priority is ​rescue ​operations. Once they ​are completed, the procedural and ​investigative actions ‌will be carried ​out,” ​he said.

The incident occurred at about 7am local time around ​​the Zimnitsa road junction in both directions of traffic on the Trakia highway, according to the Dnevnik news site, which reported that at least 31 people have been injured.

The US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is leading the American delegation alongside Jared Kushner - Donald Trump’s son-in-law – has just posted on X with details of their meeting with European and Ukrainian officials ahead of the trilateral talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia.

Witkoff said the meeting helped to coordinate their efforts to end the war and “establish the conditions for a durable peace”, including support for “robust security guarantees” for Kyiv. He said officials from Europe, the US and Ukraine shared the same objectives and all held a commitment to “Euro-Atlantic security”.

double quotation markParticipants emphasized that any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine.

The shared objective is to develop a practical and mutually reinforcing security framework that strengthens Ukraine’s long-term security and builds the confidence necessary to reach a negotiated settlement.

“Participants further recognized that addressing post-war security concerns and reducing the risk of conflict are essential. They discussed how to ensure strong mechanisms for managing risk and avoiding dangerous escalation,” Witkoff added.

Witkoff, a property developer and a longtime friend of Donald Trump took a leading role in Ukraine-Russia negotiations with little diplomatic experience, effectively doing the role usually reserved for the secretary of state.

Donald Trump has said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

After meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.

The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”. “We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

We are restarting our Europe live blog ahead of the US-led trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi that seek an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on the eve of the talks that Ukrainian battlefield successes were strengthening Kyiv’s position in negotiations.

The ⁠three-sided talks between Ukrainian, Russian and ⁠US negotiators ​are to open on Tuesday and will be the first substantive talks since February aimed at ending the war, which has raged on for more than four-and-a-half years.

“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. “Every task that is fully accomplished – every defensive operation that ⁠increases Ukraine’s strength and delivers results – strengthens Ukraine and, above all, strengthens us in negotiations.”

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner (who is also Donald Trump’s son-in-law) are to lead the American delegation at the talks, which are scheduled for two ⁠days. In Washington, ⁠Trump said on Monday that the US was seeing ​a “very strong inclination” towards ending Russia’s war, and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.

A US official said security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic for the discussions, including the potential for Kyiv to be granted a Nato-style article 5 defence, which protects member states in case of an attack. Any territorial agreement would probably come at the end of negotiations once other items were agreed upon, including a postwar security architecture, the official said.

But Ukraine and Russia have both been adamant about territory, with neither side willing to make any major concessions during previous rounds of diplomacy. Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, wants to obtain all of eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region.

European officials, ⁠including from France, Germany and the European Commission, ⁠will not directly take part in negotiations, as per Russia’s insistence. But instead the Ukrainian delegation, led by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, will meet separately to brief their European allies on progress.

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The two US envoys met Ukrainian and European officials in Abu Dhabi ahead of the trilateral talks this morning. “Our key priorities are ending the fighting, securing reliable postwar security guarantees, ensuring Ukraine’s economic recovery and development, and taking humanitarian steps,” Umerov wrote in a social media post.

European officials, who have been largely excluded from peace talks, wanted to be involved directly in the talks amid concerns the US administration could try to force through a deal favourable to Russia. Stick with us as we bring you the latest developments from the negotiations and other Europe-related news.

articles.title: Sarah Ferguson in touch with ex-Prince Andrew as expert warns royal downfall 'has further to go' after arrest
articles.excerpt:
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner discusses Sarah Ferguson's denial of tell-all rumors and the potential consequences for daughters Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windso...
articles.body_text:
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner discusses Sarah Ferguson's denial of tell-all rumors and the potential consequences for daughters Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor may have lost his royal titles, but the scandal surrounding his ties to Jeffrey Epstein continues to follow him — and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson.

People magazine reported that while it's unclear whether the former Duchess of York has seen her ex-husband recently, the two remain in contact.

"They have an ongoing cordial and supportive relationship as co-parents and co-grandparents," a spokesperson for Ferguson told People.

FORMER PRINCE ANDREW, SARAH FERGUSON DUBBED ROYAL FAMILY’S ‘BONNIE AND CLYDE’ AS EPSTEIN FALLOUT GROWS: AUTHOR

Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025 in London. People magazine reported that the former Duchess of York has been in touch with her ex-husband. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Ferguson's spokesperson for comment.

"It is not surprising," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "If Andrew came to court, she might well be called as a witness. Much depends on whether the police in Britain can obtain the unredacted Epstein files. But there is no way back for Andrew. He hasn't helped the FBI. He has no support. He has no reputation to lose. It can't get much worse. His fall is unique. It has further to go."

Sarah Ferguson and former Prince Andrew, Duke of York attend day 4 of Royal Ascot at Ascot Racecourse on June 19, 2015, in Ascot, England. (Samir Hussein / WireImage)

Andrew has been issued a witness summons in a civil fraud case, marking what is believed to be the first such summons issued to a member of the British royal family since 1870, The Associated Press reported.

WATCH: SARAH FERGUSON DENIES TELL-ALL BOOK AMID ROYAL FAMILY CONCERNS: EXPERT

The summons comes after a High Court judge in London ruled in October that Andrew could be called to testify about a payment he received in connection with the case. Andrew may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify, the AP reported.

The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former advisor, Selman Turk, misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound (approximately $1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Andrew in 2019. The younger brother of King Charles III repaid the money in 2021, and he is not a party to the lawsuit. Turk denies dishonesty.

From left: The former Prince Andrew, King Charles III and Prince William attend Katharine, Duchess of Kent's Requiem Mass service at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025, in London. Andrew was arrested on Feb. 19, 2026. Thames Valley Police confirmed to Fox News Digital he was released hours later. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Police Scotland confirmed to Fox News Digital that active inquiries are underway into information concerning Andrew and Epstein at Balmoral Castle, the royal family's Scottish estate. They noted that the inquiries are at a "very early stage."

Balmoral Castle in Scotland is seen here. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

The confirmation follows a report by the Scottish Daily Express that police inquiries concern allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate, where Andrew hosted Epstein and his longtime associate, Ghislaine Maxwell.

"We have received information and active enquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage," a Police Scotland spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "All enquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those enquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The former Prince Andrew, Duke of York attends the Easter service at St. George's Chapel on April 20, 2025, in Windsor, England. He lost his princely title in October of that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

Police declined to specify the focus of the inquiries or whether Andrew is the subject of an investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to Andrew's attorney for comment. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital the palace does not speak on Andrew's behalf because he is no longer a working royal.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

England's King Charles III formally stripped his brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor (pictured here) of his royal titles on Nov. 6, 2025. An announcement was previously made on Oct. 30, 2025. Andrew said he would stop using his royal titles on Oct. 17, 2025. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Andrew lives in seclusion on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk. A spokesperson for Ferguson told People that she has been spending time with their daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and her five grandchildren since returning to the U.K. in late August.

"She's resettling here, lying low while she looks at the next stage. She's happy spending time with her family and focusing on her relocation," the spokesperson said.

Sarah Ferguson (left) and Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent, at Westminster Cathedral in London on Sept. 16, 2025. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press)

People reported that Ferguson is renting a house in the Home Counties, a region of counties surrounding London. She previously spent time in the Austrian Alps.

Representatives for Sarah Ferguson shut down rumors she is preparing to write a tell-all memoir. (Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images)

"Sarah Ferguson will be deliberately lying low to allow any tension involving the royal household to die down," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. "Right now, Sarah is probably staying away from Sandringham to avoid adding to the melodrama. Obviously, Sarah is concerned about Beatrice and Eugenie. Any repercussions attached to her may fall on their shoulders too."

"The Andrew and Sarah story and their continued love for each other have always been strong," Turner said. "Most days, when they were living together at Royal Lodge, they would make time for each other."

Andrew Lownie, author of "Entitled," dubbed Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor as the royal family's "Bonnie and Clyde," as they remained deeply loyal to each other while navigating scandals and public scrutiny throughout the years. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

On Feb. 19, Andrew's 66th birthday, Thames Valley Police arrested him on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that he shared confidential information with Epstein while serving as a British trade envoy. He has not been charged. The investigation followed the king's decision in 2025 to strip his brother of his remaining royal titles and honors over his ties to Epstein.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, younger brother of Britain’s King Charles, formerly known as Prince Andrew, leaves Aylsham Police Station in a vehicle, on the day he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

On Oct. 8, Andrew secured a legal victory when a High Court judge in London ruled that search warrants used to raid two properties linked to him were unlawful because police had relied on the wrong legal provisions. The judge, however, said "the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful."

Andrew has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.

This undated photo shows the former Prince Andrew and Jeffrey Epstein at Ascot in the U.K. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Ferguson retreated from public life after the release of Epstein-related documents renewed scrutiny of her past relationship with the convicted sex offender. She has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with the financier, who died in federal custody in 2019.

Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor leave after attending the Easter Mattins Service at St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, in Windsor, England, on March 31, 2024. (Hollie Adams/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Emails released as part of the Epstein files revealed that Ferguson continued to praise the convicted sex offender even after his 2008 conviction, including referring to him as a "supreme friend," renewing scrutiny of their relationship.

"For 30 years, Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor sold us the much-debated story: Married. Divorce. Living together at Royal Lodge. Co-parenting. The 'happiest divorced couple in the world,'" British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital.

Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor are seen here on their wedding day in 1986. (Derek Hudson/Getty Images)

Chard believes Ferguson is prioritizing her family even as her relationship with Andrew remains "publicly cordial for their daughters but privately fractured."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

On March 22, 2026, a spokesperson for Sarah Ferguson denied U.K. reports that she was participating in a reality TV series about cloning the late Queen Elizabeth II's corgis. (Stephane Cardinale - Corbis/Corbis via Getty Images)

"Sarah is loyal," Chard said. "However, she is also loyal to herself and will do what she needs to spring back. She realizes her own Epstein emails, calling him a 'supreme friend' and more has cost her charities, book deals, her title. Her much-needed invitations also dried up, although she still has a close circle of friends."

On Oct. 29, Ferguson made a rare public appearance alongside her daughters at a memorial service in London for her former boyfriend and longtime friend, Paddy McNally, who died in July at age 88.

Princess Beatrice (left) and Princess Eugenie are seen at the funeral of their grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, in 2022. (Justin Goff Photos/Getty Images)

"It was no coincidence," Chard said. "Paddy was the one who helped her navigate her most trying time living away from her loved ones, in the Austrian Alps, in exile, cut off from royal life. His guidance, his support, his belief in her gave her the strength to come back to the U.K. to resettle and rebuild. Paddy's legacy is still carrying her through."

Sarah Ferguson, the Duchess of York, is accompanied by friend Paddy McNally in the paddock at the British Grand Prix at Silverstone, date unknown. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Ferguson's plans for the future remain unclear, People reported. While she is looking to "forge an independent life," her spokesperson told People she is not working on a tell-all memoir. Ferguson has written several books.

Sarah Ferguson is seen here with her book "A Most Intriguing Lady" at The 92nd Street Y New York, on March 6, 2023, in New York City. (Michael Loccisano/Getty Images)

Andrew has also remained largely out of public view as he faces an ongoing police investigation and a witness summons in a separate civil fraud case.

The former Prince Andrew, the Duke of York, and Sarah Ferguson photographed at Buckingham Palace after the announcement of their engagement on March 17, 1986. (Tom Stoddart/Getty Images)

"As long as Sarah is tied to Andrew, a comeback with King Charles, Prince William and Princess Catherine is almost impossible," Chard said. "William is reportedly taking an even tougher line. With her daughters, grandchildren and close friends around her, she no doubt is plotting her public revival. Her Falklands hero and exiled ex Prince Andrew will not be in tow."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: House leadership up for grabs as GOP reckons with devastating losses
articles.excerpt:
Capitol Hill freshman orientation begins as incoming progressive Democrats demand major policy updates. Fox News' Chad Pergram details House leadership battles.

Internal House and Senate party leader...
articles.body_text:
Capitol Hill freshman orientation begins as incoming progressive Democrats demand major policy updates. Fox News' Chad Pergram details House leadership battles.

Internal House and Senate party leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises to unfold on Capitol Hill.

Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic.

But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing. However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And — perhaps more importantly — it’s about the math.

Republicans are up first with elections in both chambers starting Tuesday morning.

THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, left, and US House Speaker Mike Johnson, during a news conference at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Nov. 5, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

For Minority Leader, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. Current House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is not seeking to stay in leadership once his party isn't in charge anymore.

If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All incoming House Republicans (including non-voting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in conference. The selection of Minority Leader does NOT go before the entire House like Speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88.

The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for Minority Whip.

Senate Republican leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running to keep his leadership position for the party in the new Congress.

Meanwhile, Democrats will begin elections for their House leader on Wednesday where Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to secure that nomination. No internal Democrat Senate leadership election date has been set.

There are some progressives and Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Democrats who will be House Members next year who want someone other than Minority Leader Jeffries keep his position.

Who do they want instead? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black Speaker of the House.

For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for Speaker in their Caucus. That needs a simple majority. So surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for Speaker.

The Speaker of the House is the Constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government – much like the President is for the executive branch and the Chief Justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for Speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on January 3.

There are 435 Members. If all Members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So that is not going to happen. He might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly.

The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference work much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for Majority Leader in the Democratic Caucus and Minority Leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate Majority Leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate Majority Leader" has only been around since the early 20th Century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House Speaker being the head of this branch of government.

It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would not become Majority Leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beat down.

First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is very popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for Majority Whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz if something happens with Schumer.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said he wants to look at his options and endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for Majority Leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer.

But again, you can’t beat someone with no one.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and the GOP are gearing up for a floor battle with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats over Trump-backed voter ID legislation. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in Caucus and he’s the next Majority Leader.

There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But a group of Senate Republicans are calling on a delay in leadership elections slated for Tuesday. Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes.

So for the next couple of weeks, there’s a lot of counting. Counting about votes for impeachment. Counting in leadership elections. And next year, counting votes as Democrats try to enact their agenda.

Democrats will say voters are counting on them. And Republicans, well, they may be counting the days.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, warned that they was a "problem" with the Senate's bipartisan housing package. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Everything in the new Congress will come down to the math. And there's the issue of impeaching Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth.

But forget about Democrats pushing the move next year. Try Republicans — THIS year.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is reintroducing articles of impeachment for Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth this week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth.

Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September. That nixed Massie’s effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) condemned the effort by the Kentucky Republican. But Johnson insisted that he didn’t send Members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth.

Massie attempted to execute a parliamentary move which would compel the House to consider the impeachment articles right away. But they expired once the House went out of session. But Massie will resuscitate them.

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS

Massie authored a total of eight articles of impeachment, ranging from the "kidnapping" of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro to how the Pentagon is running the war in Iran.

It’s possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans are grumbling about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work.

All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach Hegseth. Some Republicans are exasperated by Hegseth and have said privately they’d like to impeach. There are even more Republicans trying to build distance between themselves and President Trump after the midterms. That’s augmented by the fact that Republicans believe the war in Iran cost them control of Congress. Thus, even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Republican Members who lost – or were shocked that they lost – might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House than Republicans. And don’t forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election.

A simple majority is necessary to impeach.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is seen on Oct. 15, 2026, at the Pentagon in Arlington, Va. ( )

If adopted, the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate. Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That’s what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence.

It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Believe it or not, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote? That’s to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young, R-Ind., and others.

It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial.

In addition, unlike legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and health care?

Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week’s electoral shellacking?

Some of this hinges on who both parties in each body select as their leaders.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Quiet serial killers may hide in plain sight as DNA unmasks dead 1970s Pennsylvania strangler, expert says
articles.excerpt: Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former FBI behavioral analysis consultant and LAPD psychologist, discussed why serial killers often have more victims than they are linked to after DNA tied a dead Pennsylvania ma...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former FBI behavioral analysis consultant and LAPD psychologist, discussed why serial killers often have more victims than they are linked to after DNA tied a dead Pennsylvania man to two 1970s killings.

Quiet serial killers may be hiding in plain sight, an expert warns, after new DNA technology helped unmask a Pennsylvania man authorities say killed at least two women in the 1970s.

At a Thursday news conference, Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the man who sexually assaulted and strangled Brenda Ritter, 18, and Susan Rush, 21, in the 1970s.

Rush vanished on Nov. 24, 1976, after leaving a shopping mall, according to the City of Washington Police Department. She was supposed to meet her family at church but never arrived. Her brother spotted her car along a street the next morning, Thanksgiving Day, and her body was discovered in the trunk.

TED BUNDY LINKED TO ANOTHER DECADES-OLD HOMICIDE NEARLY 40 YEARS AFTER HIS EXECUTION

Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr., who died in 2023, as the man who killed Brenda Ritter and Susan Rush in the 1970s. (Pennsylvania State Police)

Ritter disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977, police said. Her body was later found on a hillside, and authorities determined she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.

The suspect, Clark Sr., died at 66 on July 17, 2023, of natural causes.

DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

In late 2008, evidence from Ritter's killing was sent to the state police crime lab, which produced an unknown male DNA profile. The DNA was put into an FBI database, CODIS, which was searched weekly with no match. In May 2025, testing at Cybergenetics' laboratory showed the same man was responsible for the deaths of both women.

Clark left DNA at both crime scenes, according to police, and advances in testing at several labs, including Identifinders International, helped investigators zero in on him before more testing sealed the match.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Brenda Ritter, 18, disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977 and was later found sexually assaulted and strangled on a hillside, police said. (Pennsylvania State Police)

Police said Clark would have been 20 at the time of Ritter's homicide and 19 when Rush was killed.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky said he thinks there may be more victims.

"I believe that once you're a serial killer, you're always a serial killer. I believe there could potentially be more victims out there," Petrosky said.

Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former LAPD psychologist and FBI behavioral analysis consultant, told Fox News Digital it's "normal" for the number of known victims to fall short of a serial killer's true toll, and that new technology is often what closes the gap.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I think it's normal and normative that the number of known cases is always less than what has been detected," Mohandie said. "These kind of guys often have more victims out there than they've been known to be connected to. The reality is that there are usually more crimes attributable to serial offenders than they're ever held to account for."

Susan Rush, 21, vanished after leaving a shopping mall on Nov. 24, 1976, and her body was found the next morning in the trunk of her car, police said. (Pennsylvania State Police)

Mohandie said it's not unusual for a serial killer to go quiet for years, either because they sense investigators closing in or because their lives get busy with things like raising a family.

"There are a lot of cases where they do go dormant, what we call a cooling-off period, and that can be because they realize it's too hot for them to continue to offend, that they'll get caught, so it's a strategy to avoid being captured. It may mean that they've had a close call with being captured, and it spooked them, so they'll go quiet for a while because of that," he said.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Popular cooking methods may destroy key health benefits of broccoli, experts warn
articles.excerpt: Cooking broccoli at high temperatures may reduce certain nutrients, but experts say a few easy kitchen adjustments, including adding mustard powder, could help retain more of the vegetable's beneficia...
articles.body_text:
Cooking broccoli at high temperatures may reduce certain nutrients, but experts say a few easy kitchen adjustments, including adding mustard powder, could help retain more of the vegetable's beneficial properties.

Not all methods of cooking broccoli are created equal, and some simple tips can ensure you get the most nutrients out of it.

Whether it's steamed, roasted or added to a stir-fry, broccoli is a healthy option packed with vitamins such as A, C and K, minerals such as calcium, potassium and iron, fiber and even a potentially cancer-fighting compound, the Washington Post recently reported.

But certain ways of cooking broccoli can ensure you get the most out of the cruciferous vegetable and preserve those compounds.

YOU'RE PROBABLY COOKING RICE WRONG, AND CHEFS REVEAL THE SIMPLE MISTAKE TO AVOID

Boiling broccoli can cause water-soluble nutrients and compounds to leach into the cooking water, while prolonged or high-heat cooking, including roasting, can reduce antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cancer-fighting properties.

Cruciferous vegetables provide fiber, vitamins and plant compounds being studied for potential health benefits. (iStock)

"Boiling causes the most loss in nutrients," Sol Figueroa, a Florida-based registered dietitian nutritionist with Mochi Health, told Fox News Digital. "Vitamin C and glucoraphanin dissolve in water, so a lot of them end up in the cooking water that gets poured down the drain."

NATURAL COMPOUND IN BLUEBERRIES AND GRAPES MAY UNLOCK FAT-BURNING PROCESS IN MUSCLE CELLS

Glucoraphanin is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables and, when it is digested, it can be converted into sulforaphane, a compound studied for potential antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects and possible benefits for liver, metabolic and gut health, as well as cancer prevention.

Figueroa offered several tips to help get the most out of your broccoli. One way to preserve some of the nutrients is to use as little water as possible when boiling, she said.

Chopping broccoli and letting it rest before cooking may give sulforaphane, a plant compound studied for potential health benefits, time to form. (iStock)

Another is to sprinkle mustard powder on cooked broccoli. Mustard seeds contain myrosinase, an enzyme that helps convert glucoraphanin to sulforaphane and that can be lost during cooking.

COMMON GRILLING MISTAKE COULD STRIP FISH OF KEY NUTRIENTS AND RUIN YOUR MEAL, EXPERTS WARN

Some simple prep also may help preserve sulforaphane, according to Figueroa.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising."

"Chopping the broccoli and letting it sit for about 30 to 40 minutes before cooking gives sulforaphane time to form first," she said.

FOUR COMMON KITCHEN HABITS THAT CHEFS SAY HOME COOKS NEED TO STOP DOING IMMEDIATELY

Most of the research related to broccoli's health claims has been conducted in labs and animals, Figueroa added.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising," she said.

Broccoli stalks are edible and can be trimmed, sliced and cooked alongside the florets. (iStock)

Steaming is one of the best ways to preserve broccoli's enzymes, and while the method often reduces vitamin C in other foods, research shows broccoli might be an exception, the Washington Post reported.

Quickly microwaving broccoli may help preserve nutrients, according to the outlet, and using broccoli's cooking water in soup or stew can help retain some water-soluble vitamins.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Felice Kaufman, a Florida-based food blogger at Cooking in the Keys and former New York Whole Foods Market chef, said she usually steams broccoli, cutting the florets into similar sizes and checking for doneness after about three minutes.

Steaming broccoli briefly may help preserve nutrients and compounds that can be reduced by prolonged cooking. (iStock)

"Taste a piece. If you'd eat it right then, take it out of the pot," Kaufman told Fox News Digital. "The heat keeps cooking the broccoli after it comes out of the pot."

Kaufman also recommends using the stalk, which she trims, slices and cooks with the florets.

She prefers steaming to boiling, in part to preserve vitamin C, but said that's not always possible.

"If the sink is full — it happens — I'll throw the broccoli straight into the boiling water," she said. "One less thing to wash."

Experts say the most important thing is to eat broccoli, whether it's steamed, roasted or prepared another way. (iStock)

No matter how it's served, getting some broccoli into your diet is key, experts agree.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The most important thing is eating broccoli at all," Figueroa said.

If roasting is the way your family likes it best, do that, she added.

Kaufman echoed that advice, saying, "Five ounces of broccoli, organic, conventional or frozen, is better than any processed food you can eat."

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile
articles.excerpt:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according ...
articles.body_text:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a new passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.

Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.

Despite her conviction and the party’s ban, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.

The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.

Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.

Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

articles.title: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’
articles.excerpt:
France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks...
articles.body_text:
France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday.

“I can also tell you that we rule nothing out and will take all measures – including those we may not disclose publicly – that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” he added.

Barrot, speaking on France Info ‌‌television, said the government would push for European Union sanctions in response to what he called an “attack of unprecedented scale and aggression in our country”.

He said firm measures would be taken “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again”.

On Monday, Barrot said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind cyberattacks targeting more than 700 French supermarkets on October 11 and 12, when refrigerators were remotely accessed “to initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles”.

Raised temperatures in fridges forced the supermarkets to throw away all perishable food.

Millions of euros’ worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday she had opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit of the IRGC, over the attacks.

The prosecutor’s office has requested international arrest warrants be issued for two Shahid Kaveh officials.

Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.

In a suspected cyberattack on November 2, temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

Jody Westby, chief executive of Global Cyber Risk LLC, said tracking down the group directly responsible for the attacks is “very difficult” because of poor cooperation on international cybercrime investigations.

“It’s been a problem for 20 some years, and now it’s a little better, but only marginally so,” Westby told Al Jazeera. She said that it was difficult to track and trace the origin of such attacks “because of the nature of packet switching”.

In recent days, European air traffic has also been disrupted by false bomb alerts against dozens of flights, although the origin of those threats has yet to be determined.
