articles.title: At least one person killed as Russia and Ukraine trade strikes overnight
articles.excerpt:
Overnight strikes between Russia and Ukraine have killed at least one person and damaged a Russian oil refinery.

The ⁠⁠Kirishi refinery in the ⁠⁠Leningrad region was set on fire following a Ukrainian...
articles.body_text:
Overnight strikes between Russia and Ukraine have killed at least one person and damaged a Russian oil refinery.

The ⁠⁠Kirishi refinery in the ⁠⁠Leningrad region was set on fire following a Ukrainian ‌‌drone attack, Leningrad Regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Monday in a post on Telegram.

One woman was killed by falling drone debris, Drozdenko said.

Also on Monday, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that his country had agreed to establish a new mechanism to allow European Union funds to be deployed more quickly in response to Russian attacks  against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The Kirishi refinery is Russia’s ⁠⁠second-largest, and the Leningrad region is a major hub ‌‌for the country’s oil and grain exports via the Baltic Sea.

Leningrad’s governor also said air defence forces had downed 113 Ukrainian drones, and that an apartment in Kirishi ⁠⁠had been damaged in the ⁠⁠same overnight attack on the region.

Russian forces struck three ⁠⁠power substations across ⁠⁠Ukraine overnight on Monday and also hit ‌‌a cargo ship in the Black Sea that Moscow ⁠⁠said was providing ⁠⁠arms to Ukrainian forces, Russian state ⁠⁠news agencies ⁠⁠reported.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify those claims.

Russia has kept up regular attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, including energy sites across the country.

“Right now, many of our cities and communities are facing a very difficult situation with power, water, and heating supplies due to Russian strikes,” Ukraine’s president said in a post on X on Monday.

Zelenskyy said that he had agreed with Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, to “activate a special emergency mechanism” that would allow European funding “for what is needed most”.

“Our teams are already working on this,” Zelenskyy added.

The Kyiv, Dnipro, Sumy, and Donetsk regions, as well as Kherson, are facing the most acute energy crisis, the Ukrainian president said.

articles.title: Iran’s authorities harden domestic security controls amid US strike threats
articles.excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Iran’s domestic security apparatus is on high alert and hardening its approach in dealing with issues that authorities perceive to be jeopardising their control of the country during th...
articles.body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s domestic security apparatus is on high alert and hardening its approach in dealing with issues that authorities perceive to be jeopardising their control of the country during the war with the United States.

Iranian authorities have issued warnings to the public about tough sentences if they protest against the government and are tightening their control in public spaces after months of loosened restrictions on how people dress.

In short, the Iranian authorities appear to be trying to project an image that they will not yield on the principles of the Islamic Republic after eight months of war and amid the threat of a new, wider, more intense wave of US attacks.

Mahjoob Zweiri, director of the Gulf Studies Center at Qatar University, said the authorities have also been able to publicly mobilise supporters dedicated to the continuity of the government in Tehran amid these tensions.

“They include not only IRGC but also some civilians, and this is likely to continue until the war finishes,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a military entity established to safeguard the principles of the 1979 Islamic revolution.

Iranian authorities routinely deploy harsh punishments to deter any form of dissent. The war, which began on October 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iranian leaders, has only accelerated this process.

On Sunday, the judiciary said three young men arrested during nationwide protests in January were executed for allegedly attacking government offices and damaging public property near Tehran to benefit the US and Israel.

The authorities consider the antigovernment protests a “coup” attempt by “terrorists” affiliated with the US and Israel. But an independent United Nations fact-finding mission found the authorities had committed crimes against humanity during a violent crackdown on protesters that human rights groups said killed thousands of people, mostly on the nights of January 8 and 9.

Foreign-based rights organisations said many political cases that result in executions are marred by allegations of torture, forced confessions and other violations of due process.

This year, Iran’s government has executed at least 79 political or religious prisoners, including 40 people arrested during the January protests, according to the Norway-based Hengaw Organization for Human Rights. Some were executed after espionage convictions.

“Iran is a country at war with the world’s lone superpower, whose strategy toward Tehran remains unclear, and with Israel, whose government pursues a declared policy of overthrowing the regime in Tehran, whether through economic and military warfare or by partitioning Iran through a US- and Israeli-backed civil war,” political scientist Ali Alfoneh said.

“Taking these circumstances into consideration, the authorities of the Islamic Republic are no more repressive than any other regime facing similar threats.”

In some cases, authorities have loosened their enforcement of laws on the mandatory headscarf, the consumption of alcohol, the use of narcotics and other social issues in what Alfoneh said was in part to keep people busy with activities that might distract them from political activism.

“Repression appears to be reserved for matters of political freedom and for antiregime uprisings,” Alfoneh said.

There are signs that authorities are now cracking down on what they perceive to be public opposition to the principles of Iran’s theocracy as the war continues.

In Tehran on October 30, hundreds of mostly Gen Z Iranians celebrated Halloween by wearing makeup or costumes and gathering in cafes on artsy Iranshahr Street.

Within hours, motorcyclists and plainclothes security personnel arrived to disperse the crowds and close down cafes. Assaults and detentions were reported. People enjoying the evening in nearby Artists Park were reportedly ordered away.

The authorities did not officially comment on the incident but have since set up pro-government stations and booths on the same street, where supporters chant “revolutionary” slogans in praise of the government and wave flags.

Pro-government demonstrators have blocked city squares and streets in Tehran since the war began in perceived messages of defiance to domestic and external opponents.

As part of the “self-sacrifice” Janfada campaign, some of them receive gun training and other support at these locations to serve as part of the Basij, a domestic IRGC paramilitary force, which has been used to crack down on antigovernment protests.

Even before Halloween, police criticised gatherings on Iranshahr, Sanai and other streets in Tehran that have become popular gathering spots for young Iranians looking for space to express themselves amid deteriorating living conditions resulting from the war, an economic crisis and domestic mismanagement.

“Those streets have unfortunately turned into a place where people cruise and walk around,” Tehran traffic police chief Teymour Hosseini said last month. He also hinted that the gatherings of young people were the reason cafes and businesses have been shut down by police in recent months.

The government also continues to impose a dress code, especially for women, since shortly after the 1979 revolution. But since the nationwide Mahsa Amini protests of 2022-2023, women have increasingly ditched their headscarves in public in Tehran and other cities in defiance of the law.

Hossein Shariatmadari, a hardline media figure, wrote in an article that loose hijabs were “one of the levers used by the enemy in the coming war” and must be taken seriously.

“The enemy has been defeated in military confrontation with Islamic Iran and has now shifted a considerable part of its abilities towards war in economic and cultural areas, particularly through expanding loose hijab,” he said.

State crackdowns have also attracted some limited attention in local media although for different reasons.

“A tense night in Iranshahr”, the reformist Shargh newspaper wrote about the operation on the eve of Halloween, urging policymakers to study what people want and provide attractive cultural opportunities. The Rouydad24 news website questioned the usefulness of treating the cultural preferences of young people as security problems.

The ultraconservative Keyhan newspaper wrote that Halloween celebrations were evidence of “cultural alienation” that was weakening knowledge of ancient traditions like Nowruz, the Persian New Year.

But Iranian authorities over the years have politicised domestic traditions too, namely by restricting and shooting at Chaharshanbe Suri fire festival celebrations during the protests.

Qatar University’s Zweiri said whether Iran and the US manage to end the war through a negotiated resolution or engage in a more devastating conflict would play a role in determining if more nationwide protests take place in Iran.

Some Iranians feel that any kind of protest currently could be interpreted as allying with foreign powers.

“The second level of reality is the identity of being Iranian, which means no Iranian wants to be affiliated to an enemy that attacks and destroys the country,” Zweiri said.

“Whether there is a deal or more war in the future will determine how Iran will be developing economically and politically and socially.”

articles.title: Rubio says war on Iran unpopular but ‘necessary’ to stop nuclear threat
articles.excerpt:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that ...
articles.body_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran to safeguard the world from Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Rubio told reporters in Florida on Sunday that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Trump addressed “difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary”, Rubio added.

On diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough”. He added that although Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

Rubio comments came after Trump had said that “a lot of people didn’t like” Vice President JD Vance recent comments blaming the US-led war on Iran for the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s US midterm elections.

Trump said that although he mostly agreed with Vance, he did not regret the decision to go to war against Iran. It “will go down as one of the best things we ever did”, he said, adding that if Tehran were to have a nuclear weapon, “they would blow up the world”.

Trump also told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday that as long as Washington sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement”, it is “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” for the US to resume strikes.

For Iran’s part, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that it was “time for the White House to make its own” decision on the war.

“American voters have made their choice,” Araghchi wrote on X, referring to the midterm election results.

He added that Tehran’s “2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results”.

“Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Iran has offered to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the United States meets its conditions.

Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.

Tehran is reviewing proposals presented by Qatar aimed at addressing differences with Washington, according to the Associated Press news agency.

In recent days, Rubio has also denied “unfounded” speculation that he was quitting as the top US diplomat to run for higher office in 2028.

articles.title: JOHN MIZE: Democrat victory just means the fight for life has added importance
articles.excerpt:
Wendy Faustin and attorney Roger Byron speak exclusively with Fox News Digital about Colorado's abortion clinic 'bubble law' and their First Amendment concerns.

Tuesday, Nov. 3, Americans cast their ...
articles.body_text:
Wendy Faustin and attorney Roger Byron speak exclusively with Fox News Digital about Colorado's abortion clinic 'bubble law' and their First Amendment concerns.

Tuesday, Nov. 3, Americans cast their votes and turned congressional majorities against the pro-life cause.

It may be easy to despair, especially following two years of strong, pro-life leadership that accomplished a historic year of defunding many abortion providers from federal Medicaid dollars, but the pro-life movement has fought through hostile waters before — and won.

Here’s how we navigate the next two years.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Defending legacy pro-life provisions must be a first priority. We have known for months that the Hyde Amendment, protecting taxpayers from being forced to directly fund abortions, has been in the crosshairs for the next pro-abortion Congress.

Anti-abortion rights demonstrators march to the Supreme Court for the 52nd annual March For Life in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 24, 2025. (Bryan Dozier/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

But conscience protections for healthcare entities that choose not to provide abortions under the Weldon Amendment may also be on the line.

This pro-abortion majority wants to make Americans complicit in their extremism.

Both the Hyde and Weldon amendments have survived pro-abortion majorities before, including the 117th Congress. In 2021, the House Appropriations Committee advanced a Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education spending bill that omitted both Hyde and Weldon rider language.

Even though both chambers were led by pro-abortion majorities, pro-life organizations were able to rally, telling Congress that these protections are not up for negotiation.

This is the same message we must carry over the next two years.

Congress must also be reminded that preserving these riders is in its own best interest, attaining bipartisan public support.

According to the 2026 Knights of Columbus/Marist polling, 54% of Americans opposed taxpayer funding of abortion and 63% support conscience protections for healthcare providers.

'EXTREMIST' AND 'BARBARIC': MASSACHUSETTS DEMOCRATS BREAK RANKS OVER NEW ABORTION LAW

Pro-abortion members of Congress are also likely to urge the passage of the Women’s Health Protection Act. This bill is intended to codify the state of abortion extremism under Roe v. Wade, preventing any state or locality from restricting abortion before viability.

If this became law, it would also erase necessary safeguards for women like mandatory ultrasounds to confirm pregnancy or rule out ectopic pregnancies, eliminate waiting periods and allow unrestricted mail-order abortion.

Both the Hyde and Weldon amendments have survived pro-abortion majorities before, including the 117th Congress.

What pro-life groups have more accurately called the "Women’s Health Endangerment Act" has been fended off since it was first introduced in 2013. Under the 117th Congress, this bill passed the House of Representatives but did not reach the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome cloture in the Senate.

However, this new Congress is signaling less political restraint and may eliminate the filibuster to evade the necessary checks-and-balances of cloture. Pro-life groups must be unified in opposing this extreme tactic.

It is essential to remember that Congress is only one cog in the political machine, and we can still fight for life within the Trump administration and among the many states.

The pro-life movement has overcome many cycles of pro-abortion control since Roe and yet still was able to achieve the historic victory in Dobbs not too long after the 117th Congress.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Administrative agency action is still on the table. The Food and Drug Administration’s review of the abortion pill is still pending, and its latest update to the courts suggest final results will be available to the public by March 2027.

Restoring in-person dispensing requirements as a minimum repair to mifepristone’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy is still on the table. It’s even more essential now that the agency’s review is airtight and able to withstand partisan scrutiny.

The Trump administration still has the authority to finally rescind the Biden-era Office of Legal Counsel’s politicized Comstock opinion and fully enforcing the law through the Department of Justice.

Stopping the mail-order abortion scheme harming women across the country will be essential to combatting the losses of this week.

Still, we must not waver from our collective efforts in all 50 states. Losses in Texas showed us that we cannot become complacent in protecting life where we believe it to be the most secure.

American politics is a cultural battle and, as Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia stated, "[t]he permissibility of abortion, and the limitations upon it, are to be resolved like most important questions in our democracy: by citizens trying to persuade one another and then voting."

John Mize is the CEO of Americans United for Life, the nation's leading pro-life legal advocacy organization.

articles.title: PAUL TELLER: Foreign investors are milking US taxpayers. Congress should stop them
articles.excerpt:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveils a massive federal investigation into alleged multi-million-dollar fraud in Minnesota.

America has become too litigious. Even the slightest wrong seems to yiel...
articles.body_text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveils a massive federal investigation into alleged multi-million-dollar fraud in Minnesota.

America has become too litigious. Even the slightest wrong seems to yield a lawsuit these days, lining the pockets of trial attorneys who profit from pitting Americans against Americans. But did you know that a new brand of lawsuit has emerged in recent years that has foreigners fueling the litigation and then taking the winnings at a lower — or even zero — tax rate?

Here’s how it works. A foreign sovereign wealth fund or other investment fund overseas eyes a potential or existing lawsuit in the United States and speculates that it could earn a significant financial return by contracting with one party, often the plaintiff’s side, to underwrite the large and growing costs of the lawsuit. When the plaintiff receives a financial reward from the court, the winnings tend to be taxed as ordinary income (i.e., at a higher rate).

WAVE OF OVERLOOKED 'LEFT-WING' LAWSUITS COULD COME WITH AN UNEXPECTED PRICE TAG FOR AMERICANS

But when the foreign underwriter that financed that same lawsuit collects its share of the winnings (decided in advance as a condition of funding the lawsuit), that money can be treated as a capital gain and therefore taxed at a lower rate than the plaintiff herself pays. And since foreign investors generally owe no U.S. tax on capital gains from American sources, the tax rate for the foreigner is often zero, even as the American plaintiff pays the ordinary income tax rate.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks at a news conference, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, at the Treasury Department in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

TREASURY FLAGS $8B IN SUSPICIOUS FOREIGN-DIRECTED TRANSFERS THROUGH US MONEY SERVICES FIRMS

Recently, in a Capitol Hill hearing, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply criticized this scheme of foreigners fueling American lawsuits and running away with a greater share of the winnings. Bessent is exactly right: Foreign financing of American lawsuits is indeed "a malignancy" on our judicial system, as he called it, that is draining money out of the U.S. economy, driving up prices across the board for American consumers and further encouraging litigiousness in American society.

As the secretary noted, these foreign financiers are asserting preferential tax treatment, avoiding U.S. taxes entirely and getting away with it. The result: American taxpayers are in fact subsidizing a practice that is driving up costs for American businesses and fostering higher prices for all Americans at the grocery store and at the pump.

SUPREME COURT CLIMATE CASE COULD BANKRUPT OIL COMPANIES, SEND GAS PRICES SOARING, EXPERTS WARN

What’s particularly offensive about this practice is that the impetus behind the capital gains tax rate being lower than the ordinary income tax rate on the same amount of money is the wholeheartedly American desire to reward risk-taking investment aimed at production and growth. But the foreign hedge funds and other international wealth funds that underwrite American lawsuits at the lower or zero tax rate are not investing in economic growth. Quite the opposite. They are seeking to profit from the restraint of growth, from lawsuits that siphon resources from the profit margins and bottom lines of American producers.

REPUBLICANS AREN’T STOPPING: GOP TO UNLEASH ANOTHER ‘BIG, BEAUTIFUL BILL’ WITH A NEW TARGET

Congress should close this unAmerican, abusive loophole this year and put the billions of dollars in increased revenue toward pro-growth tax relief in America. In typical Beltway fashion, some politicos will assert that there’s not enough time to make this fix this year. That’s inaccurate. Right now, Congress is scheduled to be in session for at least five more weeks this calendar year, and there is room in the calendar to schedule additional days and (God forbid!) late nights in session. Yes, this might mean coming back to the office after scurrying around town to lavish holiday parties, but so be it. This issue is worth it.

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

Many in Congress, including House Republican leaders, have said that this year they want to pass another "reconciliation" bill (a special type of legislation not subject to the Senate filibuster, regarding revenues going in and out of the Treasury). That would be the ideal legislative vehicle in which to fix this foreign loophole and direct the resulting revenues back to the American taxpayer.

As the secretary noted, these foreign financiers are asserting preferential tax treatment, avoiding U.S. taxes entirely and getting away with it.

But if Congress can't get its act together soon, the White House should work with Bessent to see what actions the executive branch may legally take on its own to address this boon for foreign financiers.

Either way, this would be an easy win for American consumers and businesses, while defunding left-wing trial attorneys who continue to enrich themselves on the backs of excessive lawsuits.

Paul Teller, president of Teller Strategies, worked all four years in the Trump-Pence White House, was Sen. Ted Cruz’s chief of staff and served U.S. House conservatives for 13 years.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's FAA touts new AI-powered tool helping thousands of passengers avoid flight delays
articles.excerpt: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy slams Democratic Rep. Don Beyer for calling the FAA's new AI tool an unproven system. Duffy defends the predictive technology on 'Fox & Friends' with Brian Kilmeade...
articles.body_text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy slams Democratic Rep. Don Beyer for calling the FAA's new AI tool an unproven system. Duffy defends the predictive technology on 'Fox & Friends' with Brian Kilmeade, labeling the criticism as complete stupidity. He explains how the tool coordinates schedules to prevent flight delays and safely manage American airspace instead of keeping planes in ground stops.

EXCLUSIVE: The Trump administration's new AI-supported air traffic management tool has already helped reroute nearly 180 flights carrying approximately 24,000 passengers to avoid congestion, cutting flight times by more than 10 minutes on average, according to new Department of Transportation (DOT) data shared exclusively with Fox News Digital.

The Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART, has been operational for nearly six weeks, helping air traffic controllers identify more fuel-efficient routes and anticipate potential disruptions.

According to DOT, the technology has also saved nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight on average, offering an early glimpse of how the Trump administration hopes to reduce flight delays and cancellations.

TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy discusses the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART technology, which uses flight and weather data to help air traffic controllers identify congestion and recommend more efficient routes. (Courtesy Department of Transportation)

"Under President Trump, we are making historic progress to revitalize air traffic control and improve the passenger experience for millions of Americans," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Duffy also said the technology would deliver broader benefits as the program expands.

"SMART will slash frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices."

One example came in October when a flight carrying 147 passengers from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Orlando International Airport avoided expected congestion after SMART recommended an alternative route.

SEVERE TURBULENCE DIVERTS NEW YORK CITY FLIGHT TO MIAMI, 8 INJURED

The FAA's Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system helps air traffic controllers identify more fuel-efficient routes and anticipate potential disruptions. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

The flight had been scheduled to depart during a period when congestion was expected along its original path. SMART identified a route farther west, which air traffic controllers accepted, shortening the journey by 11 nautical miles and saving six minutes of flight time, according to DOT.

The technology combines 200 data streams, including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics, into a centralized platform.

Its AI-supported engine helps aviation specialists anticipate where congestion could develop and recommend more efficient routes before congestion builds.

The technology is also designed to improve how the FAA manages severe weather, a source of disruptions for U.S. air travelers.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

Aviation specialists work inside the FAA's SMART Center, where technology combines weather, flight path and air traffic data to help identify potential congestion and improve flight efficiency. (Courtesy Department of Transportation)

According to a DOT fact sheet, the agency's existing approach involves blocking off large rectangular sections of airspace affected by storms, even though weather systems are often irregularly shaped and safe corridors may remain available.

SMART is intended to provide a clearer picture of changing weather conditions, allowing aviation specialists to identify routes around storms and determine when restricted airspace can safely reopen.

Despite its AI-supported capabilities, SMART does not independently direct aircraft or replace human air traffic controllers.

A team of aviation specialists analyzes and validates SMART's data before sending scheduling recommendations to the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center. Those recommendations are then forwarded to local air traffic control facilities, where officials decide whether to accept them.

The initiative comes as the nation's busiest airports handle millions of flights annually.

According to DOT, approximately 6.5 million flights operate each year at the nation's 30 busiest airports. About 300,000 receive reroutes before departure, while 3.6 million experience airborne reroutes, vectoring or holding.

The FAA initially limited SMART's rollout to the National Capital Region in September before beginning validation efforts with air route traffic control centers in Miami, Jacksonville and Atlanta in October.

The agency plans to continue testing the system as it works toward expanding SMART to all 22 air traffic control centers nationwide.

While the early results involve a relatively small share of domestic U.S. flights, DOT says the technology is intended to help airlines operate more predictable schedules and ease pressure on air traffic controllers.

For travelers, the Trump administration's goal is fewer delays for passengers, shorter flights and less time lost to flight congestion.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

articles.title: Congress returns to brutal lame-duck stretch with shutdown deadline, leadership races: 'Closet is full of s—'
articles.excerpt:
Several newly elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

Lawmakers are back on Capitol Hill this week for the first time si...
articles.body_text:
Several newly elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

Lawmakers are back on Capitol Hill this week for the first time since the midterm elections, and Republicans have a slew of responsibilities in front of them before Democrats take over the reins of power in January.

"The lame duck is like that closet in your house where everybody's throwing a bunch of s--- into it," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. "And the closet is full of s--- now, and now we got to figure out how to get it all out of there."

Current federal funding levels run out on Dec. 11, and without another deal in place, Congress risks plunging the government into another shutdown. Some Democrats signaled to POLITICO that they could use President Donald Trump’s war in Iran as leverage in spending talks — which could very well lead to a fiscal cliff that could paralyze federal agencies.

But one House Republican, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told Fox News Digital they expect another short-term extension of current funding levels, called a continuing resolution (CR), through February or March of next year. The current CR was passed to cover the end of the last fiscal year ending Sept. 30 through next month.

TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson will have to navigate a busy lame-duck period before Congress changes hands. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"No one wants a shutdown, I would think," that House Republican said. "Not even Dems."

HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS

Other legislative priorities Congress will have to reckon with in the next few weeks include the farm bill, which is passed every five years and sets food and agriculture policy for the country. Republicans are also aiming to pass a bill to revitalize the country’s transportation infrastructure and a bipartisan tax package before the end of the year.

Then there is also the looming debt ceiling deadline coming in January, which Trump will likely call on Republicans to deal with before Congress changes hands.

GOP lawmakers shared varying levels of optimism when asked about how productive they would be.

"It can be. It should be," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., said. "But my faith in some of my Senate colleagues is not real high, because I feel like they have a personal vendetta towards the president, and it's more about that than it is about passing legislation. We should do our business in Congress."

Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, said, "I think it's gonna be difficult to get a whole lot done. But we have done a lot of work leading up to the lame-duck session to prepare for passing a number of important bills, many of which are bipartisan."

But first, both House and Senate Republicans will need to face their losses in person — and consider how to rebuild.

WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images)

"It’s going to feel like a funeral," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "It’s depressing even for those of us who won, because we lost so many good, quality members."

The first order of business this week will be choosing their new leaders for the next Congress.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running for the minority leader role unopposed for now.

And House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is vying for the minority leader role against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio.

MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS

But Moran and Stutzman both said Republicans would unify quickly after that drama is resolved.

"It should be immediate," Stutzman said. "If we're not paying attention to the American people, and we're focusing on leadership positions and personality fights, we're gonna continue to lose."

HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES DEFENSE PLAN TO SHIELD TRUMP FROM LOOMING DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATIONS

Moran said, "We understand now more than ever how important it is for us to come back together, coalesce and to regroup for the next election, and to prepare for the defense of democracy."

On Democrats’ side, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to glide into the speaker role after leading his party to a commanding victory.

Democrats’ leadership elections will take place the week after Republicans’ do.

And on the productivity front, Stutzman also called on the Senate to pass the election security-focused SAVE America Act, which Republicans are attempting to accomplish via the budget reconciliation process to sidestep the need for Democrat support. The House passed a blueprint for the bill in July.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., gestures while addressing Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison during a hearing on Capitol Hill on Feb. 16, 2026. (CSPAN)

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has been working on the structure of that package for some time, but wasn’t so sure that if Republicans lost, it would be something the GOP had the political will to finish.

"It might turn to some people's attitudes in terms of support for it," Johnson said.

Then there’s permitting reform, which was on thin ice heading into Election Night until the White House and Senate Democrats struck a deal for a variety of wind projects to move forward. Whether Democrats support that now, and give Trump and the GOP a win on their way out, remains to be seen.

"First thing we need to do is make a motion to add a 13th month to the calendar, because we've got so much stacked up to do that's really important for the country," Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Russell Brand to be sentenced for rape and sexual assault today – latest updates
articles.excerpt:
Disgraced comedian was convicted last week and was warned he faces a ‘signficant’ prison term

Good morning. Russell Brand will be sentenced today after being found guilty of raping a woman and sexual...
articles.body_text:
Disgraced comedian was convicted last week and was warned he faces a ‘signficant’ prison term

Good morning. Russell Brand will be sentenced today after being found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others in seperate incidents between 2005-2009.

The disgraced former comedian and Hollywood star has been behind bars since he was convicted by a jury last Thursday, denied bail by his trial judge who ruled that he posed a flight risk.
 
 
 During the four-week trial, prosecutors had argued that Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator” who pursued women relentlessly and exploited his fame and power to get what he wanted from them sexually.

The 51-year-old father of three is now facing a “significant” prison term, Justice Joel Bennathan said last week.

The sentencing is taking place in Southwark Crown Court in London and commences at 10:30am GMT. I’ll bring you all the developments.

The four-week trial kicked off in September. The court heard that Brand had struggled to convince friends and former colleagues to provide evidence for him.

His wife, Laura Brand, 39, was the only one who took the stand on 29 October to give evidence to his good character. The couple had first met when she was 19 and he 31.
 
 
 She said Brand was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”.

She said she had been aware of his infidelities and promiscuity. She said she had never felt sexually pressured by him.
 
 
 “The way he treats me is to really know me, I feel very seen by him, in a way I’ve never experienced before. I love him very much.”

“We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage. It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest.”

Laura Brand has been in court everyday at her husband’s rape trial, and arrived earlier for his sentencing.

Following his conviction last week, the Met Police revealed that they were investigating further rape allegations against Brand, including one involving a then 16-year-old girl.

The Met said they had already questioned Brand on further complaints from two other women, and have submitted the files to crown prosecutors.

The lead detective in the case, Det Supt Andy Furphy, told the Guardian last week he believed there could be more victims.

double quotation markIf you get a conviction then it tends to encourage other people to come forward because they see the courage and the bravery and the resilience that these women have had to go through this criminal justice process, and they feel their own strength as a result of that. They want to come forward and have their story told.

The Met’s investigation into Brand, named Operation Actinolite, involved tracing and speaking to more than 100 witnesses, reviewing more than 1,400 documents and taking more than 340 statements, including from Brand’s former employers, colleagues and associates.

Brand has also been accused of sexually assaulting a woman at his mansion in Los Angeles in 2008, in a civil claim filed at the high court in London.

The former actor-comedian was transported to Southwark Crown Court in a white prison van. He was held at HMP Wandsworth on the weekend.

His wife, Laura Brand, who has been a steadfast and loyal supporter by his side, has also just entered the court. She gave testimony on his behalf, attesting to his good character during the trial.

The couple have three young children together.

The actor-comedian had been free but was taken into custody immediately after the jury returned the guilty verdicts last Thursday.

His defence lawyer Ian Winter KC had put in a plea for bail, arguing for Brand to have the weekend to say goodbye to his wife and three children.

But this was rejected by Justice Bennathan on the grounds that Brand, with his money and connections, posed a flight risk.

There were substantial grounds to “fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence”, the judge said.

double quotation markI regret the hardship caused to the children, of course.

But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father.

Sitting in the courtroom last week, Brand had closed his eyes when the guilty verdict for the rape charge was read out. After his bail was denied, he gestured OK to his lawyers and repeated “I’m good, I’m good, I’m good”, before being taken away by guards.

The jury of eight men and four women deliberated for more than eight hours last week to return a unanimous verdict where they found Brand guilty on four of the seven charges.

He was found guilty of one count of rape and three incidents of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one attempted incident.

Brand had pleaded not guilty to all the offences, telling the court he believed he never had non-consensual sex.

But the jury found he had committed crimes against four women between 2004-2009 in different locations, in a central London bar, a radio station, recording studio and his former home in Hampstead, London.

He was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman at a colleague’s birthday party in a bar in Soho, London in 2004, but found not guilty of orally raping her in a bathroom.

He was found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005

He was convicted of anally raping a fan at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009

He was found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during an advert recording in 2009.

He was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party annual conference in Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the bathrooms in the London offices of MTV music channel.

articles.title: Polanski says Labour has ‘shocking record’ on climate issues as ministers expected to cut EV targets for car industry – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Louise Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter

Good morning. Monday is often the busiest day of the week at Westminster but, with the Commons still enjoying a mini ...
articles.body_text:
Louise Haigh is expected to agree to cut a target for EV sales by about a quarter

Good morning. Monday is often the busiest day of the week at Westminster but, with the Commons still enjoying a mini November recess, today is looking a bit quiet. Andy Burnham is on a visit to a hospital this morning and he wants to talk about a £40m programme in England to try to keep vulnerable patients out of hospital. The Department of Health and Social Care has the details here, and Andrew Gregory explains it all here.

But Burnham may find he ends up taking more questions from the media on another Guardian story, Kiran Stacey’s scoop about the government being on course to water down electric vehicle (EV) targets.

With Burnham attending the Cop climate crisis summit later this week, the revelations won’t boost Burnham’s credentials with environmentalists.

The final EV decision has not yet been taken, but the Greens are already outraged. These are from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader.

double quotation markThis week leaders meet for the UN climate summit.

The context? A summer of heat deaths. Scientists saying 2026 will be the hottest year ever.

To bend over backwards to the car industry, and scrap plans for rapid electrification.

double quotation markThis Government is building up a shocking record of backsliding and bad decisions on climate issues.

At a time when we desperately need leadership, they bend to the will of polluters by slashing key rules and pushing ahead with fossil fuel extraction.

And this is from the former Green leader Caroline Lucas.

double quotation markA truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time. The shift to electric vehicles is government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy. Cutting EV targets would send a message on eve of #COP31 that UK is no longer serious about #climate action.

Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a hospital in Hertfordshire.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

The Tories have criticised the Scottish government for posting a message on its X social media account about a Sikh festival at 11am yesterday – as the nation was observing the two-minute silence for Remembrance Sunday. Harriet Cross, the shadow Scottish secretary, said:

double quotation markIt is hard to see their decision to post about a Sikh festival at precisely 11am, at the very moment that people across the country were observing a two-minute silence to honour our war dead, as a coincidence.

There is no reason why they couldn’t have recognised both - not least out of respect to the 83,000 Sikhs killed fighting in both World Wars.

This failure to mark Remembrance Sunday shows a total disregard for the sacrifice our soldiers made and continue to make in defence of our country.

At 11am yesterday John Swinney, the Scottish first minister, was with other leaders in Edinburgh laying a wreath at a remembrance ceremony.

Businesses which trade goods made with slave labour will have to withdraw them from sale, the government has said, revealing it will change the law to enforce the new ban. The Press Association reports:

double quotation markJonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said he plans to introduce new legislation to introduce mandatory human rights due diligence for companies, which will require them to remove products made with forced labour and modern slavery.

He outlined the move in a letter to the Commons business committee, which has been calling for new business safeguards against modern slavery for nearly two years.

The new duty will apply to British businesses with a global turnover of more than £350m, and non-UK businesses with a UK-generated turnover of more than £350m.

Those who do not comply with the new duty may be forced to withdraw products from sale which have come from forced labour or modern slavery, Reynolds said.

The commitee has been calling for modern slavery protections to be strengthened since it heard evidence from Chinese-owned clothing company Shein in January 2025.

In that session, the firm repeatedly declined to confirm whether its products contained cotton sourced from China, including Xinjiang, where it is believed that the Uyghur minority are subject to forced labour.

Here is an article by Fiona Harvey and Jasper Jolly published last month on what the consequences would be if the government were to relax its EV targets, as the Guardian today reports now seems inevitable. (See 9.26am.)

double quotation markThe end goal of 2035 is likely to remain, but under a consultation that ended on Friday, the 2030 targets could be weakened to 70% or even as low as 50% of new cars. Taken with previous watering down of the policy to allow more sales of hybrid cars – which use both electric and combustion engines – that change would lead to emissions greater than burning all the gas in the Jackdaw field, according to the ECIU [Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit].

If the mandate were cut more drastically to require only 50% of sales to be EVs by 2030, this could mean an additional 147 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, which would equate to about 58% of the likely emissions from burning the oil produced by the Rosebank field.

Jess Ralston, an analyst at the ECIU, said weakening the target would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China as increasing numbers of people opt for EVs. It would also not benefit the public because EVs can be £1,750 a year cheaper to run, and potentially more with oil prices rising.

The final EV decision has not yet been taken, but the Greens are already outraged. These are from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader.

double quotation markThis week leaders meet for the UN climate summit.

The context? A summer of heat deaths. Scientists saying 2026 will be the hottest year ever.

To bend over backwards to the car industry, and scrap plans for rapid electrification.

double quotation markThis Government is building up a shocking record of backsliding and bad decisions on climate issues.

At a time when we desperately need leadership, they bend to the will of polluters by slashing key rules and pushing ahead with fossil fuel extraction.

And this is from the former Green leader Caroline Lucas.

double quotation markA truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time. The shift to electric vehicles is government’s single biggest decarbonisation policy. Cutting EV targets would send a message on eve of #COP31 that UK is no longer serious about #climate action.

Morning: Andy Burnham is visiting a hospital in Hertfordshire.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

articles.title: RILEY GAINES: Voters sent two midterm messages, and Democrats will only hear one
articles.excerpt: In this episode of The Riley Gaines Show, Riley examines the political contradictions emerging from the 2026 election results. While Democrats celebrated victories, ballot measures concerning biologic...
articles.body_text:
In this episode of The Riley Gaines Show, Riley examines the political contradictions emerging from the 2026 election results. While Democrats celebrated victories, ballot measures concerning biological sex and female athletics in states including Colorado, Washington, Arizona, and Nebraska sent a different message about the future of women's sports. Riley argues that the results reveal a growing divide between voters' economic concerns and their positions on cultural issues—and that both political parties would be making a mistake by ignoring it.

I’ll admit it. Tuesday night was disappointing.

I expected Republicans to lose more seats than they flipped. History suggested as much. But I certainly didn’t expect the results to be quite that bad.

Still, buried beneath the headlines celebrating Democratic victories was a rather inconvenient development for the political left. Americans may have voted to elect Democrats, but that doesn’t mean they’ve suddenly developed an appetite for the progressive social agenda again.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

In fact, on one of the most contentious cultural issues of the last several years, voters delivered a remarkably consistent message.

In Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington, voters backed measures protecting female athletic competition on the basis of biological sex.

And these weren’t just Republican strongholds. Colorado and Washington are reliably blue states whose political leadership has spent years embracing progressive gender policies.

Yet the same electorate willing to put Democrats in positions of power also voted to reject a central pillar of the modern progressive agenda.

I don’t know how much clearer voters can make themselves.

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

For years, elected Democrats and their allies in the mainstream media have insisted that protecting women’s sports is an extreme position and that anyone who dares advocate for it is a hate-filled bigot. And believe me, that’s one of the nicer things I’ve been called.

I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too.

We’ve been told that acknowledging biological differences between men and women is transphobic. That girls who object to sharing locker rooms or competing against male athletes are the problem. That sports should prioritize inclusion and kindness, even when doing so comes at the expense of fairness and safety.

I’ve personally experienced what happens when you challenge that orthodoxy. I’ve also watched countless female athletes lose opportunities, endure public ridicule and face enormous pressure to remain silent simply for asking for something as basic as a fair shot.

I’ve watched politicians, university administrators and athletic organizations bend themselves into knots trying to explain why women should be expected to sacrifice their own opportunities in the name of inclusion.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

Voters made their position clear in 2024, when the Republican agenda prevailed nationally. Apparently, even after voting for Democrats in 2026, they still aren’t buying what the progressive left is selling on this issue.

Opponents of the girls’ sports initiative reportedly raised roughly $4 million, with substantial backing from unions and progressive organizations, including Planned Parenthood. Proponents raised approximately $200,000, largely through grassroots efforts.

They prevailed despite being outspent nearly 20 to 1.

That’s a staggering disparity, and an even more telling result. At what point does the political left accept that this is a losing issue and give it a rest?

Women’s sports protections are not some fringe position held exclusively by Republicans. The issue cuts across party lines, and the people who have spent years insisting otherwise have a serious problem on their hands.

The cultural shift is evident well beyond the ballot box.

Look at the response WNBA player Sophie Cunningham has received.

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

After publicly expressing support for protecting women’s sports, Cunningham didn’t issue a groveling apology. She wasn’t shunned into professional exile. Quite the opposite.

Her public profile exploded. Her social media following and engagement skyrocketed. Her merchandise became some of the most sought-after in the league, and her Adidas shoes reportedly sold out almost immediately.

On Halloween, I saw countless young girls wearing her jersey and dressing up as Sophie Cunningham.

Riley Gaines and Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham pose for a photo following Sunday's game at Target Center against the Minnesota Lynx. (Riley Gaines/XX-XY Athletics)

The notion that expressing a common-sense view about women’s sports is automatically a career-ending offense looks increasingly ridiculous.

For years, corporations, celebrities and athletes were conditioned to believe that stepping outside progressive orthodoxy would destroy their reputations.

That threat doesn’t carry quite the same weight anymore.

And I think that’s worth celebrating, particularly after an election that otherwise gave conservatives plenty of reasons to believe a serious reckoning is overdue.

But there’s another part of Tuesday’s results that Republicans would be foolish to ignore.

DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING

Affordability is a real problem. And I believe that was the bigger message voters sent on Tuesday by voting for Democrats.

Americans are tired of working harder just to afford less. They’re tired of watching their grocery bills climb, calculating how much they can spend at the gas pump and wondering whether homeownership will ever be a realistic possibility.

Riley Gaines holds a sign thanking Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham for speaking out to protect women's sports. (Riley Gaines/XX-XY Athletics)

Riley Gaines, Sophie Cunningham, and XX-XY Athletics founder Jen Sey pose courtside after an Indiana Fever game with a sign thanking Cunningham. (Riley Gaines/XX-XY Athletics)

Young people, in particular, are confronting an economy that often feels stacked against them. And when they express their frustration, they’re too often dismissed as lazy or entitled.

Sometimes that criticism is warranted. Most of the time, it isn’t.

I believe Americans have remarkably short memories about just how bad inflation became under the Biden administration. But telling a struggling family that things used to be worse isn’t going to make their next grocery bill any easier to pay.

People vote based on the lives they’re living, not just the economic statistics politicians would prefer they remember.

And when people feel financially desperate, promises of sweeping government intervention can sound awfully attractive.

That’s part of what makes socialism so dangerous. The promise of essentially free everything is appealing, particularly to generations that have never been adequately taught its historical consequences. Of course, nothing is actually free. The bill always comes due, whether through higher taxes, mounting debt or diminished economic opportunity.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

But dismissing every voter concerned about affordability as ignorant or entitled would be a serious mistake.

I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too.

But I don’t think the voters’ message of "affordability" in voting for Democrats is what Democrats will hear.

Elected Democrats will be tempted to interpret their victories as permission to expand DEI mandates, advance gender-transition policies for minors, allow boys access to the girls’ locker room, raise taxes, advocate for more lax immigration policies and continue placing ideological priorities ahead of the concerns of ordinary families.

TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING

Winning an election doesn’t mean voters have endorsed every plank of your platform. And it certainly doesn’t mean they’ve abandoned their common sense.

Tuesday’s ballot initiatives should serve as a warning against making that assumption.

They should also give Republican lawmakers in politically competitive states some much-needed confidence.

Take Pennsylvania, where legislation protecting women’s sports has faced significant political resistance.

For too long, some Republicans have treated this issue as politically radioactive, apparently convinced that defending female athletes is too controversial to be worth the fight.

Well, voters in Colorado and Washington just offered a pretty compelling rebuttal.

If these protections can earn majority support in states that routinely elect Democrats, what exactly are Republicans in purple states so afraid of?

Of course, winning at the ballot box doesn’t mean the fight is over.

MATT CALKINS: AFTER YEARS OF THREATS AND INTIMIDATION, THE BULLIES IN THE WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE FINALLY LOST

Colorado’s newly elected Democratic governor, Phil Weiser, has already suggested that the state’s transgender-related ballot measures may need legislative adjustments.

And we’ve seen elsewhere, including Maine, how officials such as Secretary of State Shanna Bellows have resisted efforts to restrict male participation in girls’ sports.

I fully expect more legal challenges, political maneuvering and attempts to weaken these protections.

But those efforts only reinforce the larger point. When the public is given a direct say, the progressive establishment doesn’t always like the answer.

For a party that prides itself on defending democracy, it might consider respecting the democratic process even when the outcome is inconvenient.

As for the next two years, Democrats will have an opportunity to show Americans what their governing priorities actually are.

And if recent history is any indication, I suspect they’ll provide plenty of reminders of why voters rejected their national agenda in 2024. For some reason, this is the hill they continually choose to die on.

Republicans, meanwhile, have work to do. They need to take affordability seriously, offer credible solutions and stop assuming that winning the cultural argument automatically translates into winning elections. It doesn’t.

Voters can agree with you on cultural issues and still vote against you when they feel their financial concerns aren’t being addressed. Tuesday’s midterm election results proved that these realities can coexist, and Republicans would be wise to recognize it.

Still, I refuse to confuse one disappointing election night with a wholesale cultural reversal.

I’ve spent years speaking with parents, students and female athletes across the country. I’ve seen firsthand how much the conversation has changed.

People who once whispered their concerns are increasingly willing to say them publicly. They’re less intimidated by the accusations, less willing to accept obvious contradictions and less interested in being lectured by institutions that have spent years squandering their trust.

That’s not something that disappears because one party has a good election night.

Political power changes hands. Cultural convictions are often much harder to reverse.

Democrats won important elections Tuesday. Republicans should take those losses seriously, learn from them and make the necessary adjustments.

But the voters also made something unmistakably clear once again. They haven’t suddenly decided that women and girls are undeserving of their own athletic categories, free from mediocre men.

And if the progressive left believes Tuesday was a mandate to resurrect every unpopular cultural crusade Americans have spent years rejecting, they’re in for a rude awakening.

Democrats may have won the election. They haven’t won the culture.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM RILEY GAINES

Riley Gaines is a 12-time NCAA All-American who competed for the University of Kentucky NCAA swim team before retiring from competition and focusing on political activism. Riley is host of "The Riley Gaines Show" podcast. Watch "The Riley Gaines Show" on YouTube, or listen on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and anywhere you get your podcasts. New episodes drop Wednesdays and Fridays.
